t: The historical position of Leninism and its contemporary significance
zh: 列宁主义的历史地位及其当代意义
paras: Wang Xiaoju asks how Leninism should be assessed historically and what it means today. The article argues that Lenin advanced Marxism to a new stage, that Leninism made an original contribution to Marxist theory, and that inheriting, defending and developing it remains a major task for the prospects of world socialism. In Wang's view it also bears on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and on Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first sets out Leninism's historical position under five headings: Marxism adapted to its era, to Russia, to practice, to the future, and to internationalism. The second surveys and rebuts anti-Leninist currents, from Khrushchev and Gorbachev to Russian historians, Vladimir Putin, Western scholars such as Erich Fromm and Karl Korsch, and some Chinese scholars. The third turns to four present-day implications.

Wang's central claim is that Leninism is Marxism developed for the age of imperialism and proletarian revolution, and confirmed in practice by the October Revolution, the New Economic Policy and the founding of the USSR. Wang cites Lenin's theory of imperialism, his view that socialism could first win in one country, and his notion that each nation would reach socialism in its own way. Wang treats the evaluation of Lenin as a political question as well as a scholarly one, and rejects what the article calls historical nihilism. Putin's remark that Lenin's national self-determination planted a 'bomb' under the Soviet state is rejected as untenable. Wang argues that the federation Lenin proposed was meant to secure the Soviet state against intervention, and that the USSR's dissolution cannot be blamed on Leninism.

For the present, Wang argues that Leninism offers a basis for understanding world history, including the continuing validity of the 'two inevitables' of Marx and Engels. It also gives a scientific basis for reading the changing world order, including digital and platform capitalism, and supports a fairer international order and multilateralism. For Chinese modernization, Wang draws on Lenin's formula for learning from foreign technology and management, and on the New Economic Policy as an inspiration for the socialist market economy. Wang calls for close reading of the classics. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences historian defends Lenin against Russian, Western and Chinese critics and ties Leninism to current Chinese policy.
quoteEn: How to evaluate Lenin and Leninism is not only a major academic question but, even more, a major political one.
quoteZh: 如何评价列宁和列宁主义，不仅是一个重大的学术问题，更是一个重大的政治问题。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to each historical period. The article extends the same logic to Lenin's adaptation of Marxism to Russia.
The official name for the Party's path of modernization, set out prominently after the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
In official Chinese usage, a label for interpretations that deny or belittle the revolutionary and socialist past. The article applies it to anti-Lenin and anti-Soviet narratives.

The thesis from the Communist Manifesto, as the article presents it, that capitalism will inevitably perish and socialism will inevitably triumph. The article treats it as still the main trend of world history.

The policy Lenin introduced in Soviet Russia in 1921, replacing grain requisitioning with a tax in kind and allowing limited market activity. Chinese official discourse often cites it as a precedent for reform.

t: An analysis of the roots of the degeneration of Karl Kautsky's view of Marxism
zh: 卡尔·考茨基马克思主义观蜕变的根源论析
paras: Why did Karl Kautsky, a leading theorist of the Second International and the German Social Democratic Party who once contributed importantly to Marxist theory, end up opposing Marxism? Zhuang argues that the shift came from an incomplete and wavering grasp of Marxism's basic principles. The author reads this as the product of both theoretical roots and personal, subjective factors set against the transition from peaceful capitalism to imperialism.

The article has three parts. The first sets out four theoretical roots of Kautsky's degeneration. The second turns to three subjective factors in his character and politics. The third draws lessons for the Chinese Communist Party's theoretical innovation in the new era, and a short conclusion follows.

On the theoretical side, Zhuang says Kautsky made Marxism's scientific character positivist, treating it as an empirical science rather than a philosophy and reducing historical materialism to a method. He is said to have made its revolutionary character abstract: his stance moved from delaying revolution to obstructing, opposing, attacking and finally slandering it. He is said to have vulgarised the Marxist view of development through Darwinian evolutionism and dissolved its class character through the theory of "ultra-imperialism" and "pure democracy". Citing Lenin's criticism, Zhuang presents Kautsky's war-time and post-1917 positions as a blurring of the class nature of war and democracy. On the subjective side, Zhuang points to his weak theoretical independence, which left him under outside influences such as Bernstein's. The author adds that he failed to grasp imperialism and revisionism as products of the new epoch, and lacked the practical ability to apply theory, preferring a compromise that kept the Party formally united.

Zhuang concludes that Kautsky's case warns that theory loses vitality once it departs from Marxism's essential attributes. The author calls for unwavering adherence to dialectical and historical materialism, to the unity of science and revolution, of thorough theory and conscious practice, and of class character and popular character. The article ties this to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, to Chinese modernization, and to the Two Integrations. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-scholarly account of Kautsky as a negative example, and of how it is used to frame current theoretical innovation.
quoteEn: The root of the degeneration of Kautsky's view of Marxism lies in his incomplete and unsteady understanding of the basic principles of Marxism.
quoteZh: 考茨基马克思主义观蜕变的根源，在于其对马克思主义基本原理的认知不彻底、不坚定。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: An official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxist theory to China's conditions and to contemporary developments.
The official term for China's own path of modernization, promoted by the Party since the early 2020s as distinct from Western models.
The Party's formula of integrating Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.

t: Two paths beyond modernity: Marx and Strauss
zh: 超越现代性的两条道路：马克思与施特劳斯
paras: Hao Zhichang and Liu Xiaona compare how Karl Marx and Leo Strauss diagnose the crisis of modernity and what each proposes in response. The article argues that the two thinkers represent opposed directions: Strauss seeks a return to classical political philosophy, while Marx seeks to go beyond capitalist modernity through social revolution. The authors hold that the difference rests on rival views of history, and that Marx's historical materialism reaches the deeper root of the crisis.

The article has three main sections and a conclusion. The first sets out Strauss's critique of historicism, his account of the 'quarrel between ancients and moderns', and his appeal to natural law, teleology and the best regime. The second presents Marx's analysis of capital, its 'great civilising influence', its limits in production, consumption and human relations, and the abolition of capitalist private property and the restoration of individual ownership. The third weighs the two paths as a choice between value reconstruction and social transformation, and briefly sets aside Nietzsche, Heidegger, Löwith and Arendt. It closes with Baudelaire's view of modernity and a remark of Althusser's.

In the authors' reading, Strauss treats the crisis as theoretical: modern historicism dissolves any standard of good and bad, and an 'eternal history' embodied in the classical best regime is the remedy. The authors judge this a one-sided, partly romantic and conservative, ultimately utopian approach that never reaches the real source of the crisis. They cite Engels to argue that social change originates in modes of production and exchange, not in ideas, and note that Western cultural traditions existed long before modernity arrived. Marx, by contrast, locates the crisis in the capital relation, so overcoming it requires changing the material mode of production. The authors add that Strauss's charge that Marx's future humans are 'last men' fails, since Marx envisages free, many-sided activity.

The authors conclude that the crisis of modernity is total, at once theoretical and practical, and that Strauss and Marx complement each other. Strauss lacks a dimension of practical reality; Marx's project should absorb Strauss's ethical concern and his reminder not to forget inherited human values. Even so, they insist on viewing Strauss through Marx's lens, discarding his unrealistic social imagination, and judge that the most urgent crisis is capital's 'colonisation and control' of life. Read the original if you study Marxist critiques of Western conservative thought, or want a Chinese academic account of how Marx and Strauss can be set against each other on modernity.
quoteEn: Strauss did indeed grasp the absence of the value dimension, but this is not the whole or the more fundamental truth; the crisis that modern society urgently needs to resolve is capital's colonisation and control of life.
quoteZh: 施特劳斯的确捕捉和意识到了价值维度的缺失，但这不是全部或更为根本的真相，现代社会亟须解决的危机是资本对生活的殖民与控制。

t: On the logical evolution of Lukács's ethical thought
zh: 论卢卡奇伦理思想的逻辑演变
paras: Yan and Liu take up a common periodisation of Georg Lukács's ethics: a Romantic phase before Marxism, a revolutionary ethics after his turn to Marxism, and late cultural critique and democratic politics. They argue that this scheme hides the links between the phases. In their view, the evolution of Lukács's ethics, its substance and its present-day relevance can be understood only within an overall 'individual–class–species' (ge ti–jieji–lei) framework. They also hold that Lukács never built a systematic Marxist ethics, but his critique of dogmatised Marxism opened a path for constructing one today.

The article follows Lukács's ethics chronologically in four parts. It begins with the metaphysical individual ethics of Soul and Form and Theory of the Novel and its move towards the proletarian class ethics of 'Tactics and Ethics'. It then examines the ethical predicament of History and Class Consciousness. Next it treats the late works: the Aesthetic, the Ontology of Social Being and The Process of Democratization. It closes with an assessment. The authors draw on commentators such as István Mészáros, Ágnes Heller, Norman Levine, György Márkus and Gareth Stedman Jones.

The authors present Lukács's shifts as responses to the problems of his time and to impasses in his own theory, not as irrational breaks. In History and Class Consciousness, individuals are subordinated to the class and the Party. Class consciousness is treated as the proletariat's 'ethics', and Lenin's idea of 'injecting' it from outside is endorsed. The authors see the book's real difficulty as the relation between material base and consciousness: Lukács tried to resolve capitalist contradictions through consciousness, which underestimated capital's logic. After 1956, influenced by the 1844 Manuscripts, he replaced 'class' with 'species'. Aesthetics then sought the unity of individual and species, and the later democratization work tied socialist democracy, teleology and non-alienated labour to that unity, extending to everyday life.

Yan and Liu conclude that Lukács's work has a deeper continuity, which they call a steadfast 'cultural watchfulness' grounded in concern for human existence and fate. They cast the Ontology as overcoming the subjectivism of History and Class Consciousness, and The Process of Democratization as a development of Leninist state theory. They add that his ethics strongly influenced Western Marxism, especially Eastern European neo-Marxism, and that, as Lukács himself said, theoretically mistaken parts often have the greatest influence. They therefore call for a critical attitude. Read the original if you study Lukács, the history of Marxist ethics, or how Chinese scholars read the continuity of his thought across his career.
quoteEn: Although Lukács never systematically constructed a Marxist ethics, his critique of dogmatised Marxism opened a path for the contemporary construction of Marxist ethics.
quoteZh: 卢卡奇虽未系统建构马克思主义伦理学，但他对教条化马克思主义的批判却为马克思主义伦理学的当代建构开辟了道路。

t: The 180th anniversary of The German Ideology: retrospect and prospect
zh: 《德意志意识形态》问世180周年：回顾与展望
paras: Marking 180 years since Marx and Engels began writing The German Ideology in 1845–46, Zhao Yulan offers a short retrospective and research outlook in a newspaper commentary. The author treats the work as the birthplace of the materialist conception of history. The main claim is that Chinese scholarship has long tracked international editorial work and should now aim to lead as well as follow, above all by settling its own edition and by debating the editors of the second Marx-Engels Complete Works historical-critical edition (MEGA2).

The article first traces the work's publication history. It runs from the single chapter Marx published in 1847, through the partial printings by Mehring, Bernstein and Mayer in the early twentieth century, to Riazanov's 1924 and 1926 publication of the 'Feuerbach' chapter and Adoratsky's 1932 MEGA1 volume, the first complete edition in the original language. It then follows the post-1962 rearrangements of the 'Feuerbach' chapter by Bagaturia and Taubert and the 2017 MEGA2 volume. Finally it sets out the Chinese editions, from Guo Moruo's 1938 translation to the 1960 first Chinese Complete Works, the 1988 new 'Feuerbach' chapter, the 2003 selection and the 2009 Collected Works.

Zhao argues that the 2017 MEGA2 volume largely returns to the MEGA1 logical structure. In Zhao's reading, it nonetheless rests on a judgement that the text was a quarterly-journal project made up of separate texts, and it inserts Engels's notes on Feuerbach into the 'Feuerbach' chapter, which undermines the chapter's status as a chapter. The second Chinese Complete Works, which is based on MEGA2, should therefore follow MEGA2 for textual content but decide its own arrangement through independent research. Zhao also contends that Chinese scholars have already made a case for treating the text as a 'work' rather than a 'quarterly', and doubts that the order in which the manuscripts were written shows a major 'Stirner shock' to Marx.

Zhao concludes that the work remains an important growth point for Marxist research. The author calls for a new Chinese complete edition, for international dialogue in which Chinese scholars lead the discussion, and for continued study of the text's documents, theory and contemporary value. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-authored overview of the editorial history of The German Ideology and of how Chinese scholars position themselves toward MEGA2.
quoteEn: The new Chinese edition of The German Ideology may certainly take MEGA2 as its basis for textual content, but in arranging the text it must step outside the MEGA2 framework and decide its own arrangement on the basis of its own independent research and judgement.
quoteZh: 中文新版《德意志意识形态》固然可以在文本内容上以MEGA2为依据，但是在文本编排上必须跳出MEGA2的框架，依据自己的独立研究和独立判断来确定自己的编排方式。

t: Engels's critique of "True Socialism" and its lessons for today
zh: 恩格斯对“真正的社会主义”思潮的批判及其启示
paras: Fu Chenchen examines how Engels criticised "True Socialism", a current of 1840s German thought that tried to graft English and French utopian socialism onto German idealist philosophy. The article argues that Engels's first systematic critique, in the preface and concluding remarks of his 1845 text Fragments on Fourier's Trade, exposed the current as an abstract, ethicised, anti-proletarian doctrine. Fu also argues that this critique still offers methodological lessons for ideological work in the new era.

The article has four parts. It first traces the historical formation of True Socialism: the split of the Young Hegelians (Strauss, Bauer, Feuerbach) and the way utopian socialism was received and distorted in a Germany with a weak bourgeoisie and a large petty bourgeoisie. It then sets out four theoretical features of the current, drawing on figures such as Karl Grün, Hermann Kriege and Friedrich Beck. A third part analyses Engels's methods of critique, and the last turns to present-day implications.

Fu identifies the four features as follows: an abstract theory of human nature with a moralising bent; a "supra-class" ethical utopia of universal love in place of class struggle; a vulgarising misreading of Fourier; and, at root, the conservatism of the German petty bourgeoisie. In Fu's account Engels's method rests on historical materialism, class analysis and scientific abstraction, which he sets against the "empty abstraction" of True Socialism. Fu stresses Engels's contrast between Fourier, who reached his vision of the future after correctly understanding past and present, and the True Socialists, who arbitrarily arrange history and then point to where the future should go. Fu also cites the position of True Socialists during the 1844 Silesian weavers' uprising as evidence of the current's reactionary function.

In the final part Fu draws three lessons for China today, each tied to statements by Xi Jinping. These are to uphold historical materialism against historical nihilism and abstract speculation; to treat theoretical resources scientifically and avoid vulgarised readings or mechanical grafting of Western concepts; and to hold to Party spirit and a people's standpoint against ideological deception. Fu links petty-bourgeois illusions to what the article calls "welfare populism", "universal values" and ideological infiltration. Read the original if you want a close textual study of Engels's Fragments on Fourier's Trade, or an example of how classical critiques of rival socialisms are applied to present-day ideological work in China.
quoteEn: The rise and fall of True Socialism also shows that the vitality and truth of scientific socialism lie in this: only by insisting on abolishing private ownership through class struggle, and by basing social critique on analysis of relations of production, can one see through ideological illusion and realise the real movement that abolishes the existing state of things.
quoteZh: “真正的社会主义”思潮的兴衰也昭示了科学社会主义的生命力与真理性在于，只有坚持以阶级斗争消灭私有制、立足生产关系分析展开社会批判，才能穿透意识形态幻象，实现消灭现存状况的现实运动。

glossary.explanation: A German intellectual current of the 1840s (Karl Grün, Moses Hess and others) that recast French and English socialism in terms of Feuerbachian human essence and love. Marx and Engels criticised it in The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto.
A group of radical followers of Hegel in 1830s–40s Germany who criticised religion and the Prussian state. Marx and Engels belonged to it before breaking with its idealism.

In official Chinese discourse, a label for views that question or negate the Party's account of the revolution, socialist construction and reform. The article treats it as a present-day relative of True Socialism's abstract speculation.

t: On the relationship between the "two inevitabilities" and the "two never wills": a reflection based on Marx's idea of bypassing the capitalist "Caudine Forks"
zh: 论“两个必然”与“两个决不会”的关系——基于跨越资本主义制度“卡夫丁峡谷”设想的反思
paras: Li Jian takes up a gap in Chinese scholarship on the "two inevitabilities" (capitalism will inevitably perish, socialism will inevitably triumph) and the "two never wills" (no social order perishes before all the productive forces it can contain have developed; no new relations of production appear before their material conditions mature). Existing work, the author says, analyses their logic at the level of what ought to be and neglects how the "two never wills" actually serve as conditions for the "two inevitabilities". Li argues that Marx's late idea of bypassing the capitalist "Caudine Forks" does not overturn this condition. It deepens it and shows a special route to realising the "two inevitabilities" in backward countries.

The article has three sections. The first reads the relationship through historical materialism, tracing the two formulas to the Communist Manifesto, Capital and the 1859 Preface. The second examines how the Russian-commune idea both challenges and sustains the framework. The third draws lessons for building the theoretical system of Chinese modernization, citing Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and Engels's 1885 letter to Vera Zasulich.

Li's central move is to reject two misreadings of the "two never wills": a dogmatic \"capitalist-conditions theory\" requiring every country to pass through full capitalism, and an abstract talk of \"general material conditions\" detached from history. The Caudine Forks idea is said to acknowledge diverse paths and multiple sources of the material conditions, which can be partly absorbed from capitalist civilisation abroad and combined with reactivated communal forms. Li then argues that it leaves the framework intact on four grounds. The bypassable path is particular while the unbypassable law is universal, a dialectical \"concrete universality\" rather than an either/or. What can be bypassed is capitalist relations of production and their suffering, not the development of productive forces. Subjective initiative operates within objective limits, which Li reads into Marx's remark that a society can shorten and lessen the birth-pangs. The classical and bypass paths are complementary, operating at different analytical levels.

Li concludes that the Russian-commune idea upholds both the trend and its preconditions while extending historical materialism's grasp of diversity. For Chinese modernization, Li draws three implications. It is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party. It must proceed from national conditions, separating socialism's unchangeable essence from its selectable forms. It must follow the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, using capital while ultimately transcending capital's logic. Li adds that replacing capitalism is a long, peaceful competition. Read the original if you study the Marxist theory of non-capitalist paths, the Caudine Forks debate, or how Chinese scholars link Marx's late writings to Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: What can be bypassed here are capitalist relations of production and the concrete path, not the material foundation it creates or the process by which productive forces develop.
quoteZh: 这里可跨越的是资本主义的生产关系和具体道路，而非其创造的物质基础和生产力的发展过程。

glossary.explanation: The thesis that capitalism will inevitably perish and socialism will inevitably triumph, derived from the Communist Manifesto's claim that the bourgeoisie's fall and the proletariat's victory are equally unavoidable.

Marx's formulation in the 1859 Preface: no social order perishes before its productive forces are exhausted, and no new relations appear before their material conditions mature. Chinese theorists treat it as the precondition of the "two inevitabilities".

A reference to Marx's late writings on Russia, where he considered whether the rural commune could reach socialism without passing through the capitalist stage, the Caudine Forks being the place where Roman soldiers suffered a humiliating defeat.

The official concept for China's path to modernization under Communist Party leadership, presented as distinct from Western modernization and used as an organising theme in Party theory since the 2020s.

t: A historical analysis of who proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance
zh: 工农联盟提出和创建的历史辨析
source: Marxist Theory Studies in Colleges and Universities (Gaoxiao Makesi zhuyi lilun yanjiu), 2025 no. 4
paras: Who first proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance? Li Wei takes up a question that surfaced in a 2010 debate in Marxist Studies over whether Marx and Engels held the idea at all. The article argues that the alliance was proposed and created by Lenin, not by Marx and Engels or by the nineteenth-century European socialists and workers' parties, who never developed it in theory or practice.

Li first sets out two conflicting readings in Soviet and Chinese editorial prefaces: Lenin's 1894 work is said to have first proposed the alliance, while the prefaces to Marx and Engels's Selected Works credit Marx's The Class Struggles in France and The Eighteenth Brumaire. The article then reviews how Marx and Engels's views on the peasantry changed between 1848 and the 1890s. It examines Engels's 1894 "The Peasant Question in France and Germany", and closes with Lenin's creation of the alliance and its development by Mao Zedong and later Chinese Communists.

Li argues that passages usually cited for an early alliance idea come from the 1848 revolutionary period and were later revised by Marx and Engels themselves. Li notes that Marx deleted one such passage from the 1869 edition of The Eighteenth Brumaire. After the Paris Commune, they concluded that peasants could obstruct workers' revolutions. Reading Engels's 1894 text, Li finds that the European parties took up the peasant question only after half a century, and that they regarded peasants essentially as voters to be won in parliamentary elections. In Li's account, the worker-peasant alliance instead grew from armed struggle against landlords and the bourgeoisie, from proletarian leadership of the peasantry in the bourgeois-democratic revolution, and from the Leninist party. Only Lenin's Bolsheviks, in Li's view, found "the correct way of approaching the peasants".

Li concludes that the alliance emerged only when the proletarian revolution reached a higher stage, and that Europe's early workers' movement had no peasant movement to learn from. Li treats this as no fault of Marx and Engels, since each era solves the tasks it is able to pose. The article presents the Chinese Communists under Mao Zedong as the culmination of the alliance in practice and theory, and refers to Xi Jinping's thought as guiding its current consolidation. Read the original if you work on the history of Marxism, the peasant question or Lenin's relation to Marx and Engels, and want a detailed argument against the view that Marx first proposed the alliance.
quoteEn: The worker-peasant alliance and its theory could arise only in the struggle against the landlord class and the big bourgeoisie, and this historical task fell to the Bolsheviks led by Lenin.
quoteZh: 工农联盟及其理论思想只有在与地主阶级和大资产阶级的斗争中才能产生，这一历史的任务落在了列宁领导的布尔什维克身上。

glossary.explanation: The political alliance between the working class and the peasantry under proletarian leadership. In Soviet and Chinese Marxism it is treated as the class foundation of revolution and of the socialist state.

The set of theoretical and practical problems about the peasantry's role in revolution and socialism. Engels used the term in 1894, and Lenin and Mao later gave it a different content centred on land and struggle against landlords.

t: The Holy Family and the formation of the materialist conception of history
zh: 《神圣家族》与唯物史观的形成
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 14 April 2026
paras: This short commentary in a Chinese academic newspaper asks what role Marx and Engels's The Holy Family (1844–45) played in the formation of the materialist conception of history. Gong Qin argues that the book is a key link in that process. Its "real humanism" is a key step towards a science of real human beings and their historical development, going beyond Feuerbach while still showing his influence.

The book's main target is the Berlin "Free" circle around the Bauer brothers, whom Marx and Engels treat as a caricatured completion of Hegelian dialectics in a philosophy of self-consciousness. Gong organises the discussion around three questions: what real humanism is, how humanist materialism relates to historical materialism, and how to understand Marx's critique of the "mystical side" of Hegel's dialectic. The article draws on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, the Theses on Feuerbach, Engels's later work on Feuerbach and the afterword to the second edition of Capital, Volume I.

On the first question, Gong notes that contemporaries such as Ruge and Stirner read Marx and Engels as members of a Feuerbachian "humanist school", stressing the "humanism" in the phrase. Gong stresses its "real" side: the distinction between interests and ideas, and the claim that history originates in material production. On the second, Gong argues that Marx moved from using "materialism" pejoratively to engaging French and English materialism, linking it to humanism, the critique of private property, socialism and communism. The Holy Family and the Theses on Feuerbach thus mark a move from reflecting on humanist materialism to historical materialism. On the third, Gong reads the critique of Hegel's "speculative structure" (the hypostatisation of ideas and the turning of substance into subject) as a long exploration. It ran through the analysis of civil society and material production and ended in Capital's historical, materialist and dialectical exposure of the capitalist mode of production.

Gong concludes that the decisive step beyond Feuerbach was the construction of a dialectical, historical and practical materialism within the critique of political economy and the exploration of socialist and communist practice. Rereading the book today, Gong says, means taking from Marx and Engels the habit of starting from reality, grasping social structure and historical trends, welcoming dialogue between different views, and advancing theoretical innovation with methodological self-awareness. Read the original if you want a compact orientation on how The Holy Family connects Feuerbach, Hegel's dialectic and the emergence of historical materialism, as seen by a Chinese scholar of Marxist intellectual history.
quoteEn: This is to construct a dialectical, historical and practical materialism within the critique of political economy and the exploration of socialist and communist practice.
quoteZh: 这就是在政治经济学批判和社会主义共产主义实践的探索中，建构辩证的、历史的、实践的唯物主义。

glossary.explanation: The label Marx and Engels gave their own position in The Holy Family (1844–45), drawing on Feuerbach's humanism while turning towards real human beings and their material conditions. Chinese scholars treat it as a transitional stage towards historical materialism.
The standard Chinese term for historical materialism, Marx and Engels's theory that material production and social relations shape history.

t: A historical analysis of who proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance
zh: 工农联盟提出和创建的历史辨析
source: Marxist Theory Studies in Colleges and Universities (高校马克思主义理论研究), 2025 no. 4
paras: Who first proposed and created the worker-peasant alliance in the history of the international communist movement? Li Wei notes that Soviet and Chinese editorial prefaces give two contradictory answers: Lenin in 1894, or Marx in 1850. The article argues that Marx, Engels and the European socialists of the nineteenth century never formulated or built such an alliance, and that Lenin first tried and partly solved the problem in practice and theory.

Li first reviews how the Soviet Marx-Engels-Lenin Institute and, later, China's Central Compilation and Translation Bureau interpreted the classics in prefaces to the Selected Works and Collected Works. He then traces the nineteenth-century record, from the 1848 revolution through the Paris Commune and Engels's 1895 Introduction to Marx's The Class Struggles in France to Engels's 1894 essay on the peasant question in France and Germany. The second half turns to Lenin, the Bolsheviks and the Chinese Communists, ending with Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping.

Li argues that the oft-cited 1848–52 remarks on peasants joining workers reflect the thinking of Marx and Engels as young men, and that they later revised it. Li points to Marx's deletion of a passage from the 1869 second edition of The Eighteenth Brumaire and to his 1875 judgement that peasants can obstruct workers' revolutions. On Li's reading, Engels's 1894 essay shows that European socialist parties took up the peasant question only late and treated peasants chiefly as voters in parliamentary contests. Lenin, by contrast, fought for proletarian leadership in the bourgeois-democratic revolution and treated the land question as its core. He then drew on 1905 Moscow uprising and armed struggle to form peasant, worker and soldier soviets, whose alliance carried the October Revolution.

Li concludes that the alliance emerged from revolutionary practice against landlords and the big bourgeoisie, and marks the passage of Marxism into the era of Leninism. The Chinese Communists, in Li's account, then brought it to completion through rural revolutionary bases and land reform. Li adds that the absence of the idea among Marx and Engels is no cause for regret, because each era sets its own historical tasks. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based challenge to the view that Marx originated the worker-peasant alliance, or want to see how Chinese editorial prefaces shaped that view.
quoteEn: The worker-peasant alliance and its theory could only arise in the struggle against the landlord class and the big bourgeoisie, and this historical task fell to the Bolsheviks led by Lenin.
quoteZh: 工农联盟及其理论思想只有在与地主阶级和大资产阶级的斗争中才能产生，这一历史的任务落在了列宁领导的布尔什维克身上。

t: Foucault and Marx: from Capital to the genealogy of power
zh: 福柯与马克思：从《资本论》到权力谱系学
paras: Was Foucault a Marxist, an anti-Marxist, or something in between? Ouyang Qian takes up this long-contested question and argues that the answer should start from Foucault's own statements. The article focuses on Foucault's remark that his work on disciplinary power was guided by Volume II of Capital, which he called a genealogy of capitalism. Ouyang concludes that Foucault used Marx selectively and that the two thinkers' critiques of capitalism are complementary.

The article first surveys Western views on the relationship, from claims that the two are unconnected to Jacques Bidet's reading of a relation both close and exclusionary, and Étienne Balibar's reading of Foucault's work as a confrontation with Marx. It then sets out the French intellectual context: the post-war prestige of Marxism, Sartre's "horizon", the structuralist turn, and the shock of May 1968. Next it examines what Foucault said about Marx, before comparing Capital Volume II with Foucault's analysis of power under three headings. It ends by applying both thinkers to digital capitalism.

Ouyang argues that Foucault separated Marx from "Marxism", rejected economic determinism, the base–superstructure model and utopian teleology, and kept Marx's critique of political economy and historical analysis as a toolbox. Since Foucault never explained the debt to Volume II, Ouyang offers a tentative comparison. Capital's circulation corresponds to power as flow and network. Reproduction of capital corresponds to the reproduction of "docile bodies" and qualified subjects through disciplinary institutions. Circulation obstacles and crises correspond to the inevitability of resistance within power relations. In Ouyang's formulation, Marx deals with the power of the economy and Foucault with the economy of power, and Foucault preferred to cite Marx "secretly".

Ouyang proposes combining the two: Marx's macro-level analysis of class and exploitation with Foucault's micro-level analysis of discipline and biopolitics. The article argues that this combination explains digital capitalism, where data serve as a factor of production and source of surplus value, platforms accumulate monopolistically, and algorithms act as invisible overseers of labour. It contends that both critiques remain valid while private ownership of the means of production, capital logic and unequal power relations persist. Read the original if you study Foucault's relation to Marx, or want a Chinese philosophical reading that links Capital Volume II to the analysis of power and digital capitalism.
quoteEn: Marx's critique of political economy and Foucault's critique through the genealogy of power together constitute theoretical tools for the critique of capitalist modernity.
quoteZh: 马克思的政治经济学批判和福柯的权力谱系学批判，共同构成了资本主义现代性批判的理论工具。

glossary.explanation: Foucault's term, central to Discipline and Punish, for power exercised through training, surveillance and norms in institutions such as prisons, schools and factories.
Foucault's term for forms of power that manage life itself, such as population regulation and health policy, rather than relying on repression alone.
Foucault's phrase for bodies made useful and obedient through disciplinary techniques.

t: A critique of positive philosophy: Feuerbach and Marx
zh: 肯定哲学批判：费尔巴哈与马克思
paras: Liu Senlin takes up Feuerbach's little-studied 1838 essay "Critique of Positive Philosophy", the first Young Hegelian review of the late Schelling's positive philosophy. The article asks what the essay reveals about Feuerbach's shift of thought and about the path from Hegel through Schelling and Feuerbach to Marx. Liu argues that the essay criticises Schelling's positive philosophy and, beyond it, the "negative" speculative philosophy that Hegel represents, while pointing towards a "new and only positive philosophy".

The article reconstructs the essay's two senses of the relation between "philosophy" and "speculation", then traces its echoes in Marx and Engels. It draws on The Holy Family, The German Ideology, Marx's letter to Feuerbach, Feuerbach's later writings on Hegel, and commentary by Frank, Xian Gang and Wang Ding. It also brings in Stirner, whose key concepts Liu presents as reversed borrowings from Schelling's Philosophy of Revelation.

Liu's core claim is that Feuerbach inherits Schelling's stress on sensuousness, becoming and existence but finds Schelling's positive philosophy half-hearted: still subordinate to negative philosophy, bound to religion and myth, and prone to arbitrary subjectivity. Feuerbach wants to free it and reduce theology to anthropology. Liu uses Marx and Engels's remark that Feuerbach "first attacked Hegel" with sober philosophy against drunken speculation to argue that it refers to this essay, not to the 1839 critique of Hegel. In Liu's account, Feuerbach's overcorrection against subjectivity pushes him into contemplative naturalism. He drops the subjectivity and active practice that Schelling, Hegel and Stirner kept, and Marx later criticises this.

Liu concludes that Marx and Engels corrected Feuerbach in several ways. They replaced "positive philosophy" with positive science, treated the sensuous as needing critical reflection and as practice, and combined sensuousness with rationality and essence. Marx's Hegel, Liu says, is the Hegel already criticised by Schelling and Feuerbach, so historical materialism emerged from reworking the Hegel–Schelling dispute over negative and positive philosophy. Read the original if you study the Hegel–Schelling–Feuerbach–Stirner–Marx lineage and want a detailed textual argument about how Marx's practical materialism emerged.
quoteEn: Marxist philosophy was born in the creative transformation and innovative development of the achievements of these two philosophical transformations.
quoteZh: 马克思主义哲学就是在对这两种哲学变革成就的创造性转化、创新性发展中诞生的。

t: An analysis of the roots of the degeneration of Karl Kautsky's view of Marxism
zh: 卡尔·考茨基马克思主义观蜕变的根源论析
paras: Karl Kautsky was a leading theorist of the Second International and the German Social Democratic Party and once contributed significantly to Marxist theory. Zhuang asks why his understanding of Marxism changed over time until, in the article's account, he ended up opposing it. The thesis is that the root lies in an incomplete and unsteady grasp of Marxism's basic principles, which Zhuang traces to three sources: his misreading of Marxism's essential attributes, a vulgar evolutionary view of development, and the pressures of the transition to imperialism together with his own personal weaknesses.

The article first examines how Kautsky understood the essential character of Marxism. It then follows what Zhuang calls the parabolic course of his political outlook, from the revolutionary tactics of the 1905–1909 period to his wartime and post-1917 positions. Zhuang draws on Kautsky's own writings, on remarks by Lenin, and on his intellectual biography, including his father's nationalism, Darwinism and his friendship with Bernstein. The final sections draw lessons for developing Marxism today.

Zhuang's central move is that Kautsky turned Marxism into a positivist empirical science. He denied it was a philosophy, reduced historical materialism to a method, and set its scientific character against its revolutionary and class character. His Darwinian idea of development as adaptation, Zhuang says, led him to fatalism, technological determinism and a view of democracy as gradual expansion. From this Zhuang derives his later positions: 'ultra-imperialism', defence of the fatherland in the First World War, and 'pure democracy' set against proletarian dictatorship. A second move is that Kautsky failed to see imperialism and revisionism as products of the new epoch. Zhuang adds that he lacked theoretical courage, sought a middle path between left and right, and put the appearance of unity first.

Zhuang concludes that Kautsky's case warns that theoretical innovation loses vitality once it departs from Marxism's essential attributes. The article proposes holding firmly to dialectical and historical materialism. It also calls for uniting science with revolutionary character, thorough theory with conscious practice, and class character with the people's interests. These principles are linked to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, to the Two Integrations, and to Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist assessment of Kautsky's trajectory and how it is used to argue for theoretical orthodoxy in current Chinese theory work.
quoteEn: The root of the degeneration of Kautsky's view of Marxism lies in his incomplete and unsteady grasp of Marxism's basic principles.
quoteZh: 考茨基马克思主义观蜕变的根源，在于其对马克思主义基本原理的认知不彻底、不坚定。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and to contemporary developments.
Formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
The Party's official term for China's own path of modernization, used as the framework for national rejuvenation.
Kautsky's theory that rival imperialist powers might unite to exploit the world jointly and peacefully; Lenin sharply criticised it.

t: Marx's threefold critique of List's political economy
zh: 马克思对李斯特政治经济学的三重批判
paras: Marx named the free-trade versus protective-tariff debate as the first spur to his economic studies, and Friedrich List's national political economy was the leading case for tariff protection. Writing in Chinese Social Sciences Today (March 2026), Zhang Hongliu argues that, despite its progressive role in anti-colonial and national-industry struggles, Marx exposed List's thought as 'vulgar' on three grounds: class standpoint, theoretical claims and philosophical basis.
The short piece takes each ground in turn, drawing on Marx's early writings. It then places the critique in Marx's diagnosis of German 'anachronism' and the problem of catching up with Britain.

On class standpoint, Zhang says List's work expressed the weakness and self-interest of the German bourgeoisie. That class needed protection to build a home market but feared British and French expansion, so it was a hesitant 'fence-sitter' rather than a catch-up economics. On theory, List's 'stages' and 'productive forces' doctrines lumped social, technical, economic and political categories into a national concept of production that, in Marx's words, lost any scientific value. Philosophically, List rested on the historical school of law, whose Hugo, Zhang writes, misread Kant and set reason against history.

Zhang concludes that List offered a 'German plan' combining going with and against British power, from a bourgeois standpoint. Marx faced a similar predicament but, from the proletarian standpoint, sought to transcend both German theory and German reality through a 'world plan'. Zhang holds that elaborating this plan is a task for contemporary Marxism and that the critique of List is a key reference. Read the original if you want a brief guide to how Marx's early texts treat List, protectionism and late development.
quoteEn: List's political economy is not a 'catch-up economics' but a stale 'vulgar economics'.
quoteZh: 李斯特政治经济学不是一种“赶超经济学”，而是一种陈腐的“庸俗经济学”。

t: Lenin's critique of Machism in Materialism and Empirio-Criticism
zh: 《唯物主义和经验批判主义》对马赫主义的批判
paras: This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2026, reconstructs the logic of Lenin's Materialism and Empirio-Criticism. Wang and Zhu argue that Lenin's critique of Machism, which tried to "revise" Marxist epistemology in the context of Second International revisionism, remains a core statement of the Party spirit of philosophy and a resource against idealist tendencies today.

The authors set out Lenin's critique in four layers: ontology (the doctrine of "elements"), epistemology (experience and practice), the theory of truth, and the class character of supposedly "neutral" philosophy. They also note the limits of the critique, which they say targets Mach's philosophy and not his physics, and its historical setting.

Wang and Zhu read Lenin as showing that the "neutral elements" of Mach and Avenarius, and the claim that bodies are complexes of sensations, make subjective experience the ultimate basis of the world and so slide into idealism. Against the resulting agnosticism, they report, Lenin made practice the first and basic standpoint of epistemology and the test of truth. They also say Lenin set the objectivity of truth and the dialectic of absolute and relative truth against Machism's "economy of thought" relativism. In the authors' account, Lenin finally argued that no "non-partisan" philosophy exists in a class society, and that Machism became a channel for bourgeois ideology in the workers' movement.

The authors conclude that the critique dismantled Machism, advanced dialectical-materialist epistemology and laid an ideological foundation for the Bolsheviks and the international communist movement. They hold that studying the book strengthens the ability to recognise and resist ideological currents amid today's diverse thought. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented summary of how Chinese scholars present Lenin's anti-Machist argument and its present-day use.
quoteEn: Lenin's critique of Machism not only comprehensively dismantled the structure of the theory but also greatly advanced dialectical-materialist epistemology, laying a firm ideological foundation for the Bolshevik Party and the international communist movement.
quoteZh: 列宁针对马赫主义展开的批判，不仅全面瓦解了该理论的体系架构，还极大地促进了辩证唯物主义认识论的进步，为布尔什维克党以及国际共产主义运动筑牢了思想根基。

glossary.explanation: The philosophical current based on Ernst Mach's empirio-criticism, which Lenin attacked in 1908–09 as disguised subjective idealism. In Russia some Bolsheviks, such as Bogdanov, had adopted it.

Lenin's thesis that philosophy takes sides in the struggle between materialism and idealism, and that this reflects class interests. Chinese Marxist writing often uses it to justify a committed ideological stance.

t: Combining scientific achievements with dialectical thought: Engels's Dialectics of Nature at one hundred
st: A retrospective and outlook
zh: 科技成果与辩证法思想结合——恩格斯《自然辩证法》出版百年的回顾与展望
paras: Marking a century since the first full publication of Engels's Dialectics of Nature in 1925, Liu Dachun asks what this unfinished manuscript still offers. Liu argues that, although incomplete, it shows Engels's insight into the laws of nature and of the natural sciences and his aim of joining scientific results to dialectical thought. In Liu's account, its study keeps generating new vitality and remains a source for views of nature, science and technology, and scientific method.

The commentary has three parts. The first tells how the manuscript was written between 1873 and 1883, interrupted twice (by Anti-Dühring and by the editing of Capital), withheld by the Second International and finally published in Moscow under David Riazanov. The second traces its fortunes in China in three stages: translations from 1932 and Yan'an study groups; disciplinary institutionalisation from 1956; and the post-reform-era growth of societies, journals and graduate courses. The third offers a centenary outlook.

Liu's core claim is that the text can be "activated" for the twenty-first century. Liu lists five ways it stays alive: John Bellamy Foster's reading of Engels as a founder of ecology and of the metabolic cycle; Stephen Jay Gould's link between labour in the transition from ape to human and gene–culture coevolution; Western workshops on a "digital dialectics of nature" applying Engels's laws to deep learning and AI explainability; Prigogine and Stengers's use of dialectical models in complexity science; and its role as a base for the interdisciplinary field of science, technology and society. Liu then names four contemporary values: refining the Marxist view of nature, supporting technological innovation, training interdisciplinary talent, and serving as a tool of practical critique for technology ethics and AI governance.

Liu concludes that the manuscript, written in nineteenth-century Europe and still unfolding across three centuries, is steadily completing its "unfinished" mission. The article links the work to green development, ecological civilisation, high-quality development and new quality productive forces. Read the original if you want a concise account of how Dialectics of Nature was published and taught in China, and how a Chinese philosopher of science presents its present uses.
quoteEn: Dialectics of Nature is not merely a document in the history of ideas but a theoretical treasury capable of dialogue with contemporary scientific and technological change.
quoteZh: 《自然辩证法》不仅是一份思想史文献，更是一部能够与当代科学技术变革进行对话的理论宝库

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping from 2023, referring to advanced productive forces driven by technological breakthroughs and innovation, as opposed to growth based on resources and inputs.
An official economic goal since 2017 that stresses quality, efficiency and innovation over speed of growth.
An official policy goal of integrating environmental protection into economic and social development, written into Party and state documents since the 2010s.

Engels's term for the dialectical laws operating in nature. In China it also names an academic field, now called philosophy of science and technology, taught as a Marxist theory course to science graduate students.

t: How latecomer countries can develop productive forces: starting from Marx's critique of Friedrich List's The National System of Political Economy
zh: 后发国家如何发展生产力——从马克思的《评弗里德里希·李斯特的著作〈政治经济学的国民体系〉》谈起
source: Studies on the Marxist Theory Discipline (Marxism Theory Discipline Research), 2025 no. 5
paras: Marking the 180th anniversary of Marx's 1845 manuscript on Friedrich List's The National System of Political Economy, Chen Liangbin asks how latecomer countries can develop their productive forces. Chen argues that List's programme for German catch-up serves the German bourgeoisie, that Marx both criticised and surpassed it, and that Marx's own theory of productive forces gives scientific guidance to latecomers. The renewed interest in a 'neo-Listian school' in the early twenty-first century is the stated reason for revisiting the text.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs List's theory of national productive forces, which rests on a critique of Adam Smith's cosmopolitan free trade and has three components: state intervention, priority for industry and protective tariffs. The second sets out Marx's critique of each component, then traces how Marx's productive-forces theory developed from the German Ideology through the Grundrisse and Capital to the 1859 Preface, and finally his late view of Russia and the 'Caudine Forks of capitalism'. The third draws implications for developing new quality productive forces.

In Chen's reading, Marx saw List's state intervention as the hypocrisy of a weak German bourgeoisie seeking state protection while dressing its interests in the language of national spirit. List's industrial priority confused the forces that industry awakens, meaning the workers, with the capitalist industrial system that will eventually be broken by them. List's protective tariffs, Chen says, are the same capital logic as free trade, binding a country to the world market. Chen holds that Marx surpassed List by adopting a proletarian standpoint and locating Germany's backwardness in the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production. Chen distinguishes a micro level, with subjective and objective productive forces and science and technology, from a macro level, the contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production.

Chen concludes that new quality productive forces require science and technological innovation, reform of production relations to create what Xi Jinping calls new-type production relations, and better coordination of production factors such as data and knowledge. Once List's class standpoint is sublated, Chen adds, his emphasis on state intervention, tariff protection and national spirit still has relevance. Chen links these to the new-type whole-nation system, resistance to foreign trade protectionism and promotion of the Chinese national spirit. Read the original if you want a Chinese account that links Marx's critique of List to current debates on new quality productive forces and technological self-reliance.
quoteEn: Therefore, the inevitable result of protective tariffs is to tie the country to the war chariot of capital's expansion of the world market.
quoteZh: 因此，保护关税的必然结果是将国家绑上资本拓展世界市场的战车。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping put forward in 2023–24. It refers to advanced productive forces driven by innovation, high technology and high efficiency, and is used in current policy discussion of economic upgrading.
A policy term for mobilising state, market and social resources nationwide to achieve breakthroughs in strategic fields such as core technologies.
In Marxist theory, the social relations people enter into in production, above all ownership relations. The article treats their fit with productive forces as decisive for development.
The Hegelian-Marxist notion of Aufhebung: simultaneously negating, preserving and transcending. Chen uses it for taking over what is useful in List while discarding his class standpoint.

t: The epochal yardstick of Marxist ethics
zh: 马克思主义伦理学的时代标尺
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 23 October 2025
paras: Li Yitian asks what should decide whether Marxist ethics exists and what scope it should have. The short commentary argues that the test is not whether Marx and Engels wrote a dedicated ethics treatise, but whether Marxism responds to real ethical problems. Li calls this the "large yardstick" and presents Marxist ethics as an undertaking of large scale in three senses.

The piece is organised under three headings: "large scale" and "large size", "large ethics" and "large theory", and "large history" and "large practice". It begins with the scattered textual basis in Marx and Engels, then turns to the normative structure of Marxism, and ends with the historical and practical setting of the field.

Li notes that Marx's key moral passages sit in unpublished manuscripts, and that Engels's Anti-Dühring devotes only three sections to ethics. Even so, Li holds that Marx and Engels meet the criteria of systematic moral thought and ethical normativity. Li draws from the classics three positive themes (freedom, equality, association) and three negative ones (alienation, exploitation, division), and argues that these can be understood only by moving beyond ethics into economics, sociology and anthropology. Ethics must also engage politics, economics and religion, using historical materialism to critique them and then to construct their normative principles, especially under socialism. Li adds that Marxist ethics needs a long-term historical view, including its own "changes from ancient to modern" over two centuries.

Li concludes that Marxist ethics should not be confined to speculation about good and evil or to a narrowly drawn moral domain. It should place the present within long historical time and take in social phenomena arising from great practice, which Li says will help build and refine its body of knowledge. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of how the scope and legitimacy of Marxist ethics are being framed.
quoteEn: What truly decides whether Marxist ethics exists has never been the \"small standard\" of whether a dedicated ethical work was written, but the \"large yardstick\" of whether it responds to real ethical problems.
quoteZh: 真正决定马克思主义伦理学是否存在的，从来就不是“是否撰写专门的伦理著作”这种“小标准”，而是“是否回应现实的伦理问题”的“大尺度”。

t: Sandel's critique and reconstruction of the Rawlsian conception of the self
zh: 桑德尔对罗尔斯式自我观念的批判及重构
paras: This research article examines Michael Sandel's critique of the conception of the self in John Rawls's A Theory of Justice, and Sandel's attempt to replace it. Zhu Huiling takes Rawls's claim that the self is prior to its ends, and so the right prior to the good, as the logical starting point of Rawls's theory and the target of Sandel's most distinctive philosophical work. Zhu concludes that Sandel's critique is incomplete and his reconstructed self probably unsuccessful, yet that the effort remains philosophically important.

The article is built in three parts. The first treats the defects Sandel finds in the deontological self as a moral subject: an impoverished, 'unencumbered' self and a possessive subject that cannot support claims of desert. The second turns to the self as agent and discusses possession, choice and reflection, including the original position and the veil of ignorance. The third sets out Sandel's 'constitutive self', which Sandel links to Alasdair MacIntyre's 'narrative self' and to Confucian ideas, and then assesses it. A short conclusion draws out its significance for Sandel's later thought.

In Zhu's account, Sandel argues that Rawls's self stands at a distance from its attributes and so cannot ground a thick sense of desert. Rawls's 'choice' amounts to taking inventory of existing desires, and reflection is limited to outward calculation. Behind the veil of ignorance, parties do not choose principles but recognise them, which in Sandel's reading shows a hidden reliance on an intersubjective self that Rawls officially excludes. Zhu rejects critics such as Will Kymlicka and Philip Pettit, who hold that Sandel's revisable self is no different from Rawls's, and maintains that the two differ in the nature of the subject, not only in its capacities. Zhu nonetheless finds that Sandel cannot say how far the community constitutes the self or reconcile free will with constitution. Citing Jack Crittenden, Zhu also points to a dilemma: if the self is framed by its community's ends it cannot reflect on them, and if it can reflect on them they do not constitute it.

Zhu concludes that Sandel's critique has three lasting merits. It makes people reconsider the community and its values, though Zhu says it should not be read as communitarianism, since Sandel's common good is a reflectively formed one. It prepares the ground for Sandel's revival of civic republicanism and his later critiques of the market society and meritocracy. And it invites reconsideration of Confucian ideas of self, society and state, where Zhu notes that Western divisions between private and public are absent. Zhu urges readers to look at their own society's conditions and Chinese classical thought to find their own questions and solutions. Read the original if you are interested in the Sandel–Rawls debate on the self, or in how a Chinese scholar assesses it and relates it to Confucian thought.
quoteEn: Whether the capacities of the subject are homogeneous or heterogeneous is beside the point; what plays the decisive role is the nature of the subject itself.
quoteZh: 主体能力本身无所谓同质还是异质，具有决定性作用的还是主体的性质本身。

t: Marx's view of spiritual life and its contemporary embodiment
zh: 马克思精神生活观及其现实体现
paras: Kulaixi Yibulayin asks what historical materialism says about spiritual life and how Marx's view should guide the enrichment of people's spiritual world today. The author argues that Marx's historical materialism is not a 'soulless materialism'. In this reading, Marx returned spiritual life from abstract speculation to material production and to the question of human emancipation. The article ties this to Xi Jinping's call at the 20th Party Congress (2022) to meet the people's growing spiritual and cultural needs, and to Chinese modernization.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the essence of spiritual life in Marx: its basis in material production, its subject as the 'real social human being', its mode as universal free intercourse, and its aim of all-round human development. It then examines Marx's criticisms of four kinds of 'unscientific' spiritual life, and his constructive alternatives. The last part turns to present-day applications in China.

Kulaixi presents Marx's critique as aimed at four targets. These are the 'abstract' spiritual life of Hegel and Feuerbach, the 'illusory' life of religion's other-worldly consolation, the 'reified' life under capital's logic, and the 'one-sided' life produced by the capitalist division of labour. Each critique, the author says, comes with a positive programme. It calls for a practice-based spiritual life that changes the world, a this-worldly life for real people, and a human-centred life built on social rather than capital logic. It also calls for an all-round life in a communist society of freely associated individuals. The author stresses that, for Marx, ideological forms are overcome only by overthrowing the social relations that produce them.

In the final section the author draws practical conclusions. Enriching the people's spiritual world requires advancing socialism with Chinese characteristics across economic, political, cultural, social and ecological fields, and holding to a 'people-centred' value orientation. It also requires promoting mutual learning among civilizations and shared human values, and holding firm to communist ideals while rejecting bourgeois false ideology. The author connects this to creating a new form of human spiritual civilization. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar draws on Marx's texts to ground current Party policy on cultural and spiritual construction.
quoteEn: Spiritual life takes 'material production practice' as its basis, the 'real social human being' as its subject, 'universal free intercourse' as its mode, and 'the all-round development of the human being' as its orientation.
quoteZh: 精神生活以“物质生产实践”为基础，以“社会现实的人”为主体，以“普遍自由交往”为方式，以“人的全面发展”为指向。

glossary.explanation: The official Party framing of China's development path, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It lists enriching the people's spiritual world among its essential requirements.
The official name for China's current socialist system and path since the reform era. It is the framework within which Party theory places present-day practice.

t: The multiple meanings of "socialist revolution" and "socialism" in Lenin's writings after the October Revolution
zh: 十月革命后列宁著述中“社会主义革命”“社会主义”概念的多重含义
paras: Why did Lenin call Soviet Russia's revolution "socialist" and call certain emergency measures "socialism", when he also said the country had not yet built a socialist society? Yu argues that these terms in Lenin's post-October writings are not simple descriptions of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the people's current practice. In Yu's reading they carry a long-range view of the future, a global view, praise for heroic struggle, and a resolve to keep the cause advancing.

The article follows Lenin's usage from late 1917 through the civil war to the New Economic Policy of 1922. It draws on his speeches to peasant and soviet congresses, "The Immediate Tasks of the Soviet Government", his remarks at the Seventh Party Congress (1918) and a 1920 review of the revolution's first three years. It is organised in three sections, one for each of three claims, plus a conclusion that links Lenin's concepts to the Chinese Communist Party today.

First, Yu holds that Lenin joined present practice to its future. Measures such as land redistribution, workers' control and bank nationalisation were compatible with capitalism, but they led towards socialism, so the revolution could be called socialist. Soviet Russia was a "socialist republic" because it had set out on that road, while it remained in a "transition period" consistent with Marx and Engels. Second, Lenin tied the Russian revolution to European and world revolution, describing Russia as one link in a world chain and insisting that victory could not be secure without it. Third, Yu says that when Lenin called accounting and control, or grain collection, "socialism" or "living socialism", he used the word loosely. Yu argues he did so to praise the masses' creativity and to mark measures on which the survival of Soviet power depended, while keeping the classical view that socialism lacks commodity production, classes and the state.

Yu concludes that these concepts reflect experience gained in the revolutionary struggle and in building a new system. The author sees the same qualities in the Chinese Communist Party of the new era: the "Two Centenary Goals" show a future vision, a community with a shared future for mankind shows a global vision, and the campaign against poverty shows heroic struggle. Yu presents this as adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you study Lenin's changing use of the word "socialism", or want to see how Chinese scholars link Leninist concepts to current Party discourse.
quoteEn: When Lenin said that "accounting and control" is socialism, he was discussing the matter in a non-strict sense; in fact he had not changed his view that a socialist society is one with "three absences".
quoteZh: 列宁说“计算和监督”是社会主义，是从非严格意义上论述问题的，实际上他没有改变关于社会主义社会是“三个没有”的社会的思想。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for cooperation and shared security and prosperity among countries.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for fitting Marxist theory to China's conditions and to the current era. It was extended to include 'of our times' in recent Party documents.
In Marx, Engels and Lenin, the historical stage between capitalism and a developed socialist or communist society. Lenin described Soviet Russia as being in this stage.
Official goals of building a moderately prosperous society by the Party's centenary (2021) and a modern socialist country by the centenary of the People's Republic (2049).

t: The historical dialectic of the state and capitalism in Capital and its manuscripts
zh: 《资本论》及其手稿中国家与资本主义的历史辩证法
paras: Guo Qiang argues that scholarship on Capital has concentrated on its economics and neglected its theory of the state, while work on Marx's theory of the state has turned mainly to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and The Civil War in France. The article contends that Capital and its manuscripts contain a systematic account of the state's origin, essence, functions and future, derived from the state's link to the capitalist economy. Guo points to Marx's "five-part" and "six-book" plans, both of which reserve a separate section for the state.

The article is organised in five parts. It treats in turn the essence of the bourgeois state, its functions, relations between states in foreign trade and the world market, the historical limits of the state form, and Marx's anticipation of the state's withering away. Guo draws on Capital, the 1857–58 manuscripts, the preface and introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, the London Notebooks, and related passages from Engels.

Guo's central claim is that Marx explains the state from civil society, meaning material life relations, rather than from the state itself. The bourgeois state emerged with primitive accumulation, relying on the colonial system, public debt, modern taxation and protective tariffs, and its laws (enclosure acts, labour statutes, factory acts) serve capital even when they concede to workers. Guo reads the state's dual functions as public affairs arising from the nature of all societies and specific functions arising from the opposition between government and the mass of the people. The state's dependence on capital's command over labour, hidden behind formal freedom and equality, is said to be the "most hidden secret" of the state form. The contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation, Guo argues, makes the state a "collective capitalist" unable to resolve the opposition between universal and particular interests.

Guo concludes that Marx foresaw replacing the "illusory community" of the state with an association of free individuals who own the means of production in common and distribute means of consumption according to labour time. In this account, society would then take back state power, and the state apparatus would be consigned to a museum of antiquities. Guo presents this as the completion of human emancipation beyond merely political emancipation. Read the original if you want a close, text-based reconstruction of the state theory in Capital and its manuscripts, drawing on Marx's planning schemes and economic categories.
quoteEn: Marx did not discuss the state in terms of the state alone, but understood its essence from the standpoint of the relationship between society and the state.
quoteZh: 马克思不是就国家谈论国家，而是从社会与国家关系的角度理解国家的本质的

glossary.explanation: Marx's term, used in Capital and earlier in the Communist Manifesto, for a future society in which producers work with commonly owned means of production and consciously plan social labour.
A phrase from The German Ideology describing the state as a seemingly common interest that in fact serves the ruling class.
Hegel's term for the sphere of material life relations and market exchange. Marx took it as the base from which the state and legal forms must be explained.
The plan in the 1859 Preface covering capital, landed property, wage-labour, the state, foreign trade and the world market. Capital realised only the first part.

t: The 21st century still needs Lenin
st: On Žižek's defence and rehabilitation of Leninism
zh: 21世纪依然需要列宁
zhSub: 论齐泽克对列宁主义的辩护和正名
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2025 no. 2
paras: Why has Lenin returned to Western radical-left debate, and how does Slavoj Žižek defend him? Luo and Guo argue that Lenin has been misread and stigmatised as a symbol of totalitarianism because his critique of bourgeois freedom threatens the legitimacy of liberal democracy. They present Žižek's call to "repeat Lenin" as the most prominent response, while holding that it also exposes the predicament of the Western left.

The article has four parts. It first describes how Lenin was labelled totalitarian and why this served capitalism. It then sets out Žižek's defence across his Lenin books, from Repeating Lenin (2001) to Lenin 2017 (2017). A third section explains why Žižek holds that the century still needs Lenin, and a conclusion assesses this Western turn from the authors' own standpoint.

The authors report three moves in Žižek's defence. First, Leninism does not necessarily lead to Stalinism: Žižek reads Lenin's economic and nationality policies and his "political testament" as incompatible with Stalin's course, and ranks the October Revolution with the French Revolution as a world-historical "event". Second, Lenin opened a revolutionary path from a desperate situation after 1914, when the Second International collapsed into patriotism. Third, "repeating Lenin" means recovering what Lenin failed to do and the courage to make the impossible possible, not returning to Lenin. Žižek, in this account, uses Lacanian theory to show that liberal "freedom of choice" is a framed, forced choice, and that Western Marxism has been tamed into cultural critique.

Luo and Guo conclude that the Western left's turn to Lenin reflects its difficulties: a muted working class, short-lived protests such as Occupy Wall Street, and a defanged critical theory. Whether it will help remains, they say, to be seen. They propose a more realistic option: recognising socialism with Chinese characteristics as an inheritor and developer of Leninism that is opening a new phase of world socialism. Without this, they argue, "repeating Lenin" risks becoming an empty slogan. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic assessment of Žižek's Leninism and of how Chinese scholars view Western radical-left thought.
quoteEn: The misreading and stigmatisation of Lenin is a product of the workings of capitalist ideology, aimed at containing the revolutionary potential of Leninism and thereby preserving the order of capitalist rule.
quoteZh: 列宁被误读和污名化是资本主义意识形态运作的产物，其目的在于遏制列宁主义所具有的革命潜能，从而维护资本主义统治秩序。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up. Official texts present it as adapting Marxism to China's conditions.

t: A historical-materialist reading of the complex link between cultural forms and the development of an age, and its contemporary implications
st: An analysis based on Marx's Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy
zh: 文化形态与时代发展复杂关联的唯物史观阐释及其当代启示
zhSub: 基于马克思《〈政治经济学批判〉导言》的分析
source: Studies on Marxism (马克思主义研究), 2025 no. 4
paras: Wang Xiaofeng asks how Marx's 1857 Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy explains the relationship between an age and its culture, using ancient Greek art as the main case. The article argues that Marx treats culture as bound to the social conditions that produce it, yet not mechanically determined by material production. Wang presents this as a theoretical basis for current Chinese debates on cultural construction and the 'Second Integration'.

The article has five parts. The first discusses Marx's claim that classical art can no longer be produced in its 'epoch-making' classical form. The second takes up why classical art still gives enjoyment and serves as a norm. The third covers culture's tie to 'a definite form of social development'. The fourth treats the uneven relation between material production and art. The fifth draws lessons for the study of Chinese culture. Wang draws on Engels, Mao Zedong and Marx's other works, and on examples from Greek myth, the Renaissance, the Enlightenment and Chinese history.

Wang makes three main moves. First, cultural 'revivals', whether the Renaissance or the Hundred Schools of Thought in China, are said to be new cultures with new content that borrow older forms, so Marx's remark is read as affirming real, non-abstract progress through the negation of old forms. Second, classical works still move people because they express the essence of their time or shared human feeling, such as love of nature and longing for freedom. Their charm is tied to immature social conditions that cannot return, and rigid classical norms can also restrict a culture's spread, as Wang says happened with classical poetry. Third, Wang stresses the uneven relation between material and cultural development: undeveloped eras can produce major art, individual talent matters, and backward countries such as Germany and France could lead in philosophy. Wang adds, citing Engels, that economic development retains the final say.

Wang concludes that Marx's text points to a path of creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional Chinese culture, guided by Marxism. The article warns against two errors: dismissing tradition as worthless, and exaggerating its achievements, for instance by claiming that socialist ideas could arise in an old peasant economy. Wang also says ancient concepts, such as 'the people', must be distinguished from their modern meanings rather than matched by surface analogy. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar uses Marx's Introduction on art and the age to support current Party policy on integrating Marxism with traditional culture.
quoteEn: Therefore, in the discussion of combining the basic principles of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture, the key question is not whether to 'integrate', nor even why, but how.
quoteZh: 所以，关于马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合的讨论，其关键问题不在于要不要“结合”，甚至也不在于为什么“结合”，而在于怎样“结合”。

glossary.explanation: The combination of the basic principles of Marxism with China's fine traditional culture. Xi Jinping put it forward in 2021–2023 as the second of the Two Integrations, alongside integrating Marxism with China's concrete realities.
The official term for the parts of China's cultural heritage that the Party regards as worth preserving and developing, as distinct from elements it treats as outdated.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.explanation: A formula associated with Xi Jinping for treating traditional culture. It means recasting old forms to fit current needs and adding to the content of tradition.

keywords: Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy

t: Critique of the logic of capital in Marx's theory of world history and its contemporary significance
st: A textual study based on Capital and its manuscripts
zh: 马克思世界历史理论视域下的资本逻辑批判及其当代意义
zhSub: 基于《资本论》及其手稿的文本研究
source: Economic Vertical and Horizontal (Jingji zongheng), 2025 no. 4
paras: Wang Xinsheng and Zhang Jianrong ask what the logic of capital is, why it governs modern society, and how it can be overcome. They propose reading Marx's critique in Capital and its manuscripts through his theory of world history, rather than treating it in isolation.
