Their thesis is that Marx's critique of capital's logic unites the critique of the "old world" with the discovery of a "new world", and that it still offers resources for understanding contemporary capitalism.

The article has three main parts. The first traces how the logic of capital arose in world history: its premises, its spatial and temporal expansion through the world market, its historical limits and its effects. The second examines the world-historical dimension of Marx's critique, including its dialectical basis and its three strands, which the authors label real, historical and value critique. The third draws out four contemporary meanings, namely digital capitalism, socialist construction in China, alternative paths to modernization, and human development.

The authors argue that capital's logic, the inner law of ceaseless pursuit of surplus value, built the world market and remade human society. They hold that it is also self-contradictory: rising organic composition, falling profit rates and general overproduction mean that capital's own limits constrain it. Marx's critique is an immanent, dialectical one, unlike that of classical economists, who treated capital as eternal, or of utopian socialists, whose criticism was external. The authors say the critique exposes fetishism and abstract domination, the temporary character of capitalism, and the inversion that makes people servants of capital. They claim the same contradictions create the material base and the proletariat for a communist world history.

The authors conclude that Marx's critique remains valid because digital capitalism, in their account, intensifies rather than abolishes exploitation on a private-ownership basis. For socialism with Chinese characteristics at the primary stage of socialism, they say it justifies using capital as a factor of production to develop the productive forces while regulating its negative side and preventing disorderly expansion. They also argue that capitalist modernization is not the only route to modernization, and that sublating capital means absorbing its achievements while overcoming its defects, in order to achieve people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a text-based, Capital-centred account of how Chinese scholars link Marx's critique of capital to digital capitalism and to the regulation of capital in China today.
quoteEn: As long as the logic of capital continues to spread across the globe, Marx's critique of it retains world-historical significance.
quoteZh: 只要资本逻辑还在全球蔓延，马克思资本逻辑批判就还有世界历史意义。

glossary.explanation: The official Chinese Communist Party assessment that China is still at an early, long-lasting stage of socialism with underdeveloped productive forces. It is used to justify a market economy and multiple forms of ownership.
The official name for China's path and system since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, a socialist market economy and national conditions.

In Marxist usage, the account that capital's expansion and the world market turn local histories into one interconnected global history. Chinese scholars treat it as a core part of historical materialism.
The Hegelian-Marxist notion (Aufhebung) of overcoming something while preserving its positive content.

t: Marx's dialectic of labour and the limits of Western modernity
st: With a commentary on Heidegger's account of the relation between Marx and Hegel
zh: 马克思的劳动辩证法与西方现代性的限度
zhSub: 兼评海德格尔论马克思和黑格尔的思想关系
source: Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2025 no. 3
paras: Liu Guixiang takes up Heidegger's claim that Marx merely inherited and applied Hegel's dialectic of labour, so that Marxism remains inside the subject-centred metaphysics of modernity. The article argues that Heidegger correctly identifies Hegel as the source of Marx's concept of labour but mistakes this source for the nature of Marx's thought. In Liu's reading, Marx's dialectic of labour sublates Hegel's and points to a critique of modernity and the communist movement, which together answer the 'riddle of history'.

The article is organised around three questions: what Heidegger actually says about Marx and Hegel (drawing on the Letter on Humanism and 'The Principle of Thinking'); how Marx inherits and goes beyond Hegel; and how Heidegger assesses the contribution and limits of each. Liu traces Marx's five critiques of Hegel, from the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right to the Paris Manuscripts, The Holy Family, The German Ideology and The Poverty of Philosophy. The article then places the Marx–Heidegger dispute within the wider field of modernity debates, citing Löwith, Marcuse, Lukács, Althusser and Habermas.

Liu's central move rests on Marx's Paris Manuscripts. Marx credits Hegel with grasping labour as the self-generation of humanity, but faults him for knowing only abstract, mental labour, so that objectification stays 'a circle within thought'. Marx replaces self-consciousness with the sensuous human being and makes 'objective activity' the starting point of a new materialism. Liu presents this as an ontological revolution that predates Heidegger's Being and Time by more than eighty years. Heidegger's analysis, by contrast, is ontological and phenomenological, whereas Marx's is practical and dialectical-materialist. Liu also notes that Heidegger acknowledged communism as an experience of world-historical significance, yet still read Marx through Feuerbach's humanism.

Liu concludes that Marx's dialectic of labour overcomes the opposition between humanism, which fixes on human essence, and historicism, which appeals to time, by showing history's diachronic and synchronic dimensions arising together in humanity's dealings with the world. Reunification, in this account, comes through the critique of capitalism and the communist movement rather than Hegelian triads or Heideggerian meditation on Being. Liu holds that this points to a new form of human civilisation beyond capitalism. Read the original if you want a Marxist rebuttal of Heidegger's reading of Marx and Hegel, grounded in close reference to the Paris Manuscripts.
quoteEn: The limit of Hegel's dialectic is in fact the limit of modern society as a whole, and this limit is reproduced through the intellectual dispute between Hegel and Marx.
quoteZh: 黑格尔辩证法的限度，其实就是整个现代社会的限度，这个限度通过黑格尔和马克思的思想争执被再现出来。

t: Being born from nothing: the logical beginning of Capital
zh: 有生于无：《资本论》的逻辑开端
source: Fujian Forum (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 3
paras: Dai Ligang takes up the question of where Capital logically begins, a problem the author ties to constructing the "rational form" of Marx's historical dialectic. Dai argues that the value-form school, which makes value and its forms the beginning, reads the relation of being and non-being the wrong way round. On Dai's account, Marx's critique reverses "non-being arises from being" into "being arises from nothing".

The article opens by dismissing both the Soviet textbook reading of dialectics as an essential "law" and the Heideggerian-phenomenological existential reading. It then reviews the debate over the beginning: Rosenthal and Ilyenkov's realist reading with the commodity as starting point, Hans-Georg Backhaus's value-form dialectic, and Chris Arthur's New Dialectic, which draws on Hegel's Logic and Roy Bhaskar's account of absence. It also covers critical realist objections that put production at the core. Dai then returns to Marx's method of critique, drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno, and examines the German terms verschwindet and Verrücktheit in the Grundrisse.

Dai distinguishes two moments of critique, following Adorno: Critique I shows how capitalism constructs a fetishised "second nature", and Critique II pierces its false objectivity and shows the historical, non-eternal character of the value form. Dai charges Backhaus and Arthur with keeping only Critique I. By treating use-value and value as potentiality and realisation, they make the illusion permanent, and they substitute value-form determinism for the labour theory of value. Dai holds that Marx instead uses "disappearance" as a verb, so that use-value and concrete labour become a non-being that is absent but still stands in negative, heterogeneous relation to value. Verrücktheit ("derangement") describes value's domination over use-value, which appears only as "abstract chaos". The same negativity recurs in the relation of capital and labour, and Marx's late "Notes on Wagner" is cited as showing that the commodity, not value, is the starting point.

Dai concludes that the beginning of Capital is the commodity's internal contradiction, not a self-realising value form. Dai also revises Arthur's table of the relations between production and exchange. Post-structuralist readings such as Hardt and Negri's, and practice-based or phenomenological readings, are said to miss the mechanism of dialectical movement. In Dai's view, that movement is driven by absent non-being negating being, which also allows the ideological illusion to be pierced. Read the original if you work on value-form theory, the New Dialectic or the Hegel–Marx relation, and want a critical Chinese reassessment built on close reading of Marx's German terms.
quoteEn: The above argument for the fundamental status of \"non-being\" (nothing) aims to show that the beginning of Capital is not the value form with its power to dominate and synthesise, but the internal contradictoriness of the commodity.
quoteZh: 以上对“非存在”（无）的根本地位的论证旨在说明《资本论》的开端并不是有着统摄和综合能力的价值形式，而是商品的内在矛盾性。

t: Re-examining the "method of inquiry" and "method of presentation" in Marx's Capital
zh: 马克思《资本论》的“研究方法”和“叙述方法”再审视
paras: How should the method of Marx's Capital be understood? Bai and Wang argue that reading it only as ascent from the concrete to the abstract (inquiry) or from the abstract to the concrete (presentation) narrows Marx's dialectic and its materialist horizon. They contend that the two methods must be grasped as a unity, and that this unity, with Marx's concept of the "power of abstraction", marks the "critical and revolutionary" character of Capital's methodology.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the "two paths" of political economy in Marx's 1857 Introduction and the distinction between inquiry and presentation. The second returns to Capital to read the unity of the two methods through Marx's reply to the Russian critic Kaufman, Engels's "logical and historical" principle, and Marx's break with Hegel and Proudhon. The third turns to the "power of abstraction", the critique of commodity fetishism and the question of how capitalism's real conditions of life are revealed.

Bai and Wang hold that the method of inquiry appropriates material and traces the inner connections of its forms, while the method of presentation reproduces the "life of the material" in thought so that it looks like an a priori construction. Reading Marx's description of presentation as "scientifically correct" as a verdict against inquiry, they say, hides Capital's materialism. Against Kaufman, who saw Marx as a Hegelian idealist, they stress Marx's inversion of Hegel: the logic of things, not the "thing of logic". The order of categories is set by their place in the structure of modern bourgeois society, with capital as a "universal light", not by historical sequence. The authors present Marx's power of abstraction as a "real abstraction" arising from social practice. It differs from the intuitive abstraction of classical political economy and the speculative abstraction of Hegel. In the commodity, social relations between people appear as relations between things, and the contradiction between use-value production and value valorisation drives capital to undermine itself.

The authors conclude that the methodological revolution of Capital lies in critically inheriting both classical political economy and German philosophy through the power of abstraction. They say this let Marx explain the capital–labour relation scientifically for the first time and turned dialectics into a revolutionary weapon against capitalist society. They also treat Capital as, in effect, a critique of Hegel's logic. Read the original if you work on the methodology of Capital, the Marx–Hegel relationship, or the debate over inquiry versus presentation and real abstraction, and want a densely sourced argument.
quoteEn: To grasp the method of Capital as a whole, one must understand the "method of inquiry" and the "method of presentation" as a unity; only then can one truly grasp the "critical and revolutionary" methodological essence of Capital.
quoteZh: 因此，要想对《资本论》的方法进行整体性的把握，只有将“研究方法”与“叙述方法”二者统一起来加以理解，才能真正把握《资本论》“批判的和革命的”方法论本质。

glossary.explanation: In Marx's Afterword to the second edition of Capital, the stage of mastering material, analysing its forms and tracing their inner connections. The article ties it to the path from the sensuous concrete to abstract determinations.
The stage in which the results of inquiry are set out, ascending from abstract determinations to the concrete totality. Marx called it "scientifically correct" in the 1857 Introduction.

Marx's phrase in the Preface to Capital, where it replaces the microscope and chemical reagents in analysing economic forms. The authors read it as a dialectical force that grasps social relations behind things.

An abstraction that arises from the practice and exchange relations of people in society, not from thought alone or from the intuition of things. The article contrasts it with the intuitive abstraction of classical political economy and the speculative abstraction of Hegel.

t: The historical dialectic of the state and capitalism in Capital and its manuscripts
zh: 《资本论》及其手稿中国家与资本主义的历史辩证法
paras: Guo Qiang argues that scholarship on Capital has concentrated on its economic theory and neglected the theory of the state it contains. Studies of Marx's state theory, in turn, tend to rely on the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right or The Civil War in France. The article holds that Capital and its manuscripts reveal the origin, essence, functions and future trend of the state through the state's links with the capitalist economy.

The article first notes that Marx's 'five-part' and 'six-book' plans both reserved a separate section for the state. It then moves through five themes: the essence of the bourgeois state, its functions, relations between states in foreign trade and the world market, the historical limits of the state form, and the prospect of the state's withering away. Evidence is drawn from the 1857–58 manuscripts, the Preface and Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy, the London Notebooks, Capital, and Engels.

Guo's central claim is that Marx explains the state from civil society, not from the state itself. Capital's rule over labour, rooted in private ownership of the means of production, is said to translate into political domination, so that formal freedom and equality conceal exploitation. On this reading, the state has a dual character: it performs 'public affairs' arising from the nature of all societies and 'specific functions' arising from the opposition between government and the mass of the people. Its economic role runs through the colonial system, public debt, modern taxation and protective tariffs, and factory legislation is presented as a concession won by class struggle. Guo adds that the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation cannot be cured by a state that is, in effect, the 'total capitalist'. In the world market, bourgeois society 'oversteps the bounds of the state', bringing both development and colonial oppression.

Guo concludes that Marx foresaw replacing the 'illusory community' of the state with an 'association of free individuals'. In it, means of production would be socially owned, labour would be joint, and individual ownership would be re-established on the basis of cooperation. Free time, not labour time, would become the measure of wealth. The state machinery would then be placed in a museum of antiquities, and society would take back state power. Read the original if you want a source-based account of how Capital and its manuscripts treat the state, tracing the planned 'state' section through to the withering away of the state.
quoteEn: Capital's domination over labour operates not only in the economic sphere but also deeply shapes the political sphere, and is the social root of the bourgeoisie's monopoly of state power.
quoteZh: 资本对劳动的支配不仅在经济领域，还深刻影响政治领域，是资产阶级垄断国家政权的社会根源。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term in Capital and the Communist Manifesto for a post-capitalist society in which producers work with common means of production and consciously plan social labour.
A phrase from The German Ideology describing the state as a seemingly common interest that in fact serves the ruling class and stands apart from society.
Hegel's term for the sphere of material and economic relations, which Marx identified with bourgeois society and treated as the basis of law and the state.

glossary.pinyin: wǔ piān jìhuà yǔ liù cè jìhuà
glossary.explanation: Marx's successive outlines for his critique of political economy, in the 1857 Introduction and the 1859 Preface. Both include a separate part on the state.

t: A historical-materialist reading of the complex relation between cultural forms and the development of an era, and its contemporary implications
st: An analysis based on Marx's Introduction to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy
zh: 文化形态与时代发展复杂关联的唯物史观阐释及其当代启示
zhSub: 基于马克思《〈政治经济学批判〉导言》的分析
source: Marxism Studies (马克思主义研究), 2025 no. 4
paras: Wang Xiaofeng asks how Marx's 1857 Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy explains the relation between an era and its culture. Wang argues that Marx's remarks on Greek art supply a historical-materialist framework for contemporary work on culture, and in particular for the debate on how to achieve the second of the Two Integrations, the union of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture.

The article is organised in five parts. The first four read Marx's text closely, with supporting passages from Engels, Mao Zedong and the Eighteenth Brumaire. They take up why classical art cannot be reproduced in its classical form, why it still gives aesthetic enjoyment, how culture is bound to 'a definite form of social development', and the uneven relation between material production and art. The fifth part draws implications for Chinese cultural policy. Examples range from Greek myth, the Renaissance and the Enlightenment to the Hundred Schools of Thought, Tang and Song poetry and Yan'an-era works.

Wang's central claim is that cultures arise and fade with the social conditions that produced them, so any cultural 'revival' is a new culture with new content rather than a repetition. Classical works nonetheless keep their charm because they speak to shared human feeling, natural beauty and the aspiration to freedom, as an adult can enjoy a child's naivety without becoming a child again. Wang also stresses that Marx rejected mechanical determinism. Art can flourish where production is backward, individual talent matters, and the relative independence of consciousness lets economically backward countries, such as Germany in philosophy, produce advanced culture. Wang adds, following Engels, that this cannot be made absolute.

For Chinese cultural construction, Wang concludes that the real question for the Two Integrations is how to integrate, not whether. Wang warns against both dismissing tradition and idealising it beyond its era or class. The author proposes creative transformation and innovative development of tradition, a distinction between traditional culture and its enduring spirit, and critical sublation instead of surface analogies between ancient and modern concepts. Read the original if you want a close Marxist reading of the Introduction's aesthetics applied to current Chinese debates on tradition and the Two Integrations.
quoteEn: Therefore, in the discussion of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture, the key question is not whether to 'integrate', nor even why, but how.
quoteZh: 所以，关于马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合的讨论，其关键问题不在于要不要“结合”，甚至也不在于为什么“结合”，而在于怎样“结合”。

glossary.explanation: Formula in Party theory: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities (the first) and with excellent traditional Chinese culture (the second). The second was stressed especially from 2021 to 2023.
Official phrase for the parts of China's cultural heritage regarded as worth inheriting, as opposed to elements deemed outdated or reactionary.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.explanation: Formula associated with Xi Jinping for treating tradition: reshaping old forms with new content and modern expression, and supplementing and extending the substance of traditional culture.
The Hegelian-Marxist notion (Aufhebung) of simultaneously negating, preserving and surpassing an earlier stage. Chinese texts use it for a critical, selective inheritance of tradition.

keywords: Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy

t: Critique of the logic of capital from the perspective of Marx's theory of world history, and its contemporary significance
st: A textual study based on Capital and its manuscripts
zh: 马克思世界历史理论视域下的资本逻辑批判及其当代意义
zhSub: 基于《资本论》及其手稿的文本研究
source: Economic Vertical and Horizontal (Jingji zongheng), 2025 no. 4
paras: Wang and Zhang ask what the logic of capital is, why it governs modern society, and how it can be overcome. They propose reading Marx's critique of it through his theory of world history, arguing that the two are inseparable: the logic of capital governs the formation of world history and human development, while world history supplies its origins, limits and the path to its sublation.

Drawing on Capital and its manuscripts, the article has three parts. The first traces how the logic of capital arises and expands historically: its preconditions, its spread through the world market, its limits and its effects. The second examines the world-historical dimension of Marx's critique. The third draws out four contemporary implications, which the authors tie to digital capitalism, socialism with Chinese characteristics, modernization and human development.

The authors argue that Marx's critique is an immanent, dialectical one. It differs from classical economists, who treated capital as eternal, and from utopian socialists, whose criticism was external. Marx exposes the logic of capital through three linked critiques: of reality (fetishism and abstract domination), of history (capital's own limits, the 'barrier' to capitalist production being capital itself) and of values (the reduction of people to one-sided, alienated beings). Its aim is to find within the old world history the new one that sublates it. On this reading capital has a dual character: a civilising side as a factor of production and a destructive side as a relation of production. The authors say it should therefore be neither wholly negated nor justified.

Wang and Zhang conclude that the critique remains a 'pathology of capital' of world-historical significance. They claim it shows that digital capitalism is a more concealed form of exploitation on a private-ownership basis. They also say it explains why capital has a place in the primary stage of socialism, where its positive side is to be used and its disorderly expansion regulated. In their account it undermines the idea that capitalist modernization is the only path and points towards the free and all-round development of the person. Read the original if you want a text-based account of how Chinese scholars link Marx's world-history theory and critique of capital to digital capitalism and the role of capital under socialism.
quoteEn: Although capitalist modernization opened world history, it is not the one to bring it to an end.
quoteZh: 资本主义现代化虽是世界历史的开启者，但并非世界历史的终结者。

glossary.explanation: The official Chinese Communist Party thesis, formalised in the 1980s, that China is still at an early, long stage of socialism. It is used to justify developing the productive forces and a market economy.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

t: The significance of Herder for the formation of Marx's thought
zh: 赫尔德对马克思思想形成的意义
paras: Ma Jianqing asks whether Johann Gottfried Herder (1744–1803), a leader of the Sturm und Drang movement, influenced Marx, and if so which elements, to what degree and by what routes. The article argues that the link is real but fragile and thinly documented. Marx's German heritage, it holds, should not be reduced to Hegelian speculative philosophy, since it also includes wider eighteenth-century currents that Herder helped shape.

After a brief review of scholars who mention the connection (Isaiah Berlin, F. M. Barnard, Allen Wood, among others), the article proceeds in three parts. It first reconstructs channels of dialogue: Marx's 1839 folk-song collection drawing on Herder's Stimmen der Völker in Liedern, his reading notes of 1844–47, and references in letters. It also traces indirect mediation through Hegel, Feuerbach, Savigny, Goethe and Gans. It then compares Herder and Marx on the human being, language and history, and finally assesses the relation between anthropology and historical materialism.

Ma argues that Herder's view of human nature as self-expression through action anticipates the objectification theory of the 1844 Manuscripts. Herder's thesis that thought and language are inseparable, and his naturalistic account of language's origin, are said to resonate with Marx's remarks on language as social and as the element of thought in The German Ideology and the Grundrisse. Herder's treatment of history as natural, causal and organic is likened to Marx's idea of history as the true natural history of man and of society as an organism. Most of this influence, Ma suggests, reached Marx through Hegel and Feuerbach.

Ma concludes that both thinkers faced a shared task at the secularising turn of philosophy: reconciling ideal and real, universal and particular. Herder's anthropology, however, still relied on metaphysics, on God and on an inflated role for spirit, and in the sense of Marx's critique of German ideology it remained idealist. Historical materialism, grounded in practice and material production, is presented as dissolving the tensions in Herder's thought. The author warns against both exaggerating the link and opposing the two thinkers absolutely. Read the original if you study the intellectual genealogy of Marx's early work or the German Romantic and Sturm und Drang background to historical materialism.
quoteEn: Both Herder and Marx were committed to the unity of philosophy and life, theory and practice.
quoteZh: 赫尔德与马克思都致力于哲学与生活、理论与实践的统一。

t: The machine narrative in Marx's context and its conceptual genealogy
zh: 马克思语境中的机器叙事及其概念谱系
paras: Existing scholarship reads Marx on machines mainly through the philosophy of science and technology or through the critique of political economy. Zhao argues that this work rarely shows how Marx's machine-related concepts are connected to one another. The article contends that Marx's machine is not an isolated object but part of a narrative with an internal generative logic and a conceptual genealogy.

Working from Marx's own texts, the article traces a sequence: traditional tool, machine tool, machine, automaton and machine system; then the automatic machine system and the automatic factory; then the factory system, factory legislation and wider social institutions. It is organised in three main sections, followed by a short conclusion. Zhao also draws on Charles Babbage, Lewis Mumford and Andrew Ure to show where Marx follows or departs from them.

In the first move, Zhao says Marx goes beyond Babbage's structural account by adding the 'subjective' side of the modern machine, the automaton with 'mechanical' and 'intelligent' organs. Marx treats the machine system as the bridge from the machine as a single object to the machine as a social-historical element. In the second move, Zhao argues that capitalist machine production reverses the relation between worker and machine. This is not a loss of human subjectivity in general. It is one class, the capitalists, appropriating the subjectivity of another through ownership of capital. Machines are dead labour that transfer value, while only living labour creates surplus value, and this is why capitalists build the factory system and have it codified in factory legislation. Zhao presents these as arrangements that stabilise capitalist relations and socialise the conflict, without changing the underlying relationship.

Zhao concludes that, for Marx, the source of alienation is capitalist private ownership of the means of production and its capital logic, not the machine itself. Zhao reads Marx as warning that smashing machines will not free workers. Instead, the contradiction between private ownership and the socialisation of machine production points towards public ownership and the use of machines for people's free and all-round development. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based reconstruction of Marx's machine concepts and their links to the factory system and factory law, rather than a debate on contemporary technology.
quoteEn: The machine in Marx's context is not an isolated objective entity but forms a distinctive machine narrative and conceptual genealogy.
quoteZh: 马克思语境中的机器并不是某种孤立的客观存在，而是构成了独特的机器叙事及其概念谱系。

t: The historical presence of philosophy
st: Origins and position of Hegel's theory of the history of philosophy
zh: 哲学的历史性在场
zhSub: 黑格尔哲学史理论的渊源与定位
paras: The modern idea that philosophy is inseparable from its history owes much to Hegel's Lectures on the History of Philosophy. Feng Jiahui argues that this position was not a self-evident premise for Hegel but a theoretical solution to a problem in his own development. For post-Kantian thinkers seeking a scientific, systematic philosophy, the fact that philosophy has a history was a serious challenge, and Hegel's answer is traced here through its stages.

The article follows Hegel from his early Jena years to his mature system. It first examines the 1801 'Differenzschrift' and the 1801/02 lectures on logic and metaphysics, then the mid-Jena turn to the historicity of spirit and the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807). It then turns to the six lecture courses on the history of philosophy given from 1819, with discussion of Hegel's Logic, Karl Vieweg's recent reconstruction, and critics such as Fulda.

Feng's central claim is that Hegel moved from asserting the supra-historical unity of philosophy to the principle of the 'agreement of history and logic'. Early on, reason was single and its system lay beyond history. Three insights then changed this: knowledge's history is constitutive of knowledge, contradiction drives thought forward dialectically, and 'spirit' covers both individual moments and the whole. The Phenomenology offered a preparatory account but, as an introduction to the system, did not settle the matter. In the mature theory, the author stresses, Hegel speaks of the 'identity' of history and logic, not their 'unity', and does not claim one-to-one correspondence. Citing Fulda, Feng reads the principle as holding at the main nodes of philosophy's history, like supporting points in a building, not at every detail.

Feng concludes that Hegel founded the philosophical study of the history of philosophy, which becomes philosophy's own theoretical task, not a branch of intellectual history. The author also identifies a cost. Hegel's historicity concerns the living present, not the future, so a completed logic sits uneasily with a history of philosophy that cannot end. Either philosophy has exhausted its possibilities, or Hegel's logic is itself only a historical product. Read the original if you study Hegel's development, post-Kantian systematic philosophy or the relation between history and logic, and want a close textual account of how this principle emerged and where its limits lie.
quoteEn: What matters in essence is rather the self-manifestation of spirit: it does not permeate every detail of reality, but on the larger scale its historical process becomes transparent in logical determinations.
quoteZh: 事关本质的毋宁在于精神之自身展现（sich manifestieren）；它不渗透于实在的每一个细节，但在大的尺度之中，其历史进程在逻辑规定中变得透明。

t: The construction and transcendence of "moral politics": Rousseau, Hegel and Marx
zh: “道德政治”的建构与超越：卢梭、黑格尔与马克思
paras: Zhang Dang takes up the relation between morality and politics, which the article treats as a basic tension of modernity. The thesis is that Rousseau saw the separation of the two and proposed rebuilding a "moral politics", and that Hegel tried to repair the proposal with "ethical politics". On Zhang's reading, both remained trapped in the same predicament, and only Marx resolved it by moving the question from morality and will to property relations.

The article, published in Philosophical Research in 2025, is organised in three parts. The first sets out why moral politics was needed, tracing Machiavelli's split between morality and politics and the positions of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau on the state of nature and the social contract. The second examines Rousseau's "general will" and his proposals on inequality, then Hegel's critique, with a side glance at Kant. The third follows Marx from his 1843 reading notes on Rousseau to the critique of political economy.

Zhang argues that Rousseau located inequality and servitude in society rather than nature, but then defended property as a sacred right, which conflicts with his attack on private property. Hegel, in Zhang's account, rightly criticised Rousseau's voluntarist freedom, its link to Jacobin terror, and Kant's empty moral law. By distinguishing morality from ethical life (Sittlichkeit), Hegel made freedom concrete, but his rational state left the economic basis of the political state unexplained. Marx, Zhang says, used historical materialism to reject the premise of the individual as will, and in The German Ideology treated the state as a form through which the bourgeoisie secures its property. In Capital he separated private property based on the producer's own labour from that based on exploiting others' labour. Zhang holds that Rousseau and others blurred this distinction and so indirectly defended capitalist private property.

Zhang concludes that Marx went beyond moral politics by taking the proletariat as the revolutionary subject, abolishing capitalist private property and re-establishing "individual ownership" on the basis of associated labour. In this reading Marx dissolved the split between modern morality and politics and gave a scientific guide to reducing the wealth gap and achieving real democracy and equality. Read the original if you study Marx's relation to Rousseau and Hegel, or the history of political philosophy on property, democracy and the state.
quoteEn: By distinguishing the forms of property rights in the course of history, Marx thoroughly criticised bourgeois property rights and thereby went beyond the path of rebuilding a bourgeois "moral politics".
quoteZh: 马克思通过区分历史进程中的财产权形式，彻底批判了资产阶级的财产权，从而超越了重建资产阶级“道德政治”的路径。

glossary.explanation: The author's term for Rousseau's project of grounding the political order in moral principles, above all the general will, against the modern separation of morality and politics.
The author's label for Hegel's response, in which the state is an ethical totality (Sittlichkeit) that unites universal and particular, going beyond subjective morality.
Rousseau's volonté générale, the universal will of citizens aimed at the common good, distinguished from the mere sum of particular wills.
Marx's phrase in Capital for the property form that replaces capitalist private property, based on cooperation and common possession of the means of production.

t: The historical basis of production and the logical beginning of exchange: Marx's value-form theory in the process of research and the process of presentation
zh: 生产的历史基础与交换的逻辑开端：基于马克思价值形式理论研究与叙述过程的探讨
paras: Li Qiankun takes up a dispute over whether production or exchange has priority in Marx's critique of political economy. Since the second half of the twentieth century, Li says, Western left theory has given exchange discourse logical priority and has tried to replace or reject Marxism's categories of production. The article argues that in his research Marx found production to be the historical basis of exchange, but in presenting the capitalist mode of production in Capital he made exchange the logical beginning. Together these two processes make up the distinctive method of his value-form theory.

The article opens with the Western currents Li has in mind: Western Marxism and Western Marxology, the New Reading of Marx, the New Dialectic, Uno school and regulation theory, Habermas and Baudrillard. It then follows Marx's treatment of money from On the Jewish Question and the 1844 manuscripts through the Grundrisse, the 1859 Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, and the 1861–63 and 1863–65 manuscripts. A final section reads the opening of Capital Volume 1 and closes by discussing Heinrich's position.

Li's central claim is that Marx's early explanations of money rested on exchange, private property and the division of labour. In the Grundrisse and the 1859 work, Li argues, he had not yet joined labour-power and surplus-value theory to value and money, and still confused exchange-value with value. Only with the theory of average profit and prices of production in 1861–63 did he explain money from the total process of capitalist production, since the commodity as a product of capital contains paid and unpaid labour whose quantity cannot be directly measured. Li holds that this is why value must take the money form. In Capital, Marx begins with exchange because the commodity form is the cell form of bourgeois society, because value and money can only be explained through value-form analysis, and because the analysis of exchange leads to labour-power as the special commodity behind money becoming capital. Li adds that this order of presentation is a 'circle' that presupposes the earlier grasp of production.

Li concludes that Marx unites the logical and the historical: production brings contradiction, struggle and historical change, while exchange brings formal norms and synchronic structure. Both aspects, Li says, belong to the capitalist mode of production. Heinrich, in Li's reading, keeps the logic of presentation but drops the historical dimension and the foundational place of production. Li contends that left theories starting from exchange risk confirming capitalism's validity and dissolving history. Read the original if you work on value-form theory, the New Reading of Marx or the research/presentation distinction, and want a close textual account of how Marx's treatment of money developed.
quoteEn: In the course of Marx's research for the critique of political economy, it was production, not exchange, that formed the entire foundation of his intellectual framework.
quoteZh: 在马克思的政治经济学批判研究过程中，是生产而非交换，构成了其思想构架的全部基础。

t: Critique of the logic of capital in Marx's theory of world history and its contemporary significance
st: A textual study based on Capital and its manuscripts
zh: 马克思世界历史理论视域下的资本逻辑批判及其当代意义
zhSub: 基于《资本论》及其手稿的文本研究
source: Economic Vertical and Horizontal (Jingji zongheng), 2025 no. 4
paras: Wang Xinsheng and Zhang Jianrong ask what the logic of capital is, why it governs modern society and how it can be overcome. They propose a perspective that reads Capital and its manuscripts through Marx's theory of world history. Their thesis is that Marx's critique of the logic of capital unites the criticism of an 'old world history' with the discovery of a 'new' one, and that this critique keeps its significance for the present.

The article has three main parts. The first traces how the logic of capital came to shape world history: its preconditions in primitive accumulation and the separation of labourers from the conditions of labour, its expansion through the world market, its historical limits and its historical effects. The second examines the world-historical dimension of Marx's critique. The third draws out four contemporary implications: for understanding digital capitalism, for building socialism with Chinese characteristics, for exploring modernization paths and for the free and all-round development of the human being.

The authors argue that Marx's critique is dialectical and immanent. It does not defend capital as eternal, as classical economists do, and it does not criticise it from outside, as the utopian socialists do. It has three strands: a critique of reality (the abstraction and fetishism through which relations between people appear as relations between things), a historical critique (capital's own barriers, such as the falling profit rate and crises of overproduction) and a critique of values (capital's reduction of people to one-sided, alienated beings). For the authors, the contradictions of capital also generate the material and social conditions for communism as a new world history. On this basis they hold that digital capitalism leaves the exploitative essence of capital unchanged. They also argue that capital has a civilising side as a factor of production and a destructive side as a relation of production.

The authors conclude that the critique of capital's logic is a 'pathology of capital' with world-historical meaning. They call for regulating its negative aspects and making full use of its positive ones in socialism with Chinese characteristics, and for recognising that capitalist modernization is not the only route to modernity. Read the original if you want a systematic, text-based Chinese account of how Marx's world-history theory is used to link the critique of capital to digital capitalism, the regulation of capital in China and alternative modernization.
quoteEn: The critique of the logic of capital is the key by which Marx perceived and revealed this secret.
quoteZh: 资本逻辑批判则是马克思洞察和揭示这一秘密的锁钥。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's political and economic system since reform and opening up. It combines Party leadership, a socialist market economy and the aim of building socialism in Chinese conditions.

A concept in Chinese Marxist scholarship for the inner law of capital as a social relation, which is the unending pursuit of surplus value. Scholars use it to explain how capital comes to organise society as a whole.
Marx's notion, from The German Ideology onwards, of history becoming a worldwide, interconnected process through the world market. Here it is tied to the global expansion of capital.

t: Marx's endogenous money thought
st: A comprehensive discussion based on money types and theoretical structure
zh: 马克思的内生货币思想
zhSub: 基于货币类型和理论结构的综合性探讨
source: Journal of the History of Economic Thought (Jingji sixiang shi xuekan), 2025 no. 1
paras: Marx praised Ricardo's value theory but repeatedly criticised his monetary theory. Wang asks what Marx's own theory of money was and why it diverged from Ricardo's quantity theory. The article argues that Marx built an endogenous money theory, in which prices determine the quantity of money, drawing on the Banking School rather than on Ricardo. It holds that Marx distinguished metallic, credit and fiat money, and that endogenous and quantity-theory logics apply to different types.

The article first traces the intellectual sources: the Currency School versus Banking School dispute, the earlier bullionist controversy, and the quantity theory and endogenous theory as modern schools. It then examines the money types of Marx's time (metallic money, credit money, and the question of whether sterling was fiat money), using the pound's history from 1694. Finally it reconstructs the theoretical structure in three parts: the endogenous money equation, the real bills doctrine and the law of reflux. Wang relies on close reading of Marx's texts and on writers such as Schumpeter, Blaug, Hodgson and Shaikh.

Wang's central claim is that the same currency can follow different laws under different regimes. Sterling was convertible, and so endogenous, in 1694–1797, 1821–1914 and 1925–31, but exogenous and fiat in 1797–1821, 1914–25 and after 1931. Ricardo wrote during the 1797–1821 suspension of convertibility, which explains his preference for the quantity theory. Marx wrote during the gold standard's height. Wang reads Marx's equation PQ/V = M as running from prices to money, and reads his treatment of real bills and reflux as linking money to capital movement. On this reading Marx anticipated Keynes's liquidity trap through his remark that credit-based money turns into metal-based money in crises.

Wang concludes that Marx's criticism of Ricardo may be one-sided, given the different monetary regimes each faced, and that Marx did not clearly count bank deposits as money. Wang nonetheless sees Marx's endogenous framework as close to post-Keynesian thinking and relevant to China, where deposit money dominates M2 and the 2024 Central Economic Work Conference put social financing before money supply. Money is held to play a passive, secondary role in economic fluctuations. Read the original if you study Marx's monetary theory, the Currency–Banking School debate, or the historical grounding of endogenous money.
quoteEn: An important finding of this article is that the same currency (represented by sterling) can follow different laws of monetary circulation in different historical periods and under different monetary systems.
quoteZh: 本文的重要发现是同一种货币(以英镑为代表)在不同历史时期和不同货币制度下可以遵循不同的货币流通规律。

t: Revisiting the mercantilist and physiocratic views of wealth and their subject
st: Starting from "Private property and labour" in Notebook III of the Paris Manuscripts
zh: 再论重商主义和重农学派的财富观及其主体之思
zhSub: 从《巴黎手稿》笔记本Ⅲ“私有财产和劳动”谈起
source: Journal of Renmin University of China, 2025 no. 1
paras: Huang Zhijun takes up the section "Private property and labour" in Notebook III of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. There Marx, following Adam Smith, treats the mercantilists as placing labour outside wealth, the physiocrats as moving labour into wealth as its subjective essence, and Smith as making general labour the universal essence. Huang calls this a widely accepted "strong logic" of transition and argues that it is too simplified and labelled. Going back to the mercantilist and physiocratic texts, Huang proposes a "weak logic" instead: labour is a subjective element of wealth in mercantilism, and a subjective component, not the subjective essence, in physiocracy.

The article has three parts. The first re-examines mercantilism on money and wealth, on circulation and wealth, and on the forms of existence of people in the mercantilist age, drawing on Smith, Schumpeter, Marx, William Stafford, Thomas Mun and Fernand Braudel. The second turns to Quesnay and physiocracy, covering their view of the nature of wealth, the composition of wealth through the "net product", and the understanding of the subject, including the classes of the Tableau économique. A conclusion then assesses traditional histories of political economy, Marx's early and late views, and the link between views of wealth and ways of human existence.

On mercantilism, Huang argues that Smith's label of "confusing money with wealth" fits only some early writers. Citing Schumpeter, Stafford and Mun, Huang holds that later mercantilists located the source of wealth in manufacture and production, so labour was already an internal element. On physiocracy, Huang follows Marx in crediting it with moving the study of surplus value into production, and sees a tension between declaring labour the essence of wealth and treating labour as an element of land. Huang's reading of Quesnay is that land remains the sole source of wealth. Agricultural labour only shapes natural products, and agricultural labour is therefore the subjective component, not the subjective essence, of wealth.

Huang concludes that Marx's 1844 judgements still relied on Smith, because Marx had not yet developed his theories of value and surplus value. In Capital and its manuscripts, Marx divides mercantilism into early and late phases and credits physiocracy more accurately. Huang also criticises Rosenberg's history of economic thought for repeating Smith's picture and for reading the physiocratic view of value as labour-created. Huang adds that the mercantilist age had varied modes of human existence, while physiocracy tied the subject to land and agriculture, which modern industry would negate. Read the original if you study the history of political economy, Marx's early economic reading of his predecessors, or the Smithian framing of mercantilism and physiocracy.
quoteEn: In my view, for the physiocrats agricultural labour is the subjective component of wealth, not its subjective essence.
quoteZh: 笔者认为在重农学派那里，农业劳动是财富的主体构成，而非主体本质。

t: Pursuing the appeal of theory through the long course of history
st: On "A Study of the Historical Development of the Two Theoretical Cornerstones of Scientific Socialism"
zh: 在历史长河中追寻理论的魅力
zhSub: 读《科学社会主义两大理论基石的历史发展研究》
paras: This is a book review, published in Guangming Daily on 3 July 2025. Wang Fuxin reviews Professor Zhu Dapeng's monograph A Study of the Historical Development of the Two Theoretical Cornerstones of Scientific Socialism (People's Publishing House). Wang argues that the book shows scientific socialism to be a theory with lasting appeal, and that studying its theoretical foundations as a whole is a key to understanding that appeal.

The two cornerstones are the materialist conception of history and the theory of surplus value. According to Wang, Zhu analyses how they relate to the overall development of scientific socialism. The book looks at its historical course, its present circumstances and its future trends, and it combines theory with practice. Wang organises the review around four qualities the book brings out: depth, sincerity, breadth and vitality.

Wang gives each quality a ground. Depth comes from resting on the long course of human history. As an example, Wang cites the apparent paradox that the surplus-value theory was completed in Capital (1867), after scientific socialism was founded in the Communist Manifesto (1848). The book resolves this by pointing to a fairly complete theory of the working class already held by Marx and Engels, which linked the two cornerstones. Sincerity comes from holding the moral high ground, in the aim of human liberation. Breadth comes from addressing real problems of the age, including current disputes over the production and distribution of surplus value. Vitality comes from driving new practice. The book lists present challenges to the materialist conception of history, which Wang says can be settled fully only through new practice.

Wang concludes that scientific socialism advances in stages only when it holds to the stance, viewpoint and method of the two cornerstones. The review presents socialism with characteristics of China as the current achievement of this process, one that opens space to lead the times and guide practice. Read the original if you want a short Chinese-language account of how this monograph frames the two cornerstones and why a Party-affiliated scholar considers it significant.
quoteEn: Problems are the voice of the times, and the fundamental task of theory is to answer them and guide their solution.
quoteZh: 问题是时代的声音，回答并指导解决问题是理论的根本任务。

glossary.explanation: The doctrine founded by Marx and Engels, which grounds socialism in the analysis of history and capitalism rather than in moral ideals. Chinese texts treat it as the core part of Marxism.
Marx and Engels's account of history as shaped by material production and class relations. It is conventionally listed as the first of the two cornerstones of scientific socialism.

t: A political-economy analysis of "techno-feudalism"
zh: “技术封建主义”的政治经济学分析
paras: Pan Yue and Cheng Enfu examine the "techno-feudalism" thesis advanced by left-wing scholars such as Cédric Durand, Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean. Varoufakis claims that rent has defeated profit, that "cloudalists" rather than the proletariat will end bourgeois rule, and that techno-feudalism rather than socialism will replace capitalism. The authors answer that digital platforms have not surpassed capitalism. In their reading, "cloud rent" is a form of ground-rent-like income that ultimately derives from surplus value created by wage labour.

The article first reconstructs the theory's categories: cloud capital, cloudalists, cloud fiefs, cloud rent and cloud serfs. It then defines digital space and digital platforms as the "land" on which people work and live, and sets out a classification of platforms. The next sections explain how platform monopoly generates rent and apply Marx's theory of ground rent to e-commerce platforms. The final section assesses the theory's claims about markets, profit and historical trend.

The core move is an analogy with Marx's rent theory. Platform ownership, the authors argue, is ownership of virtual labour space, and platform revenue combines interest on invested capital with true "cloud rent" (which they call "platform rent"). They identify differential platform rent I and II, arising from uneven traffic and from additional investment, and absolute platform rent. The latter is illustrated with a formula showing that e-commerce shortens circulation and reduces commercial capital, yielding excess profit. Monopoly platform rent rests on monopoly prices. They also argue that data rent is only a surface phenomenon, since monopoly of digital space underlies it.

The authors conclude that markets and profit have not disappeared, because exchange persists even where platforms isolate buyers from one another. Cloud rent is paid out of production, merchants' profit or workers' wages, so it derives from industrial workers' labour. They see techno-feudalism as a technological extension of capitalist relations that intensifies exploitation and monopoly and accelerates capitalism's decline. They credit the theory with exposing digital capitalism but fault its metaphor of regression and its neglect of the proletariat's historical role. Read the original if you want a Marxist rent-theory critique of Varoufakis and Durand, including the e-commerce rent model.
quoteEn: The essence of "techno-feudalism" is a technological extension of capitalist relations of production, further confirming the parasitic nature of capitalism, which upgrades exploitation through technological restructuring.
quoteZh: “技术封建主义”的本质是资本主义生产关系的技术化延伸，进一步印证了资本主义通过技术重构实现剥削升级的寄生性本质。

glossary.explanation: A thesis associated with Cédric Durand, Yanis Varoufakis and Jodi Dean. It holds that digital platforms have replaced markets and profit with rent-extracting domains, so that capitalism is giving way to a new, feudal-like order.

In the techno-feudalism literature, the rent that platform owners collect from users for access to digital platforms and cloud services. The authors argue it is a form of ground-rent-like income derived from surplus value.
The term for digital platforms viewed as fiefs: monopolised digital domains that replace markets. The authors treat them as virtual land.
The authors' shorthand for cloud rent on e-commerce platforms, analysed by analogy with Marx's differential, absolute and monopoly ground rent.

t: "One Step Forward, Two Steps Back": Lenin's critique of the Menshevik view of organisation and its present-day lessons
zh: 《进一步，退两步》批判孟什维克关于组织的观点及其现实启示
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2025 no. 3
paras: Huang and Liu revisit Lenin's polemical work One Step Forward, Two Steps Back (written February–May 1904) to ask what its critique of the Menshevik view of organisation says about building a proletarian party. They argue that Lenin exposed the substance and harm of Menshevik organisational ideas and set out basic principles of party-building that still apply. Writing in 2025, they present the text as guidance for the Chinese Communist Party's drive to strengthen the political and organisational functions of Party organisations, as called for by the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024).

The article has five sections. Four reconstruct Lenin's rebuttals of Martov and the Mensheviks on four issues: blurred membership boundaries, the party's relation to trade unions and mass organisations, "autonomism" versus centralism, and party discipline. The fifth draws four lessons for the present: building a tightly knit organisational system, upholding the authority of the Central Committee and centralised, unified leadership, upholding and improving democratic centralism, and tightening Party discipline and rules.

In the authors' reading, Lenin held that the party must be an organised whole and not a loose political alliance, and that it must be kept distinct from the class. They also report his view that the party leads unions and other mass organisations, which cannot stand outside its guidance. Centralism, he argued, must be written into party rules, because the minority must yield to the majority and the part to the whole. The authors distinguish this from bureaucratic centralism. They say Lenin traced Menshevik hostility to discipline to the psychology of bourgeois intellectuals, whereas the factory trains workers in organisation. For Lenin, discipline rests on Marxism and binds leaders as much as ordinary members.

The authors conclude that Lenin's critique offers a model for the Party's full and rigorous self-governance. They call for optimised grassroots organisations, higher-quality members, strengthened Party political-building, and better mechanisms to implement central decisions. They also propose education in democratic centralism, a more developed system of Party regulations, and stronger enforcement of political discipline. They cite Xi Jinping on persistent problems such as weakened implementation of Party leadership, "deliberation without decision" and disregard of discipline. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party-school style reading links Lenin's 1904 organisational polemic to current Party-building doctrine.
quoteEn: Lenin points out that the party's discipline is founded on Marxism.
quoteZh: 列宁指出，党的纪律以马克思主义为基础

glossary.explanation: The organisational principle of Leninist parties, combining discussion and election with binding discipline of the minority to the majority and lower bodies to higher ones. The CCP describes it as its fundamental organisational principle.

keywords: One Step Forward, Two Steps Back

t: An interpretation of "standing on the right side of history" through historical materialism
zh: “站在历史正确的一边”的唯物史观阐释
paras: Xi Jinping has repeatedly called on China to "stand on the right side of history". This commentary, published in Guangming Daily in June 2025, asks what the phrase means when read through historical materialism. Tang Aijun argues that historical materialism supplies the basic theoretical framework for interpreting it, and that the phrase asks historical agents to choose correctly at a historical crossroads.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the context in which the formulation appears: a world history of growing interdependence, set against sluggish economic recovery, unilateralism, protectionism and what the author calls hegemonic bullying. The second gives the underlying philosophical logic in three points. The third draws out practical requirements for the historical subject.

Tang's core move is to reconcile historical determinism with subjective choice. History advances in a spiral, with setbacks and "countercurrents", so that its actual course has a right and a wrong side. Because, in Marx and Engels's words in The Holy Family, it is real, living people who make history, agents can act correctly or incorrectly. Tang then names three senses of the "right side": grasping and applying historical laws; discerning the great trends of the age, by looking at the past, seeing essences behind appearances, identifying the principal contradiction and finding certainty amid uncertainty; and standing with human progress. For the last, Tang takes productive-force development as the objective measure and the free and all-round development of the individual as the subjective measure. This means serving the interests of the great majority, upholding historical justice and international morality, and promoting shared human values.

Tang concludes that the right side of history demands an active historical spirit, summed up in three tasks: "observe the broad trends", "respond to changes" and "turn crises into opportunities". The author presents these as drawing on the dialectical conversion of danger into opportunity and as calling for a fighting spirit under geopolitical pressure. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists ground a leader's slogan on international affairs in historical-materialist philosophy.
quoteEn: Historical correctness is the unity of conformity to laws and conformity to purpose, of the objective measure and the subjective measure.
quoteZh: 历史正确性是合规律性与合目的性、客观尺度与主体尺度的统一。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory of history, which treats the development of productive forces and social relations as the basis of historical change. Chinese official discourse presents it as the Party's basic method for understanding history.
An official concept promoted by Xi Jinping, listing peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom as values shared across civilisations.

keywords: great changes unseen in a century

t: An analysis of research on the political roots of contemporary European and American populism
zh: 当代欧美民粹主义政治根源研究探析
source: Journal of Shaanxi Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 1
paras: This review article surveys Western political-science scholarship on why populism has risen in Europe and the United States, with a focus on the third wave of populism. The authors argue that Western research, while it has made some progress in tracing populism to tensions inside liberal democracy, is marked by idealism, metaphysical thinking and a failure to identify any fundamental way out of the capitalist democratic predicament. Only socialism, they conclude, can resolve the crisis.

The article first sets out the field. It contrasts the older "normal pathology" view of radical-right populism with Cas Mudde's "pathological normalcy" thesis and his definition of populism as a thin-centred ideology, and notes that economic-insecurity and cultural-backlash explanations have dominated. It then reviews three clusters of work on political roots: the conflict between two faces or pillars of democracy (Margaret Canovan, Yves Mény and Yves Surel, Rudy Andeweg and Tom Louwerse, Peter Mair); deeper paradoxes of democracy (Canovan, Yannis Papadopoulos, Cesare Pinelli); and a representation-crisis reading using principal–agent logic (Herbert Kitschelt, Kenneth Roberts, Paul Taggart, Oliver Schmidtke).

The authors credit this literature with three advances: a shared working definition built around ideology, the pure people, the corrupt elite and popular sovereignty; a first treatment of populism as internal to democracy; and a recognition of the contradictions between democratic principles and institutions, such as empowerment undermining transparency. Their critique is Marxist. They say the scholars treat ideas as the main driver and so invert the relation between material conditions and consciousness; that they split elites and the people into a metaphysical opposition, sharing the elitist tradition they study; and that they trust Western democracy's capacity for self-correction. Citing Levitsky and Ziblatt on polarisation, the authors argue that this trust is misplaced, and they present Lee Drutman's proposed electoral reforms as an example of reform that does not escape Canovan's paradox.

The authors conclude, from historical materialism, that patching the capitalist political and economic system cannot stop populism's challenge or capitalist democracy's decline. In their view, only a socialist revolution that replaces capitalism with socialism addresses the underlying contradictions and overcomes populist tendencies. They also say the 2024 European Parliament elections and Donald Trump's re-election show the relevance of the topic. Read the original if you want a detailed map of Western theories of populism's political origins and a Chinese Marxist critique of them.
quoteEn: Populism, as a radical reaction to the crisis described above, is in fact the product of the interplay of internal and external contradictions in Western democratic politics.
quoteZh: 民粹主义作为对上述危机的一种激进反应，实际上是西方民主政治内外部矛盾运动的产物。

t: Towards a positive philosophy: Marx and the philosophical transformation of modern civilization
zh: 走向实定哲学：马克思与现代文明的哲学转型
paras: Liu Senlin asks how Marx's philosophy responds to a modern world in which, in the words of the Communist Manifesto, all that is solid melts into air and all that is holy is profaned. The article argues that the loss of old certainties demands a new grounding of certainty, which Liu terms 'positivity' (shiding xing, from the German 'positiv'). Building a world that is grounded, open to the future and meaningful is, in Liu's view, the core of Marx's philosophical change and of his reflection on modernity.

The article has four parts. It first traces the shifting meaning of 'positiv' from officially or traditionally 'posited' authority, through Hegel, late Schelling, Feuerbach and the empiricist 'culture of fact', to experience-based verification. It then examines Marx and Engels's call in The German Ideology for a 'genuine positive science'. The third part treats reification as a second modern source of positivity, and the fourth turns to positivity in the spiritual sphere and the problem of nihilism, drawing on Nietzsche, Weber and William McGaughey.

Liu argues that positivity reached Marx from several channels: the humanities (Schelling, the early Romantics), the natural sciences, and above all the social sciences, especially political economy. Only after engaging political economy did Marx stop subordinating empirical reality to reason and begin to rebuild theory on a positive foundation, which for Liu marks the turn to the critique of political economy. Liu reads reification dialectically: as a progressive stage of the 'dependence on things' that raises productivity and fairness over personal dependence, yet as a limit when judged from the stage of free individuality. The article also criticises Max Stirner's 'Unique One' as a petty-bourgeois fantasy.

Liu concludes that Marx sought more than fair distribution of wealth and rights. Capital dissolves every sacred value into the calculable and exchangeable, which paves the way for modern cynicism, the 'last man' and a flattened civilization. Liu holds that material productive forces are the foundation of positivity but not all of it, and that a transcendent, spiritual dimension is also required. Liu also proposes that ontology and the split between theoretical and practical philosophy be rethought, and leaves open how Marx's anti-metaphysics relates to twentieth-century philosophy. Read the original if you are interested in Marx's relation to German classical philosophy, Schelling and Feuerbach, or in philosophical readings of reification and nihilism.
quoteEn: How to understand and construct this certainty, or positivity, and how to build on a positive world a modern world that is grounded (not illusory), has prospects (not fixed) and has meaning (not nihilistic) is the root of the change Marx brought to philosophy and the key to his thinking on modernity.
quoteZh: 如何理解、构建这种确定性或者实定性，如何在实定世界的基础上构建有根基(非虚幻)、有前景(非固化)、有意义(非虚无)的现代世界，是马克思哲学变革的根本之处，也是马克思的现代性思考的关键之处。

t: Marx and Engels's theory of civilization and its contemporary value
zh: 马克思恩格斯的文明理论及其当代价值
paras: Zhang Sanyuan starts from the recent prominence of "civilization" in Chinese scholarship, following the claim that Chinese modernization has created a new form of human civilization. The author argues that a "return to Marx" is the necessary route for addressing it. Marx and Engels wrote no dedicated treatise on civilization, Zhang says, yet historical materialism is itself a scientific theory of civilization, and recovering it gives Chinese modernization its "soul-vein" (hún mài, the deep lineage that sustains it).

The article has four parts. It first sets out five principles for interpreting the theory: orientation to the people, critique, thoroughness, process and wholeness. It then presents the theory's core content, its distinguishing features, and its contemporary value. Zhang also outlines four periods in the theory's formation, from the early 1840s to Engels's later writings, but treats these only briefly.

The central claim is that civilization arises from "the production of the immediate material means of life", not from ideas, so that historical materialism supplies a "practical history" of civilization rather than a "history of ideas". Civilization develops through the basic contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and it is open and processual. Its theme is human emancipation and all-round development, which can be realised only on the basis of highly developed productive forces. Zhang finds the theory marked by unities of ideal and practical, class and human, critical and constructive, systematic and developmental. Capitalist civilization is a unity of civilization and barbarism, and communist civilization, the "association of free individuals", supersedes it dialectically rather than discarding it wholesale.

Zhang concludes that the theory is not outdated. The author argues that the world still lives in Marx's "age of civilization", so his critique of capitalist barbarism remains valid. On that basis Zhang presents Chinese modernization as a creative application of the theory. It is said to surpass Western modernization through a self-reliant, holistic and global view of civilization, with the Second Integration of Marxism and traditional Chinese culture as the key to a modern Chinese civilization. A community with a shared future for mankind is described as a real step towards the communist ideal. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how Chinese Marxist scholarship derives a theory of civilization from classical texts and links it to Chinese modernization.
quoteEn: Marx and Engels's theory of civilization is not a closed theoretical system but an open one, advancing with the times and with practice, continually drawing on humanity's latest achievements of civilization and developing innovatively.
quoteZh: 马克思恩格斯的文明理论不是一个封闭的理论体系，而是一个开放的理论体系，与时代俱进、与实践同行，不断借鉴吸收全人类最新文明成果，实现创新性发展。

glossary.explanation: The official Party concept of China's own path of modernization, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western modernization.
An official phrase, used since Xi Jinping's 2021 speech marking the Party's centenary, for the civilization that Chinese modernization is said to create.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept of international relations based on cooperation and shared interests. It is also used as a guiding idea in Chinese foreign policy.
The Marxist theory that material production and social relations ultimately shape politics, ideas and historical change.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Historical materialism as a transcendence of Feuerbach's philosophy
st: An inquiry into foundational questions for the discipline of the history of Marxism
zh: 历史唯物主义是对费尔巴哈哲学的超越
zhSub: 马克思主义发展史学科基础问题探究
paras: Heng Lin asks how Feuerbach's philosophy related to the emergence of historical materialism in the particular conditions of nineteenth-century Germany. The article argues that Feuerbach's anthropological materialism supplied a direct theoretical premise and a transitional link for Marx and Engels. Historical materialism, in this reading, then criticised and transcended Feuerbach by bringing practice and social-economic relations into materialism.

The article is arranged in five parts. It first sets out the German background: industrialisation and the 1847 crisis, political fragmentation under feudal power, Hegel and the Young Hegelians, and utopian socialism. It then traces Marx's changing relation to Feuerbach, from the Rheinische Zeitung period and the 1843–44 correspondence to the break marked by the Theses on Feuerbach. Two textual comparisons follow: the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 against Feuerbach, and the Theses against the Feuerbach chapter of The German Ideology. A conclusion draws these threads together.

Heng's central claim is that Marx took over Feuerbach's materialist starting point, his view of humans as natural, sensuous beings, and his theory of religious alienation. Marx then recast these through political economy. In the Manuscripts, alienated labour is analysed through wages, profit and rent, so that Feuerbach's critique of religion becomes a critique of capitalist relations. The article says the Theses mark a qualitative leap: Feuerbach's materialism is faulted as merely contemplative, and the human essence is redefined as the ensemble of social relations. The Feuerbach chapter, Heng argues, then develops the full system: social being determines consciousness, and the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production drives social change. Heng presents the Theses as an initial statement and the German Ideology chapter as a mature, systematic theory.

Heng concludes that historical materialism arose from several interacting factors: German classical philosophy, Feuerbach's materialism, Germany's social contradictions, and Marx's and Engels's own theoretical work and practical activity. Feuerbach was indispensable but limited, and those limits pushed Marx and Engels on. The article presents historical materialism as critical, inheriting and innovative, not a wholesale rejection of earlier thought. Heng also cites Xi Jinping on practice and on Marxism as a guide to action. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-by-text account of the Marx–Feuerbach relationship, as presented in Chinese scholarship on the history of Marxism.
quoteEn: Historical materialism achieved a critique and transcendence of Feuerbach's philosophy.
quoteZh: 历史唯物主义实现了对费尔巴哈哲学的批判与超越。

t: The conceptual logic of "the critique of capital"
st: The core of the "doctrine of the concept" in Marx's political economy
zh: “资本批判”的概念逻辑
zhSub: 马克思政治经济学“概念论”的核心要义
source: Contemporary Economic Research (当代经济研究), 2024 no. 7
paras: Liu Daoyi asks how Marx's critique of capitalism is organised as a system of concepts, and what the "logic of Capital" requires of later critiques of capital. The article argues that Capital is built as a body of concepts moving around one core concept that defines the essence of the capitalist economic system. It holds that this "concept-movement" reflects the real "contradiction-movement" of capitalism and so gives later theory a model of "logical normativity".

The article first traces the idea of concept-movement to Hegel's speculative logic and Marx's inversion of it. It then sets out four basic forms of conceptual movement in Capital: critique of old concepts, definition of new ones, remodelling of concepts and conversion between concepts. A second section follows the genesis of this logic across the 1844 Manuscripts, the 1857–58 and 1861–63 manuscripts and Volume I. A third section works through the logic of Capital's three volumes: the production process, the circulation process and the total process of capitalist production.

Liu's central claim is that Marx's research ran through repeated cycles from the concrete to the abstract and back to the concrete. The first cycle fixed "alienated labour" as the core concept. After the later manuscripts, "surplus value" replaced it as the core. Abstract and concrete are relative: commodity is abstract relative to money, money relative to capital, and surplus value relative to profit. Liu reads Volume I as the full definition of surplus value, Volume II as the mediating forms of capital's circulation, and Volume III as its concrete forms (profit, average profit, price of production, commercial profit, interest, rent). The final part, "Revenues and their sources", is likened to the "absolute idea" in Hegel's logic and is read as a critique of vulgar economics and its "trinity formula".

Liu concludes that this conceptual system, centred on surplus value, rejects the "factor theory" and other defences of capitalism, and differs from Hegel's reconciled "absolute spirit". The author argues that it therefore drives practical change through critique of unjust, unequal economic orders and a scientific vision of a good life. Liu presents it as necessary for any critical study of present-day global capitalism and human emancipation. Read the original if you want a detailed, Hegel-informed account of how Capital's categories are derived and related, drawing on the manuscripts as well as the published volumes.
quoteEn: "Concept-movement" thus takes the real "contradiction-movement" as its source of normativity.
quoteZh: “概念—运动”就是这样以现实的“矛盾—运动”为规范性的来源(Source of Normativity)

glossary.explanation: The author's term, drawn from Hegel's logic, for the development of concepts in a system. Liu argues that in Marx this development mirrors the real contradictions of capitalism.

glossary.zh: 从具体到抽象再从抽象上升到具体
glossary.pinyin: cóng jùtǐ dào chōuxiàng zài cóng chōuxiàng shàngshēng dào jùtǐ
glossary.en: from the concrete to the abstract and back to the concrete
glossary.explanation: Marx's method of exposition, set out in the 1857 Introduction. Research moves from concrete material to abstract determinations and then rises again to a concrete totality.
The core concept of Marx's 1844 Manuscripts. In the article it is the first core concept defining the capitalist system, later replaced by surplus value.
The view, associated with Say and Smith, that value comes jointly from labour, capital and land. The article treats it as a defence of capitalism.

t: The "Locke factor" in the construction of Marx's thought
st: The critique of the "theory of innate ideas" as an example
zh: 马克思思想建构中的“洛克因素”
zhSub: 以对“天赋观念论”的批判为例
paras: Nie Jinfang asks how far John Locke shaped the philosophy Marx called the "new materialism" or "modern materialism". The article contends that Marx's thought contains many "Locke factors" that earlier scholarship has treated only in broad, abstract terms. Nie takes one case: Locke's critique of the theory of innate ideas in Book I of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding. The argument is that Marx inherited Locke's line of attack and then surpassed it by grounding it in the history of capitalist society.

Using a textual ("文本学") method, Nie reads the Essay against Marx's doctoral dissertation, the Rheinische Zeitung and Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher writings, the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the 1844 Manuscripts, The Holy Family and The German Ideology, with Engels's Anti-Dühring as a supplement. The article has four sections.
