They cover the "innate principle" as a groundless hypothesis, the absence of universal consent, reason and its link to reality, and the testing of particular ideas (identity, mathematical axioms, substance) against social history. Nie notes that Locke's labour theory of property and his liberal politics are left for separate studies.

Nie's central claim is that Locke's rebuttals are largely abstract and logical, while Marx's are placed in time, place and class. Locke argued that religious ideas vary across peoples and that no principle commands universal consent. Marx, in Nie's reading, reduces religion to the self-consciousness of an alienated world and shifts criticism from heaven to earth. He also shows through the "Jewish question" that there is no consensus on "emancipation", and builds a ladder from political to social to human emancipation. On reason, Nie points to the Paris Manuscripts, where Marx sets wages, profit and rent side by side and so treats them as parts of a social whole governed by capital. On identity, mathematics and substance, Nie argues that Marx and Engels treat identity as grounded in difference and mathematical axioms as drawn from reality. They also contrast speculative "substance" (the "Fruit" of The Holy Family) with a materialist one, tracing the latter through Locke's influence on French materialism.

Nie concludes that Marx replaced the "innate principle" of ideas with a "real principle" and located the origin of ideas in practice. He did so by moving from critique of religion and the state to the political economy of civil society. Nie adds that the Locke case shows Marxism's inseparable link with the Western intellectual tradition, and it also shows how Marx's changes of thought tracked social change. Read the original if you work on the intellectual sources of Marx's materialism, or want a close, text-by-text comparison of Locke and Marx on ideas, religion and reason.
quoteEn: Examining the "Locke factor" in the construction of Marx's thought, and the surpassing it achieved, reflects, through one case in the history of ideas, the inseparable inner connection between Marxism and the Western intellectual tradition.
quoteZh: 辨析马克思思想建构中的“洛克因素”及其所实现的超越，既从一个思想史“个案”的视角反映了马克思主义与西方思想传统之间不可分割的内在关联

glossary.explanation: A name Marx used for his own philosophical position, distinguishing it from earlier idealism and from older, contemplative materialism. Chinese scholarship often pairs it with "modern materialism".
Another label for Marx's philosophy, used here for a materialism that works within the relations of subject and object, spirit and matter, idea and reality.
The view, held by Plato, Descartes and others, that some principles are present in the mind before experience. Locke attacked it in Book I of his Essay.

t: How labour ownership was alienated into capital ownership
st: From Locke and Hegel to Marx
zh: 劳动所有权何以异化为资本所有权？
zhSub: 从洛克、黑格尔到马克思
source: Journal of Jiangsu Ocean University (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 1
paras: Scholars have recently disputed whether Locke's theory of labour ownership justifies capitalist exploitation and whether Marx seriously criticised Locke. Hu Shun sets this dispute aside and traces an internal line of development from Locke through Hegel to Marx. The article argues that Locke established the identity of labour and property, Hegel grounded it metaphysically and noticed its negative effects, and Marx showed labour and ownership coming apart, so that labour ownership turned into capital ownership. Hu concludes that it is better to criticise views that confuse capital ownership with labour ownership than to argue over whether Locke or Hegel defended exploitation.

The article has four sections: the identity of labour and ownership in Locke, the negative effects of that identity in Hegel, the separation of labour and ownership in Marx, and a short conclusion. Hu reconstructs Locke's argument against Filmer, his limits on accumulation and his treatment of money. Hu then follows Hegel's route from will and personality to possession of the body and of things, and his analysis of poverty in civil society. The Marx section runs from the 1842 debate on gathering fallen wood to the 1844 Manuscripts and the 1857–58 manuscripts.

Hu reads Locke's argument as a descending sequence from God to person (body), then labour, then thing. In this reading, Locke's money is a means of exchange and hoarding, not self-expanding capital, so his theory stays monistic, with labour as the only ground of property. Hegel's sequence runs from person, as the unity of will and body, to possession and then to the thing. Hegel sees that the labour-ownership principle produces the paradox of poverty amid excess wealth and the rabble, which his proposed remedies cannot solve. Marx, in Hu's account, moves from treating ownership as a legal relation to treating it as a historical relation of production. He then shows that capitalists exchange surplus value from earlier rounds of production for labour-power, so that ownership means appropriating others' products for the capitalist and, for the worker, treating one's own product as another's property.

Hu concludes that the line from Locke and Hegel to Marx runs "labour, property, poverty, exploitation", and that Marx's work lifts modern political philosophy to the level of the critique of political economy. Neither Locke nor Hegel discussed exploitation, and Marx did not label their theories apologetics. In Hu's view, apologists nonetheless use them to present capital ownership as naturally just labour ownership, and Hu holds that Marx's critique targets private ownership of the means of production, with public ownership as the principle of scientific socialism. Read the original if you study the relation between Marx and early modern political philosophy, or want a close account of how Marx's view of ownership changed between 1842 and 1857.
quoteEn: Rather than arguing over whether the property theories of Locke and Hegel defend capitalist exploitation, it is better to criticise those views that confuse capital ownership with labour ownership.
quoteZh: 与其争论洛克、黑格尔的财产权理论是否为资本主义剥削辩护，不如批判那些将资本所有权混同为劳动所有权的观点。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist term for socialism grounded in the analysis of capitalism's historical development, as opposed to utopian socialism. Hu uses it for the position that a future society must rest on public ownership of the means of production.

t: Keeping firmly to the right direction in research on the War of Resistance against Japan
zh: 牢牢把稳抗战史研究方向
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2025, shortly after Xi Jinping's article in Rossiyskaya Gazeta on the 80th anniversary of victory in the Soviet Great Patriotic War, Xu Zhimin asks how research on the War of Resistance against Japan should be oriented. The commentary argues that scholars must resist two errors: denying the Communist Party's role in the resistance, and ignoring China's contribution to the world anti-fascist war while exaggerating that of the United States and Britain.

The piece is built around four themes drawn from Xi Jinping's statements on the war: the significance of the 18 September 1931 Incident, the Party as the 'mainstay' of the resistance, China as the main Eastern theatre, and defence of the postwar order. It closes with proposals for the discipline.

Xu argues that the 1931 Incident opened the world anti-fascist war, and notes that a growing number of Chinese and foreign scholars date the Second World War from it rather than from 1939. The author describes the Party as the political guarantee of final victory through its united front and its war behind enemy lines. Citing casualty and economic-loss figures, Xu holds that the Chinese theatre pinned down the main Japanese army, thereby supporting the Soviet Union and the Allied strategy. Historical nihilism and revisionism in Germany, Japan and in resistance-war studies are presented as threats to the postwar order.

Xu calls for building the discipline's 'three systems' (disciplinary, academic and discourse), developing an autonomous body of knowledge with original concepts, using big data and artificial intelligence on sources, and spreading a correct view of the war. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official line on wartime historiography is framed for Chinese historians in 2025.
quoteEn: To speed up building the 'three systems' of the discipline and construct an autonomous body of knowledge, we must uphold historical materialism and take Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as our guide.
quoteZh: 加快构建抗战史学科“三大体系”，建构抗战史自主知识体系，必须坚持唯物史观，坚持以习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想为指导

glossary.explanation: A phrase meaning a pillar standing firm in a rushing river. Official Chinese accounts use it to describe the Communist Party's role in the resistance war.
An official Chinese term for interpretations seen as denying or distorting the Party's history and revolutionary achievements.
The disciplinary, academic and discourse systems that Chinese leaders call on scholars to build, so that Chinese social science has its own distinctive framework.

t: The core and distinctive features of the new round of scientific and technological revolution from the perspective of historical materialism
zh: 唯物史观视域下新一轮科技革命的核心与特质
paras: Zhang Jianyun asks what lies at the centre of the current round of scientific and technological revolution and what it means for the mode of production. The article's thesis is that the leading force is a digital-intelligence technology system, formed by the convergence of information technologies. Its core, in Zhang's reading, is artificial intelligence that builds models from massive data and so liberates mental labour. This in turn merges cultural and material production, and Zhang argues that capitalism's logic runs against these new productive forces while socialism complements them.

The article has three sections. The first traces the technological convergence: twentieth-century computers, digitisation, AI, the internet and mobile communications, joined from the 2000s by cloud computing, the Internet of Things and blockchain. The second examines how AI assists the human brain and why this is the revolution's key content. The third turns to changes in the means of production, forms of labour and the organisation of cooperation, and contrasts capitalist and socialist institutions. Zhang draws on Marx's Capital, the 1844 Manuscripts and statements by Xi Jinping, and refers to DeepSeek as a recent case.

Zhang uses Marx's method of ascending from abstract determinations to the 'concrete in thought' and names data as that concrete: the individual technologies are all organised around producing, circulating and using data. Following Marx's account of labour as ideal construction before material transformation, Zhang says machine learning simulates this process of 'conceptual construction'. Just as the machine system freed manual labour in the nineteenth century, AI frees mental labour today. Zhang holds that AI-generated content cannot objectify human emotion or serve as a final product, so it cannot replace human labour. Data, being easily copied, non-exclusive and gaining value when shared, undermines private ownership. Digital cultural production, small-scale and distributed, fits socialist public ownership better than capitalist mass hiring. Blockchain-based internet cooperation, Zhang suggests, makes Marx's 'one social labour force' conceivable.

Zhang concludes that capitalist private ownership and the logic of capital, together with the hegemonic thinking of Western states, obstruct digital-intelligence productive forces, while socialism is suited to them and will reshape human civilisation in a fair and reasonable way. The article presents new quality productive forces and a community with a shared future for mankind as outcomes of this alignment. Read the original if you want a Marxist-theoretical account, from within Chinese Party scholarship, of AI, data as a factor of production and mental labour.
quoteEn: The value of data lies not in possession but in use.
quoteZh: 数据的价值不在于占有，而在于使用。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2023, referring to advanced productive forces driven by technological breakthroughs and innovation, especially in digital and high-tech sectors.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept advanced by Xi Jinping, stressing shared interests and cooperation among states.
A term the author links to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) for the combined system of digital and AI technologies.
Labour carried out chiefly by the brain; the author treats it as the process of 'conceptual construction' inherent in all human labour.

t: Contemporary interpretations of Marx's theory of alienation and their significance
st: David Harvey's "universal alienation" and Hartmut Rosa's "new alienation"
zh: 马克思异化理论的当代阐释及其意义
paras: Since the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 appeared, Marx's theory of alienation has been continuously disputed. Zhou Ke divides recent foreign interpretations into a textual-interpretation school (Allen Wood, Bertell Ollman, Robert Tucker, Allen Buchanan, Andrew Sayers and others) and an "application and development" school (Erich Fromm, Herbert Marcuse, Henri Lefebvre). The article argues that David Harvey's "universal alienation" and Hartmut Rosa's "new alienation" continue the second path and offer useful lessons for understanding contemporary capitalism and exploring alternatives to it.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs Harvey's account, drawn mainly from Seventeen Contradictions and the End of Capitalism and a 2018 essay for Marx's bicentenary. The second sets out Rosa's social-acceleration theory and his notion of resonance, from Social Acceleration (2005) and Resonance (2016). The third assesses what both contribute to the critique of capitalism.

On Zhou's reading, Harvey takes alienation to run through all capitalist contradictions, from production to consumption, debt, politics and ecology. He traces its intensification to deindustrialisation, technology and consumerism, and to the circulation of capital through production, realisation and distribution. He therefore proposes a "revolutionary humanism", opposed to Althusser's expulsion of alienation from Marxism. Rosa locates alienation in the time structure of late modern society. Technological acceleration, acceleration of social change and acceleration of the pace of life are driven by competition, a cultural promise and a self-propelling feedback loop. He identifies five forms of alienation (spatial, of the world of things, of action, of time, and of self and society), and proposes "resonance" as a non-alienated relation between subject and world.

Zhou concludes that both thinkers carry on Marx's scholarly tradition, extend his total critique of capitalism to wider domains, and explore alternatives to capitalism. The author also judges that Harvey's proposals and Rosa's resonance projects remain content with local reforms and normative principles, avoid deeper questions of institutions and the revolutionary subject, and so carry a utopian and reformist character. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's assessment of Harvey and Rosa as heirs of Marx's alienation concept, including its critical verdict.
quoteEn: Both continue Marx's approach of total critique and, from different angles, deepen understanding of the operating logic of contemporary capitalist society.
quoteZh: 他们都延续了马克思的总体批判思路，从不同角度深化了对当代资本主义社会运行逻辑的认识。

t: Marx's critique of Eurocentrism and its implications
zh: 马克思对西方中心论的批判及其启示
paras: Some Western scholars, especially on the left, now describe Marxism as a typical case of Eurocentrism. Yang Shengping cites Andre Gunder Frank's ReOrient (published in Chinese as 'Silver capital'), which charges Marx and Weber with seeking the origins of capitalism in European particularity. Yang argues the opposite: historical materialism and the theory of world history are the most thorough critique of Eurocentrism, though Marx's own break with it developed over time. The article draws lessons for cultural development in China today.

The article has three parts. The first shows that the founding of historical materialism was itself a critique of Eurocentrism, and distinguishes a historical 'centre' from 'centrism'. The second traces how Marx's critique developed in stages, from the 1840s to his death, and tests it on the late writings on Russia and the 'Kafkaesque' passage, the 'Caudine Forks of capitalism' (Marx's own phrase). The third turns to present-day implications for China, chiefly the building of 'cultural subjectivity'.

Yang contends that, because Marx grounds history in material production, he avoids Hegel's spirit-based Eurocentrism, and that a leading country at a given stage is only a temporary centre, not a permanent one. Yang divides Marx's later work into phases and argues that his earlier remarks on India and the Asiatic mode of production still bore the mark of Western sources, while his work from the 1870s, with first-hand material on Russia, rejects both 'European uniqueness' and 'Eastern stagnation'. Yang rejects readings that treat the Western path and the Russian 'leapfrog' path as unrelated, saying this risks an 'anti-Eurocentric Eurocentrism'. In Yang's account the two paths are linked within a world history dominated by capitalism. A leap is possible only given external conditions, such as Western example and support, and productive forces cannot be skipped.

Yang concludes that criticism of Eurocentrism is a means, not an end, and that the aim is theory that can guide China's development. Cultural subjectivity should be judged first by cultural advancement, not nationality, and should absorb the best achievements of all peoples, including developed capitalist countries. Eurocentrism as a view of history and as a political and value stance should be rejected, while Eurocentric modes of thinking and discourse can be selectively transformed and used. Yang adds that national character should be open and combined with advancement in a new organic cultural whole. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Marx's late writings on Russia and non-Western paths, and its link to current debates on cultural subjectivity and an independent knowledge system.
quoteEn: Therefore, the national character of culture is not a narrow nationalism but an open and inclusive one, and it must keep developing and being reconstructed as the times advance.
quoteZh: 因此，文化的民族性不是狭隘的民族性，而是开放包容的民族性，并且这种民族性需要随着时代的发展而不断发展和重构。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese official and academic discourse on cultural construction, referring to a people's capacity to build its own culture actively and independently. It is closely tied to the drive to build an 'independent knowledge system'.
A slogan in recent Chinese academic policy calling for social-science concepts and theories rooted in China's own experience. Yang treats it as the form, not the substance, of cultural subjectivity.
Marx and Engels's account of how the expansion of commerce and industry joins separate peoples into one interacting historical process. Yang contrasts it with Hegel's idealist version.

The view that takes the West as the standard for judging other societies and treats the Western model as the only path of development. Yang distinguishes it as a view of history, as political and value stance, and as a mode of thought and discourse.

t: The discursive resolve of Marx's critique of capitalism
zh: 马克思资本主义批判思想的话语定力研究
paras: What gives Marx's critique of capitalism its lasting power? Jiang Linteng and Qiao Ruijin argue that it lies in an internally unified body of discourse, which they call its "holistic discursive resolve" (zhengtixing huayu dingli). The article sets out to show how Marx articulated his theory, in order to deepen understanding of the essence of Marxism and to advance its development.

The authors analyse this discourse in three dimensions, each organised around a question Marx kept asking: the form of the discourse (what is the root of social alienation?), its content (how can the world be changed?) and its significance (how is human emancipation possible?). Each section follows Marx's path from the Rheinische Zeitung period and the 1844 manuscripts through the German Ideology, the Communist Manifesto, Capital and the 1857–58 manuscripts to his late anthropological and historical studies. A short conclusion draws the three together.

In the authors' reading, Marx moved from philosophical and political critique to the critique of political economy, tracing alienation from alienated labour through the theory of surplus value and commodity fetishism to capital's domination. This opens onto the question of change, where Marx's starting point of "real individuals" and "revolutionary practice" makes people the subjects who transform the world. Finally the authors present human emancipation as the aim of Marx's whole discourse: communist revolution by the proletariat, the sublation of private property, wage labour, the division of labour and classes, and the "three forms" of social development. They stress that communism is an ongoing movement and not a panacea.

The authors conclude that the three questions correspond to "explaining the world", "changing the world" and unifying the two. This lets Marx combine grand and micro narratives, avoiding both relativism and absolutism, and makes his writings a coherent "artistic whole". They add that studying this resolve helps in understanding Marxism's essence, in developing Marxism in the new era and in building a discourse system with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a systematic, Chinese-language reading of Marx's thought as one discursive whole organised around alienation, practice and emancipation.
quoteEn: Marx's critique of capitalism did not invent new phrases to explain the existing world; it started from the surface of social life and its contradictions, probed their roots until it found a fundamental and reasoned explanation, and on that basis sought to genuinely change the existing world.
quoteZh: 马克思资本主义批判思想不是编造新的词句来解释现存世界，而是从社会生活的表象及其矛盾入手深究其根源，直至找到根本性的合理解释，并在此基础上寻求对现存世界的真正改变。

glossary.explanation: The authors' term for the internal coherence and staying power of Marx's theoretical language, which they say rests on its form, content and significance.
Marx's starting point in The German Ideology: living people in definite social relations, as opposed to abstract notions of humanity.
A phrase from Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, denoting the unity of changing circumstances and human self-change; the authors treat it as the only real way of transforming the world.
Marx's goal of emancipating all humanity, distinguished from merely political emancipation; the authors treat it as the core of his whole theory.

t: Marx's thought on proletarian poverty as institutional poverty
zh: 马克思关于作为制度性贫困的无产阶级贫困思想
paras: The article asks where Marx located the cause of proletarian poverty. Mou and Wang define institutional poverty as poverty produced by the injustice of a society's or state's institutions. They contrast Marx with Hegel, who held that a rabble arises 'naturally' from individual differences. In their reading, Marx held that proletarian poverty is overwhelmingly caused by the institutional injustice of capitalist society, not by individual differences among workers. Marx did not rule out individual poverty, but it was not his focus.

The authors build the argument around three roots of this poverty: alienated labour as the social root, class rule as the political root, and surplus value as the economic root. They draw mainly on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, The Class Struggles in France 1848 to 1850, Capital and the Communist Manifesto. They also clarify concepts, such as alienation, externalisation and reification, and the Marxian categories of labour, labour-power and capital.

On alienated labour, the authors set out four features. It strips labour itself of its essence, it strips the worker of theirs, it does the same to the idle appropriator, and it distorts all human relations. They treat private property, wages, capital, profit and rent as consequences of alienated labour. On class rule, they analyse the properties of ruling power and use Marx's account of French classes to show an asymmetrical structure in which the proletariat sits at the bottom. On surplus value, they follow Marx from the commodity to the free wage-worker, who is formally equal but sells labour-power. Surplus value is then accumulated and divided among industrial, commercial and loan capitalists and landowners as profit, interest and rent.

The authors conclude that, because all three roots rest on the capitalist system, that system is the ultimate source of proletarian poverty. They hold that the proletariat must therefore abolish bourgeois ownership, rise to become the ruling class and win democracy. It must then take over capital step by step and centralise the instruments of production in the hands of the state, while increasing productive forces. They present this as the theoretical basis of Marx's idea of the fundamental emancipation of the proletariat and of all humanity. Read the original if you want a systematic account of Marx's early and mature critique of capitalism read through the concept of institutional poverty.
quoteEn: Proletarian poverty is caused by the institutional injustice of capitalist society, not by individual differences among proletarians.
quoteZh: 无产阶级贫困是由资本主义社会的制度性不公而非无产阶级的个体性差异所造成的

t: Lenin's exploration of the role of politics in the social development of backward countries
zh: 列宁关于发挥政治在落后国家社会发展进程中的作用的探索
paras: The article asks how Lenin, after the October Revolution, tried to use politics to drive economic and social development in a country with a backward economy and culture. Wang and Wang argue that this was a consistent thread in his thinking, which they call the "political-axis model". Under this model politics is the pivot that pulls the other elements of society along with it. They say the model passed through two stages, and that its lessons bear on China's present modernization.

After a literature review, the authors say existing Chinese scholarship concentrates on political structures, the Party and the state. In their view it neglects how political functions act on the economy, culture and society during socialist construction. They then set out the general laws of social development and trace Lenin's practice in two periods: 1917–1920, when political power was used to remake the economic base directly, and 1921–1924, when he turned to political reform and cultural work. The article closes with lessons for contemporary China.

The central argument starts from the Marxist claim that productive forces and the economic base decide in the long run, while the superstructure, and politics above all, can play a decisive role under particular historical conditions. Wang and Wang set Lenin against Plekhanov and Kautsky, whom they accuse of "vulgar determinism". During war communism, they say, Lenin used state power to remould ownership, distribution and resource allocation through nationalization, requisitioning and the abolition of money. This brought some successes but also peasant unrest and economic decline, and Lenin admitted the error. The authors then say the New Economic Policy shifted the focus to the superstructure: clearer division of powers between Party and soviets, stronger oversight, less bureaucracy, and investment in education and rural culture. They stress that the aim of this reform remained the liberation and development of productive forces.

The authors draw two lessons. Using politics as the axis must conform to economic laws, which for China means respecting the market's decisive role in allocating resources alongside government regulation and the development of new quality productive forces. It must also keep improving the superstructure, through Chinese modernization, the modernization of the system and capacity for governance, and whole-process people's democracy. They add that China's conditions differ greatly from those of Soviet Russia and call for combining Marxism with China's circumstances. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of Lenin's war communism and NEP as an account of the part politics plays in modernizing backward countries, and of how that reading is tied to current Party discourse.
quoteEn: Giving full play to the key role of politics became a logical thread running through Lenin's theoretical thinking and practical exploration of socialist construction after the October Revolution.
quoteZh: 充分发挥政治的关键作用也成为贯穿列宁在十月革命后关于如何进行社会主义建设的理论思考和实践探索的一条逻辑主线。

glossary.explanation: The authors' own label for Lenin's post-1917 approach, in which politics is the pivot that moves the other elements of society and aligns the superstructure with the economic base.
The Soviet policy of 1918–1921 of grain requisitioning, nationalization of industry and state distribution, introduced during the Civil War.
The policy adopted in 1921 that replaced requisitioning with a tax in kind and allowed limited markets and private enterprise under state control.
The official term for China's path of modernization, which Party discourse presents as having distinctive features such as huge population size and common prosperity.
A concept promoted by Xi Jinping from 2023, referring to productive forces driven by innovation and advanced technology.
The official description of China's democratic system, said to involve popular participation at every stage of decision-making.

t: Marx's Manchester Notebooks and his study of socialist doctrine
zh: 马克思《曼彻斯特笔记》对社会主义学说的研究
paras: Kong Weiyu takes up Marx's Manchester Notebooks, which the author presents as his first systematic study of socialist doctrine. The article asks what Marx took from English socialist writers and how that work bears on the formation of historical materialism and scientific socialism. Kong's thesis is that two logics were at work: a utopian logic in the English socialists and a realist logic in Marx, who in criticising the former also sublated the residue of his own humanist logic. The article is prompted by the 2015 publication of the notebooks' second half in MEGA2, which revived international scholarship (Matthias Bohlender, Lucia Pradella, David Leopold).

The article has four parts. It begins with Marx's picture of the proletariat's misery in Manchester, drawn from excerpts of Eden, Wade, Thompson, Bray and Parkinson. It then examines socialism's practical conditions, its means of realisation and its envisaged future, mainly through William Thompson and John Francis Bray. A third part treats Robert Owen on the relation between people and environment. The last part sets out the two logics and reads Bray's "two voices" through Bohlender's analysis.

In Kong's reading, the excerpts on child labour, slavery and unequal exchange convinced Marx that the worker has become a literal "thing" rather than a philosophical "alienated" being. They also convinced him that hope cannot rest on the rich, so liberation must come from the proletariat itself. Kong traces to Bray the roots of later ideas: the producing class as the revolutionary subject, the worldwide character of the proletariat, machine production as the basis of social change, and the base–superstructure metaphor. Kong also sees in Bray's joint-stock scheme a possible spur to Marx's later attention to joint-stock companies. Marx rejects Bray's gradualism, his reliance on reason and his rejection of revolution, as well as Thompson's "ought" and Owen's external determinism. Kong notes that Marx's "Umstände" and "Umwelt" differ from Owen's environment, because Marx makes people and circumstances shape each other through practice.

Kong concludes that Marx's "changing the world" was no mere slogan but a programme grounded in social laws, marking the birth of a new worldview. The utopians "interpret" a better future, whereas Marx studies the real movement that abolishes the existing state of things. The notebooks, Kong argues, show Marx learning from the utopians in order to break with them. Read the original if you study the genesis of historical materialism and want a close, text-based account of Marx's reading of Bray, Thompson and Owen in the Manchester Notebooks.
quoteEn: Marx's focus is on how to overthrow the existing bourgeois system. Owen is \"interpreting the (future) world\" while Marx is \"changing the world\"; this is the greatest theoretical heterogeneity between them and an important anchor of Marx's realist logic.
quoteZh: 马克思的关注重点则是如何推翻现有的资产阶级制度。欧文是在“解释（未来）世界”，而马克思是在“改变世界”，这是两者最大的理论异质性，也是马克思现实逻辑的重要落脚点。

t: The spread of Marxism and Marxism-Leninism in China before the founding of the Communist Party
zh: 中国共产党成立之前马克思主义与马克思列宁主义在中国的传播
paras: Lin Jianhua traces how Marxism, and later Marxism-Leninism, reached China before the Communist Party was founded in 1921. Written to mark the centenary of Lenin's death and of the term "Marxism-Leninism" (first used by the Comintern in 1924), the article argues that before the October Revolution Marxism was only sporadically introduced in China. After 1917, it contends, a Russian-mediated Marxism-Leninism was spread widely and deliberately, and this prepared the ground for the Party.

The article has three parts. The first surveys the period from the 1870s to the 1910s, when Marxism arrived by two routes: European diplomats, students and missionaries, and Japan, through reformists, revolutionaries (Sun Yat-sen's circle, Zhu Zhixin, Song Jiaoren) and anarchists. The second covers the post-1917 route through Soviet Russia, centred on Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Chen Wangdao's 1920 translation of the Communist Manifesto, Mao Zedong's conversion, and the communist groups formed in 1920–21. The third examines why Marxism-Leninism took root and what was emphasised.

Lin's central claim is a "two-way meeting" between Marxism-Leninism and China. In Lin's account, Marxism's mission of human liberation matched modern China's tasks of national independence and liberation. Pre-revolutionary Russia's conditions resembled China's, Soviet Russia pursued an equal policy toward China, and imperialist aggression ended illusions about the West. Lin argues that early Chinese Marxists, driven by the aim of national salvation, selectively stressed historical materialism and class struggle, drawing on the October Revolution's lessons. Lin discusses Lenin's continuation and development of Marx and Engels, and notes that early Party documents wrote in proletarian dictatorship, class struggle and violent revolution.

Lin concludes that Marxism is not a dogma but requires concrete analysis of concrete conditions, so Marxism-Leninism in China had to adapt to local conditions while innovating. Lin links this to Mao Zedong Thought, the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and holds that upholding the last means upholding Marxism-Leninism. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-historiography account of early translations, journals and figures, with many Chinese transliterations of Marx's name.
quoteEn: The recognition, acceptance and application of Marxism and Marxism-Leninism by the Chinese people was a historical process of continuous expansion and deepening.
quoteZh: 马克思主义、马克思列宁主义被中国人民所认知、接受、运用,是一个不断拓展和深化的历史过程。

glossary.explanation: The term was first used by the Comintern's Fifth Congress in 1924, after Lenin's death, for Marxism as developed by Lenin. In China it became the Party's foundational doctrine, and the article traces its adoption in Party documents from 1925.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017. It is presented officially as the latest stage of adapting Marxism to China.
The official name for the path and system developed since reform and opening up began in 1978. The Party presents it as Marxism applied to Chinese conditions.

glossary.literal: rushing toward each other from both directions
glossary.explanation: A recent colloquial phrase the author uses for the mutual attraction between Marxism-Leninism and China, which the author presents as historically necessary.
The ruling party of the People's Republic of China, founded in 1921. The article treats its birth as the result of the spread of Marxism-Leninism.

t: The evolution of modern Western idealist views of history and the methodological revolution of historical materialism
zh: 近代西方唯心史观的演进逻辑与历史唯物主义方法论变革
source: Studies on Marxism (马克思主义研究), 2024 no. 12
paras: Li Chengwang asks how Marx and Engels moved beyond the tradition of modern Western idealism to answer what the article calls the history–freedom riddle: how human history can realise the free and all-round development of each person. The article argues that this became possible only when they exposed the real, material source of the premises of idealist thinking, and so founded a new method for understanding history in productive labour.

The article is built in three parts. The first traces the path of Western idealist views of history from Greek philosophy and Christianity through Vico, Voltaire, Rousseau and Kant to Hegel, and sets out the contradictions in Hegel's philosophy of history. The second examines how the Young Hegelians, namely Bauer, Feuerbach and Stirner, tried to answer the riddle through a philosophy of self-consciousness. The third presents the methodological revolution of historical materialism, as developed mainly in The German Ideology. Li says earlier scholarship has paid less attention to the intellectual genealogy that explains why German idealism dissolved and why the Young Hegelians fell back into idealism.

Li contends that Hegel treats history as the development of spirit, so that finite human beings become a stage in an infinite spirit's movement. In this reading, universality and necessity dominate particularity and individual freedom. The Young Hegelians, in Li's account, replace Hegel's absolute spirit with self-consciousness (Bauer), sensuous human essence and love (Feuerbach) or the egoistic 'unique one' (Stirner). They stay on speculative ground and oppose phrases with phrases. Marx and Engels respond in four steps. They start from the 'pure empirical' premise of the production of material life. They develop a theory of comprehensive production, comprising means of subsistence, new needs, human reproduction, social relations and mental production. They hold that individual freedom depends on social relations and can be fully realised only in a real community that abolishes capitalist private ownership. They identify the proletariat as the historical subject of that transformation.

Li concludes that Marx and Engels replaced the substance-thinking and conceptual dialectic of idealism with a dialectic of concrete production, so that history appears as the history of material production. This, the article says, brought the materialist principle fully into the study of historical laws and made the philosophy 'realistic'. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how the Chinese journal Studies on Marxism frames the move from Hegel and the Young Hegelians to historical materialism.
quoteEn: Human history is fundamentally the history of material production.
quoteZh: 人类历史从根本上是物质生产史

t: Re-examining the relationship between "alienated labour" and "private property" in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
zh: 《1844年经济学哲学手稿》中“异化劳动”与“私有财产”关系的再审视
source: Studies on Marxism (马克思主义研究), 2024 no. 12
paras: Wang Yue takes up a long-running dispute over the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844: whether Marx argues in a circle when he relates alienated labour to private property, running from private property to alienated labour and back to private property. The article argues that the charge of "circular reasoning" rests on a prior claim that Marx's thought broke decisively after the Manuscripts, and that this claim does not hold. Read in the light of the continuity of Marx's development, Wang contends, the relation between the two concepts can be answered scientifically and the Manuscripts' significance reassessed.

The article first sets out the debate. Those who see circularity attribute it to Marx's thin knowledge of political economy, to defects in alienation theory, or to a humanist presupposition about the human species-essence. Those who deny it work mostly within the text and rarely address the underlying assumption of a rupture, so the two sides talk past each other. Wang then examines three propositions behind the rupture thesis: the Manuscripts' method, their concept of the human being, and the nature of alienated labour. A final section places the Manuscripts between Marx's earlier work (the Rheinische Zeitung period, the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question) and his later work.

Wang's central argument is that the Manuscripts apply, in an early form, the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete that Marx later formulated in the 1857–58 manuscripts. In this reading, "alienated labour → private property" describes the internal structure of modern capitalist society at the level of essence, whereas private property appears as the cause only at the level of appearance. The order of economic categories within capitalism is therefore not their historical order. Wang adds that Marx's "human being" is a real, sensuous, social being, different from Hegel's and Feuerbach's, and that alienated labour is a description of existing economic facts, not a moral postulate. The logical chain is thus resolved by distinguishing private property as the real starting point from the human being engaged in alienated labour as the theoretical starting point.

Wang concludes that the Manuscripts supply the premise of historical materialism, a first attempt at the laws of capitalist society that leads toward Marxist political economy, and the first systematic statement of Marx's views on communism, containing seeds of scientific socialism. Wang traces this line through the Comments on James Mill, The Holy Family, the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology. Read the original if you work on the young Marx, on the "rupture" versus continuity debate, or on Chinese scholarship on the Manuscripts, and want a detailed textual argument against the circular-reasoning charge.
quoteEn: In sum, the argument of the Manuscripts is not a purely philosophical one, but an "attempt" by Marx at the political-economic method of "ascending from the abstract to the concrete".
quoteZh: 综上所述，《手稿》中的论证不是纯粹的哲学论证，而是马克思对“从抽象上升到具体”的政治经济学研究方法的一次“尝试”。
keywords: ascent from the abstract to the concrete

t: Two critiques of Proudhon and the formation of Marx's labour theory of value
zh: 对蒲鲁东的两次批判与马克思劳动价值论的形成
source: Marxism and Reality (马克思主义与现实), 2024 no. 6
paras: Studies of how Marx's scientific theory of value took shape have concentrated on classical political economy. Chen Zheng argues that a Proudhon factor has been neglected. The article holds that Marx's two critiques of Proudhon's view of money, in The Poverty of Philosophy (1847) and in the 'Reflection' of 1851, played distinct and important roles in building Marx's labour theory of value.

The article covers the late 1840s and early 1850s. It begins with Proudhon's 'constituted value' and his labour-money scheme, and with his People's Bank of 1849. It then examines the first critique in The Poverty of Philosophy and the second in the 'Reflection', written in March 1851 and included in the London Notebooks of Marx's third period of economic study. A short conclusion draws out four points.

Chen argues that the first critique pushed Marx to adopt Ricardo's position openly. Proudhon's attempt to equate labour time with the 'value of labour' exposed Smith's confusion of two measures of value. Marx therefore came to see Ricardo's theory as a scientific account of bourgeois society and as the critical starting point for his own theory. Chen adds that Marx still took over Ricardo's quantity theory of money to refute Proudhon, so this critique remained flawed. In the second critique, drawing on the Currency School–Banking School dispute, Marx broke with that quantity theory. He located the root of crises in the whole system of production resting on capital, not in the monetary system. Proudhon and the bourgeois economists, in Marx's words, wanted to keep money without its properties. Chen reads this as a shift of perspective from exchange and circulation to relations of production.

Chen concludes that Marx's struggle with Proudhon's view of money laid the methodological basis for his theory of value. It later underpinned his analysis of capitalist production and exploitation, and served as a bridge to his mature historical materialism and political economy. Chen also calls for the theory to confront the challenges that artificial intelligence poses to the labour theory of value, on the basis of historical materialism. Read the original if you study the intellectual history of Marx's economics, his relation to Ricardo and the London Notebooks, or the Proudhon–Marx dispute over money.
quoteEn: The renewed critique of Proudhon's view of money in the 'Reflection' was a key step, and a necessary theoretical prelude, to Marx's eventual construction of his own scientific theory of value in A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, Part One.
quoteZh: 《反思》中针对蒲鲁东货币观的再批判，是马克思最终在《政治经济学批判。第一分册》中建构起自身科学价值理论的关键一步和必要的理论前奏

t: Lenin's critique of erroneous currents of thought in the period of the New Economic Policy
zh: 新经济政策时期列宁对错误思潮的批判
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2024 no. 6
paras: After the New Economic Policy (NEP) was launched in spring 1921, Russian intellectual life became increasingly lively and a range of mistaken currents of thought, the article argues, disturbed public opinion and undermined the ideological basis on which the Party led the people. Wang Jianing examines how Lenin criticised the main currents and what ideas he developed in doing so. The author holds that revisiting this critique still has practical significance today.

The article is organised around four targets of Lenin's criticism. These are: petty-bourgeois reformism and petty-bourgeois revolutionism over the NEP; the mechanical economic determinism of Sukhanov and others on Russia's road of development; the anarcho-syndicalism of the Trotskyists, the Workers' Opposition and the Democratic Centralists in the trade-union debate; and the Proletkult's narrow and impatient view of culture. Wang draws on Lenin's texts such as 'On the Tax in Kind', 'Our Revolution' and 'Better Fewer, But Better', and on the positions of Plekhanov, Kautsky, Bogdanov and Pletnev.

Wang reports that Lenin read the NEP debate as a question of where Russia was heading. He answered the Change-of-Landmarks group, who expected degeneration into capitalism, by insisting that capitalism be developed under a socialist orientation, and he answered the 'revolutionary phrase-mongers' by arguing that capitalism, compared with small-scale production, was a step forward. For Lenin, in Wang's account, the Party had to learn to use and master capital, directing it into state capitalism. Against Sukhanov's economic determinism, Lenin held that the general laws of history presuppose particular forms of development, so Russia could first seize power and then create the conditions for socialism. Against anarcho-syndicalism, he insisted on the Party's centralised, unified leadership and on trade unions as schools and transmission belts rather than state organs. Against the Proletkult, he stressed Party leadership of culture, reliance on the broad masses and specialists, and raising the people's cultural level, starting with literacy and the status of teachers.

Wang concludes that Lenin's critiques defended the socialist direction of the NEP, the political legitimacy of the October Revolution, the Party's leadership and a realistic approach to cultural construction. Wang presents them as ideas of lasting relevance for socialist construction. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of Lenin's late polemics, from the NEP to the trade-union and Proletkult debates, as presented in the Chinese Marxist literature.
quoteEn: Lenin pointed out that the most urgent task was to raise the people's cultural level, a key link in whether the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) could govern smoothly and successfully.
quoteZh: 列宁指出，最迫切的任务是提升人民文化水平，这是事关俄共（布）能否顺利执政和成功执政的关键环节。

t: Chinese modernization theory and practice continually enrich and develop Marxist principles
st: An interview with Cheng Enfu, Academic Member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences
zh: 中国式现代化理论和实践不断丰富发展马克思主义原理
zhSub: 访中国社会科学院学部委员程恩富教授
paras: This is an interview with Cheng Enfu, Academic Member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, conducted by the journal Studies on Marxism. It asks how the theory and practice of Chinese modernization enrich and develop basic Marxist principles. Cheng answers that they do so in six areas: the people as the subject of history, the two civilizations, the driving forces of social development, ecological civilization, the community, and the leadership of the proletarian party.

The interview moves through six headed sections, each pairing a classical Marxist principle with the Chinese Communist Party's historical practice. Cheng draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, then follows Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and the leaders who followed them. He gives most space to Xi Jinping's formulations since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024).

Cheng presents each area as continuity plus innovation. He contrasts the Marxist "people as subject" with Rousseau's bourgeois popular sovereignty, which in his reading ignores the economic sphere. He argues that Chinese practice coordinates material and spiritual civilization where capitalist modernization produced a split. He reads comprehensive reform as the Party's handling of the contradiction between relations of production and productive forces. Marx's idea of a "true community", set against the illusory communities of class society, is for Cheng carried forward by a community with a shared future for mankind, together with the global initiatives on development, security, civilization and AI governance. Cheng also says the "three unwaverings" must not be split into preserving fundamentals and innovating, and that Party leadership decides the direction and fate of modernization.

Cheng concludes that Chinese modernization, led by the Party, has added new content to Marxist theories of the people, civilization, social dynamics, ecology, the community and party leadership, and offers humanity "a new choice" of modernization. He treats Xi Jinping's statements as the latest stage of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed official-scholarly account of how Chinese modernization is theorised as a development of Marxist principles, with extensive citation of Party leaders.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization in practice prominently displays a grand narrative of the worldview and methodology of "problem orientation", "systems thinking", "upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground" and even "having the world in view".
quoteZh: 中国式现代化实践突出展示出对“问题导向”“系统观念”“守正创新”以至“胸怀天下”的世界观和方法论的宏大叙事

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of modernization, stressed in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). The Party presents it as distinct from Western models.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations, presented as a vision of global cooperation and common interests.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Lenin's exploration of preventing and curbing bureaucratism and formalism
zh: 列宁对防治官僚主义形式主义的探索
paras: Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party has treated improving its work style as an entry point for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and Xi Jinping has repeatedly said that formalism and bureaucratism "kill". Lü Weizhou and Liao Bin ask what Lenin's theory and practice against these two ills can offer the Party today. They argue that Lenin, leading the first socialist state, identified their forms, harms and roots and devised practical remedies that remain instructive.

The article is organised in three parts followed by a short conclusion. The first part covers Lenin's exposure of bureaucratism and formalism in Soviet state and Party organs and the harms he ascribed to them. The second analyses their political, economic and cultural roots. The third sets out the measures Lenin proposed and carried out, drawing on his speeches, telegrams, decrees and organisational initiatives.

The authors report Lenin as listing three forms of formalism: endless meetings, a paper-bound "document culture" and dilatory procedure. They present him as tracing the roots to the Tsarist legacy, to a small-producer economy (backed by figures on Soviet output in 1920 and on collectivisation) and to mass illiteracy that left administration without effective supervision. They also cite the later Soviet record, from privilege under Stalin to life tenure under Brezhnev, as showing that neglecting the problem helped bring down the Party and state. Lenin's remedies fall into four groups: socialist democracy (contact with the masses, elections and recall, pay no higher than a skilled worker's, supervisory bodies); socialist legality (prosecuting negligent officials); slimmer state organs, individual responsibility and shorter meetings; and a purer Party membership, including strict admission, the 1921 purge of some 170,000 members, cadre training and assessment, and rewards.

The authors conclude that the Chinese Communist Party has drawn on Lenin's approach and developed it in the new era. They stress that the two ills are stubborn and recurrent, so the struggle must be sustained, long-term and meticulous. They call for further study of the conditions that breed them, and of new and hidden forms, in order to provide an institutional guarantee for the Party's leadership of deeper reform and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of Lenin's anti-bureaucracy measures as presented in current Party-theory writing on work style.
quoteEn: In Lenin's view, an oversized apparatus easily leads staff to shift blame and evade responsibility, so he treated streamlining organs as a fundamental measure for overcoming bureaucratism and formalism.
quoteZh: 列宁认为，机构庞大容易造成工作人员互相推诿、不负责任,因而将精简机构作为克服官僚主义和形式主义的根本举措。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Xi Jinping era covering discipline, anti-corruption and work-style campaigns within the Chinese Communist Party.
The official name for China's path of modernization, promoted since 2021 as distinct from Western models.
In Party usage, a work style of officials who stand above and apart from the masses, seek status and privilege, and neglect real problems.
In Party usage, pursuing outward form, such as meetings, paperwork and show, while neglecting substance. It is usually named together with bureaucratism as one of the "four undesirable work styles".

t: The spread and transformation of the concept of "nihilism"
zh: “虚无主义”概念的传播与衍变
paras: This short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (27 February 2025) asks how the term "nihilism" (xuwu zhuyi) entered Chinese and why its meaning has remained so unclear. Zhang notes that "nihilist party", "nihilism", "Narodnik", "anarchist party" and "anarchism" were often used interchangeably, so that the sense of each shifted with the speaker's stance. The article's thesis is that in early twentieth-century Chinese usage "nihilism" meant Western Nihilism, anarchism and Daoist "emptiness and non-action" all at once.

The piece follows the term in three stages. It begins with the ancient Chinese word xuwu, found in Daoist texts such as the Laozi commentaries, the Zhuangzi and the Guanzi. It then traces the Western Nihilist/Nihilism from its Russian origins through late Qing transliterations and the Japanese translation "nihilist party". Finally it looks at dictionaries and at attempts by Liao Zhongkai and Zhou Zuoren to clarify the concept.

Zhang's central reasoning is that the term arrived through two channels that blurred it. Drawing on Jiang Lu, the article says Nihilism was used in Russia from 1829 as a term of abuse, then attached to the democrats and assassins of the Narodnik movement. Late Qing writers mostly transliterated it. The translation "nihilist party" came via Japan, where Kayama Sentaro's book on modern anarchism was repeatedly introduced to China under "nihilist party" titles. This led, in Zhang's account, to nihilism, populism and anarchism sharing one label. The article shows the confusion in the dictionaries of Yan Huiqing (1908) and Hemeling (1916), which separated a philosophical sense from a political one.

Zhang reports that Liao Zhongkai (1906) listed socialism, anarchism and nihilism as three separate doctrines but later translated a book on anarchism under a "nihilist party" title. Zhou Zuoren (1907) argued that assassination was a political tactic and that nihilism was a philosophical doctrine rooted in materialism. Zhang judges that these efforts had little effect, because intellectuals of the period used many new terms without studying them systematically. Read the original if you want a compact, source-based account of the term's early Chinese history, from Daoist usage to the translations of the late Qing and early Republic.
quoteEn: In sum, in the Chinese context of the early twentieth century, "nihilism" meant Nihilism, meant Anarchist (anarchism), and was also closely tied to the Daoist "emptiness and non-action", presenting a complex picture of unclear meaning.
quoteZh: 总而言之，在20世纪初的中文语境中，“虚无主义”既指Nihilism，又指Anarchist（无政府主义），还与道家的“虚无、无为”密切相关，呈现出语义不明的复杂图景。

glossary.explanation: A classical Chinese term, common in Daoist texts, for the formless, empty ground of the Dao. It was later used to translate Western "nihilism".
A Japanese-derived translation of Nihilist, applied in China to Russian revolutionaries, especially the assassins of the Narodnaya Volya. It was often equated with anarchists.
The doctrine opposing the state, influential among Chinese radicals in the early twentieth century. The article shows it was often conflated with "nihilism".

t: Why Marx was not an egalitarian
zh: 马克思为什么不是平等主义者
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), via China Social Sciences Net; posted on marxism.cass.cn 2025-01-15
paras: Was Marx an egalitarian of some kind, or a political philosopher of equality? Bao Dawei argues that he was not. Read as egalitarian political philosophy, Marx's texts cannot account for his position, and the author holds that only the "grand historical view" of historical materialism can separate Marx's thought from the various egalitarianisms. This is a short newspaper-style essay in the history of Marxism.

The essay first explains why Marxism so often looks like egalitarianism. Equality is an everyday experience and a basic norm of modern political ethics. Marxism also draws on egalitarian sources, namely French and English utopian socialism and left Hegelianism. Early workers' movements, including Weitling's, pursued egalitarian aims, and Western Marxist readings have sometimes fused Marxism with egalitarianism. It then sets out three reasons why inequality is, for Marx, only a phenomenon, and ends with how equality can actually be achieved.

Bao's three reasons are as follows. By the measure of historical progress, inequality does not mark backward productive relations, and Marx and Engels criticised Proudhon's teleological moralising about equality. By the logic of capitalist relations of production, equality is the bourgeoisie's own ideology, under which "equal exploitation of labour-power" is capital's first human right, and Enlightenment thinkers also attacked inequality. By theoretical radicalism, moral judgement stays at the level of appearances, whereas Marx sought to grasp "the root of the matter". In Bao's reading, Marx's early critique in On the Jewish Question and the Communist Manifesto shows that legal equality makes people isolated monads and legitimises new class exploitation. Real equality depends on a revolutionary reconstruction of the superstructure and on the abolition of classes, which lies beyond egalitarian political philosophy.

Bao concludes that Marxist theoretical radicalism must stay "on the road", because egalitarianism cannot escape what Rancière calls the "embarrassment" of modern politics: what the shifting mix of equality and inequality actually consists of. The author notes that scholars disagree, citing Kai Nielsen, who stresses Marx's concern with equality, and Allen Wood, who denies that Marx treated social equality as good in itself. Bao sides with separating Marx from egalitarianism. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language statement of the case against reading Marx as an egalitarian, and a map of the scholars it engages, including Cohen, Wood, Nielsen and Rancière.
quoteEn: But Marxism is, after all, not a form of egalitarianism, and Marx was not an egalitarian of any kind.
quoteZh: 但是，马克思主义毕竟不是一种平等主义，马克思也不是某种平等主义者。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese scholarship and official discourse for assessing events over long historical spans and in their overall laws of development. Here the author uses it to name the method of historical materialism.

t: In what respects the idea of self-reform inherits and develops Mao Zedong's thought on Party building
zh: 自我革命思想在哪些方面继承和发展了毛泽东党的建设思想
source: Research on Ideological and Political Work (《思想政治工作研究》), 2024
paras: Li Jie asks how the idea of the Party's self-reform, formed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), relates to Mao Zedong's thought on Party building. The author argues that self-reform is an original contribution of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In Li's account, it moves the Party's long search for a way out of the historical cycle of rise and decline from a "first answer" to a "second answer", and it inherits and develops Mao's thought in four respects.

The article is a short theoretical essay in four parts, each pairing a Maoist principle with its post-2012 development. The four topics are the view of the people, the view of discipline, building the Party ideologically, and the "Two Musts". Each part quotes Mao's texts and Xi Jinping's statements, and each names the relationship that the new thought is said to handle better under present conditions.

On the people, Li treats serving the people wholeheartedly and the mass line as Mao's red thread, which Xi extends by putting "putting the people first" at the head of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. On discipline, Li links Mao's 1938 restatement of Party discipline to the present stress on intra-Party regulations, on placing discipline ahead of law, and on the "four forms" of supervision, which is said to improve the handling of Party discipline and state law. On ideology, Mao's rectification campaigns and the Yan'an model of education lead to the concentrated study campaigns of recent years, with Party political building leading all other areas. On the "Two Musts", Li presents Mao's Yan'an "first answer", that the people must supervise the government, as completed by the "second answer" of self-reform. Li cites the anti-corruption campaign as evidence, and sets it against those who praise Western multiparty rotation and the separation of powers.

Li concludes that the Party must not lose itself amid praise, and must keep to the spirit of self-reform. Quoting Xi, Li calls for a "great self-reform" to lead a "great social revolution", and the reverse, so that the Party remains the core of leadership. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how current Party-building doctrine is tied to Mao's thought, and of how Party media frame the claim of a "second answer".
quoteEn: The Party's greatest political strength is its close ties with the masses, and the greatest danger after taking power is becoming divorced from them.
quoteZh: 党的最大政治优势是密切联系群众，党执政后的最大危险是脱离群众。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The Party's slogan, in use since the 18th Party Congress (2012), for stricter discipline, anti-corruption work and internal regulation. It is often rendered "strictly governing the Party in an all-round way".
Official term for the Party's capacity to purge and improve itself without outside pressure. It was developed under Xi Jinping and is presented as the Party's "second answer" to the historical cycle.
Mao-era principle that the Party must draw its policies from the masses and return them to the masses. It is treated as the Party's fundamental work method.
Mao's 1949 call for Party members to stay modest and prudent and to keep up the habit of hard struggle, before the Party took national power.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name of Xi Jinping's body of ideas, written into the Party constitution in 2017.

t: The history of reform and opening up: the key logic of education in common ideals and convictions
zh: 改革开放史：共同理想信念教育的关键逻辑理路
paras: This short piece asks why education in the common ideals and convictions of socialism with Chinese characteristics should be embedded in the history of reform and opening up. Wan Jun argues that doing so rests on a philosophical rationale and follows the first methodological principle of ideological and political theory courses. The author presents this as methodological guidance for university teachers who want students to hold these convictions firmly.

The article has two parts. The first sets out two philosophical grounds drawn from Marxist epistemology and dialectics. The second shows how the approach applies the principle that political orientation and academic rigour must be unified in teaching.

On the philosophical side, Wan holds that logic must follow history. The abstract, law-like understanding of socialism with Chinese characteristics should therefore be returned to the winding history of reform and opening up. Likewise, essence appears through phenomena, so dry laws become persuasive only when illustrated by historical figures, events and facts. On the methodological side, Wan treats academic rigour as the foundation and political orientation as the soul. The author credits the Party's leadership, a people-centred stance and a political commitment to socialism with helping China avoid the "subversive errors" of Eastern European socialist states. Convictions without theoretical support lose vitality, while those without politics lose direction.

Wan concludes that teachers who grasp this logic can answer students with thorough theoretical analysis rather than empty indoctrination, which raises the appeal and effectiveness of their courses. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese ideological and political education justifies teaching ideals through the history of reform and opening up.
quoteEn: Ideals and convictions without theoretical support lose their vitality, and those without a political dimension lose their direction; the two are highly unified.
quoteZh: 没有学理性支撑的理想信念就失去了生命力，没有政治性的理想信念就会迷失方向，二者高度统一。

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping. Official narratives treat it as the starting point of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The Communist Party's official name for its theory and path of socialism, developed since reform and opening up.
The shared commitment to socialism with Chinese characteristics and national rejuvenation that official education seeks to instil, especially in students.
Compulsory courses in Marxism and Party ideology taught at Chinese schools and universities.

t: The evolutionary logic of ecological civilization from the perspective of epistemology
zh: 认识论视野下的生态文明演进逻辑
paras: Zhou Guangxun and Chen Xuancheng ask how Marxist epistemology can guide human understanding of the relationship between people and nature, at a time when the rapid development of artificial intelligence has produced new accounts of how knowledge arises and what it is. They argue that Marxist epistemology keeps its scientific vitality and remains the theoretical guide for understanding and transforming the world and for achieving harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature. On this basis they present ecological civilization as the culmination of an evolution in human cognition and in forms of civilization.

The article has three parts. It first sets out the two features of Marx's theory of knowledge as the authors read it: a practice-based epistemology and a theory of "reproduction" (zaixian). It then proposes surveying the history of civilization through a "grand historical materialism", drawing on Engels, Freud and Oswald Spengler. Finally it compares three ecological currents: deep green, light green and red-green.

The authors hold that the process of knowing runs from practice to knowledge and back to practice, and that it moves "concrete–abstract–concrete". In their account, Marx's epistemology is not mere mirroring but a creative reworking of reflections in the mind. They argue that Western scholars have wrongly portrayed Marx as anti-ecological, Promethean and anthropocentric. In their reading, a grand historical materialism examines changes in the human–nature relation as well as in human–human relations. They map Marx's sequences of social forms, of human interdependence and of economic forms onto fishing-and-hunting, industrial and ecological civilization. The three green currents are assessed against this frame. The authors say deep green, centred on ecocentrism, ignores human relations and so misses capitalism as the source of ecological crisis. Light green, centred on modern anthropocentrism, relies on technology and economic accounting but overlooks the logic of capital. Red-green, with ecological Marxism as its mainstream, is said to sublate both by criticising the capitalist system.

The authors conclude that ecological civilization is neither a return to a pre-modern society nor a postmodern rejection of growth and technology. In their view it is a civilization in which science and technology are used to transform nature in line with real human needs. Economic growth, ecological protection, social progress and free and all-round human development would advance together, and the "two reconciliations" (of humanity with nature and of humanity with itself) would be realised. Read the original if you want a short Chinese Marxist statement of how epistemology, historical materialism and the typology of Western green thought are linked to the concept of ecological civilization.
quoteEn: Ecological civilization is not a return to a pre-modern society that abandons the transformation of nature and the development of human society, nor a postmodernist position opposed to economic growth and scientific and technological development.
quoteZh: 生态文明不是放弃自然改造和人类社会发展而向前现代社会的复归，不是反对经济增长和科学技术发展的后现代主义主张

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese official and academic discourse for a form of civilization built on harmony between people and nature. It has been written into Party documents and the state's development goals since the early 2000s.
A term used by some Chinese scholars for a broad reading of historical materialism that covers not only human–human and human–society relations but also the human–nature relation.
The authors' label for Marx's epistemology, which they distinguish from simple mirroring (reflection theory). On this view the mind creatively reworks reflected objects to grasp their essence.
A formulation, drawn from the early Marx, of the reconciliation of humanity with nature and of humanity with itself. The authors treat it as the goal of ecological civilization.

t: Excavating and drawing sensibly on China's fine traditional economic thought
zh: 挖掘并合理借鉴中华优秀传统经济思想
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in October 2024, Zhao Mairu asks what traditional Chinese economic thought can offer to present-day economic practice and theory. The article argues that this thought holds considerable wisdom, and that excavating it and drawing on it sensibly will help further the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics, in practice and in theory.

The piece is organised around the four moments of social reproduction in Marxist political economy: production, distribution, exchange and consumption. Each section takes one traditional idea or cluster of ideas, such as Li Kui's "exhausting the potential of the land", "storing wealth among the people", the "Ji Ran strategies" of trade, and spending "for the people". Each is then linked to a contemporary policy position.

On production, Zhao presents Li Kui's Warring States reforms as intensive, careful farming that joined land and labour, and cites yield ratios that the author says were far higher in China than in Western Europe. On distribution, the people-as-foundation tradition (Mencius, Xunzi, Guanzi, Tang Zhen) is said to favour national wealth built on popular wealth, which the author connects to common prosperity and to the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on income distribution. On exchange, Zhao reads the Ji Ran strategies, Bai Gui, Sima Qian's view that one should follow market tendencies, and Guanzi's counter-cyclical "heavy and light" intervention as early grasp of price laws and macro-regulation. On consumption, the author notes the dominant ethic of thrift. Zhao stresses that Xunzi, Sima Qian, Guanzi and Lu Ji, a Ming thinker, saw government spending on water works, relief and public goods as strengthening the economic base.

Zhao concludes that each of these strands has "reference value" for today. They bear on liberating and developing the productive forces, on common prosperity, on building a high-standard socialist market economy, and on strengthening consumption's basic role in economic development, as the 20th Party Congress (2022) put it. The piece is brief and programmatic, and it offers no critical assessment of the traditional ideas. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese scholarship links classical Chinese economic thinking to current policy language.
quoteEn: The productive wisdom embedded in ancient Chinese production thought such as "exhausting the potential of the land", which aims to use all factors of production and methods of management to keep liberating and developing the productive forces, should be further excavated in our own time.
quoteZh: 积淀在“尽地力之教”等中国古人生产思想之中、旨在利用一切生产要素和管理方法不断解放和发展生产力的生产智慧应当在当代被进一步挖掘。

glossary.explanation: A goal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, stressed by Deng Xiaoping and again under Xi Jinping, meaning prosperity shared by all rather than polarisation of wealth.
The official name for China's path and system since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, a socialist market economy and Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions.

glossary.en: exhausting the potential of the land
glossary.literal: teaching to exhaust the strength of the land
glossary.explanation: A policy associated with Li Kui of Wei in the Warring States period, promoting intensive cultivation, crop diversification and timely harvesting.
A traditional principle that national wealth rests on popular wealth, so the state should let the people prosper rather than accumulate in the treasury.
Commercial and price-management maxims attributed to Ji Ran, recorded in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian and said to have been used by Fan Li.

glossary.zh: 高水平社会主义市场经济体制
glossary.pinyin: gāo shuǐpíng shèhuì zhǔyì shìchǎng jīngjì tǐzhì
glossary.explanation: A phrase from the Third Plenum of the 20th Central Committee (2024) on deepening reform, referring to a more developed and better regulated socialist market system.

t: Immaterial labour and digital labour: an examination from the standpoint of the materialist conception of history
zh: 非物质劳动与数字劳动的唯物史观考察
paras: Contemporary capitalism is changing its forms of labour, production organisation and exploitation. Mo Lei compares two much-discussed accounts of these changes: Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri's "immaterial labour" and Christian Fuchs's "digital labour". The article, a short commentary in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, argues that the two share a "family resemblance" but diverge on information, subjectivity, the measurement of exploitation and the realisation of the common.

The piece has three parts. It first sets out the resemblances in background, concept and theoretical aim. Hardt and Negri start from Empire and the global biopolitical order, while Fuchs starts from financial capitalism and the rise of the internet and platforms; both work within "transnational informational capitalism". It then lists five differences, and finally asks what theoretical logic lies behind them.

On resemblances, Mo notes that both approaches stress the production of knowledge, information and affect, the feminisation of work, and free communication and cooperation. Both hold that the appropriation of workers' activity and creativity is the main form of exploitation. On differences, Fuchs objects that "immaterial" implies a split between mind and matter, since information work is still brain-based material work. Mo replies that Hardt and Negri's "immaterial" refers mainly to the product. Fuchs extends Marx's rate of surplus value to include users' unpaid time, concluding that it tends towards infinity and calling users "internet slaves". Hardt and Negri reject quantification, treating exploitation as a qualitative matter of life and social relations. Fuchs also seeks platforms owned in common and a "working-class social media". Hardt and Negri focus on producing common subjectivity and on the multitude.

Mo traces these differences to two sources. Hardt and Negri start from living labour and subjectivity, offering an immanent critique of how subjects produce themselves. Fuchs studies the internal mechanism of value formation through the relation between audience commodity, media and advertising.
