They argue that modernization since the Industrial Revolution has taken three forms: capitalist early-starting predatory, capitalist late-starting dependent, and socialist late-starting independent. In their account, capitalist modernization was flawed from the outset and is exposed in the third wave of modernization, while Chinese modernization is presented as the leading example of the socialist independent type.

The article first reviews theory in three parts: post-1945 Western development economics (structuralist and neoclassical), the social-development thought of Marx, Engels and Lenin, and the radical left tradition of dependency theory and world-systems analysis. It then examines the practice of capitalist modernization, using Britain, France, the United States, Germany and Japan as predatory early starters and South Korea as a dependent case. Finally it turns to socialist independent modernization, taking the Soviet experience from the New Economic Policy to the five-year plans, and then China's path.

The authors argue that structuralists and neoclassicals differ on the role of the market but share a class standpoint, since neither touches the question of ownership. Radical thinkers such as Paul Baran, Samir Amin and Immanuel Wallerstein, by contrast, belong to the Marxist paradigm and criticise the capitalist order. Drawing on Marx and Lenin, the authors define "predation" as unequal value transfer and colonial exploitation, and dependence as control of a country's economy, politics, culture and military by international finance capital. They cite South Korea's chaebol, foreign shareholding and US military command as evidence. They hold that public ownership and foreign-trade monopoly allowed the Soviet Union to modernise without plunder or foreign loans, and attribute its collapse to the degeneration of the Soviet Communist Party rather than to the Soviet model.

For China, the authors identify four features of its independent path: strengthening Party leadership through self-reform, a people-centred orientation, theoretical innovation through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and independence and self-reliance. They conclude that only adherence to socialism can produce independent modernization. They also warn against copying Western models. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist typology of modernization that links dependency and world-systems theory to official accounts of Chinese modernization and the Soviet experience.
quoteEn: The fundamental standard for judging whether a path of modernization is outdated or backward lies not in whether it appeared early or late, nor in how long it has existed, nor in how many countries follow it, but in whether it accords with the fundamental interests of the broadest masses of the people.
quoteZh: 衡量现代化道路是否过时、是否落后，根本标准不在于它出现的时间是早或晚，也不在于它存在的时间是长或短，更不在于走这条路的国家是多或寡，而在于它是否符合最广大人民群众的根本利益

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's development path under Communist Party leadership, promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as a distinct alternative to Western modernization.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official formula for applying Marxist principles to China's concrete conditions and its traditional culture, and updating them for each era.
A school, largely Latin American and Marxist-influenced, holding that underdevelopment in the periphery results from exploitation by core capitalist countries.
Soviet policy introduced in 1921 that replaced grain requisition with a tax in kind and allowed limited markets and state capitalism.

t: The elements, structure, distinctive features and systematic construction of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation
zh: 中华民族现代文明的要素结构、显著特征与系统建设
source: Marxist Studies (马克思主义研究), 2024 no. 3
paras: Responding to Xi Jinping's call, at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, to build a modern civilization of the Chinese nation as a new cultural mission, Luo Liang asks three questions: what this civilization is, what is distinctive about it, and how it should be built. The article, published in Marxist Studies in 2024, answers by treating the civilization as a complex system whose elements, relations, structure and functions can be analysed in turn.

The text has three parts. The first sets out the system's element structure: five component civilizations, four pairs of relations, three structural levels and four functions. The second identifies four distinctive features. The third proposes construction paths organised around three system properties, which Luo calls self-activation, self-emergence and self-adaptation.

In Luo's account, the five components are a material civilization of high-quality development, a political civilization of the people being masters of the country, a spiritual civilization of all-round human development, a social civilization that brings benefits to the people, and an ecological civilization of harmony between humanity and nature. The relations are tradition and modernity, upholding fundamental principles and innovation, the real and the virtual, and the local and the global. The structure comprises an ontological layer (civilizational thinking and existence), a categorial layer (ideas, artefacts, conduct, institutions) and an operational layer (cultivation, practice, creation). The functions are continuing the national spiritual lineage, the cultural lineage, the root lineage of traditional culture, and the soul lineage of Marxism. The four features are dynamism through casting off the old and establishing the new, unity of group and self, inward cohesion and wholeness, and an inclusive openness. Luo contrasts the last two with what the article describes as a capitalist hegemonic logic of Western-centrism.

For construction, Luo calls for Party leadership at every level, the Two Integrations and socialist core values as the basis of practice, and evaluation by the people's interests. The article also urges strengthening the civilization's communication, influence and guiding power internationally, and its adaptation to global pluralism, digitalization, civilizational conflict and rival domestic currents of thought, which it says must be countered under Marxist guidance. Read the original if you want a systematic, system-theory framing of how official discourse conceptualises the modern civilization of the Chinese nation, with its component parts and proposed construction tasks.
quoteEn: The modern civilization of the Chinese nation, as a new form of human civilization, is an aggregate composed of material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization.
quoteZh: 中华民族现代文明作为人类文明新形态，是由物质文明、政治文明、精神文明、社会文明、生态文明等要素构成的集合体。

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture. It is presented as the method of adapting Marxism to China.

An official economic goal, stressed since 2017, that prioritises quality, innovation and efficiency over speed of growth. The Party describes it as the primary task of building a modern socialist country.

keywords: modern civilization of the Chinese nation

t: Beyond "labelling" and bias
st: A reflection on the abuse of the authoritarianism paradigm in Western political science
zh: 超越“标签化”与偏见
zhSub: 对西方政治学研究中威权主义范式滥用问题的反思
paras: Lin Yi and Wang Qiaochu ask why Western political science has so persistently classed non-Western political systems as "authoritarian", and what Chinese scholarship should do about it. Taking the Economist Intelligence Unit's 2022 Democracy Index as a starting point, they argue that the "authoritarianism" paradigm has become a standardised, prejudiced label that serves ideological competition more than analysis. The authors hold that Chinese scholars must move beyond it and build indigenous concepts if they are to explain Chinese modernization on its own terms.

The article has three main parts. The first describes how overseas scholars apply the label (centralised authority, elections that fail liberal-democratic standards, state will placed above citizens' rights) and how the notion of "authoritarian resilience" explains survival within the same frame. The second traces the paradigm's abuse and its conceptual and theoretical roots in political development theory, the "transition paradigm" and the "democracy/non-democracy" dichotomy. The third sets out the political context and intellectual lineage behind the paradigm and then proposes alternatives.

The core argument is that "authoritarianism" is a residual category between totalitarianism and democracy, defined against a Western liberal benchmark. Lin and Wang note that sub-concepts such as "fragmented", "competitive" or "participatory" authoritarianism pair a pejorative noun with neutral or favourable adjectives, which they read as patching a concept that cannot explain real achievements. They add that the "grey zone" of hybrid regimes shows the dichotomy's blind spots, that the third wave of democratization ended in reversals in many transition states, and that the label has been stretched even to Western cases such as the Trump administration. In their account, scholars such as Larry Diamond reveal how democracy itself is being ideologised and "exported" to protect Western international standing.

The authors conclude that the paradigm fails both as theory and as description, and that democracy has many forms, so no single standard can define it. For Chinese political studies they propose four lines of work: the Second Integration of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture, systematic study of the experience of the People's Republic, critical but creative borrowing from Western discourse, and a firm socialist orientation centred on the people. They also call for turning local concepts into discourse able to compete with Western ones. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic critique of the "authoritarianism" label in Western political science and the case for an indigenous political-science discourse.
quoteEn: The authoritarianism paradigm cannot uphold genuine objectivity: all of its analysis rests first of all on a value choice that treats Western democracy as the standard.
quoteZh: 威权主义研究范式无法秉持真正的客观性，它的一切分析都首先建立在以西方民主为圭臬的价值选择之上。

glossary.explanation: Official term for China's own path of modernisation, promoted by the Party leadership since the early 2020s as distinct from Western models.

Formula, prominent from 2021–2023, calling for the basic principles of Marxism to be combined with fine traditional Chinese culture. It is the second of the Two Integrations, the first being combination with China's concrete realities.

The research framework in Western political science that classifies regimes as authoritarian and studies their resilience or transition. The authors treat it as a biased, ideologically loaded approach.
The theoretical framework, from the third wave of democratization, that assumes authoritarian regimes will eventually move to Western-style liberal democracy.

t: Can the West escape the crisis of neoliberalism?
zh: 西方能否摆脱新自由主义危机
paras: Dai Weilai asks whether the West can escape the crisis of neoliberalism, rebuild the international order and keep its dominant position. This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, argues that neoliberalism, which has shaped US economic policy since the 1970s, now faces crises in the economic, social and political spheres. Dai holds that escaping them will not be easy.

The article first sets out the three crises in turn: the crisis of the free market, of social values and of political consensus. It then turns to the Biden administration's response at home and to its attempt to reshape the global order.

On the economy, Dai argues that financial deregulation fed speculation, hollowed out industry and produced financialisation, and that the 2008 financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic exposed the limits of self-regulating markets. Dai describes neoliberal "freedom" as freedom for capital owners to set rules in their own favour, and cites wealth inequality, protest movements and polarised politics as signs of lost consensus. The article reads the "New Washington Consensus" set out by Jake Sullivan in April 2023 as an end to neoliberal foreign policy. In Dai's account, it combines industrial policy, public investment, welfare expansion and labour protection at home with protectionism, high-technology barriers and a more fragmented global order abroad.

Dai concludes that neoliberalism, presented as a "universal value", must change profoundly. The question, Dai writes, is also one of how Western values will be repositioned in a changing social order. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic view of how the US shift away from neoliberalism is being interpreted.
quoteEn: Neoliberalism is not real freedom, but the freedom of capital owners to make and enforce rules that favour themselves.
quoteZh: 新自由主义并非真正的自由，而是资本所有者制定并执行有利于自己规则的自由。

t: Hou Wailu's three identities in exploring the sinicization of Marxism
zh: 侯外庐探索马克思主义中国化的三重身份
paras: How did the historian Hou Wailu approach the adaptation of Marxism to China? Yuan Zhiwei argues that Hou pursued it along three paths, revolution, historiography and thought, and so combined the identities of revolutionary, historian and thinker. In Yuan's reading, these three identities explain the purpose and the scholarly contribution of Hou's history writing. The piece appeared in the China Social Sciences Daily in November 2023.

The article is organised around the three identities. It first looks at Hou as a revolutionary who "fought with the pen", then as a historian who sought truth for practical use, and finally as a thinker who explored the future of Chinese culture. Yuan draws on Hou's biography, from his student activism and contact with Li Dazhao to his translation work and wartime editing, and on his studies of Chinese thought and society from the Shang-Zhou transition to the early twentieth century.

As a revolutionary, Yuan says, Hou joined the Communist-led national salvation movement and the New Democratic Revolution. He co-translated the first volume of Capital with Wang Sihua in 1936. Yuan holds that his scholarship was meant to supply historical grounds for the revolution and for Marxism's spread in China. As a historian, Hou built a "trinity" of economics, philosophy and history and combined social history with the history of thought. He also required a world-historical, comparative outlook, summed up as "a world perspective, Chinese problems". As a thinker, Yuan argues, Hou criticised the autocratic, religious and land-nationalising features of traditional thought while valuing its materialist, atheist and anti-despotic strands. He judged that Chinese tradition lacked an internal dynamic of self-transformation and needed scientific Marxism as a new cultural force.

Yuan concludes that Hou's aim was to "ask after the future way out of Chinese culture", that is, to find answers for China's independence, prosperity and the liberation of the Chinese nation. In this account Hou also tried to build confidence in a Chinese scholarly paradigm grounded in historical materialism. Yuan says these experiences still offer theoretical reference for current discussion of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and of Chinese culture's direction. Read the original if you want a concise, sympathetic overview of Hou Wailu's career and method as a case of Marxist historiography in China.
quoteEn: The purpose of Hou Wailu's scholarship was to "ask after the future way out of Chinese culture", that is, to look for answers for China's independence and prosperity and for the liberation and freedom of the Chinese nation.
quoteZh: 侯外庐学术研究的目的是“叩问中国文化的未来出路”，即为中国的独立和富强、中华民族的解放和自由寻找答案。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formulation for applying Marxism to China's conditions and to the present era. The article uses the earlier shorter form 'Marxism's sinicization (中国化)' for Hou's work.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution led by the Communist Party against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism, as a transition towards socialism.
The Marxist theory that material and economic conditions shape social structures and the development of history. Hou treated it as the guiding method for studying Chinese thought and society.

t: Can the West escape the crisis of neoliberalism?
zh: 西方能否摆脱新自由主义危机
paras: Dai Weilai asks whether the West can escape the crisis of neoliberalism, rebuild the international order and keep its dominant position. This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, argues that neoliberalism, which has dominated US economic policy since the 1970s, now faces crises in three areas: the economy, society and politics. In Dai's view, escaping it will not be easy.

The article first sets out the three crises: the failure of the free market, a crisis of social values and a collapse of political consensus. It then turns to the US response, both at home and in the international order, and ends by placing neoliberalism within the longer history of Western political thought.

Dai argues that deregulated finance produced speculation, hollowed-out industry and rising inequality. The article cites a record "misery index", stagnant incomes for the bottom 90 per cent and protest movements such as Occupy Wall Street. It also describes political polarisation, with left and right both attacking neoliberalism. Dai reads the "new Washington consensus", which national security adviser Jake Sullivan outlined in April 2023, as a turn towards industrial policy, state-led development, labour protection and protectionism. The article presents this as a US attempt to restore its hegemony. According to Dai, it will diversify global economic policy, sharpen competition, put a "iron curtain" around high-technology trade and make cooperation on issues such as climate harder, while the rise of developing countries redistributes power.

Dai concludes that neoliberalism, presented as a "universal value", cannot avoid crisis as social practice changes, and must undergo deep adjustment. Whether the West can escape is, in this view, a question about repositioning Western values in an evolving social order, not only about its political-economic system. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic view of the US shift away from neoliberalism.
quoteEn: Neoliberalism is not true freedom, but the freedom of capital owners to make and enforce rules that favour themselves.
quoteZh: 新自由主义并非真正的自由，而是资本所有者制定并执行有利于自己规则的自由。

t: "Rules-based" as a discursive trap of the United States and the West
zh: 基于规则”是美西方的话语陷阱
paras: Wang Lei takes up the phrase "rules-based international order", which US and Western leaders use frequently. The commentary argues that these leaders are not defending international rules. In Wang's reading, the phrase carries a set of Western values and calculated self-interest.

The piece first sketches the historical record. It runs from the Westphalian system through the Vienna, Berlin, Versailles–Washington and Yalta systems, which Wang describes as orders "based on power". It then covers the post-1945 UN-centred system and the post-Cold War promotion of the "Washington Consensus". It ends with the shift of power from West to East and from North to South.

Wang argues that the vagueness of "rules" suits US instrumental needs, because international law would bind the United States. In this account, the United States subordinates international law to its "rules", reshapes them pragmatically (for example a "new Washington Consensus"), and applies them selectively. Wang cites three points: US non-participation in key multilateral treaties, policies at odds with general principles of international law, and the "trimming" of law in the name of rules. On this view the formula erodes the unity and authority of international law, and the United States becomes its "number one destroyer". It also divides friends from foes, labelling China and Russia "revisionist".

Wang presents China as a firm defender of an order based on international law. Rules should be made jointly, serve public-goods values, and apply to all without exceptionalism or double standards. Only a return to such an order, together with reform of international law, would bring lasting peace and development, in Wang's view. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentary criticises the "rules-based order" concept and sets it against international law.
quoteEn: The "rules-based international order" is in essence a hegemonic view of order advanced by the United States and other Western countries, who use international law and rules when they suit them and discard them when they do not, choosing entirely by their own interests.
quoteZh: “基于规则的国际秩序”实质是美国等西方国家倡导的霸权秩序观，它们对国际法和国际规则“合则用，不合则弃”，完全是以自身利益为取舍。

t: The inner paradox of neoliberalism's anomalous survival
zh: 新自由主义反常存续的内在悖论
paras: Neoliberalism is blamed for the Asian and Latin American crises of the 1990s and the US financial crisis of 2007–2008, yet it did not perish and has become the ideology of mainstream Western parties. Chen Xuefei asks why it persists and argues that this survival is anomalous. In Chen's view it has not resolved neoliberalism's underlying difficulties but deepened the internal crisis of modern Western society, so it cannot last.

This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in December 2023, traces neoliberalism genealogically. It moves from mercantilism and French physiocracy to classical liberalism, then to the two post-war neoliberalisms, German ordoliberalism and American neoliberalism, before turning to their domestic and international effects.

Chen's central claim is that liberal governance has always carried a paradox between freedom and security: freedom must be produced and managed at once. Ordoliberalism made security subordinate to the freedom of market competition, and American neoliberalism pushed this furthest. It recast the population as human capital, treated every person as an enterprise, applied economic analysis to marriage, family and politics, and made the market a tribunal judging government. Domestically, Chen argues, the interest mechanism worsens the Matthew effect in income and wealth, and measures such as minimum-income schemes or pandemic relief protect freedom rather than the population. Internationally, Chen calls neoliberalism a new imperialism that globalises North Atlantic standards.

Chen concludes that neoliberalism's persistence reflects not vitality or universality but the shelving of its own paradox by states that have become containers for global capital. Placing the freedom mechanism above everything else serves the hegemonic expansion of globalised capitalism and deepens Western society's crisis. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese critical genealogy of neoliberalism that draws on Foucault-style governmentality analysis.
quoteEn: The anomalous survival of neoliberalism has not fundamentally resolved the difficulties it faces but has deepened the internal crisis of modern Western society, and it therefore cannot last.
quoteZh: 新自由主义的反常存续，未能从根本上解决其面临的困境，反而加深了现代西方社会的内在危机，因此，其必然也就无法持久。

t: Living up to a great era, shouldering a glorious mission
zh: 不负伟大时代 担负光荣使命
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 17 May 2024
paras: This commentary, published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2024, asks what Chinese philosophers and social scientists must do to meet the expectations Xi Jinping set out at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences work. Peng Qinghong takes Xi's call to "stand at the forefront of the times, connect the changes of past and present, and sound the first notes of new thought" as a framework. The author argues that this call gives researchers both a direction and a set of values to follow.

The piece is organised under three headings drawn from Xi's formulation: standing at the crest of the times, being skilled at connecting past and present, and daring to voice new ideas first. Each heading is divided into three requirements. The text quotes Xi throughout, including on Chinese modernization, the Two Integrations, the people-centred orientation of scholarship, and academic misconduct.

Under the first heading, Peng says scholars should solve problems, anticipate risks and lead, by focusing on the Party's and the country's major questions, moving from passive response to active foresight, and identifying the broad logic of social development. Under the second, the author calls for cultural confidence, adherence to the Two Integrations and "upholding fundamental principles while innovating". Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is presented as a model of this approach. Under the third, Peng requires scholars to put the people first, practise seeking truth from facts, and show the boldness to speak. Peng cites the 1978 article "Practice is the sole criterion of truth" as an example of the second requirement. On the third, Peng calls on scholars to consolidate Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere and to counter what the author describes as demonization of China abroad. They should act as "fighters" rather than "gentlemen" who guard their reputations.

Peng concludes that if scholars follow these three requirements, they will not fail in their mission and will make larger contributions to building a strong country and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official commentary translates Xi Jinping's expectations of social scientists into concrete duties, or if you are studying the language that frames academic work in China's new era.
quoteEn: Philosophy and social science workers must show real ability and achieve good results in researching and solving major problems of overall, fundamental and critical importance to the Party and the country.
quoteZh: 哲学社会科学工作者必须在研究解决事关党和国家全局性、根本性、关键性的重大问题上拿出真本事、取得好成果。

glossary.explanation: A formula associated with Xi Jinping: combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture.
The official term for China's own path of modernization, presented by the Party as distinct from Western models and as rooted in Chinese civilization.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central national goal, associated with the Chinese Dream, of restoring China's strength and international standing by the mid-twenty-first century.
A slogan in Party discourse that calls for keeping to correct principles and the Marxist orientation while pursuing new ideas and practice.

t: The Party's practical path in building a modern civilisation of the Chinese nation
zh: 党推进中华民族现代文明建设的实践脉络
paras: This short commentary, first printed in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2024, asks how the Communist Party of China has approached cultural construction and how it should now build a modern civilisation of the Chinese nation. Starting from Xi Jinping's June 2023 remarks at the symposium on cultural inheritance and development, Chen argues that this task is the Party's new cultural mission and follows from a long line of practice in developing socialist culture.

The article moves in three steps. It first recalls the Party's cultural mission since its founding and in the early People's Republic. It then reviews what has been achieved since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including Xi's theoretical contributions on culture. Finally it sets out the requirements for the new journey: cultural confidence, openness and inclusiveness, and keeping to fundamental principles while innovating.

Chen's central claim is that the Party has always led advanced culture and also inherited traditional culture. After 1949, in Chen's account, it established Marxism's guiding position, adopted the principles of making the past serve the present and foreign things serve China, and issued the "let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend" policy. Since 2012 the Party has combined Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture, which the article treats as the basis for the Two Integrations, especially the "second integration". Chen lists many strands of Xi's thinking, among them the Party's overall leadership of ideological work, core socialist values, a Chinese philosophy and social science, the protection of cultural heritage, international communication and the Global Civilization Initiative. Chen holds that cultural confidence means turning Chinese experience into Chinese theory. Openness means drawing on all outstanding civilisational achievements. "Upholding fundamental principles" means keeping the Party's cultural leadership and the Chinese nation's cultural subjectivity, and never abandoning Marxism or traditional culture.

Chen concludes that the new form of human civilisation created by Chinese modernization is both Chinese and global, and calls for guidance by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The article also calls for the Two Establishes, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds, so that a model modern civilisation can be offered to the world. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated commentary presents the lineage and current requirements of the cultural mission.
quoteEn: Only by upholding fundamental principles can we avoid losing ourselves and our direction; only through innovation can we grasp and lead the times.
quoteZh: 守正才能不迷失自我、不迷失方向，创新才能把握时代、引领时代。

glossary.explanation: Formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities (the first) and with fine traditional Chinese culture (the second). The "second integration" was stressed by Xi Jinping in 2023.
The official term for China's own path to modernity, set out by the Party especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A 2021 Party formulation affirming Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Party and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought.
The Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Party Central Committee and in the whole Party, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.
Confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
A 2023 proposal by Xi Jinping promoting respect for the diversity of civilisations, shared human values and exchange between civilisations.

keywords: modern civilisation of the Chinese nation

t: Promoting the high-quality development of philosophy and social sciences
zh: 推动哲学社会科学高质量发展
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 17 May 2024
paras: This commentary, published on 17 May 2024 in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, responds to Xi Jinping's speech at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences work. Lü Peiming argues that the speech answers fundamental questions about the long-term development of the field and sets the direction for philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, style and manner. The article asks how universities, taking Tongji University as the example, can turn this guidance into high-quality development.

The piece has three parts. The first describes the new situation facing university philosophy and social sciences over the eight years since the 2016 symposium. The second reports what Tongji University has already done to promote interdisciplinary integration. The third sets out five new lines of action for the future.

On the current situation, Lü names three factors: Xi Jinping's new requirements, including the call to build China's own knowledge system; new Party Central Committee plans such as the 2017 opinions on accelerating the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics and the 2022 action plan to 2035; and the challenge of a new technological revolution, which is pushing the restructuring of the humanities into a 'new liberal arts'. Lü presents Tongji's response as organisational innovation: discipline clusters, organised interdisciplinary research on topics such as AI governance and digital cities, cross-field platforms and think tanks focused on 'city' and 'Germany (Europe)'. The five future tasks are deepening research on Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era under the Two Integrations; moral education for a new generation; serving national strategy; developing the new liberal arts with AI; and building China's external discourse system.

Lü concludes that universities should integrate Marxist theory with engineering, science and medicine, and train versatile talent. They should also produce original scholarship that supports the building of China's own knowledge system and the effort to build a community with a shared future for mankind. The text is a university leader's programmatic statement more than an analytical study. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese university translates central directives on philosophy and social sciences into institutional plans, platforms and priorities.
quoteEn: Accelerating the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics ultimately means constructing China's own autonomous knowledge system.
quoteZh: 加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学，归根结底是建构中国自主的知识体系。

glossary.explanation: Formula in Xi Jinping-era Party theory: combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with China's fine traditional culture.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations and global governance, used in official foreign-policy and discourse-building language.
An education-policy initiative to restructure humanities and social science disciplines through interdisciplinary integration with science, engineering and digital technology.
Slogan stressed by Xi Jinping in 2022, calling for Chinese scholarship to build its own concepts and theories rather than rely on Western frameworks.

t: Understanding new quality productive forces as a key variable
zh: 理解作为关键变量的新质生产力
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 22 May 2024
paras: This text is a Chinese translation of a commentary by the Lebanese author Linda Matar. It takes up Xi Jinping's call of 31 January 2024 to accelerate new quality productive forces and asks what the concept means. Matar argues that it is a key variable of economic growth and should be read through Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In this reading it is an upgrade of productive forces within a socialist, people-centred framework, not a paradigm shift or a turn to capitalism.

The piece begins with China's development path since 1949, which Matar sums up as policy autonomy and a link between security and development. It then cites figures on research and development spending, export growth in the "new three" products (electric vehicles, lithium batteries, solar cells) and technological leadership. Further sections cover the Marxist theory of productive forces, the Party's reform-era policy, whole-process people's democracy, poverty reduction and inequality, and the place of innovation and national security in high-quality development.

Matar contends that mainstream growth models, which treat technology as endogenous or exogenous, hide the question of which social forces direct development and who benefits. In her account, the difference between socialist and capitalist production lies in its purpose: satisfying people's needs rather than creating private surplus value. She argues that the state's control of capital, together with the Party's leadership, keeps workers united with the means of production. Matar rejects Western media claims that the concept repackages old slogans or that the Party commands from above, and points to consultative democracy. She presents democracy and development as mutually reinforcing: people's control of resources is, in her view, the substance of democracy.

Matar concludes that new quality productive forces are a roadmap for China's socialist modernization and cultural-ethical progress. She holds that high-quality development keeps economy and politics united and protects China's global position and its voice in science and technology under Western restrictions. Development, innovation and national security form a "trinity", in her words, and technology serves the aim of making the economy serve the people. Read the original if you want to see how a foreign sympathetic commentator frames the concept, and how she answers Western media interpretations, for a Chinese-language audience.
quoteEn: The main difference between China's socialist model of production and the Western capitalist model lies in the ultimate goal of production.
quoteZh: 中国的社会主义生产模式与西方资本主义生产模式的主要区别在于生产的最终目标。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping stressed in 2023–24, describing advanced productive forces driven by high technology, high efficiency and high quality, with a large rise in total factor productivity at their core.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Chinese Communist Party, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–18.
An official goal, prominent since 2017, that shifts emphasis from speed of growth to quality, innovation and balance.
The official term, promoted by Xi Jinping since 2019, for China's democratic model, which stresses participation beyond elections.

t: A theoretical analysis of the modern civilization of the Chinese nation
zh: 中华民族现代文明的理论探析
paras: Shang Zhixiao takes up a concept introduced by Xi Jinping in 2023: "the modern civilization of the Chinese nation", presented as part of a new cultural mission alongside cultural prosperity and building a strong socialist culture. The article argues that this new formulation needs to be understood theoretically before it can be put into practice. Its answer is that the modern civilization of the Chinese nation is, in essence, a socialist modern civilization: the latest form of Chinese civilization, built on socialism and the Party's leadership.

The article has four parts. It first distinguishes civilization from culture and sets out what it sees as the distinctive features of Chinese civilization. It then traces how Xi came to the concept, from his remarks at the Yin Ruins in Anyang in October 2022 to the symposium on cultural inheritance and development in June 2023. The third part defines the concept and its internal structure. The fourth traces its historical course since 1949 and its link with Chinese modernization.

Shang's core argument has three moves. First, Chinese civilization is described as unbroken, deep, distinctive and far-reaching, with five outstanding features (continuity, innovation, unity, inclusiveness, peacefulness); the modern civilization is said to inherit these. Second, the concept is analysed on two levels. Conceptually it has a subject (the Chinese nation), a historical position (the modern era) and a form (culture). In practice it rests on the Party as leadership core, the people as the force relied upon, and socialism with Chinese characteristics and advanced socialist culture as guiding direction. Civilization is the inner essence and advanced socialist culture its outward form. Third, the author places its starting point in the founding of new China and the establishment of the socialist system, and argues that it grows together with Chinese modernization. In this reading the concept goes beyond both traditional Chinese civilization and capitalist civilization, and also escapes the constraints of "traditional" socialism.

Shang concludes that building this civilization means promoting the creative transformation and innovative development of fine traditional Chinese culture, combining Marxism's basic tenets with that culture, and developing socialist culture and Chinese modernization together. The author presents it as both a requirement of national rejuvenation and a new model within the diversity of world civilizations. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese academic account of how the concept is defined and justified, and how it is tied to Chinese modernization and the Marxism–tradition integration.
quoteEn: The modern civilization of the Chinese nation both surpasses capitalist civilization and frees itself from the shackles of \"traditional\" socialism; in essence it is a socialist modern civilization.
quoteZh: 中华民族现代文明既领先于资本主义文明，又摆脱“传统”社会主义的羁绊，其实质是社会主义现代文明。

glossary.en: the modern civilization of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A formulation Xi Jinping first used in October 2022 and set out as a cultural mission in June 2023. It denotes the contemporary form of Chinese civilization under socialism.
The official name for China's path to modernization under Party leadership, presented as distinct from Western models. It was elaborated especially from the 20th Party Congress (2022).
The task Xi Jinping set out in June 2023: promoting cultural prosperity, building a strong socialist culture and building the modern civilization of the Chinese nation.

t: Revision notes on the 2024 edition of the textbook "Chinese Marxism and the Contemporary Era"
st: Guidance for revising and teaching the doctoral political theory course
zh: 《中国马克思主义与当代（2024年版）》修订说明
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2024 no. 5
paras: This is an explanatory note by Hou Huiqin, chief expert of the project team, on the 2024 revision of the textbook Chinese Marxism and the Contemporary Era. It is the only ideological and political theory course taught to doctoral students nationwide. Hou says the revision, only two years after the 2021 edition but spanning the 20th Party Congress (2022), aims to build the latest results of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times into the book, and offers teaching advice for the new edition.

The note has three parts. The first sets out the revision's guiding idea and principles: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era is treated through the relationship between contemporary China and the world, the Two Establishes provide the political standpoint, and updating is balanced against stability. The second argues that teaching depends on rendering Marxism in rigorous scholarly terms ("xueli hua"). The third presents the course's purpose as cultivating socialist "new-era talents" with a world outlook, with comments on students, teachers and young people's responsibilities.

Hou argues that new ideas should be integrated "organically" rather than pasted in as labels, and that about a third of the text was changed while keeping the 2021 structure. Each of chapters one to six moves from the world's problems, to how states respond, to China's answer. Chapters on contemporary capitalism and socialism are now set within the interplay of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the great changes of the century. On scholarly rigour, Hou holds that doctoral teaching must pose problems that experience cannot answer, rebut "rational" hostile ideological challenges, and reconstruct theoretical results as historical laws grounded in a worldview, not in empiricism. Hou also says teachers should stress that Chinese modernization is fundamentally different from Western modernization and reject the view that modernization means Westernization.

Hou concludes that the course should join ideological guidance with academic depth, so that doctoral students gain a Marxist worldview alongside specialist skills and take on responsibility for national rejuvenation. The closing section, on the dialectic of "when youth flourishes, the nation flourishes", urges young people to unite China's mission with the times' mission, cultivate virtue and real skills, and pair lofty ideals with hard work. Read the original if you want to see how the compilers of China's doctoral-level political theory course describe its design, its teaching method and its intended audience.
quoteEn: Without conscious grasp of a worldview, and without breaking through the limits of empirical and positivist methods, one cannot understand the laws of social history.
quoteZh: 没有世界观的自觉，不突破经验的、实证的方法局限，就无法认识社会历史规律。

glossary.explanation: A formulation from the 6th Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) affirming Xi Jinping's core position in the Party and the guiding status of his thought.

t: The new form of human civilisation in the perspective of world history, and its significance
zh: 世界历史视域下的人类文明新形态及其意义
source: Teaching and Research on Marxist Theory, 2024 no. 2
paras: Tian Yisong and Chen Weici ask how the "new form of human civilisation", presented as an inherent part of Chinese modernization and an expression of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, can be explained theoretically. They argue that Marx's theory of world history is the appropriate tool. In their account, the new form of civilisation is a creative development of that theory and its realisation in practice.

The article has three parts. The first compares Hegel's and Marx's theories of world history. The second argues that the new form of civilisation is the contemporary realisation of Marx's theory. The third presents its significance for answering Western doctrines, namely Fukuyama's "end of history" and Huntington's "clash of civilisations".

In the first part the authors contrast the two thinkers on three points. Hegel makes absolute spirit the driving force, heroic individuals the subject, and the Germanic world the highest stage. Marx locates the driving force in productive forces, the subject in the popular masses, and the final direction in communism, which in his view can only exist as a world-historical movement. The authors then argue that the new form of civilisation applies this framework. It rests on the development of productive forces, particularly through reform and opening up. It is built on socialism with Chinese characteristics and the primary stage of socialism, and it is people-centred. It is also described as a "real movement" that keeps abolishing existing conditions through the Party's self-reform, not as a finished end-state. The authors say it adds to Marx's theory in economic institutions, whole-process people's democracy, the rule of law, harmonious society and ecological civilisation.

Against Fukuyama, the authors argue that communism in Marx is an open movement, not a terminal state. They add that the new form of civilisation does not claim to be a necessary path for other nations. Against Huntington, they argue that his theory expresses Western-centrism and hides the economic and class roots of conflict. They present the new form of civilisation, together with a community with a shared future for mankind, as an alternative for developing countries to the civilisation led by capital. They conclude that it answers the "great changes unseen in a century" and surpasses Western modernization, and they call for developing it further through the creative transformation of traditional Chinese culture. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars ground official civilisation discourse in Marx's world-history theory and in a critique of Hegel, Fukuyama and Huntington.
quoteEn: The new form of human civilisation is a product of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and even more so the realisation of Marx's theory of world history.
quoteZh: 人类文明新形态是马克思主义中国化时代化的产物，更是马克思世界历史理论的现实化。

t: Several Chinese cultural concepts contained in the "Second Integration"
zh: “第二个结合”中蕴含的若干中华文化观念
source: Documents of the Party (Dang de wenxian), 2024 no. 2
paras: Cao Yingwang asks which strands of traditional Chinese culture underlie the "Second Integration", the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with excellent traditional Chinese culture. The article argues that six long-standing cultural concepts match certain Marxist ideas. In Cao's account, Communist Party members creatively transformed and innovatively developed these concepts, and they became a cultural reason why the Party has been able to keep adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The six concepts are the view of all under heaven (tianxia guan), valuing the foundation (guiben guan), self-strengthening, the relationship between heaven and humanity, continuity and change, and the unity of knowing and doing. For each, Cao sets out the classical sources, such as the Analects, Mencius and Wang Yangming. The article then pairs them with a Marxist counterpart and follows the concept through statements and policies of Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, from early Party history to the present.

Cao's central move is to show parallels between each concept and a Marxist idea. The ideal of a world of great harmony (datong) is matched with communism and, today, with a community with a shared future for mankind. Valuing the foundation is matched with the primacy of the productive forces and the people as makers of history. Self-strengthening is matched with the primacy of internal over external causes, in Mao's On Contradiction and in the principle of independence and self-reliance. Heaven and humanity is matched with Marx's view of humans and nature and with Xi Jinping Thought on ecological civilization. Continuity and change is matched with dialectical development and with "upholding fundamental principles while breaking new ground". Knowing and doing is matched with Marxist epistemology and Mao's On Practice. Cao presents the Second Integration itself as an example of continuity and change, and says Xi puts more weight on action than on knowledge.

Cao concludes that the Party's practice since its founding has given these traditional concepts new theoretical content and renewed their life in a new era. Cao says this experience offers lessons for promoting the creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional culture and for building a modern Chinese civilization. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-by-source account of how official Party scholarship links classical Chinese ideas to Marxism and to the thought of Mao, Deng and Xi.
quoteEn: The "Second Integration" rests on a foundation of excellent traditional Chinese cultural concepts, deposited over several thousand years of history.
quoteZh: “第二个结合”，有着几千年历史积淀下来的中华优秀传统文化观念基础。

glossary.explanation: Formulation by Xi Jinping (2023) of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with excellent traditional Chinese culture. It is the second of the Two Integrations, the first being Marxism with China's concrete realities.

t: Socialism with Chinese characteristics and the revival of European socialism
zh: 中国特色社会主义与欧洲社会主义的复兴
paras: This is a Chinese translation of a speech by Thürmer Gyula, chairman of the Hungarian Workers' Party, delivered at the 13th World Socialism Forum. Thürmer argues that capitalism is in deep crisis and that European socialist parties must renew themselves, drawing on socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The speech opens with a diagnosis of the present: the European Union's loss of competitiveness, the collapse of Europe's security structure and the danger of world war. It then lists several "needs" of the European socialist movement: theoretical revival, study of the Chinese Communist Party's experience, a break with the "end of history" thesis, new forms of cooperation, and a clear international orientation.

Thürmer holds that Marxism is a living theory that each party must apply to its own national conditions, as the Chinese case is said to show. He endorses Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and the Two Integrations, and calls for Marxism to be combined with Europe's own cultural and civilisational heritage. He presents China's poverty eradication and Chinese modernization as evidence that hard problems can be solved, while stressing that this is a sharing of experience and not an imposed model.

Thürmer concludes that European parties should replace profit-based capitalism with people-centred socialism, defend national sovereignty, work for a multipolar world and support a community with a shared future for mankind. He also states that some communist parties do not accept the CPC's theoretical innovations and that discussion with them should continue. Read the original if you want a European communist leader's own account of how Chinese theory is received and used in Europe's socialist debates.
quoteEn: Marxism is the common wealth of the world socialist movement, but every party has the right and the responsibility to apply Marxism according to its specific national conditions.
quoteZh: 马克思主义是世界社会主义运动的共同财富，但每个党都有权利和责任根据具体国情运用马克思主义。

t: Opposing hegemonism and power politics and actively advancing a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: 反对霸权主义和强权政治，积极推进人类命运共同体建设
paras: Kong Dan and Wang Xiangsui argue that the hegemon-centred global political order is disintegrating and a multipolar world is emerging. In this short commentary, published in World Socialism Studies in 2024, they contend that building a community with a shared future for mankind requires opposing hegemonism and power politics.

The article has three parts. It first describes the underlying logic of the current world order, then examines hegemonism and power politics as obstacles to common development and security, and finally sets out the principles of "extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits" for building the community.

The authors hold that the modern world system, which grew out of Europe from the late fifteenth century, still runs on a "law of the jungle". Citing slavery, colonial plunder, the indemnities exacted from China and the wealth drained from India, they say the developed countries became rich largely by looting the South, and that global capital still depends on excess profit from the Global South, which they call a form of "national surplus value". Hegemonism, in their definition, is a product of the imperialist stage of capitalism. They list its political, economic, trade, technological, military, information and financial forms, and say hegemons will defend their "hegemonic dividend" whatever the moral criticism. China's initiative, they warn, will therefore meet hostility from global capital.

Kong and Wang conclude that the community with a shared future for mankind means peace over war, development over poverty, cooperation over confrontation and win-win outcomes. They call for reform of existing international rules and a redesign of the global architecture, and describe opposition to hegemonism as inherent in China's view of global governance. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese statement linking the shared-future concept to a critique of capitalist hegemony.
quoteEn: Extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits constitute China's view of global governance, and opposing hegemonism and power politics is inherent in it.
quoteZh: 共商、共建、共享，是中国的全球治理观，反对霸权主义和强权政治是其题中应有之义。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s as China's vision for international relations, stressing cooperation and shared security and development. It has been cited in UN documents.

glossary.pinyin: gòng shāng gòng jiàn gòng xiǎng

glossary.explanation: A formula presented as China's principle of global governance: decisions made jointly, institutions built jointly, and gains shared by all. It is closely associated with the Belt and Road Initiative.
A term for developing countries, mostly in Asia, Africa and Latin America, which Chinese official discourse presents as a common grouping.
A term used in Chinese official and academic discourse for a stronger state's use of military, economic or other power to dominate others and shape the international order.
A Chinese political term for the practice of powerful states imposing their will on weaker ones, often under the maxim that "might makes right".

t: Postmodern theory's misreading of Marx's conception of history
zh: 后现代理论对马克思历史观的误读
paras: This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2024, asks how far postmodern criticism of Marx's concept of history holds up. Fu and Ma argue that the critiques by Jacques Derrida and Jean-François Lyotard misread historical materialism and have clear limits. They contend that Marx's view can only be fairly assessed when it is placed in its specific historical context.

The article first sets out the two critiques. Derrida, in Specters of Marx (1993), treats the conception of history as a modern ideology of a grand narrative with a single rational principle. Lyotard reads Marx's history as a singular, necessary, progressive process inherited from Enlightenment myth and still bound by metaphysics, and he favours small narratives. The authors then offer three objections.

The first objection is methodological. Fu and Ma say Derrida and Lyotard combine Marx's dialectic of part and whole with their own philosophy of the event. This is contradictory, because history conceived as unpredictable events cannot be a whole. They also say the two reduce Marx's ascent from the abstract to the concrete to a move from parts to whole, and that 'deconstruction' and 'event' lack clear meaning as bridges to historical totality. The second objection is that, once grand narratives are discarded, no comparably strong framework remains for analysing enduring structures such as the economic base and class struggle.

The third objection is that the critics overlook the historical relativity of Marx's theory, which rests on analysis of nineteenth-century Western social formations and which, in the authors' view, is open to change and rupture. The authors conclude that historical materialism seeks the dynamics and laws of social change rather than a final picture of history. Marx himself said his theory must be updated, so any critique should rest on understanding its historical conditions. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese Marxist rebuttal of Derrida and Lyotard on historical materialism.
quoteEn: Marx's historical materialism does not offer a static or final picture of history, but seeks the dynamics and laws of social change within the ever-changing flux of history.
quoteZh: 马克思的历史唯物主义不是在提供一个静态或终极的历史图景，而是在不断变化的历史流变中寻找社会变迁的动力与规律。

glossary.explanation: Marx's theory that material production and social relations drive historical change. The article defends it against postmodern critiques.

t: The scientific application of historical materialism in the Communist Manifesto
zh: 《共产党宣言》对唯物史观的科学运用
paras: Sun Min and Zhao Feng ask how the Communist Manifesto put historical materialism to work. They argue that although the materialist conception of history had largely taken shape in The German Ideology, it remained a hypothesis there, untested by a full analysis of a particular social formation. In the authors' reading, the Manifesto was the first time Marx and Engels publicly attempted, and partly completed, that task.

The short piece, published in the China Social Sciences Today in March 2024, is organised under four headings: a scientific understanding of capitalism, a scientific explanation of socialism, a scientific forecast of the future society, and a scientific revelation of historical laws. It draws throughout on passages from the Manifesto, Engels's 1883 preface, the 1872 German-edition preface and Marx's 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy.

On capitalism, the authors trace the rise of the bourgeoisie from medieval townspeople and guild masters to machine industry and a society split into two opposed classes. They stress that the Manifesto credits the bourgeoisie with a revolutionary historical role, yet holds that the contradiction between private ownership and socialised production makes capitalism's replacement by socialist relations of production inevitable. On socialism, they report the Manifesto's conclusions that the proletariat is both impoverished and united by large-scale production, that the bourgeoisie's fall and the proletariat's victory are equally inevitable, and that revolution requires the "two ruptures" with traditional property relations and traditional ideas.

The authors list five principles in the Manifesto's forecast of the future: developing the productive forces, public ownership with planned production, real democracy and the abolition of major social divisions leading to common prosperity, a staged transformation, and the building of a new culture. They concede that the Manifesto's expectation of simultaneous revolution in several developed countries differs from today's globalisation, but hold that its core principles remain sound. They conclude that, despite the unfinished critique of political economy, the Manifesto tested historical materialism through class struggle and supplied the historical basis for Marx's classic 1859 formulation. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese account of the Manifesto as a demonstration of historical-materialist method.
quoteEn: Mainly from the standpoint of class struggle, the Communist Manifesto reveals the direct form in which the basic contradictions between the productive forces and the relations of production, and between the economic base and the superstructure, appear in class society.
quoteZh: 《共产党宣言》主要立足于阶级斗争的视角，揭示了生产力与生产关系、经济基础与上层建筑之间的基本矛盾在阶级社会中的直接表现形式

glossary.explanation: A phrase drawn from the Manifesto's statement that communist revolution breaks radically with traditional property relations and with traditional ideas. Chinese commentators use it to link ownership change with cultural and ideological change.

A Chinese policy goal of shared material wealth for all, prominent in Party discourse especially since the 2010s. The authors read it back into Marx and Engels's aim of abolishing the gaps between town and country and between mental and manual labour.
The Marxist theory that material production and its social relations shape politics, law and consciousness, and that history advances through class struggle.

t: Starting from Mao Zedong's reading life
zh: 从毛泽东同志的读书生活谈起
paras: Writing for Qiushi in 2024, on the occasion of the third National Reading Conference, Chen Jin takes Mao Zedong's reading life as a model for building a "scholarly society" and for encouraging Party members and cadres to love reading, read good books and read well. The article opens with Xi Jinping's remarks on reading as his greatest hobby and as a duty of leading cadres. Chen argues that Mao's breadth of knowledge and skill in applying it were rare in Party and world history, and that his example still offers lessons.

The essay has three main sections: Mao's passion for reading, his wide-ranging reading, and his skill as a reader. It draws on anecdotes and records from his youth in Hunan, the Yan'an years and his later life. It ends by linking Mao's example to Xi Jinping's own reading habits and to Xi's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) on study by leading cadres.

Chen stresses that Mao read daily whatever his workload, using the methods of "squeezing" out time and "drilling" into problems, and kept reading until the day before his death in 1976. Mao's reading focused on Marxist-Leninist works, philosophy and history. He read Marxist classics in order to apply them to Chinese realities, philosophy as a "tool" of thought and method, and Chinese and foreign history to draw lessons and avoid cutting off the past. Chen identifies several habits of a skilled reader: rereading key texts, comparing works with opposing viewpoints, annotating and discussing in reading groups, and above all linking books to practice and to the "wordless book" of society.

Chen concludes that Mao's reading helped establish a Party tradition of treating study as a necessary route to theoretical grounding and work competence. The article presents Xi Jinping as continuing this tradition. As the country advances the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization and faces serious tests, the article calls on cadres to treat reading as a way of life, a work responsibility and a spiritual pursuit. Read the original if you want an official Party-journal portrait of Mao as a reader, and of how reading is presented as a duty for cadres under Xi Jinping.
quoteEn: Comrade Mao Zedong was not only diligent in reading but also good at it, reading, studying and thinking in earnest with heart and mind.
quoteZh: 毛泽东同志不仅勤于读书，而且善于读书，是用心用脑去真读、真学、真思考。

glossary.explanation: The official concept of China's own path to modernization, promoted by the Party leadership especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022) as the route to national rejuvenation.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal, closely associated with Xi Jinping, of restoring China to national strength and prosperity after the 'century of humiliation'.
A slogan for a society with a strong reading culture, used in national reading campaigns.

t: The meaning of Marx's concept of "world history"
zh: 马克思“世界历史”概念的意涵
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 1 April 2024
paras: Duan Guangpeng asks what Marx's concept of "world history" means once it is separated from Hegel's. Hegel, the article says, understood world history "philosophically", as the externalisation and sublation of self-consciousness. Marx reworked the concept at the level of practice and sensuous activity and started from "real human beings". Duan argues that this gave the concept a new meaning and produced a new principle for explaining history.

The article is a short essay in the history of Marxism, organised around three successive senses of world history in Marx's work. The first draws on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, where world history is the process by which humans are born through their labour. The second draws on The German Ideology, where it is the evolving history of material production. The third is a specific sense, in which world history is the expansion of the capitalist mode of production.

In the 1844 Manuscripts, Duan finds two layers. Marx adopts Feuerbach's notion of the human species-essence and treats communism as the positive sublation of alienated labour. In this layer he still follows Hegel's speculative logic of alienation and return. Marx also separates alienated labour from objectifying labour. The latter is humanity's transformation of nature and cannot be abolished, so history becomes the history of objective activity. In The German Ideology, Duan argues, Marx explains ideas from material practice rather than the reverse. He starts from real individuals acting under given material conditions, treats the production of life as both a natural and a social relation, and concludes that all history is first of all a history of production, not of ideas.

In the specific sense, Duan traces capital from landed property through medieval guild capital and merchant capital to industrial capital. Industrial capital, in Marx's account, dissolves naturally formed local and national limits and turns relations into money relations. As local and national production is drawn into the capitalist system, Duan writes, history becomes world history in the true sense. Marx mostly uses the term in this sense, Duan says. The article does not go beyond this exposition of Marx's texts. Read the original if you want a concise outline of how Marx moved from Hegelian alienation to a materialist and capital-centred account of world history.
quoteEn: By renewing and reconstructing Hegel's concept of "world history", Marx achieved an innovation in the principle of historical explanation and gave the concept of "world history" a new meaning.
quoteZh: 马克思通过对黑格尔“世界历史”概念的革新与重构，实现了历史解释原则的创新，赋予“世界历史”概念新的意义。

t: Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's important statements on ideological work
zh: 认真学习贯彻习近平总书记关于意识形态工作的重要论述
paras: This article, published in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts in 2024, takes up how Party cadres should understand and carry out ideological work under Xi Jinping's leadership. Cai argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Central Committee has strengthened centralised and unified leadership over ideology and has produced a fundamental shift in the situation in this field. The author calls on readers to study Xi's statements, take up the political responsibility of safeguarding ideological security, and build a socialist ideology with strong cohesion and guiding power.

The piece is organised in three parts. The first explains why ideological work is of the utmost importance. The second sets out why it is urgent now, looking at the state of social thinking, economic and social development, the building of a strong socialist culture, information technology and the international situation. The third lists practical measures for the coming year, drawing on Xi Jinping's cultural thought and the national conferences on propaganda and ideological work.

Cai's central claim, following Xi, is that ideological work bears on the Party's future, on the country's long-term stability and on national cohesion. The author argues that regimes often collapse first in the realm of ideas, cites the fall of the Soviet Union as a warning, and describes Western infiltration, "peaceful evolution" and "colour revolutions" as intensifying threats. Cai also says that Western "constitutional democracy", neoliberalism and historical nihilism keep reappearing in new forms, so Marxism must be established as the leading ideology amid plural currents. The article treats the internet as the main arena of struggle and says that growing competition between major powers has made the ideological contest more complex.

For practice, Cai proposes five reinforcements: arming Party members with the Party's innovative theory, positive propaganda including economic messaging and international communication, risk monitoring and prevention, tighter control of ideological positions such as schools, media, publishing and emerging technologies like AI, and stronger Party leadership. On the last point, Cai calls for revising the ideological responsibility system, with risk assessment, summons, inspection and accountability so that it has "teeth". Read the original if you want a clear example of how official Party journals set out the tasks, rationale and mechanisms of ideological work in the Xi Jinping era.
quoteEn: Ideological work is work that establishes a heart for the country and a soul for the nation, and forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation is an important part of it.
quoteZh: 意识形态工作是为国家立心、为民族立魂的工作，铸牢中华民族共同体意识是意识形态工作的重要内容

glossary.explanation: The Party's work of shaping and guiding public thought, covering theory education, propaganda, media, culture and education. It is treated as a core responsibility of Party committees.

t: Accelerating the construction of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics
zh: 加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学
paras: Chen Yulu asks how Chinese universities should carry out the Party Central Committee's call to speed up the building of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics. Citing Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) and a recent national meeting of publicity department heads, Chen argues that universities must link this task to Chinese modernization and to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The piece is a Party-theory commentary that draws its institutional examples from Nankai University.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the foundations: Marxism as the "soul" and fine traditional Chinese culture as the "root". The second turns to the three systems named in Xi's formula, namely the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems, and ties them to Chinese modernization. The third sets out what universities should do, with Nankai's history, motto and current initiatives as illustration.

Chen argues that the field must be guided by Marxism, specifically Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Researchers should be oriented to the people and to problems, and should "write their papers on the land of the motherland". The author also holds that traditional culture, patriotism and the Two Integrations give the field its roots. On the three systems, Chen calls for a balanced disciplinary layout that supports key, emerging, niche and weak subjects, and for new concepts and methods, including the use of big data and AI. Chen also wants a discourse that blends the best of Western scholarship with Chinese terms and gives China an international voice matching its standing. For universities, the central task is building an autonomous Chinese knowledge system, which Chen presents as both a practical and a theoretical need, including breaking what the article calls the Western monopoly on knowledge.

Chen concludes that universities, as one of the "five armies" of philosophy and social science, should lead in this work. Chen proposes four measures: building an autonomous knowledge system, cultivating talent under the principle of fostering virtue through education, expanding "organised research" around the major issues of modernization, and improving international communication. Nankai's forums and cultural events are offered as examples. Read the original if you want to see how a university leader presents the official agenda for Chinese philosophy and social sciences, and how Party guidance, traditional culture and institutional practice are linked in it.
quoteEn: To accelerate the construction of philosophy and social sciences with Chinese characteristics, we must proceed from the needs of Chinese modernization and further improve the disciplinary system of philosophy and social sciences.
quoteZh: 加快构建中国特色哲学社会科学，必须立足中国式现代化建设需要，进一步完善哲学社会科学学科体系。

glossary.explanation: The official concept of China's own path of modernization, promoted since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as sharing features common to all modernizations while reflecting China's national conditions.
Xi Jinping's formula for combining the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions. It is presented as the latest stage of adapting Marxism to China.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China to national strength and international standing by the mid-twenty-first century.
An approach in which universities steer research in a coordinated way toward major national needs and strategic problems, rather than leaving it to individual scholars' choices.
An official principle that the fundamental task of education is moral and ideological formation as well as teaching knowledge.

t: Who judges democracy, and how?
st: Studying and absorbing Xi Jinping's important statements on democracy
zh: 民主由谁评判、怎么评判
zhSub: 学习领悟习近平总书记关于民主的重要论述
paras: This study-and-commentary piece, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2024, asks who has the right to judge whether a country is democratic and by what criteria. Si Li answers by expounding Xi Jinping's statements on the subject. The core claim is that a country's own people, not a few outside states, judge its democracy, and that whole-process people's democracy meets the proper criteria.

The article has three parts. The first treats the question of who judges. The second sets out how a political system should be assessed, drawing on the "eight abilities" standard Xi announced in 2014 and the later "four looks, four more-so looks" formulation. The third presents whole-process people's democracy as the "most broad, most genuine and most effective" democracy, a description Si traces to the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It closes by linking this to the 70th anniversary of the National People's Congress.

Si argues that democracy belongs to all peoples and cannot be a monopoly of a few states. Judging varied political systems by a single yardstick is, in Xi's words, itself undemocratic. In Si's account, bourgeois democracy began with popular sovereignty but in practice became rule by the wealthy, and only proletarian democracy frees the democratic subject from the constraints of capital. Si holds that the Chinese model grew from China's own history and conditions. Against a model in which people matter only at election time, the article stresses substantive participation, fulfilment of promises, enforcement of laws and supervision of power. It credits the system of people's congresses, multiparty cooperation under Communist Party leadership, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots self-government with giving institutional form to the people being masters of the country.

Si concludes that whole-process people's democracy unifies process and outcome, procedure and substance, direct and indirect democracy, and the people's will and the state's will. The author presents this as a contribution of Chinese wisdom to human political civilization and calls for firmly following the path of political development of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
