Read the original if you want a short statement of the 'critical' reading of value theory, which draws on Postone, and of how it differs from the distributive-justice reading common in Chinese scholarship.
quoteEn: In its actuality, 'labour creates value' is 'wage labour creates profit'.
quoteZh: “劳动创造价值”在其现实性上就是“雇佣劳动创造利润”。

t: Is labour the foundation of Marx's critique of capitalism?
st: On Moishe Postone's interpretation of Marx's critical theory
zh: 劳动是马克思资本主义批判的基础吗？
zhSub: 论普舒同对马克思批判理论的阐释
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 7 March 2024
paras: Wu Meng takes up a common assumption in contemporary scholarship: that labour is the cornerstone of Marx's social theory, both as an ontological basis for human society and as the fulcrum of his critique of capitalism. The article examines the challenge to this view posed by the late American left thinker Moishe Postone, and argues that Postone is right to raise the question of historicity but fails to answer it convincingly. In Wu's reading, Marx does not treat labour as the foundation of capitalist society at all.

The piece is a short newspaper commentary built in three steps. It first sets out Postone's claim, in Time, Labor, and Social Domination, that the idea of labour as creator of the social world and source of wealth applies only to capitalist society, not to society in general. It then criticises Postone's account of abstract labour, and finally returns to Marx's own texts, notably the 1857–58 manuscripts, to reposition labour within Marx's thought.

Wu credits Postone with restoring a historical dimension: separating trans-historical labour from specifically capitalist labour guards historical materialism against metaphysics. But Wu argues that Postone misreads abstract labour as labour's function as a social mediating activity. For Marx, Wu says, abstract human labour expresses the equalisation of different concrete labours, a 'social effect' of the whole capitalist production mechanism and of a total 'world of commodities', not a form of labour. Wu traces this error to Postone's 'foundationalism', which looks for a homogeneous basis for capitalist totality and, in Wu's view, also obscures the class domination workers suffer from the bourgeoisie. Citing Marx, Wu contends that capitalist social structure precedes labour's apparent foundational role, which is an 'appearance'. The real question for Marx is why labour appears as value, not whether labour constructs it; the view that labour constructs value is the classical political economy Marx criticised.

Wu concludes that Postone mistook classical political economy's emphasis on labour's foundational status for Marx's own position, and so did not adequately reflect on labour's place in Marx's thought. Wu calls for facing changes in contemporary life as Marx did, in a historical-materialist way, without presupposed concepts. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese critique of Postone's reading of abstract labour and of the labour-ontology view of Marx.
quoteEn: In Marx, the prior existence of the historically specific capitalist social structure is the basic precondition that allows labour to appear as playing a foundational role, not the other way round.
quoteZh: 在马克思那里,历史性的资本主义社会结构的先行存在,是使得劳动能够表现为具有基础作用的基本前提,而不是相反。

t: The "Three Initiatives": a three-dimensional presentation of the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: “三大倡议”：人类命运共同体理念的立体化呈现
paras: Liu Zhigang asks how China's Global Development Initiative (2021), Global Security Initiative (2022) and Global Civilization Initiative (2023) relate to the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The article argues that the three initiatives follow one logic and make the idea concrete and theoretical. In Liu's account they answer three global problems, namely development, security and civilisation, and extend the Belt and Road Initiative.

After a framing section on the three initiatives as a set, the article gives one section to each. The development initiative is presented as laying the material foundation, the security initiative as ensuring lasting peace, and the civilisation initiative as building value consensus. Each section sets the initiative against Western counterparts, which the author labels "development first for the West", "absolute security" and the "clash of civilizations". Each section also lists practical steps, such as the Group of Friends of the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative Concept Paper, the Saudi–Iran reconciliation and dialogue forums among civilisations.

Liu's central claim is that the initiatives are complementary. Development supplies the material conditions for security and cultural exchange, security supplies a stable environment, and shared values supply a spiritual and ethical base. In Liu's reading, each initiative also surpasses a Western model: capital-first and self-first development, bloc-based "absolute security", and civilisational superiority and "universal values". The author cites figures to support this, including China's average contribution of 38.6 per cent to global growth over ten years and more than 70 per cent of global poverty reduction. Liu also draws on the Chinese tradition of harmony in diversity and holds that the common values of humanity differ in kind from Western "universal values".

Liu concludes that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind is a set of concrete public goods rather than empty rhetoric. The author holds that the three initiatives reshape the global economic, governance and civilisational orders. They also express a dialectical unity of the universal and the particular, and give the idea a basis in the laws of historical development. The article is written in the official voice and assesses foreign powers throughout in sharply critical terms. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Chinese scholars frame the three global initiatives as one system and contrast them with Western models.
quoteEn: The "Three Initiatives" focus on three basic human pursuits, namely material abundance, peace and stability, and spiritual richness, and reflect the holistic thinking behind China's efforts to build a community with a shared future for mankind.
quoteZh: “三大倡议”聚焦人类社会物质丰富、和平稳定、精神富有三大基本追求，体现了中国推动构建人类命运共同体的整体性思维

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept that Xi Jinping first put forward in 2013. It calls for shared development, common security and cultural exchange among states, and has been written into several UN and other multilateral documents.
Proposed by Xi Jinping at the UN General Assembly in 2021. It puts development at the centre of the global agenda and is linked to the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Put forward by Xi Jinping at the Boao Forum in 2022. It promotes "common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security" and the principle that security is indivisible.

Proposed by Xi Jinping in March 2023 at a high-level dialogue between the Communist Party of China and world political parties. It stresses respect for civilisational diversity, common values of humanity and cultural exchange.
A Chinese international cooperation initiative launched in 2013 that centres on infrastructure, trade and connectivity projects across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Cheng Jing's Marxist historiography
zh: 程憬的马克思主义史学研究
source: Historical Theory Studies (Shixue lilun yanjiu), 2024 no. 1
paras: Cheng Jing (1902–1950) is little discussed in current scholarship, though Republican-era scholars noted his work. This article asks where he belongs in the history of Chinese Marxist historiography. Li and Li argue that he was an important early pioneer: he accepted historical materialism in the early 1920s, and between 1928 and 1933 he published studies of Chinese social history whose approach matched that of Guo Moruo and Lü Zhenyu and which appeared no later than theirs.

The article first traces Cheng's route to Marxist historiography: the New Culture and May Fourth setting, study under Hu Shi, Marxist reading at Peking University, and training at the Tsinghua Institute of Chinese Classics under Liang Qichao and Wang Guowei. It then examines his social history of ancient China, followed by his history of Chinese philosophy, covering pre-Qin thought and early modern Neo-Confucianism. A final section assesses the distinctive value of his work.

On social history, the authors argue that Cheng set out a fairly complete scheme of social formations. It ran from primitive society that developed from the "horde" into the clan, through a patrilineal clan society under the Shang, to a feudal Western Zhou and a "disguised feudalism" from the Eastern Zhou and after the Qin. The authors hold that his Western Zhou and Spring and Autumn views preceded Lü's formulations and that he was closer to Lü than to Guo. On philosophy, they show him moving beyond Hu Shi's positivist model. He explained Laozi's thought through the collapse of the feudal order and answered why Confucianism suited post-Qin society. He also divided early modern Neo-Confucianism into three schools, based on principle, mind and qi, which they compare with Zhang Dainian's later scheme and place near Hou Wailu's method.

The authors conclude that Cheng's work has two distinctive values. He broke through positivist historiography from inside that camp, since he was a former secretary to Hu Shi and a friend of Gu Jiegang. His work also shows an internal, scholarly path to Marxist historiography, independent of political events such as the failure of the Great Revolution and the social history debate. They concede that his depth generally fell short of Guo and Lü. Read the original if you study the early history of Marxist historiography in China, the debates over periodising ancient Chinese society, or the Republican-era relation between positivism and historical materialism.
quoteEn: This breakthrough from within the camp of positivist historiography better demonstrates the scientific character of the Marxist path in historiography.
quoteZh: 这一来自实证主义史学阵营内部的突破，更能证明马克思主义史学道路的科学性。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory of history, which explains social change through material production and class relations. In China it was introduced and popularised from the 1910s and 1920s.
A broad controversy of the late 1920s and 1930s over the nature and stages of Chinese society, linked to disputes over the character of the Chinese revolution.
The dominant Republican-era school, associated with Hu Shi, Gu Jiegang, Fu Sinian and Wang Guowei, which stressed evidence, textual criticism and new source materials.

t: The rise and fall of late-developing modernization and the state: an analysis based on state autonomy and state embeddedness
zh: 国家与后发现代化的荣枯——基于国家自主性和国家嵌入性的分析
source: Journal of Peking University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2024 no. 2
paras: Sun Daiyao and Diao Weiqi ask what kind of state, and what kind of state–society relationship, helps late-developing countries modernize. Their answer is that two variables, state autonomy and state embeddedness, each high or low, decide whether the state plays a positive role. The authors argue that only a state combining fairly high levels of both can steer modernization well.

The article first reviews theories of state autonomy: Marx and Engels on Bonapartism, Weber on bureaucracy, the relative-autonomy debate between Poulantzas and Miliband, Huntington's political order thesis, the East Asian 'developmental state' (Chalmers Johnson), the 'bringing the state back in' school, and the later 'state in society' and 'embedded autonomy' approaches of Migdal, Evans and Weiss. It then defines the two concepts and builds a four-quadrant model. Four cases illustrate it: Argentina and India (low autonomy, high embeddedness), Nigeria (low autonomy, low embeddedness), Saudi Arabia (high autonomy, low embeddedness) and South Korea (high on both).

The authors criticise Evans for using autonomy and bureaucratic completeness interchangeably and for leaving the path from 'embedded autonomy' to performance unexplained. They define autonomy as the state's capacity to decide and enforce policy against social forces, and embeddedness as the channels through which it gathers information from, and consults, society broadly rather than only some groups. Taking resource allocation and industrial upgrading as the mediating mechanism, they argue that the state must remove barriers to resource mobility and also concentrate resources on strategic industries, withdrawing in time. In their account, early democratization in Argentina and India left the state unable to concentrate resources or overcome entrenched interests. Strong groups or ethnic forces captured resources in Nigeria, and a rentier bureaucracy absorbed them in Saudi Arabia. South Korea's planning, infrastructure and industrial policy under Park Chung-hee is presented as the successful case.

The authors conclude that late developers need relatively high autonomy and embeddedness throughout modernization, but that pushing either to an extreme, such as total state takeover of society, backfires. They acknowledge limits: the industry-and-resources lens misses political, social and cultural dimensions, and the determinants and variability of the two traits need further study. They add that a state can raise either through reform, or slide down the scale as interest groups grow. Read the original if you want a comparative framework for the state's role in late development, with case material on Argentina, India, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and South Korea.
quoteEn: Therefore, only a state combining a fairly high degree of both autonomy and embeddedness can play a positive role in both removing barriers to the free flow of resources and steering resources towards strategic industries.
quoteZh: 因此，唯有兼具较高程度自主性和嵌入性的国家，才能在排除资源自由流动障碍和促进资源流向战略产业这两方面发挥积极作用。

t: Mao Zedong's reflections on major questions of the Chinese revolution during the Great Revolution: an analysis of "The Significance of Commemorating the Paris Commune"
zh: 大革命时期毛泽东对中国革命重大问题的思考——基于《纪念巴黎公社的重要意义》的分析
paras: Tang and Chen examine a short lecture Mao Zedong gave in 1926 at the Kuomintang's political training class to mark the 55th anniversary of the Paris Commune. The text is only about 2,000 characters long, yet the authors argue that it deals systematically with the conditions, significance and lessons of the Commune. Their thesis is that, by reading the Commune closely against Chinese conditions during the First United Front, Mao thought through a series of major questions of the Chinese revolution. In their account this laid a theoretical foundation for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and for the later theory of the New Democratic revolution.

The article is organised around four themes drawn from the lecture. It first treats changes in the revolutionary situation, namely the revolution's character, its strategy and its goal. It then turns to the forces of revolution, to armed struggle as the basic form of revolution, and finally to principles and strategies for moving the revolution forward. The authors set Mao's lecture beside his other writings of the 1920s and 1930s, and beside the positions of the Comintern, the early Party congresses and Chen Duxiu.

The authors make three main moves. First, they argue that Mao saw the revolution shifting from a movement of the few to one involving the majority of workers and peasants, to be mobilised politically and aimed at a workers' and peasants' state on the Soviet model. Second, they say Mao insisted that the proletariat and its Party must lead, against the then-dominant underestimation of the working class, and that armed struggle was the basic form of revolution, to be pursued by drawing flexibly on the Commune and the October Revolution rather than copying them. Third, they report that Mao read the Commune's failure as stemming from the lack of a unified, disciplined party and of severe treatment of enemies. The authors link these points to the Party's centralised and unified leadership, to Party building, and to the principle of delivering a decisive blow to the enemy, which they contrast with Chen Duxiu's conciliatory line.

Tang and Chen conclude that the lecture marks an early, pioneering step in Mao's theoretical and practical awareness of adapting Marxism to China. They see in it the seeds of the later path of encircling the cities from the countryside and seizing power by armed force. They also urge readers today, in a period of great changes unseen in a century, to study it so as to strengthen the fighting spirit and overcome risks to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you study Mao's early thought, the Party's official historiography of the Great Revolution, or how Commune lessons are used in Chinese Marxist theory.
quoteEn: In "The Significance of Commemorating the Paris Commune", Mao's view that all backward institutions must be destroyed and a new regime representing the people's interests established inherits, and develops in a Chinese form, the Marxist-Leninist idea of "smashing the old state machine".
quoteZh: 毛泽东在《纪念巴黎公社的重要意义》中，对摧毁一切落后制度，建立代表人民利益的新政权的认识，是对马克思列宁主义关于“打碎旧的国家机器”思想的继承和中国化发展

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxism to Chinese conditions and developing it with the times. The authors treat Mao's 1926 lecture as an early example.
Mao's theory, developed in the late 1930s and 1940s, of the first stage of the Chinese revolution. It is an anti-imperialist, anti-feudal revolution led by the proletariat and an alliance of classes.

The Chinese term for the 1924–1927 national revolution, fought under the First United Front between the Communist Party and the Kuomintang. It ended with the Kuomintang's anti-Communist purges of 1927.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of the Party since the 2010s, referring to restoring China's national strength and international standing.

t: Sources and practice of Mao Zedong's idea of "proletarian revolutionary utilitarianism"
zh: 毛泽东“无产阶级的革命的功利主义”思想的源头与实践
paras: Miao Guishan examines the origins and practice of the idea of "proletarian revolutionary utilitarianism" that Mao Zedong put forward at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art in May 1942. In that talk Mao said Communists take as their starting point the unity of the present and future interests of the great majority, and so aim at the "broadest and most distant" goals rather than narrow, local ones. Miao argues that the idea has several distinct theoretical roots and was carried out in the Party's revolutionary practice, as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The article first summarises the idea's content: it is a question of standpoint (serving workers, peasants and soldiers) and of method (the mass line), it applies equally to military and cultural work, and it differs in kind from feudal, bourgeois and petty-bourgeois utilitarianism. It then has four sections on sources. These are the young Mao's reading of Friedrich Paulsen's ethics and of utilitarianism; the Communist Manifesto and the theory of the Chinese revolution; Lenin and Lu Xun on literature; and the practice of the new-democratic revolution.

Miao's central move traces the idea to Mao's 1917 annotations of Cai Yuanpei's Chinese version of Paulsen's System of Ethics, studied under his teacher Yang Changji. Mao took from Paulsen a teleological theory of self-realisation, which Miao links to his own ideal of the heroic individual and to the Chinese tradition of sacrificing life for righteousness. Miao says this ideal turned into a proletarian value outlook once Mao embraced Marxism around 1920. Miao adds that the Manifesto's claim that proletarian movements serve the immense majority, together with Mao's wartime analyses of class forces and revolutionary stages, supplied the theoretical premise. Lenin's "literature for the millions of working people" and Lu Xun's couplet about serving the people like an ox supplied the standpoint. Mao's own formula that Communists' words and actions must meet "the greatest interests of the greatest number" echoes Bentham and Mill, as mediated by Yang Changji's history of Western ethics. In the new-democratic period Mao made this a productive-forces standard, and the Party's "serve the people" purpose followed from it.

Miao concludes that the idea is true because it accords with the people's interests and has been tested in China's revolution and construction. The article also presents it as an ethical consciousness in individual Communists and an ethical spirit in the Party as a political community, citing Mao's three principles in On Coalition Government. Read the original if you study Mao's intellectual formation, the links between Chinese ethics and Marxism, or how official scholarship traces the origins of Mao Zedong Thought.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's idea of \"proletarian revolutionary utilitarianism\" began with the teleological theory of individual self-realisation that the nineteenth-century German Paulsen advanced by reworking Bentham's and Mill's utilitarianism, which Mao studied closely at Hunan First Normal School.
quoteZh: 毛泽东提出的“无产阶级的革命的功利主义”思想，肇端于他在湖南省立第一师范学校求学时研读颇深的19世纪德国人包尔生在改造边沁、密尔的功利主义基础上所倡导的目的论的个体自我实现论。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to changing eras. Mao's wartime work is treated as an early landmark of this process.

glossary.zh: 无产阶级的革命的功利主义
glossary.pinyin: wúchǎn jiējí de gémìng de gōnglìzhǔyì
glossary.explanation: Mao's phrase from the 1942 Yan'an talks. It means judging action by the combined present and future interests of the great majority of the people, as opposed to the narrow utilitarianism of exploiting classes or individuals.
The Party's working method of drawing on the masses' views and needs and then returning policy to them. It is closely associated with Mao.
Mao's term for the stage of Chinese revolution under proletarian leadership, with a bourgeois-democratic character, that was meant to precede socialism.
The Party's and army's stated purpose, made prominent by Mao in the 1940s.

t: The historical logic of East European neo-Marxism
st: On the contemporary significance of research on East European neo-Marxism
zh: 东欧新马克思主义的历史逻辑——兼论东欧新马克思主义研究的当代意义
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 23 January 2024
paras: Song Tieyi takes up a question about classification: East European neo-Marxism has long been treated as a branch or appendage of Western Marxism, so its own theoretical significance has gone under-recognised. The author argues that the two traditions share a source in Lukács's turn in Marxist theory but differ in historical logic, and that East European neo-Marxism should not be equated with Western Marxism. This short newspaper commentary also draws out what studying it means today.

Song begins with the two usual reasons for the conflation: the shared Lukácsian origin, and the fact that, apart from the Budapest School, East European currents did not survive as continuing schools. The article then uses the Czech philosopher Karel Kosík and his Dialectics of the Concrete as its main case. It proceeds in three steps: Kosík's totalising cultural critique, its extension into a critique of political economy, and its openness to history. It closes by relating the discussion to Marx's late thought and to present-day research.

The central claim is that Lukács left a double path of cultural critique and critique of political economy, and a split between methodology and ontology. Western Marxism, in Song's reading, carried on mainly as theoretical critique, whereas East European neo-Marxists, working from the practice of socialist states, tried to unite the two paths in a 'humanist socialism'. Song reads Kosík's concrete dialectics as the key example. Kosík criticises the 'pseudo-concrete' world of reified, fetishised everyday utilitarian practice, then argues that the 'economic man' of classical economics is a product of economics itself, not its premise. For Song, his dialectic is at once the self-unfolding of the 'thing in itself' and the method for pursuing it, which heals the split Lukács left. Song also links this to Marx's late writings on the Asiatic mode of production, the 'Kaufine Gorge' idea and the reply to Zasulich.

Song concludes that East European neo-Marxism was itself an expression of historical practice and stayed open to diverse historical paths on a humanist, national-cultural basis. The author connects this to adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times and to the Two Integrations, which are said to have answered the questions Marx left in his late work. Further study of East European experience is said to deepen understanding of how Marxism becomes localised worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language case for separating East European neo-Marxism from Western Marxism, centred on Kosík.
quoteEn: Therefore, unlike Western Marxism, when confronting the predicament of Lukács's theory, East European neo-Marxism consistently tried, on the basis of the historical practice of socialism, to unify cultural critique with the critique of political economy, and ultimately formed the theoretical conception of 'humanist socialism'.
quoteZh: 因此，与西方马克思主义不同，东欧新马克思主义在面对卢卡奇理论的困境时，始终基于社会主义的历史实践而尝试将文化批判与政治经济批判统一起来，并最终形成了“人道主义社会主义”的理论构想。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official formula for the Party's project of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to the current era. It is used to frame Chinese theoretical development as a continuing process.
Formula associated with Xi Jinping: combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities, and with China's fine traditional culture.
Label for the theoretical project of East European neo-Marxists who sought a socialism centred on the human being and practice, in contrast to Soviet orthodoxy.
Image used by Marx in late writings on Russia for the possibility that a society might skip the full capitalist stage of development. Rendered 'Caudine Forks' in some English editions.

t: Re-examining Marx's concept of abstract labour
zh: 重新审视马克思的抽象劳动概念
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 29 January 2024
paras: Wang Shaoliang takes up a long-running dispute over what Marx meant by abstract labour. Citing the Soviet economist Isaak Rubin's contemporary Rozenberg's early objection (1930s) to treating it as merely a physiological expenditure of labour-power, Wang argues that the physiological reading takes an epistemological sense of "abstraction" for Marx's own. In Wang's account, abstract labour is a social and ontological category specific to capitalism, not a natural property of human labour in every era.

The piece is a short theoretical commentary in three parts. It first traces the philosophical history of "abstraction" from Aristotle and Plato through Kant, Hegel and Feuerbach, and shows how this lineage produces a naturalistic reading. It then turns to Marx's ontological critique, drawing on the 1844 Manuscripts and Capital, and finally to the social determination of abstract labour and the "abstraction of labour" as a historical process. Wang also notes that Marx uses varying formulations and qualifiers such as "common", "universal" and "undifferentiated".

Wang argues that the physiological definition in Capital is a result reached "after the event", a post festum analysis that expresses capitalist commodity economy in the language of natural science and so makes wage labour look eternal. Marx, in this reading, moves abstraction into ontology: value has a "phantom-like objectivity" that is real yet detached from sensuous objectivity, and socially necessary labour time acts as a hidden structural power over workers and capitalists alike. The Latin root abstrahere, meaning separation, points to the historical separation of labourers from the means of production and from ethical ties, so that abstraction is a real, daily process in production. Wang accordingly distinguishes abstract labour from "labour in general", and criticises Paul Sweezy for equating them.

Wang concludes that abstract labour becomes the subject of modern social development only under definite historical conditions, and that attributing the substance and source of value to it can be explained only within the movement of capitalism. The analysis in Capital is said to unite scientific analysis with critique of value, since abstraction both negates individuality and gives private labour a social character. Read the original if you work on Marx's value theory or the philosophical background to Chinese debates about abstract labour and want a compact ontological alternative to the physiological interpretation.
quoteEn: Abstract labour is a social category, not a natural one.
quoteZh: 抽象劳动是一个社会范畴而非自然范畴。

t: Deconstruction and restoration: the road to rebuilding the history of Chinese Marxist historiography
zh: 解构与还原：中国马克思主义史学史的重建之路
paras: Chen Feng notes that research on the history of Chinese Marxist historiography has become a fast-growing field, drawing many young scholars, and asks how it can move beyond routine work. The article argues for two tasks: deconstructing long-standing presuppositions, and restoring the real picture of the field by returning to primary sources and engaging critically with them.

The article has two parts. The first examines four presuppositions that Chen traces to a "revolutionary history paradigm", in which Marxist historiography becomes a branch of revolutionary history. The second sets out how to restore the field's actual shape, covering which sources to read, how to read them, and the part played by the researcher's own standpoint.

In the first part, Chen challenges four assumptions. These are that Marxist historiography is the final form of historical scholarship; that it must fuse politics and scholarship; that it is the same as "Chinese Communist Party historiography"; and that its unity hides its internal differences. Chen argues the first is teleological and unhistorical, since Marxism treats everything as developing. Chen also holds that Marxism is both a revolutionary theory and a social science, so scholars could use it without sharing the political faith. Chen further distinguishes official from academic Marxist historiography and stresses breaks and disputes among its figures and periods. In the second part, Chen urges reading far beyond the few canonical authors. Suggested sources include non-Marxist periodicals, reviews, diaries and letters, popular works, ultra-left-period writings, and hostile Kuomintang criticism. Chen also proposes shifting from "confirmatory" to "discovery" reading, and treats restoration as also a reconstruction in which the researcher's present outlook meets the objective record.

Chen concludes that the field is dominated by orthodox, uneventful studies and must deliberately "defamiliarise" itself. It should dare to question inherited theories and conclusions, and aim at a "new Marxist historiography history", modelled on the shift to the "new revolutionary history" in modern Chinese history. The result, Chen says, would be a new scholarly map that is closer to the past and guides future Marxist historiography. Read the original if you study Chinese historiography or the self-critical turn in Chinese scholarship on Marxism, or want concrete source suggestions for the period before and after 1949.
quoteEn: Scholarship and belief can be joined or separated; their unity is the exception rather than the rule.
quoteZh: 学术与信仰可以相合，也可以相离——二者合一是特例而非通则。

glossary.explanation: An approach that periodises and judges historical scholarship by the stages and values of the revolutionary movement. Chen says it long shaped studies of Marxist historiography.
A recent trend in studies of modern Chinese history that revises the older revolutionary-history approach. Chen cites it as a model for a revised history of Marxist historiography.

t: Xi Jinping's inheritance and enrichment of Mao Zedong's view of traditional culture
zh: 论习近平对毛泽东传统文化观的继承与丰富发展
source: Social Sciences Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2024 no. 2
paras: Zhang Guozuo and Sun Yafang ask how Xi Jinping's attitude to traditional Chinese culture relates to that of Mao Zedong. They argue that Xi has creatively inherited Mao's view of traditional culture and enriched it with new ideas, judgements and strategic plans. The article, published in Social Sciences Journal (2024, no. 2), defines traditional culture as mainly Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist thought, and presents Xi's contribution as part of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times.

The article has three parts. The first identifies four strands in Mao's view: valuing national history, keeping the national culture primary, applying Marxism in light of Chinese characteristics, and absorbing the essence while discarding the dross. For each, the authors pair a Xi counterpart, using quotations from speeches between 2012 and 2022. The second part lists Xi's additions, and the third assesses their significance.

In the authors' reading, each Maoist idea is carried a step further. Valuing history becomes strengthening cultural confidence. Giving priority to national culture becomes holding to a Chinese cultural standpoint. Applying Marxism with Chinese characteristics becomes the Two Integrations, notably combining Marxism's basic principles with excellent traditional culture. Mao's selective method becomes 'discriminating treatment and sublating inheritance', which adds creative transformation and innovative development. The authors say Xi deepens the standing of this culture as the nation's 'root and soul' and as the root of Party theoretical innovation. They also say he gives it practical roles in governance, core socialist values, philosophy and social sciences, and literature and art. Finally, they say he sets out a systematic programme covering research, education, display, and legal protection of cultural heritage.

The authors conclude that Mao's era mostly concerned breaking down old culture and left the value, transformation and development of tradition unexamined theoretically. Xi's contribution, they argue, lies mainly in 'establishing'. They say it strengthens cultural confidence, opens a new horizon through the Two Integrations, supplies resources for a new form of human civilization and Chinese modern civilization, and underpins cultural soft power amid what they describe as hostile international pressure. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned account of how Party theorists present continuity and development between Mao's and Xi's cultural policy, with many dated Xi quotations.
quoteEn: Xi Jinping's inheritance and enrichment of Mao Zedong's view of traditional culture is mainly manifested in 'establishing', and it makes an important theoretical contribution of extraordinary significance.
quoteZh: 习近平对毛泽东传统文化观的继承和丰富发展，主要体现在“立”上，而且作出了重要的理论贡献，意义非凡。

glossary.explanation: Formula in Party theory: combining Marxism's basic principles with China's concrete realities (the first) and with excellent traditional Chinese culture (the second). Xi Jinping stressed the second integration from 2021–2023.

Official term for confidence in China's own culture, including traditional culture, revolutionary culture and socialist culture. Xi Jinping has described it as the foundation of confidence in China's path, theory and system.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official formula for the Party's ongoing project of fitting Marxism to China's conditions and to each era.

glossary.zh: 有鉴别的对待，有扬弃的继承
glossary.pinyin: yǒu jiànbié de duìdài, yǒu yángqì de jìchéng
glossary.literal: treating with discrimination, inheriting with sublation
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for handling traditional culture: sort its essence from the outdated, discard the latter, and develop the former.
A set of 24 characters in twelve values at the national, social and individual levels, promoted officially since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
Term adapted from Joseph Nye, used in Chinese policy to denote a country's cultural appeal and influence.

t: Strengthening theoretical and empirical research on China's culture and civilization
zh: 加强我国文化、文明的理论和经验研究
source: Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2024 no. 1
paras: This short editorial introduction argues that research on culture and civilization in China needs to be strengthened, both theoretically and empirically. Li Peilin notes that 'culture' is among the most widely studied yet most variously understood concepts in the humanities and social sciences. He holds that its importance in China is tied to the country's long civilizational history and to Chinese modernization, in which cultural development is one of five areas of construction.

The piece first sketches how Chinese intellectuals have treated traditional culture since the Opium War of 1840. It then distinguishes culture from civilization, notes the lack of a discipline of 'culturology', and introduces three articles by young scholars on a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences project.

Li argues that the dominant modern intellectual current, from the Westernizing Movement to the May Fourth Movement, leaned towards a break with tradition, unlike the European Renaissance. He cites Hegel and Weber as Western thinkers sceptical that Chinese culture could modernize. Two parallel strands, he says, are often overlooked: the persistence of culture in everyday life, and the deep influence of tradition on reform thought, which grew into cultural self-awareness after reform and opening up. Li also separates culture, understood as 'humanization', from civilization, which he links to writing, cities and social ritual. He says culture research is treated as interdisciplinary and mostly humanistic, which limits scholarly consensus and calls for more empirical disciplines.

Li presents building a culturally strong country and shaping a modern Chinese civilization as current tasks for Chinese social science. He introduces a 2023 national survey of residents' satisfaction with cultural development and three articles drawing on it, on cultural needs and confidence, cultural subjectivity, and cultural governance. He hopes more scholars will join, making the field more standardized and mature. Read the original if you want a brief view from a leading Chinese sociologist on how culture and civilization research is being organised in China.
quoteEn: Cultural research needs stronger disciplinary construction, and in particular needs greater participation from the empirical disciplines.
quoteZh: 文化研究需要加强学科化建设，也特别需要经验学科的更多参与。

glossary.explanation: The official Party formulation of China's own path to modernization, promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
A concept associated with the sociologist Fei Xiaotong, meaning a society's reflective understanding of its own culture. It is widely used in Chinese discussions of culture.
An official goal of building China's cultural capacity and influence, set out in Party documents.
The management and guidance of cultural affairs through state and social institutions, a topic in Chinese policy and academic debate.

t: Raising the international reach of research on contemporary Chinese history
zh: 提升当代中国史研究的国际传播力
paras: This is a reflective essay by Zhang Xingxing, editor-in-chief of Contemporary China History Studies from 2008 to 2019, written for the journal's 30th anniversary in 2024. Zhang asks how the only specialist academic journal on the history of the People's Republic could strengthen the international reach of research in this field. The answer, drawn from the author's own twelve years in post, is a combination of four practices: attending international academic events, recruiting overseas authors, co-organising conferences abroad, and publishing an English-language edition.

The essay is organised in four numbered sections, each built on dated examples. It covers the author's participation in the 2007 Beijing congress of the International Committee of Historical Sciences, the 2010 Amsterdam International Congress of Historical Sciences, and a 2015 Melbourne conference on the global nuclear order. It then lists foreign contributors, including the Russian scholar Mikhail Titarenko, Ezra Vogel of Harvard, and scholars from Japan, Sweden, Germany, Korea and Vietnam. Further sections cover joint seminars in Moscow and Hanoi, and the troubled path to an English edition with the Dutch publisher Brill.

Zhang's central claim is that the field's influence grows when Chinese scholars actively seek a voice on international platforms and build lasting institutional ties, such as the quinquennial International Senior Forum on Contemporary Chinese History run by the Institute of Contemporary China Studies. The author argues that foreign scholars' articles supply multi-perspective views and that comparative exchanges, for example between China's reform and opening up and Vietnam's renovation, help Chinese researchers understand their own development more clearly. The English edition is presented as a cautionary case: the first volume took five years, drew criticism of its translation quality, and the second carried an unapproved 21-page introduction. Zhang reports that the journal responded with stricter translator standards, content control, and a sign-off procedure before printing.

Zhang concludes that the journal is an important platform for external exchange but that much remains to be done to make it a first-rate international journal. The author calls for firm political and academic orientation, continued experimentation, and broad cooperation with scholars at home and abroad, so as to explain the Chinese path, summarise Chinese experience and tell China's story well. The essay is dedicated to the late Vogel and Titarenko. Read the original if you want a practitioner's first-hand account of how a Chinese state-sponsored history journal handled foreign collaboration, translation and publisher relations.
quoteEn: Actively going out to take part in international academic exchange and winning a voice on international academic platforms is of great importance for raising the international communication power and influence of research on contemporary Chinese history.
quoteZh: 主动走出去参加国际学术交流，争取在国际学术平台的发言权，对提升当代中国史研究的国际传播力和影响力有着十分重要的意义。

glossary.explanation: The field studying the history of the People's Republic of China since 1949, also called 国史 (national history) in official usage. It is institutionally distinct from modern Chinese history.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978. Its 30th and 40th anniversaries (2008, 2018) are the occasions for two of the exchanges the author describes.
An official slogan, associated with Xi Jinping, calling for China's experience and perspectives to be communicated effectively abroad.
A research institute of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences that publishes Contemporary China History Studies. The article abbreviates it as 当代所.

t: Theoretical precursors and practical paths in the formation of Western social law
zh: 西方社会法形成的理论先导与实践进路
source: World Social Sciences (Shijie shehui kexue), 2023 no. 5
paras: How did "social law" (shehuifa), a legal branch concerned with the livelihood of the weak, come into being in the West? Yu Shaoxiang argues that from the mid-nineteenth century the private law and market economy of capitalism produced growing social problems. Public and private law proved inadequate to them, and the two began to merge. The result was a "third domain" of law containing social law, economic law and environmental law.

The article has three parts. The first sets out five theoretical precursors: utopian socialism, the theory of state responsibility, human rights theory (including the right to subsistence), "new property" theory, and welfare economics. The second traces practice through four periods: before the Industrial Revolution, its early and late phases, and the post-industrial period. Its cases include English Poor Laws, Bismarck's social insurance in Germany, French relief and accident legislation, and the US Social Security Act of 1935. It also covers Britain's Beveridge-era reforms. The third part analyses the nature, values, aims and functions of social law.

Yu holds that social law arose from the guarantee of the right to subsistence and corrects the limits of formal equality under private law. Its values are ethical care, social security and social fairness. Its stated aims shifted over time. Bismarck's insurance is presented as an "investment" to weaken revolution, and August Bebel is cited as saying it blunted trade-union action. In modern societies, Yu says, the ideological colouring has faded and the aim is a basic safety net for all citizens. Social law also stabilises society and supports the market economy by redistribution and by stimulating consumption.

Yu concludes that social law answers objective economic and social needs and is determined by the material mode of production. The author takes this to confirm Marx's view that legal relations are rooted in material life, and that social law mainly serves to ease class conflict and resolve complex social problems. The article presents its development as a mark of a modern state's maturity. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-language overview of the Western intellectual and historical sources of social law, as background to how Chinese legal scholars frame the field.
quoteEn: Social law originates in guaranteeing the people's right to subsistence, and it is one of the important marks of the political, economic and social civilisation of the modern state.
quoteZh: 社会法起源于民众的生存权保障，是现代国家政治、经济和社会文明的重要标志之一。

t: Mao Zedong's thought on comprehensive balance of the national economy: a re-examination
zh: 毛泽东国民经济综合平衡思想再探讨
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theory, 2023 no. 8
paras: Zhou Shaodong re-examines Mao Zedong's thinking on the comprehensive balance of the national economy, which the article treats as an important part of Mao's economic thought. The author argues that Mao, applying the dialectical idea of the unity of opposites, developed a systematic account of what such balance means, what it rests on and how it is achieved. Zhou contends that, although the institutional basis and micro-level carriers of the Chinese economy have changed greatly, the core of this thought still offers guidance today.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the background: the economic recovery of 1949–52 and the sharp fluctuations in growth during the Great Leap Forward, the people's communes and the post-1959 disasters. It then discusses the meaning and nature of comprehensive balance, compares how balance is reached under capitalism and socialism, and analyses the means Mao proposed. It closes with the thought's present-day value, drawing on Mao's critical notes on the Soviet Political Economy textbook, On the Ten Major Relationships and On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People.

Zhou reads Mao's idea of balance from the theory of contradiction: imbalance is absolute and balance only temporary and relative. Balance is therefore comprehensive rather than symmetrical, meaning coordinated proportions among sectors, regions, accumulation and consumption, and centre and localities. It is also dynamic, and imbalances in the economy are in essence contradictions among the people, to be handled by unity–criticism–unity and by the principle of 'from the masses, to the masses'. Under socialism, public ownership and planned, proportionate development, led by the Party, make active balance possible. Mao's means were the 'simultaneous development' of industry and agriculture, centre and localities, large and small enterprises, modern and indigenous methods, and coastal and inland regions. Zhou links this to a 'wave-like' pattern of non-equilibrium growth and notes its resemblance to Albert Hirschman's unbalanced growth theory.

For the present, Zhou draws three lessons. Supply-side structural reform should be combined with expanding domestic demand, so as to reach a dynamic balance in which demand leads supply and supply creates demand. Macroeconomic regulation should give way to broader macroeconomic governance. Balance also needs the Party's centralised leadership, the basic socialist economic system, and the Two Unwaverings, supporting both state-owned and private firms as micro-level carriers, together with five-year plans. Zhou presents this as an example of building an autonomous knowledge system for the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-based account of how Mao's dialectics of balance is being used to frame current Chinese macroeconomic policy.
quoteEn: Comprehensive balance of the national economy is not an absolute balance between supply and demand, accumulation and consumption, long term and short term, whole and part, but a relative balance maintained in constant motion, that is, balance sought within imbalance.
quoteZh: 国民经济综合平衡并不是供给与需求、积累与消费、长期和短期、整体和局部的绝对平衡，而是在不断运动中保持相对平衡，即在不平衡中求得平衡。

glossary.explanation: A Party formula: unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector, and unwaveringly encouraging, supporting and guiding the non-public sector.
A policy line introduced under Xi Jinping around 2015 that aims to improve the quality and efficiency of the supply system by adjusting production structure and factor allocation.
A term used in recent Party documents, including the 20th Party Congress report, for a wider policy system than traditional macroeconomic regulation (fiscal and monetary policy).

Mao Zedong's 1957 category for non-antagonistic contradictions within the people, to be resolved by persuasion and criticism rather than coercion, as distinct from contradictions between the people and their enemies.

t: Mao Zedong's strategic guidance in the great War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea
zh: 毛泽东在伟大抗美援朝战争中的战略指导
paras: Marking the 130th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, Mao Xinyu asks how Mao and the Party Central Committee won the Korean War against a militarily superior United States. The article argues that victory came from a distinctive art of strategic guidance, which allowed a weaker side to defeat a stronger one and which, in the author's view, still offers lessons for handling today's risks and challenges.

The study is arranged in four parts, each ending with a short set of "lessons" for the present. It covers the decision to send troops abroad, the management of the war's course from preparation to ending, the creation of new strategy and tactics against a modernised enemy, and the use of people's war and total-war methods. Evidence comes mainly from Mao's telegrams, speeches and instructions, and from campaign history.

In the author's account, the decision to fight rested on putting political and long-term interests above immediate ones. Mao balanced economic reconstruction against survival of the new state, and chose a limited war fought outside China's borders, using the name "volunteers" and confining the conflict to the peninsula to prevent a larger one. Mao then steered the war by preparing for the worst case, shifting from counter-offensive to protracted active defence, and pursuing a negotiated settlement backed by military strength. Mao's adaptation to a modern opponent is summed up as learning from the war itself, assessing the enemy's strengths and weaknesses (US "much steel, little spirit" against Chinese "little steel, much spirit"), and devising tunnel defence, night fighting and "iron" supply lines. Finally, Mao mobilised the whole population, the Sino-Soviet alliance, diplomacy and propaganda, and fought while negotiating.

Mao Xinyu concludes that war decisions must serve the strategic whole, that war leaders must master uncertainty and develop asymmetric methods from battlefield practice, and that modern wars are won by relying on the people and on the state's total capacity. Looking to current great-power rivalry, the author calls for integrated national strategic systems, an international united front against the main adversary, and preparation for cognitive warfare, citing the Russia–Ukraine conflict. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese military-academy researcher draws on Mao's Korean War leadership to frame contemporary strategic and defence thinking.
quoteEn: War leaders must base themselves firmly on the material and technological conditions of their era, analyse both sides' strengths and weaknesses, make flexible use of time and space on the battlefield, and devise asymmetric ways of defeating a strong enemy by playing to one's strengths and avoiding one's weaknesses.
quoteZh: 战争指导者必须牢牢立足于所处时代的物质技术条件，深入分析和把握敌我双方的优劣长短，灵活利用战场时间与空间因素，探索发明扬长避短、以非对称方式制胜强敌的方法。

glossary.explanation: The name under which Chinese troops entered Korea in October 1950 instead of the People's Liberation Army. The article says the label helped avoid giving the US a pretext to declare war on China.
Mao Zedong's concept of waging war by mobilising the entire population and combining military action with political, economic and diplomatic struggle.
A strategic doctrine associated with Mao that pursues defensive aims through offensive operations, including counter-attacks beyond one's own territory.
A Party strategy of uniting diverse forces against a main enemy; here applied to international alignments to isolate the United States.

t: Searching for light: recollections and reflections at Marx's birthplace
zh: 寻找光明：马克思故居前的追忆与思考
paras: This is a first-person travel essay, first published in China Social Sciences Today in January 2024. Huo Qinghua recounts a visit in summer 2022 to Marx's birthplace in Trier, Germany, made at the end of a Sino-European study tour of vocational colleges. Huo's point is that the visit, and the exhibits in the house, show Marx's enduring significance and the continuing vitality of Marxism, above all in China.

The essay follows the visit in order. It describes the train journey from Saarbrücken, the history of Trier, and the house on Brückenstraße. It recounts how the house was identified in 1904 from a removal notice in a local newspaper, then bought by the Social Democratic Party in 1928, seized by the Nazi authorities and reopened as a memorial in 1947. Huo then goes through the three floors: the reception and family rooms, the floor on Marx's and Engels's lives, and the attic with manuscripts and editions.

Huo draws several lessons from the exhibits. Marx came from a comfortable middle-class family but chose a life of exile and struggle, in line with the school-leaving essay in which he wrote of choosing work for the welfare of humanity. Huo presents the Marx–Engels partnership as a model of comradely cooperation, with Capital as its fruit. Beside the first edition of the Communist Manifesto and the first volume of Capital, Huo notes the earliest Chinese translation by Chen Wangdao, and links them to Marx's two great discoveries, historical materialism and surplus value. Huo goes on to say that socialism suffered a setback after the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the collapse of the Soviet Union, while socialism with Chinese characteristics has since achieved remarkable results and revitalised scientific socialism in twenty-first-century China.

Huo concludes that, nearly 150 years after Marx's death, his theory still shines and will remain a beacon of human progress, thanks to its scientific, revolutionary, practical, people-centred and developmental character. Huo suggests Marxism can help in understanding the contradictions and crises of the world economic system amid what the essay calls changes unseen in a century, and in thinking about fairer and more sustainable governance. Huo ends by writing a tribute in the visitors' book. Read the original if you want a short personal account of a visit to the Trier house, with the commemorative tone in which Chinese writers present Marx's legacy to a general readership.
quoteEn: The scientific, revolutionary, practical, people-oriented and developmental qualities of Marxism will surely make it forever a beacon of human progress and development!
quoteZh: 马克思主义的科学性、革命性、实践性、人民性、发展性特质，必将使其永远成为人类进步和发展的灯塔！

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, in use since the early 1980s and combining Party leadership with a market-oriented economy.
The term for the socialism developed by Marx and Engels, which contrasts itself with earlier utopian socialism and rests on historical materialism and the critique of capitalism.

glossary.zh: 世界百年未有之大变局
glossary.pinyin: shìjiè bǎinián wèiyǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great changes in the world not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: An official formulation, used by Xi Jinping since around 2017, for a period of major shifts in the global balance of power, technology and the international order.

t: Creative transformation and innovative development of China's fine traditional legal culture
zh: 中华优秀传统法律文化的创造性转化和创新性发展
source: Studies on National Modernization (国家现代化建设研究), 2024 no. 1
paras: How should China's fine traditional legal culture be inherited and made usable for a modern socialist rule-of-law country? Li Lin argues that such culture is defined by three features: universality and commonality, advancement and civilisation, and practicality and popular orientation. Its creative transformation and innovative development should combine comparative study of foreign experience with the Two Integrations, so as to build an autonomous Chinese system of legal knowledge.

The article has three parts. The first defines key concepts, from culture and legal culture to rule-of-law civilisation and "traditional Chinese legal culture", and sets criteria for what counts as "fine". The second surveys the Chinese legal family, its influence on Japan, Korea, Vietnam and other Asian states, and China's own borrowing from abroad in civil, administrative and criminal legislation. The third introduces the author's analogy between "traditional Chinese medicine jurisprudence" and "Western medicine jurisprudence".

Li sorts inherited legal culture into three groups: elements reflecting universal human values, such as fairness, the rule of virtue assisted by punishment and cautious penal policy; elements that once served governance but are now dross, such as collective punishment and presumption of guilt; and elements, including some Legalist ideas, that were marginal then but useful now. Li then defines "Chinese-medicine jurisprudence" as China's own legal culture, legal family and Party-led rule-of-law experience, and "Western-medicine jurisprudence" as legal theory imported from the Soviet socialist, civil-law, common-law and international systems. Li holds that the two share goals as law and medicine do, and that their differences make integration both possible and necessary. Integration is to be guided by Marxism, the "soul" of the system, and by traditional culture, its "root".

Li calls for a "self-reform" of legal scholars, who should reject both the superiority of Western-style jurisprudence and the view that Chinese tradition is outdated. Li also proposes holistic study of traditional legal culture, a search for the "greatest common divisor" between the two traditions, and integration through the core branches of law, avoiding a "two-skins" outcome. The aim is a new realm of legal civilisation for Chinese modernization that supports a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a leading CASS jurist links traditional legal heritage, comparative law and the Party's theory of an autonomous legal knowledge system.
quoteEn: Innovation means creating new ideas, new discourse, new mechanisms and new forms.
quoteZh: 创新，创的是新思路、新话语、新机制、新形式

glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula of combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete realities and with its fine traditional culture.
The official name for China's own path of modernization, promoted by the Party since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept of international relations based on shared interests and values, used as a guiding idea in foreign policy and theory.
An official Party term for continuous internal renewal. Li applies it by analogy to legal scholars, calling for their "self-reform".
The traditional legal system that took shape in imperial China, culminating in the Tang Code, and which influenced neighbouring East and Southeast Asian states.

t: Rawls's threefold critique of utilitarianism
zh: 罗尔斯对功利主义的三重批判
source: Social Science Journal (Shehui kexue jikan), 2023 no. 1
paras: Rawls's criticism of utilitarianism, more than fifty years old, remains the standard backdrop for work on utilitarianism. Wang Li asks how Rawls's "justice as fairness" sought to replace it, and whether his critique holds. The article's thesis is that Rawls attacked three forms of utilitarianism with steadily weaker force, which Wang reads as showing that utilitarianism exerts a pressure on his theory that is hard to dispel.

The article follows the structure of A Theory of Justice. Three sections reconstruct Rawls's critique of classical utilitarianism (Hume, Smith, Bentham, Mill, Sidgwick), average utilitarianism and "limited" utilitarianism, each set against his two principles of justice. A fourth section then criticises the critique, drawing on rule utilitarianism and debates about decision-making under uncertainty. A short conclusion follows.

Wang reports that Rawls opposes classical utilitarianism on three contrasts: aggregate welfare against the priority of liberty and rights; extending individual choice to society against the separateness of persons; and teleology against a non-teleological view that puts the right before the good. Against average utilitarianism he cites the difficulty of calculating probabilities, the lack of a unified measure of expectation and the risk of sacrificing individuals. Limited utilitarianism, which blends the average principle with constraints such as a social minimum, is the hardest case because the argument from liberty no longer works against it. In Wang's reading, Rawls's counter-arguments are a vague utility standard and the claim that its constraints depend on intuition or on the difference principle. Wang then argues that rule utilitarianism escapes much of this critique, that Rawls's maximin reasoning is implausible, and that limited utilitarianism is best read as a special form of rule utilitarianism. Rawls's claim about the indeterminacy of utility fails once the comparison is confined to wealth and income. His claim that the difference principle secures a higher social minimum is also left without clear reasons.

Wang concludes that Rawls was not defending utilitarianism. Wang argues, however, that utilitarianism has its own strengths and resources for replying, and that "justice as fairness" would need fuller reasons to displace it entirely. The author calls for treating the two theories on equal terms through mutual critique. Read the original if you work on Rawls, contemporary utilitarianism or Chinese scholarship on political philosophy and want a detailed, sympathetic re-examination of how Rawls argued against utilitarianism.
quoteEn: For \"justice as fairness\" to replace utilitarianism completely, it must find more adequate reasons.
quoteZh: “公平的正义”要想完全取代功利主义，必须寻求更加充分的理由。

t: Self-revolution in the depths of thought: Mao Zedong's high regard for ideological and political work
zh: 思想深处的自我革命：毛泽东对思想政治工作的高度重视
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2023 no. 12
paras: Cao Yongxin asks why Mao Zedong and the Chinese Communists treated ideological and political work as a core, strategic task, and what lessons this holds today. The article argues that such work is a distinguishing feature of the Chinese Communist Party and the 'lifeline' of all other work. It holds that, under the primary stage of socialism and a socialist market economy, any slackening would put the Party's cause at risk of 'subversive mistakes'.

The article has three parts. The first traces how building the Party ideologically and building the army politically gave rise to ideological and political work. It covers the 1929 Gutian Conference resolution, Mao's 1955 remark that political work is the lifeline of economic work, and later Party documents repeating the formula. The second part sets out five lessons from Mao's leadership. The third turns to the new era and links this work to self-liberation, self-reform and historical initiative.

Cao's five lessons are theoretical preparation through Mao's writings, coordinated organisational leadership by Party committees and first secretaries, unity of knowing and doing through practice, the mass line and investigation, and a policy of 'punishing the past to warn the future and curing the sickness to save the patient'. On the last, Cao stresses persuasion over coercion. Cao also contrasts this unity of thought and practice with the self-cultivation of ancient thinkers. In the final section, Cao presents the work as the means by which the proletariat awakens its own subjectivity and liberates itself without saviours. The Party's self-reform is, in Cao's words, essentially an ideological struggle 'in the depths of the soul'.

Cao concludes that this work mobilises the most active factor in production, people, and cannot be replaced by material incentives, legal penalties or empty preaching. Citing Deng Xiaoping's 1989 remarks on weak ideological education, Cao treats neglect as costly. The article cites the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as warnings, and calls for firm leadership and initiative in this field. It also holds that historical initiative shows itself through intellectual emancipation, theoretical consciousness, active practice and a conscious choice of path. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how Mao's ideological work is being used to frame the Party's self-reform today.
quoteEn: The self-reform that the Chinese Communist Party has put forward in the new era is in essence an ideological struggle in the depths of the soul; once ideological and political work is weakened, genuine self-reform becomes impossible.
quoteZh: 中国共产党在新时代提出的自我革命，本质上是灵魂深处的思想斗争，思想政治工作一旦削弱就不可能真正做到自我革命。

glossary.explanation: The Party's systematic work of political education, persuasion and value formation among members, soldiers and the public. It originated in revolutionary-era army and Party practice and remains a standard term in Party documents.
The official characterisation of China's present stage of development, in which socialism is held to be still underdeveloped. It has been used in Party doctrine since the 1980s.
A method of leadership associated with Mao Zedong. Cadres are to go among the people, gather their views and return policies to them, and it is a core Party principle.

Official rendering of 'the Party's self-reform' (党的自我革命), the idea that the Party rectifies itself and corrects its own faults. It has been a prominent theme in Party discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The 1929 Party congress of the Fourth Red Army, held in Gutian. Its resolution established the Party's absolute leadership over the army and an early system of political work.

t: Liu Shibai: a Marxist economist in step with his times
zh: 刘诗白：与时代同频共振的马克思主义经济学家
paras: Ding Renzhong offers an appreciative portrait of Liu Shibai (b. 1925), a leading theoretical economist at Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, as a Marxist economist whose work moved in step with China's reform practice. The piece, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in November 2023, argues that Liu's research path traces a logical thread in the innovation of economic theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article opens with Liu's biography: his education-oriented family, his early reading of Capital, his studies at Wuhan University from 1942, and his teaching at Sichuan University from 1946. It notes his shift after 1958 from contemporary capitalism to socialist economic theory. Ding names three features of his scholarship: comprehensive study of economic reform, grounding in Chinese conditions, and unity of theory and practice. The body then takes up four themes: the socialist market economy, plural forms of ownership, the primary stage of socialism, and the theory of people's wealth and macroeconomic operation.

Ding stresses several of Liu's positions. In 1979 he defined the socialist economy as a socialist commodity economy and argued that a market economy is a general category, not peculiar to capitalism; Ding says this idea later entered the 1984 Party decision on economic reform. Liu argued that compatibility between the market and public ownership is settled in practice, and that state enterprises needed clear property rights and a legal-person property system. He held that socialist ownership is plural and "incomplete". Using both relations of production and productive forces as criteria, he classed China among countries emerging from a backward semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, which must pass through a long primary stage of socialism. Ding also covers Liu's idea of political economy as a study of "people's wealth", his analysis of demand shortfalls and overcapacity in the transition period, and his account of cycles under a socialist market economy.

Ding concludes that Liu consistently relied on Marxism, applied it to Chinese practice, and so advanced the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Liu is presented as a firm believer in communist ideals and in the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Ding adds that his analyses of overcapacity and cycles remain useful today. Read the original if you want a concise, officially sympathetic overview of Liu Shibai's main contributions to Chinese economic thought from 1979 to the 2000s.
quoteEn: Liu Shibai held that the question of the \"compatibility\" of the market economy with socialist public ownership can only be resolved in practice, not decided in the study.
quoteZh: 刘诗白认为，市场经济与社会主义公有制的“兼容”问题只能解决于实践之中，而不是裁定于书斋之中。

glossary.explanation: The official thesis, adopted by the Party in the 1980s, that China remains in an early, underdeveloped stage of socialism lasting a long historical period.
The official name for China's path and system since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership with a market-oriented economy.
The official description of China's economic system, formally adopted in 1992, combining market mechanisms with public ownership as the main body and state macro-regulation.

t: Wu Yifeng: a people's economist grounded in Marxism
zh: 吴易风:立足马克思主义的人民经济学家
paras: This is a biographical tribute, originally published in the China Social Sciences Today in October 2023, to Wu Yifeng (b. 1932), a first-class professor at Renmin University of China. Zhang, who was Wu's doctoral student, presents him as a Marxist economist who was also learned in Western economics and the history of economic thought. The article's thesis is that Wu combined firm Marxist conviction, critical engagement with Western economics and a commitment to serve working people, and so exemplified the "people's economist".

The piece is organised under four headings. It first traces Wu's path as a member of the first generation of economists trained after 1949, from teaching cadres in 1953 to Renmin University and the writing of his major works. It then covers his defence of Marxian economics in several debates, his work on adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, and his role as a textbook author and educator in Western economics. A final section gives a personal portrait of Wu as a teacher and friend.

Zhang reports that Wu answered critics of Marxist economics point by point. Against the claim that it ignores resource allocation, Wu argued in 1997 that allocation is subordinate to the mode of production. Against the claim that Coase had a property-rights theory and Marx did not, he argued that Marx built a scientific and systematic one a century earlier. Against the view that Marxism cannot be expressed mathematically, he co-authored work on Marx's models, while warning against using mathematics as packaging. On Western economics, Wu held that it has a dual character, class bias and usefulness under specific conditions. In Zhang's account he rejected both wholesale acceptance and wholesale rejection, calling for criticism of the ideological elements and for selective borrowing of the useful ones. Zhang also describes Wu's textbooks with Gao Hongye and his role in the 1990s seminars that countered what participants saw as the over-promotion of Coase's theorem and of privatisation-oriented theories.

Zhang concludes that Wu's emphasis on the class character of economics and on the leading place of Marxist economics in China amounts to a call for economics to serve the broad masses. Wu is said to have urged others to be "people's economists" and to have lived by this over more than sixty years of scholarship. Read the original if you want a sympathetic portrait of a leading Chinese Marxist economist, with details on his main debates, textbooks and view of Western economics.
quoteEn: He stresses that economics has a class character and that Marxist economics holds the leading position in China; in the end, this means stressing that economics must serve the interests of the broad masses of the people.
quoteZh: 他强调，经济学有阶级性，强调马克思主义经济学在中国的主导地位，说到底，就是强调经济学要为广大人民群众的利益服务。

glossary.explanation: Wu's ideal for economists who take the standpoint of working people and serve their interests, as the article presents it.

t: Moses Hess and the young Marx in historical perspective
zh: 历史性视野中的赫斯与青年马克思
paras: Since the 1960s, revived interest in Spinoza and the publication of Moses Hess's original writings have prompted renewed study of Hess's role in the formation of Marx's thought. Some scholars, including David McLellan, Isaiah Berlin, Hiromatsu Wataru and Leszek Kołakowski, stress Hess's decisive influence and even count him among the founders of the materialist conception of history. Kang Zhai accepts that Hess influenced the young Marx's communism but argues that the two men's theories differ decisively. In this account Marx's communism holds to historicity, whereas Hess's remained, in Marx's words, a "non-historical abstraction" full of moral zeal.

The article, which appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in November 2023, compares the two thinkers on three points. It first looks at their theoretical routes to communism: Marx through critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, Hess through the philosophy of history. It then asks what each meant by communism and by economic alienation. Finally it considers the political and practical consequences of these differences and closes with a critique of Hiromatsu's reading.

Kang argues that Marx reached communism by identifying the separation of civil society from the political state as the modern world's basic problem and by concluding that civil society has priority over the state. Overcoming the separation therefore meant sublating civil society. This led from the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher texts to the critique of private property through alienated labour in the 1844 Manuscripts. Hess, by contrast, moved from the religious "sacred history" of his early work, through a Fichtean philosophy of action, to a critique of money as alienated social intercourse and a vision of communism as an ethical community of love. Both used the idea of overcoming the split between individual and species. Hess's alienation, however, operates in the sphere of circulation and remains a Hegelian-Feuerbachian reworking of French socialism. Marx locates alienation in capitalist production and in the relation between labour and capital, and Kang says this reflects a deeper engagement with classical political economy.

Kang concludes that Hess's philosophical limits led him to a gradualist, morally grounded reform programme that rejected force and class struggle, with communism justified as right rather than as necessary. Such reform could not touch capitalism's basic structure, so communism stayed an "abstract ought". Kang credits Kołakowski and Hiromatsu with breaking dogmatic ideology's long concealment of Marx's early development. Kang nonetheless says Hiromatsu overstates Hess's influence and confuses Hess's view of the human essence as "intercourse and joint activity" with Marx's view of it as the ensemble of social relations. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Marx's historical standpoint is distinguished from Hess's ethical communism in current Chinese scholarship on the history of Marxism.
quoteEn: Hess, by contrast, remained throughout stuck in a dualistic opposition between a reality full of separation and alienation and an ideal state of communism.
quoteZh: 赫斯则始终停留在充满分离、异化的现实与共产主义理想状态的二元对立之中

glossary.explanation: Hegel's term (bürgerliche Gesellschaft) for the sphere of private economic interests and exchange, distinct from the political state. Marx treats it as the base of the state's form and of legal relations.
The Chinese rendering of Hegel's Aufhebung: to negate something while preserving and transcending its content.
Concept from Marx's 1844 Manuscripts: under private property the worker's labour and its products become an alien power confronting the worker.
Marx and Engels's theory that social development is grounded in material production and its relations. It is often called historical materialism.

t: Hegel's philosophy of right and the critique of Western modernity
zh: 黑格尔法哲学与西方现代性批判
paras: Marking the 180th anniversary of Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, Sun Leqiang asks how the work's scholarly value and contemporary relevance should be understood afresh, in the context of intellectual history and of East–West differences. The short essay, which first appeared in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2023, argues that the work lays bare the internal structure of Western modernity: individual, civil society, state. It also argues that Marx's claim that civil society determines the state still holds today.

Sun begins with the setting of Hegel's Elements of the Philosophy of Right, the "dual revolution" of English industry and French politics, against which Germany appears as an anachronism.
