glossary.explanation: The tradition running from Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci through the Frankfurt School and later critical theory. Chinese scholarship often extends the label to ecological and feminist Marxism, as this article does.
The mode of thought in which reason takes the form of efficiency-oriented technique and permeates social life. Chinese discussion draws on the Frankfurt School's critique of instrumental reason.
A pair of concepts derived from Max Weber. Instrumental rationality seeks efficient means, while value rationality concerns ends such as human freedom.
Lukács's term for social relations appearing as relations between things under capitalism. Here it names the society-wide process the author attributes to the capitalist use of technology.
The Marxist theory of history that explains social change through material production and social relations. Chinese authors cite it as the standpoint for evaluating foreign theories.

t: The historical practice of Chinese modernization: agrarian transformation and peasant life in contemporary Liangshan Yi areas through oral history
zh: 中国式现代化的历史实践：口述史视野下当代凉山彝族地区农政变革与农民生活
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2023 no. 2
paras: Research on Chinese modernization has mostly worked at the macro level, and Ruan Chiyin argues that concrete empirical studies are still thin. This article takes up the socialist agrarian practice of the 1950s–1970s in a frontier mountain minority region, which the author says has been less studied than Han plains villages. Using oral history, Ruan contends that collectivization and the democratic reform dismantled a slave-holding hierarchy and gave poor peasants and women new standing. The author presents this as a distinctive path of agricultural and rural modernization, different from the Western one.

The evidence comes from fieldwork in Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture in Sichuan and in Yunnan between 2013 and 2016, combined with archives and published scholarship. The article opens with the rigid caste order of pre-1956 Yi society and the effects of opium cultivation. It then presents eight elders' accounts of the democratic reform of 1956–1958 and a case study of one multi-ethnic village, "X Village", under the people's commune. It ends with the village's changes after household contracting in the early 1980s.

Ruan's central claim is that collective land ownership removed the material basis of lineage-based hierarchy. In the author's reading, the democratic reform of 1956–1958 freed slaves and redistributed land and tools. Collective production in X Village, with multiple cropping, livestock raising, processing and a "specialist team" that helped weaker teams, raised output and curbed inequality. The author also says it drew different ethnic groups into joint work. After decollectivization, Ruan reports, the two-harvests-in-a-year system and the combination of crops and livestock were abandoned. Irrigation and storage facilities decayed, and the lineage organisations regained influence. Women cadres became rare, land distribution became more uneven, and young adults left for wage work.

Ruan sums up the achievements in three areas: the economic (sustainable integrated farming and less inequality), the political (equal status for the poor and for women) and the ideological (dignity and a collective spirit). The author sees these as laying the groundwork for common prosperity. The article ends by calling for lessons from this history to guide efforts to narrow wealth gaps in a market environment. It frames this within the Party's current stress on promoting common prosperity through high-quality development and on going beyond the crisis of modernity under Western capital logic. Read the original if you want first-hand oral-history testimony from Liangshan and a village-level account of collective agriculture and its dissolution in a minority region.
quoteEn: What socialist agrarian change seeks to build is a new economic logic: while continually raising agricultural productivity, it attends to the fair distribution of wealth and power.
quoteZh: 社会主义农政变革所要建构的是一种新的经济逻辑，在不断提高农业生产力水平的同时，注重财富和权力的公平分配

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's own path of modernization, stressed in Party discourse especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as distinct from Western models.
The 1950s campaign in minority areas such as Liangshan that abolished slavery and feudal hierarchies and redistributed land. It was carried out more gradually than the land reform in Han areas.
A long-standing socialist goal of shared wealth for all, given new emphasis in Party policy in recent years.
The official economic development goal that stresses quality, efficiency and sustainability over speed of growth.
The three-tier rural collective organisation (commune, brigade, production team) that dominated Chinese countryside from 1958 until the early 1980s.
The patrilineal kin group that formed the basis of social organisation and rule in traditional Yi society.

t: Relying on tenacious struggle to open up new horizons for our cause
zh: 依靠顽强斗争打开事业发展新天地
paras: Bu Xianqun, writing in 2023 after the 20th Party Congress (2022), takes up the Congress report's call to "rely on tenacious struggle to open up new horizons for our cause". The commentary argues that the report embodies the Party's spirit of great struggle and that this spirit should guide the Party's work in the new era. In Bu's view, the spirit is a necessary mental quality and capacity for the struggles that lie ahead.

The article is organised in three parts: the theoretical, practical and cultural foundations of the spirit of struggle; its new meanings in the new era; and the guidance it offers for the future. It draws on Marxist theory, the history of the Party, the long history of Chinese civilisation, and Xi Jinping's statements since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also refers to the 19th Party Congress report (2017) on the links among great struggle, great project, great cause and great dream.

Bu contends that the spirit of struggle is inherent to Marxism, because Marxism treats the unity of opposites as the basic law of development and sees struggle as part of the contradictory movement of productive forces and relations of production. It is also described as the Party's spiritual base across revolution, construction and reform, and as a trait of the Chinese nation seen in reform, self-strengthening and vigilance in times of peace. The article lists what Xi has said the "great struggle with many new historical features" demands: firm ideals, Party leadership, vigilance against major risks, and the Party's self-reform. It notes that the 20th Party Congress report made upholding the spirit of struggle one of five major principles and called on cadres to "dare to fight and be good at fighting".

Bu concludes that great struggle is a judgement based on real conditions, an integral part of upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics, and a requirement for safeguarding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee. After the 20th Party Congress, the Party's central task is to build a modern socialist country in all respects and advance the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, and struggle is to proceed along that path. Bu calls on readers to understand the spirit of struggle through Marxism, Party and national history, and the history of Chinese civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party-affiliated historians present the 20th Congress's language of struggle and its claimed theoretical, historical and cultural roots.
quoteEn: The spirit of struggle is a defining characteristic of Marxist theory.
quoteZh: 斗争精神是马克思主义理论的特质。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Xi Jinping-era Party discourse for the struggle needed to uphold and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics. The 19th Party Congress (2017) linked it to the great project, great cause and great dream.
A phrase in Xi-era discourse for the Party's efforts to discipline and renew itself, including the anti-corruption campaign.
The official term for China's own path to modernisation, set as the Party's central task from the 20th Party Congress (2022).
The official name for the Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Marxism with China's conditions.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, often tied to the 'two centenary goals'.

t: Paradigms and practical paths for the global communication of a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: 人类命运共同体全球传播范式与实践取径
source: Journal of Hunan University (Social Sciences), 2023 no. 4
paras: Writing in 2023, Sun Lijun asks how the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, first written into the Party Congress report at the 18th Party Congress (2012) and reaffirmed at the 20th (2022), can be spread effectively worldwide. The article argues that the idea's global communication is moving through three successive paradigms: mass-media diffusion, multi-actor participation and idea reproduction. It holds that China must lead the shift from the first to the second and prepare for the third.

The article first traces how the concept was enriched over a decade, from the 2011 white paper on China's peaceful development through the Belt and Road Initiative to the "five communities" (health, security, development, humanistic and human–nature life communities). It places the concept in a longer intellectual history of "community", from Marx and Engels's The German Ideology to Ferdinand Tönnies and Western communitarianism. Using Thomas Kuhn's notion of paradigm, it then periodises the idea's communication. It closes with four practical shifts: in values, channels, narrative and discourse strategy.

Sun reports a discourse analysis of mainstream media in 18 countries and regions. In the author's account, US coverage was negative, European coverage mixed, and Belt and Road and African media most attentive, with coverage rising since 2018 and the Covid-19 pandemic. From this the author argues that government-led, single-voice diffusion has limited effect, and that NGOs, transnational firms and individuals should take part, mainly through social media. The four shifts are from "issue-based" to "people-centred" values, from one-way to multidimensional channels, from fact-based to story-based narrative, and from monologue to dialogue. Sun cites the spread of an Italian girl's thank-you cartoon and China's COVAX vaccine supply as examples.

Sun concludes that global communication is overcoming Euro-centrism and that China should raise its communication capacity, widen participation and upgrade its view of global governance. The author expects the third, reproduction paradigm to arrive only slowly, once states accept that no country can stand apart from global crises. In that stage the idea would be re-created from each country's own conditions and would also reproduce Marxist social theory under new globalisation. Read the original if you study Chinese international communication strategy, or want to see how a Chinese media scholar applies Kuhn, Rogers and social-media theory to a Party concept.
quoteEn: The ultimate aim of the global communication of a community with a shared future for mankind is to help humanity confirm that this is an indivisible community of shared risk, in which "you are in me and I am in you".
quoteZh: 人类命运共同体全球传播的终极目标在于帮助人类确证这是一个“你中有我，我中有你”不可分割、风险与共的共同体

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny for humankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept written into the Party Congress report in 2012 and promoted by Xi Jinping. It stresses interdependence, cooperation and shared benefit among states.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 to build infrastructure, trade and economic links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: The innovative value of the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics and its future development
zh: 中国特色社会主义道路的创新价值及其未来发展
paras: Taking its cue from the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022), which lists adherence to the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics as a major principle for building a modern socialist country, Zhao Yong asks what is innovative about this path and where it is heading. The article, published in Theory and Reform in 2023, argues that the path should be examined through a "grand view of history", placed within the histories of the Party, the People's Republic, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation. Zhao concludes that the path is the necessary route to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and that it offers an original option for human modernization.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the theoretical foundation (Marxism), the historical depth (the evolution from the new-democratic revolution to socialist revolution, socialist construction and socialism with Chinese characteristics) and the practical basis of the path since the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). The second identifies four forms of innovation: in path, theory, institutions and culture. The third looks ahead, proposing three perspectives for the future: subjectivity, historical initiative and international vision.

Zhao argues that the path embodies the diversity of modernization routes, both as a whole and through its many specific sub-paths, from economic and political development to the rule of law and peaceful development. In theory, Chinese modernization is said to enrich world modernization theory, to end the "end of history" thesis, to undermine the basis of "Western-centrism" and to reject capital-centred, polarising, expansionist modernization. Institutionally, Zhao sees a "three-in-one" logic of fundamental, basic and important systems that unites upholding and developing socialism with using and transcending capitalism. Culturally, the path draws on traditional Chinese civilization and offers a new form of human civilization, answering the "clash of civilizations" with exchange and mutual learning.

For the future, Zhao calls for stronger subjectivity amid great changes unseen in a century, noting that China remains in the primary stage of socialism and must keep its development in its own hands. Zhao also urges greater historical initiative, grounded in a people-centred approach, and a Chinese discourse and narrative system that raises China's international discourse power. The article is a statement of the official framing of the path and its global significance. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how Party-affiliated scholarship presents the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics after the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Chinese modernization is socialist modernization led by the Communist Party of China; it has the features common to all countries' modernization, and above all Chinese characteristics based on its own national conditions.
quoteZh: 中国式现代化是中国共产党领导的社会主义现代化，既有各国现代化的共同特征，更有基于自己国情的中国特色。

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义道路
glossary.en: the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The official name for China's development route since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, a socialist system and a market economy. The article treats it as the specific meaning of "the Chinese path".

The official concept, elaborated at the 20th Party Congress (2022), of a modernization led by the Party. It is characterised by a huge population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical balance, harmony with nature and peaceful development.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, associated with the Chinese Dream.
A framing in Party discourse that asks for current developments to be understood within long historical timeframes and world-historical trends.
The official judgement that China is still at an early, long-lasting stage of socialist development, used to justify reform and mixed ownership.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilization
glossary.explanation: A phrase in Party discourse for the civilizational model said to result from Chinese modernization, presented as an alternative to Western modernization.

keywords: path of socialism with Chinese characteristics

t: Mao Zedong's incisive analysis of why the "road of capitalist society" could not work in China
zh: 毛泽东对“资本主义社会之路”在中国行不通的深刻剖析
paras: Cao Mingchen takes up a question from modern Chinese history: why China did not and could not follow the European and American capitalist path. Drawing on Mao Zedong's writings and speeches, the article argues that the national bourgeoisie's proposals for a bourgeois republic, in whatever form, were repeatedly shown to be unworkable. In Cao's account, China's only viable course was the New Democratic and then socialist road under Communist Party leadership.

The article begins with the post-1840 semi-colonial, semi-feudal setting and then works through five reasons drawn from Mao, before a short conclusion. These are: imperialism did not permit it; socialism, as a new force in world history, did not permit it; the big landlords and big bourgeoisie firmly opposed democracy; the national bourgeoisie was weak, compromising and vacillating; and the struggle was led by the proletariat. Cao cites Mao texts from the 1920s to the late 1940s, including "On New Democracy" and his 1949 report to the Second Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee.

Cao groups the reasons into external and internal ones. Externally, Mao held that imperialism aimed to keep China a semi-colony and so blocked its national capitalism, while the October Revolution and the Soviet Union opened a new era in which colonial revolutions belonged to the world proletarian socialist revolution. Internally, the Guomindang regime represented big landlords and the bureaucratic bourgeoisie, and Chiang Kai-shek never became a Chinese "Kemal". The national bourgeoisie, economically small and afraid of the masses, was dual in character and could not lead the revolution. Cao calls proletarian leadership, exercised through the Communist Party, the decisive factor and presents Mao's "two-step" idea of a New Democratic revolution followed by a socialist one.

Cao concludes that the failure of the capitalist road had both objective and subjective causes: China's semi-colonial, semi-feudal conditions allowed neither the old Western path nor a direct leap to socialism, and the bourgeoisie lacked the strength to lead. In this reading, the founding of New China and the socialist system confirm the historical necessity of socialism. Cao says Mao's analysis helps strengthen confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a systematic, source-based account of how Mao explained China's rejection of the capitalist road, as presented in Party-history scholarship.
quoteEn: The national bourgeoisie feared the masses and dared not mobilise or rely on them, which made it a weak and powerless class.
quoteZh: 民族资产阶级害怕民众，不敢发动民众和依靠民众，决定了这一阶级是一个软弱无力的阶级。

glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's theory, developed around 1939–40, of a transitional stage of revolution in China. It is led by the proletariat and directed against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism, as a step towards socialism.
In Mao's class analysis, the Chinese capitalists not tied to imperialism or the state. He saw them as having both revolutionary and compromising tendencies.
Mao's term for the big capitalists who fused with state power and served imperialism. He associated them with the Guomindang government and its control of the economy.
The official name for China's current path and system since the reform era. The article ends by invoking confidence in it.

t: The spirit of historical initiative: its genesis, identity-building function and paths of deepening
zh: 历史主动精神：生成逻辑、认同功能与深化路径
paras: Against a background of turbulence in world history, the article asks how the Chinese nation can keep its historical resolve and confidence. It takes up the leadership's call to "strengthen historical confidence and historical initiative" and argues that the spirit of historical initiative (lishi zhudong jingshen) is a cultural form that leads people to understand and make history correctly. The authors contend that it unleashes subjects' conscious agency and strengthens popular identification with the path of Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first traces the spirit's genesis along three lines: a theoretical logic grounded in historical materialism, a historical logic rooted in the Chinese tradition of innovation, and a practical logic based on the spirit of struggle. The second sets out three identity functions: identification with a mission, with an order, and with a memory. The third proposes three ways to deepen the spirit, each aimed at a specific risk.

On genesis, the authors argue that historical materialism, with its focus on labour practice, gave birth to the spirit. They read classical Chinese ideas such as "self-strengthening without rest" and the reform programmes of Wang Anshi and Kang Youwei as sources of its innovative content, and they treat the Communist Party's struggle as its practical form. On function, the authors hold that the spirit supports the legitimacy of Chinese modernization through its "people-centred" values. They also hold that it carries national governance towards "good governance" (shanzhi) through a principle of justice, and that it consolidates historical confidence through the collective memory of national rejuvenation. On deepening, the authors prescribe a "grand historical outlook" against historical nihilism, which they link to Western "colour revolutions". They also call for "subject rationality" to disenchant capital logic and consumerism, and for strengthened "spiritual production" against technological rationality, with attention to digital technology, "technology for good" and humanism.

The authors conclude that the deeper a people's grasp of historical laws, the more it controls its own destiny. They hold that the "great changes unseen in a century" are both an opportunity and a challenge, and that seizing historical trends through initiative lets humanity advance. The text uses the vocabulary of Party theory of its period, and it reads as an attempt to ground that vocabulary in classical Marxist concepts. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese scholars link historical materialism, traditional culture and national identification to the idea of historical initiative.
quoteEn: The spirit of historical initiative has a strong orientation towards national identity and can provide legitimacy support for the path of Chinese modernization.
quoteZh: 历史主动精神有着强烈的国家认同指向，能为中国式现代化道路提供合法性支撑。

glossary.explanation: A term in recent Party discourse, linked to Xi Jinping's call to "strengthen historical initiative". The authors define it as a way of thinking and set of values by which people consciously make history.
The official name for China's path of modernization, presented by the Party as distinct from Western models.
A concept stressed by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It asks that history be viewed as a whole, across long periods and global contexts.
In official Chinese usage, a label for interpretations that question or deny the Party's historical narrative and the revolutionary tradition.
The authors use it for the highest state of national governance, an ideal balance between state and civil society.

t: Whole-process people's democracy as a necessary requirement and path of realization for Chinese modernization
zh: 全过程人民民主是中国式现代化的必然要求和实现路径
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2023 no. 3
paras: Li Feng argues that Chinese modernization and whole-process people's democracy have so far been studied separately: the first mostly in macro-economic and social terms, the second mainly as democratic ideas and institutions. The article sets out to link them, contending that whole-process people's democracy is both a necessary requirement of Chinese modernization and its political path of realization. Without that link, the author holds, democracy lacks a long-term goal and modernization lacks a democratic dimension.

The article opens by presenting Chinese modernization as a new form of human modernization and whole-process people's democracy as a new form of human political civilization. It then proceeds in two directions. The first runs from the five features of Chinese modernization (an enormous population, common prosperity, material and cultural-ethical advancement in step, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development) to the need for this form of democracy. The second runs from democracy's five links (election, consultation, decision-making, management, supervision) to their role in carrying modernization forward.

In the first part, Li draws on the scale of China's population and territory, which the author describes as imposing a heavy governance load and requiring a democracy that integrates interests under Communist Party leadership. Common prosperity is said to need both market mechanisms and economic democracy, balanced by state regulation and a guard against populism and egalitarianism. The author also rejects Western modernization theory, citing Lipset and Coppedge, as tying modernization to Western-style democracy through biased democracy indices. In the second part, Li assigns each link a task: election supplies legitimacy and efficient information processing; consultation handles complex, conflicting interests; democratic decision-making manages risk and combines democracy with centralism; management and supervision turn participation into governance effectiveness. Li contrasts this with what the article calls the gridlock and 'veto politics' of Western democracy.

Li concludes that the five features of Chinese modernization can be realized only with the values and institutional guarantees of whole-process people's democracy, and that its core meaning can be understood only within the horizon of Chinese modernization. The article promises further development of democratic forms and greater effectiveness so as to achieve modernization 'faster and better'. Read the original if you want a Party School scholar's account of how whole-process people's democracy is tied to the official framework of Chinese modernization, and of how its five links are assigned governance functions.
quoteEn: Only by examining whole-process people's democracy within the horizon of Chinese modernization can one understand its core meaning and significance.
quoteZh: 只有将全过程人民民主放在中国式现代化的视域下审视才能理解其核心内涵与重要意义。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping first put forward in 2019 and the Party has since made central to its account of socialist democracy. It describes democracy as covering election, consultation, decision-making, management and supervision, under Party leadership.

The official name for China's path of modernization, elaborated at the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is described as socialist modernization led by the Party, with five features including a huge population and common prosperity.
A goal of shared affluence for all the people, described by Xi Jinping as an essential requirement of socialism. It has been given particular emphasis in policy since 2021.

t: Towards everyday life: tracing the distinctive qualities of socialist consultative democracy
zh: 走向日常生活：社会主义协商民主的特质探源
paras: Why should consultative democracy move into people's daily lives, and what does it look like when it does? Zhang Liwei starts from the claim that consultative democracy is an important form of whole-process people's democracy. Zhang argues that moving it into everyday life takes democracy beyond its confinement to politics and makes it a way of life. This, the article holds, shows what is distinctive about the Chinese path of democracy.

The article has four parts. It first sets out why democracy should be built in everyday life, drawing on participatory democratic theory and its critique of liberal democracy. It then examines the qualities of everyday consultative democracy through historical inheritance and modern reconstruction. A third part discusses its value, engaging Henri Lefebvre's critique of everyday life and Marx on human emancipation. A short conclusion draws out the implications.

Zhang's first move is to argue that everyday life gives "participation" a social foundation. Because it is tied to personal interests, everyday participation mobilises people from below, builds trust in democratic institutions, and supplies methods for political democracy. The second move traces the inheritance of consultative democracy from the Chinese cultural ideal of harmony in diversity and the saying "when there is a problem, discuss it", which Zhang reads as seeking consensus through overlapping preferences rather than compromise. Zhang says it must also be rebuilt for the individual, social and ethical sides of the person, through equal participation, social capital and communicative ethics. The third move is that consultation restores meaning to daily life by countering alienation and strengthening intersubjectivity. Zhang links it to Marx's idea of social emancipation, citing its popular character, problem orientation and educative function.

Zhang concludes that democratic research should look beyond the political sphere and treat daily life as a new vantage point. In Zhang's account, everyday democracy complements political democracy, forms its social basis and supports a harmonious relationship between state and society. The author presents this as a creative transformation of Marxist democratic theory and a contribution to a new form of political civilisation and Chinese modernization. Read the original if you study Chinese theories of consultative democracy or want to see how Marxist, participatory and Confucian-style concepts are combined in one argument.
quoteEn: Consultative democracy in everyday life is both everyday and political.
quoteZh: 日常生活中的协商民主既是日常的，也是政治的。

glossary.explanation: A concept introduced by Xi Jinping in 2019 and later made official. It describes the Chinese system as democratic at every stage, from elections to consultation, decision-making, management and oversight.

In Chinese official usage, a form of democracy in which citizens, organisations and bodies such as the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference discuss public matters before decisions are made. It is presented as distinct from electoral democracy.
The official term for China's own path of modernisation, set out in Party documents from the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as different from Western models.

glossary.en: when there is a problem, discuss it
glossary.literal: when there is something, it is good to discuss
glossary.explanation: A common Chinese saying that Xi Jinping and official texts have adopted as a summary of consultative democracy.

t: "New materialism" and the philosophical foundations of a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: “新唯物主义”与人类命运共同体的哲学根基
source: Journal of Beijing Normal University (Social Sciences Edition), 2023 no. 4
paras: Liu Tongfang asks what philosophical ground underlies the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, which Xi Jinping's report to the 20th Party Congress (2022) describes as where the future of the world's peoples lies. Liu argues that it is rooted in Marx's "new materialism", whose standpoint, set out in the Theses on Feuerbach, is "human society or social humanity" rather than civil society. The article presents this shift of standpoint as an ontological revolution and as the basic precondition for the community's appearance in the new era.

The article has three parts. The first contrasts civil society and human society along three lines: the logical starting point, the mode of thinking, and the ultimate destination. The second links civil society to capitalist economic globalization and the "centre–periphery" order. The third moves from human society to the community with a shared future for mankind, drawing on Marx, Hegel, Lenin, Rousseau, Althusser and Western communitarian thought.

Liu contends that old philosophy begins from the abstract human being, thinks through empirical intuition and the subject–object divide, and ends in a "false community". Marx's new materialism begins from real individuals engaged in production, thinks dialectically, and aims at a "true community". Liu argues that the private interests of civil society, driven by the logic of capital, spread worldwide as unequal hierarchies of core and periphery, which the bourgeois state and its "universal values" justify. The community with a shared future, in Liu's reading, sublates this alienation as a realist and not an altruist or idealist scheme. It recognises differences between states, seeks shared interests, answers "global problems" through joint consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, and offers a measure of ethical security against modern anxiety.

Liu concludes that the community with a shared future continues Marx's project of "changing the world" in the new era and carries real world-historical significance. China's promotion of it is said to show a major-country sense of responsibility. Liu calls for deeper philosophical study of its theoretical resources and of its inheritance from new materialism. Read the original if you want a detailed philosophical genealogy that ties Chinese foreign-policy language to Marx's early writings and to the civil society debate.
quoteEn: The community with a shared future for mankind is rooted in new materialism and is the continuation and unfolding, in the new era, of Marx's programme of "changing the world".
quoteZh: 人类命运共同体植根于新唯物主义，是马克思“改变世界”方案在新时代的延续与展开。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13 as China's vision for international relations and global governance. It stresses shared interests, joint consultation and win-win cooperation.
The term Marx uses in the Theses on Feuerbach for his own standpoint, set against "old" contemplative materialism. Chinese scholars read it as the basis of historical materialism.
Marx's term, in The German Ideology, for a community of freely associated individuals. It is contrasted with the "illusory" or "false" community represented by the bourgeois state.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Upholding a world-embracing outlook: theoretical sources, a century of practice and present-day lessons
zh: 坚持胸怀天下的理论溯源、百年历程及现实启示
paras: The article examines "upholding a world-embracing outlook" (jianchi xionghuai tianxia), which the 20th Party Congress report (2022) lists as part of the worldview and methodology of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The 2021 Party history resolution also names it as one of the historical lessons of the Party's first century. Sun argues that the principle reflects the Party's Marxist stance on China's relations with the outside world. In Sun's account, it has deep theoretical roots and has guided a century of practice. It also yields lessons for advancing Chinese modernization.

The article has three parts. The first traces three sources: the Marxist idea of world history, the "all under heaven" sentiment of traditional Chinese culture, and the foreign-policy thought developed in the Sinicisation of Marxism. The second surveys the Party's practice in four periods: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era. The third draws four lessons.

Sun's core argument is that the principle joins Marx's analysis of world history with Chinese cultural concepts. From Marx and Engels, Sun takes the claim that capitalism created the world market and world history but will not end it. On this view, individual liberation and communism depend on history becoming fully world history. From the Chinese tradition Sun draws ideas such as the world as shared by all, harmony without uniformity, and benevolence towards others. Sun then follows foreign-policy thought from Mao Zedong through Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao to Xi Jinping. The article presents the practice in each period as foreign relations serving domestic tasks while pursuing independence, peace and shared development. It cites the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, foreign aid, the Belt and Road Initiative, a community with a shared future for mankind, and poverty reduction.

Sun draws four lessons. The first is to master the worldview and methodology of the Party's Sinicised Marxism. The second is to preserve centralised, unified Party leadership as the basis for handling external relations. The third is to pursue the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation through Chinese modernization, taking on greater international responsibility. The fourth is to keep to independence and self-reliance while learning from other civilisations. Sun concludes that the principle will help Chinese modernization create "a new form of human civilisation". Read the original if you want a Party-theory account of how official scholarship traces the lineage of the world-embracing outlook from Marx and classical Chinese texts to Xi Jinping's diplomacy.
quoteEn: Upholding a world-embracing outlook reflects our Party's human-centred concern that transcends class, nation and state.
quoteZh: 坚持胸怀天下，体现了我们党超越阶级、民族、国家的人类情怀。

glossary.literal: keep a heart that embraces all under heaven
glossary.explanation: A principle listed in the 2021 Party history resolution among the lessons of the Party's first century. It calls for viewing China's development in terms of humanity's shared future.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name of Xi Jinping's body of theory, written into the Party constitution in 2017.
The official concept of China's path to modernization, presented as distinct from the Western model. The 20th Party Congress (2022) made it central to its programme.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2013. It calls for countries to share interests, challenges and responsibilities.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official long-term national goal of the Party, linked to the centenary goals for 2049.
An infrastructure and economic cooperation programme launched by Xi Jinping in 2013, linking China with countries across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: An important milestone on the Chinese nation's road to great rejuvenation
st: The victory in the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea and its spirit
zh: 中华民族走向伟大复兴的重要里程碑
paras: This commentary was published in the People's Daily on the 70th anniversary of the victory in the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea. Tang takes up Xi Jinping's description of that victory as a declaration that the Chinese people had stood up, and as an important milestone on the road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The author argues that remembering the war and carrying forward its spirit should inspire the Chinese people to advance on the new journey of building a strong country and achieving national rejuvenation.

The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the victory matters historically. The second identifies four components of the Great Spirit of Resisting US Aggression and Aiding Korea. The third turns to the present and lists four resolves that remembering the war is meant to strengthen.

In the first part, Tang describes China's intervention as a just act by a just army, taken at the request of the Korean Party and government after US forces crossed the 38th Parallel and, in the author's account, threatened China's security. Tang presents the outcome as a victory of the weak over the strong. In this account it secured the new state's footing, displayed the strength of the people's army, deterred later armed attempts against China and encouraged oppressed peoples elsewhere. The four elements of the spirit are fearlessness towards bullying and hegemony, national unity under Party leadership, a willingness to fight to the death, and innovative wisdom. Tang links each to a present task: meeting risks with courage, building the broadest unity, refusing to flinch from struggle, and pioneering Chinese modernization.

Tang concludes that China must hold firm in four resolves: unity under the leadership of the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, building a strong country and achieving rejuvenation, building a world-class military under Xi Jinping Thought on Strengthening the Military, and defending world peace and justice. The last is tied to opposing hegemonism and power politics and to building a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a representative example of how official commentary in 2023 used the Korean War to support themes of Party leadership, military strengthening and national rejuvenation.
quoteEn: The great War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea was the war that founded the new China; it won, through hard fighting, the safety of the land and the peace of the nation.
quoteZh: 伟大的抗美援朝战争是新中国的立国之战，拼来了山河无恙、家国安宁。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central goal of Party discourse, associated especially with Xi Jinping's Chinese Dream. It denotes restoring China to a position of national strength and international standing after the 'century of humiliation'.

glossary.pinyin: wěidà Kàng Měi Yuán Cháo jīngshén
glossary.en: the Great Spirit of Resisting US Aggression and Aiding Korea
glossary.explanation: An official formulation, set out in the 2020 speech by Xi Jinping on the 70th anniversary of China's entry into the Korean War. It is presented as the patriotic and heroic ethos shown by the Chinese People's Volunteers.
The Party's official term for China's own path to modernization, elaborated especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as different from Western models.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Strengthening the Military
glossary.explanation: The official body of ideas on Party command of the armed forces and building a modern, world-class military. It is treated as part of Xi Jinping Thought.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept for international relations, stressing shared interests, cooperation and opposition to hegemonism. It is widely used in Chinese foreign-policy discourse.

keywords: Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea

t: The cultural construction of a community with a shared future for mankind and its world significance
zh: 人类命运共同体的文化构建及其世界意义
paras: Liu Tongfang asks what the cultural dimension of building a community with a shared future for mankind consists of, and what it offers the world. Writing in 2023, Liu argues that this cultural construction is the spiritual side of the community and has an internal structure that unites subjectivity, diversity and leadership (主导性). It has three levels, material, political and spiritual, and performs three functions: integrating, transcending and reproducing.

The article has four sections. It first defines the three features of cultural construction, then sets out the three levels, then the three functions, and finally the way cultural construction shapes a new "world civilisation body". Liu draws on Marx and Engels, Gramsci's cultural hegemony, Fei Xiaotong's idea of cultural subjectivity, Heidegger, Daniel Bell, Althusser and Bourdieu, and criticises Hegel, Fukuyama and Huntington.

Liu's central move is to ground culture in material production. The material level is the foundation, the political level (the state, institutions, political identity) is the safeguard, and the spiritual level (a spiritual home, shared values) is the aim and reacts back on the other two. The author holds that capitalist globalisation sets "universal values" against exploitation and capital accumulation, and that this produces cultural hegemony and Western "cultural centrism". The three functions are described as follows: integrating means individuals identify with community norms, transcending means critique of reality oriented to people's free and all-round development, and reproducing means cultural output is constantly renewed to meet spiritual needs.

Liu concludes that this cultural construction answers Western cultural centrism and offers a way to resolve civilisational conflict through dialogue and mutual learning, with the principle of harmony in diversity. It also points toward a new pattern of inclusive world civilisation. The author presents it as a form of Chinese wisdom that shows China's cultural consciousness and confidence and has milestone significance for human civilisation. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese-academic account of how the cultural dimension of the community with a shared future for mankind is theorised, using both Marxist and Western sources.
quoteEn: The cultural construction of a community with a shared future for mankind is a practical response to the "cultural centrism" pursued by Western powers. It stresses that civilisation itself is the decisive criterion for membership of the world civilisational community, and it enables states to take part in global governance on an equal footing.
quoteZh: 人类命运共同体的文化构建是应对西方大国推行“文化中心主义”的现实对策，其强调文明本身构成世界文明共同体准入成员的决定性准则，促使各主体国家平等地参与世界治理。

glossary.en: community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping from around 2012–2013 as China's vision for international relations and global governance. It stresses shared interests, cooperation and mutual respect among states.
A classical Chinese phrase invoked in official discourse to describe peaceful coexistence of different civilisations without forced uniformity.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Mao Zedong's economic thought: a review of research on its foundations, theoretical content and practical achievements
zh: 毛泽东经济思想的生成基础、理论内涵与实践成就研究述论
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2023 no. 1
paras: This review surveys Chinese scholarship, published since the 1980s, on Mao Zedong's economic thought, which Yang Yan treats as an important part of Mao Zedong Thought and as comparable in value to his political, military and philosophical thought. Written to mark the 130th anniversary of Mao's birth, it both explains the content of the thought and assesses the state of research. Yang's overall position is that the thought guided the historic economic changes of twentieth-century China and deserves fuller, more systematic study.

The review is organised around three dimensions: the foundations from which the thought arose, its theoretical content, and the practical achievements achieved under its guidance. It draws on monographs and articles by a long list of Chinese scholars and quotes the American scholars Maurice Meisner and Paul Samuelson on the Mao-era record. A final section sets out directions for further research.

On foundations, Yang reports that scholars trace the thought to Marxist theory, to revolutionary practice and social investigation (such as the Xunwu and Xingguo surveys), and to Chinese history and traditional thought, which Mao is said to have inherited critically. On content, the review sorts the literature into three bodies of thought: new democratic economics, the theory of socialist transformation, and socialist economic construction. The last includes stages of development, contradictions in socialist society, economic relations such as agriculture, light and heavy industry, and socialist commodity production. The review notes that scholars largely defend the General Line for the transition period, while acknowledging errors such as a single ownership form and over-hasty transformation after 1955. On achievements, it cites figures on industrial output, grain, schooling, health and life expectancy. It concludes that the Mao era was neither a utopia sustained by a personality cult nor a period of mere stagnation.

Yang concludes that research remains fragmented, because it tends to treat theory, policy and results separately, and that few studies examine how ideas were put into practice. The author calls for a full chain of logic and data running from practice to understanding and back to practice. Yang also proposes combining Marxist theory with Party history methods, and drawing on local archives and case studies, to deepen work on adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a detailed map of Chinese scholarship on Mao-era economic thought and policy, and of how that scholarship defends the Mao period's economic record.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's economic thought was by no means a utopia of a spiritual world, built under conditions of poverty on a personality cult to secure the ideological purity of the masses.
quoteZh: 毛泽东经济思想绝非在贫穷条件下，依靠个人崇拜，打造人民群众意识形态纯洁性的精神世界的乌托邦

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for the Party's ongoing effort to fit Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and contemporary circumstances. The 'times' element was added in recent Party documents.

glossary.en: General Line for the transition period
glossary.literal: general line of the transitional period
glossary.explanation: The policy announced in 1952–53 to complete industrialisation and the socialist transformation of agriculture, handicrafts and capitalist industry and commerce, often abbreviated as 'one transformation, three reforms' (一化三改).
Mao Zedong's theory of a transitional stage between semi-colonial, semi-feudal society and socialism, with a mixed economy led by the state sector.

t: The spatial production of platform capital and its limits
zh: 平台资本的空间生产及其限度
paras: Since the 2008 crisis, the "gig", "sharing" and "digital" economies have grown around platforms such as Google, Facebook and Amazon. Wang and Yang ask why and how digital platform space is produced, what role it plays in capital's valorisation, and whether platform capital has permanently overcome spatial limits. They argue that platform companies continue capitalism's tradition of spatial reorganisation by building a virtual spatial paradigm, and that this paradigm remains bound by limits inherent in capital. In their conclusion, only a socialist spatial configuration can remove these limits.

The article, published in Socialism Studies in 2023, has three main sections. The first treats the "spatialisation of capital", tracing platform capital from industrial and finance capital to the "space of flows", and describing how it builds virtual physical space, virtual social space and a psychological space of trust. The second treats the "capitalisation of space", examining the platform's capital attributes, its production process and its absorption of labour. The third examines the contradictions this process produces. The authors draw on Marx, Lenin, Harvey, Lefebvre, Giddens, Castells and Deleuze and Guattari.

In the authors' account, platform space is both a means of production and a form of capital. Virtual physical space works as a "digital factory" and is rented out for ground rent. Virtual social space turns concrete labour into homogeneous abstract labour and standardises exchange globally. Platforms extend the formal subsumption of labour into everyday life, as workers bring their own workspaces and means of production, and extend it into real subsumption by appropriating socialised collective force. The authors then identify three limits. Virtual space is infinite while real space is finite, immediate while real space is slow, and comprehensive while real purchasing power is fixed. As platform space becomes universal, the authors expect it to become structurally homogeneous, to divide users into centre and periphery, and to run out of external space for "spatial fixes". Self-driven labour and algorithmic "enslavement" are said to deepen total plunder of society and approach a new "spatial implosion".

Wang and Yang conclude that platform space production eases capital's survival crisis and carries humanity into a virtual world, but that it also exposes the exploitation of workers and of society as a whole. They hold that its spatial limits are embedded in the nature of capital and become more concrete as capital changes form. Read the original if you want a Marxist spatial-theory analysis of digital platforms that combines Marx's critique of capital with Harvey and Lefebvre.
quoteEn: Only a socialist spatial configuration can remove the spatial limits of capitalism.
quoteZh: 破除资本主义的空间限度，唯有社会主义空间构型。

t: The crisis of the neoliberal global order in the perspective of the critique of political economy
zh: 政治经济学批判视域中的新自由主义全球秩序危机
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 29 June 2023
paras: Hu Xiaokun asks how the neoliberal global order can be understood as monopolistic and crisis-ridden when read through Marx's critique of political economy and Lenin's theory of imperialism. The article, a newspaper-length commentary first published in 2023, presents the analysis of contemporary Russian left-wing scholars, above all Alexander Buzgalin and Andrei Kolganov. Hu reports their claim that twenty-first-century capitalism is returning to monopoly, which they see as the outcome of competition's own logic.

The text begins with Lenin's view that imperialism is economically monopoly growing out of free competition. It then turns to Marx's account of competition, the average rate of profit and the relation between 'capital in general' and 'many capitals'. The second half sets out Buzgalin's periodisation of monopoly capitalism since the early twentieth century and his analysis of its current forms. It ends with the Russian scholars' reading of the present world situation.

Hu argues, following Marx, that capital's inner tendencies assert themselves through competitive compulsion. Competition among many capitals produces concentration and centralisation and so turns into its opposite, monopoly. Buzgalin, in Hu's account, distinguishes three stages: early-twentieth-century imperialism, a post-war stage of social reformism, and neoliberal globalisation since the 1970s. In his view the last is reverting towards the first, under the domination of financial monopoly capital. Hu lists the features Buzgalin identifies: corporate manipulation of public life, the sale of simulated goods, speculative financial ecosystems, 'desocialisation' and escalating geopolitical conflict. Buzgalin also stresses a counter-tendency. Socialisation of production, trade unions and public-sector services built up socialist elements inside capitalism, and these now obstruct monopoly profit. The great powers respond with protectionism, militarisation and sanctions, producing what he calls a new imperialism of centre over (semi-)periphery.

Hu concludes that the Russian scholars restore Lenin's theory and Marx's critique in order to strip away neoliberal ideology's concealment of capital's logic. They also trace how the basic contradiction of capitalism spreads globally. Starting from Russia's position as a (semi-)peripheral capitalist formation, they combine geopolitical logic with the logic of capital. Hu presents this as a distinctive theoretical perspective on the 'great changes unseen in a century'. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese introduction to how Russian Marxists such as Buzgalin interpret neoliberal globalisation, de-globalisation and new imperialism.
quoteEn: In Buzgalin's view, within the framework of financial monopoly capitalism it is impossible to resolve the twenty-first-century global financial crisis, the intensification of global problems, and the series of extreme problems exposed in geopolitical and economic competition.
quoteZh: 在布兹加林看来，在金融垄断资本主义的框架内，不可能解决21世纪全球金融危机、全球性问题加剧以及在地缘政治和经济竞争中所暴露的一系列极端问题。

glossary.zh: 世界百年未有之大变局
glossary.pinyin: shìjiè bǎinián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.en: great changes unseen in a century
glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Chinese official discourse since around 2017–2018 to describe a period of profound shifts in the international order, including changes in the balance of power among states.
Marx's term for capital in its abstract, inner nature, as distinct from the 'many capitals' that compete in reality.

t: Rethinking the theoretical sources and logical course of Marx's first intellectual transformation
zh: 重思马克思第一次思想转变的理论渊源与逻辑进程
paras: Zhang Fugong takes up a long-debated question in studies of the development of Marx's thought: which theoretical sources and what logical course produced his first intellectual transformation, from idealism to materialism and toward communism. Zhang argues that earlier scholarship, which centred on Hegel and Feuerbach, neglected the latent influence of Proudhon, Moses Hess and Engels. Taking these figures into account, the article contends, gives a more exact picture of the plural background and the complicated path of the shift. The piece was published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in June 2023.

The article first reviews two interpretive routes. One, begun by Lenin, judges the shift by philosophical logic and political stance; it was hardened into a Soviet "one transformation" thesis, rejected by Western Marxism, and revived by Chinese scholars such as Sun Bo'ao through the "two transformations" thesis. The other route analyses changes of object and theme, for instance from critique of the state to critique of civil society. Zhang then proceeds in two parts: the plural theoretical background, and the stage-by-stage course through the Rheinische Zeitung period, the Kreuznach notebooks, the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question and the Introduction to the Critique.

Zhang's central claim is that Marx took over Feuerbach's anthropological materialism, not his naturalistic one, as Marx's 1843 letter to Ruge shows. Extending it to politics and economics, Zhang argues, drew on others. Proudhon offered a critique of bourgeois right and property from a theory of human nature; Hess moved from critique of political alienation to critique of monetary alienation; Engels added empirical economic study and a firmer revolutionary communist stance. Zhang holds that the "civil society determines the state" idea in the 1843 critique of Hegel was only latent social materialism, since Marx still viewed civil society negatively. The dominant logic there, Zhang suggests, was a Hess-like critique of political alienation. In On the Jewish Question Marx moved to economic alienation, and in the 1844 Introduction he tied philosophy to the proletariat, probably under Engels's influence.

Zhang concludes that in the period of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher Marx achieved a first, general transformation in philosophical logic and political stance together: Feuerbachian anthropological materialism and revolutionary communism based on it. Zhang stresses that no complete system yet existed, since alienation was still treated at the level of exchange and money, not labour, and the link between sublating alienation and communism was left to the Paris Manuscripts. Read the original if you study the early Marx and want a compact argument that Proudhon, Hess and Engels shaped his turn to materialism and communism.
quoteEn: In the author's view, Marx's dominant philosophical logic at this point was a critique of political alienation based on Feuerbach-style anthropological materialism, and this most likely came from Hess's influence.
quoteZh: 笔者认为，此时马克思的主导性哲学逻辑是基于费尔巴哈式的人本学唯物主义的政治异化批判逻辑，而这很可能来自赫斯的影响。

glossary.explanation: A reading associated with Sun Bo'ao and other Chinese scholars. It holds that Marx's early shift from idealism to materialism and communism was followed by a second, deeper break with Feuerbachian philosophy in 1845.
The Soviet-era reading, traced to Lenin, which treats Marx's turn to materialism and communism as a single shift in the early 1840s.
Feuerbach's materialism centred on the human being and human essence, as distinct from naturalistic materialism. The article treats it as the philosophical basis Marx adopted in 1843–44.

t: Main problems and solution paths in the process of Chinese modernization
zh: 中国式现代化进程中面临的主要问题与解决路径
source: World Social Sciences (Shijie shehui kexue), 2023 no. 2
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Zhao Ruyu asks what the main problem facing Chinese modernization is. Starting from the principal contradiction between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, the article argues that the central problem is the contradiction between a new industrial revolution and the urban–rural gap. The new industrial revolution is presented as the key to inadequate development, and narrowing the gap as the key to unbalanced development.

The article has five parts: the framing of the problem, the case that this contradiction is the main one, an analysis of how it arises, the paths to resolve it, and a conclusion. The historical section compares the earlier industrial revolutions and the information revolution of the 1990s in Britain, France, Germany, the United States, Japan and South Korea with the present. Zhao then examines the effects of the new industrial revolution on the countryside and the effects of the urban–rural gap on that revolution.

Zhao argues that developed countries avoided a lasting clash between industrial revolution and urban–rural relations for four reasons. Natural resources gained importance, labour-intensive industries absorbed large workforces, populations were relatively small, and the international division of labour allowed those countries to exploit developing ones. The new industrial revolution, in Zhao's account, has a dual effect. It promotes sustainability and efficiency, but it also devalues natural endowments, thins out the industrial system, expels labour and concentrates resources in very large cities, which tends to widen the rural gap. The gap in turn affects the revolution in two ways. Putting rural catch-up first could slow the revolution, whereas letting the gap widen would burden local finances, endanger food security and social stability, and weaken rural consumer demand.

Zhao concludes that neither side can be abandoned and that the gap cannot be put on hold until the revolution is finished and the 'cake' divided. The proposed path is for cities and countryside to build a modern industrial system together. It has three parts: extending new technologies such as smart agriculture, biotechnology and e-commerce to rural areas; redistributing industry spatially through metropolitan circles, virtual research clusters and small towns; and upgrading rural infrastructure and public services through in-situ urbanization. Read the original if you want a policy-oriented economic analysis of how technological change and the urban–rural divide interact in discussions of common prosperity.
quoteEn: The new industrial revolution and the urban–rural gap are not alternatives to be chosen between, but an internally unified relationship of mutual constraint and mutual promotion.
quoteZh: 新产业革命与城乡差距之间不是舍此取彼的替代关系，而是相互制约和相互促进的内在统一关系。

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal that the Party has stressed since the 2010s and especially from 2021. It refers to prosperity shared by all, with narrower gaps in income and between regions.

The official name for China's development path, emphasised at the 20th Party Congress (2022). Its stated features include a huge population, common prosperity, harmony between humanity and nature, and peaceful development.

The author's term for the wave of technological change since about 2008, covering re-industrialization with new energy, biotechnology and health, intelligent manufacturing, and the digital 'smart society'.

t: Chinese modernization: how a local narrative can become a world discourse
zh: 中国式现代化：何以从本土叙事转向世界话语
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Li Jiali asks how Chinese modernization can be turned from a locally rooted political phrase of the new era into a discourse with universal standing. The concern is practical: the author wants to guard against misreadings, especially in Western scholarship, that would turn the concept into fresh evidence for distorted accounts of China's development. Li's answer is that its universal significance must be explained in scholarly terms.

The article has three parts. The first traces the historical narrative of Western modernization discourse as Enlightenment discourse, capital discourse and development discourse, including dependency theory (Samir Amin) and Said's Orientalism. The second follows modern China's own narratives since 1840: the "Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application" approach, wholesale Westernization, and socialist modernization under the Communist Party. The third sets out three ways in which a world discourse is possible.

Li argues that modernization as a concept and its theory were built by Western thinkers, who tied it to capitalism and Western-centred world order. In Li's view, dependency theory and Orientalism remain inside Western frameworks, as anti-Western-centrism built on Western-centrism. China's earlier schemes failed, the author says, because the first kept feudal foundations and the second took capitalism as the template. Socialist modernization, from the 1945 Seventh Party Congress through the "four modernizations" to reform and opening up, is presented as surpassing both traditional socialism and Westernization.

To make the concept universal, Li calls for three moves. China's modernization should be seen as part of human modernization, sharing common features with other countries, as the 20th Party Congress report says. Its five features should be read as answers to the general problems of modernity, such as tensions between people and nature. And it should be understood as advanced because it breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and escapes the "spell of capital". Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's account of how the concept is positioned against Western modernization theory and of China's modernization debates since 1840.
quoteEn: This category is therefore not merely a particular form and local expression of human modernization in China, but a Chinese solution offered in response to the universal problems of modernity.
quoteZh: 因此，这一范畴不仅仅是人类现代化在中国的特殊形态和本土表达，而是基于现代性普遍问题而给出的中国方案。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official description of China's path to modernization, set out in the report to the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is described as socialist, led by the Party, and distinct from the Western model.

glossary.en: Chinese learning as substance, Western learning for application
glossary.literal: Chinese learning as essence, Western learning as function
glossary.explanation: A late Qing slogan, associated with Zhang Zhidong and the Self-Strengthening Movement. It urged adopting Western technology while keeping Confucian social and political principles.
A position from the New Culture era, named by Hu Shi in 1929 and defended by Chen Xujing. It held that China should adopt Western modern culture entirely.
The goal of modernizing industry, agriculture, national defence, and science and technology. It was announced in the 1950s and 1960s and became a national slogan.

t: Mao Zedong's thought on ideological and political education in universities and its contemporary implications (1949–1966)
zh: 毛泽东关于高校思想政治教育的思想及其现实启示(1949—1966)
source: Journal of Red Culture (Hongse wenhua xuekan), 2023 no. 1
paras: Luo Xiong asks how Mao Zedong approached ideological and political education in Chinese universities after 1949, and what that experience offers today. Starting from Xi Jinping's statement that this work answers the fundamental questions of what kind of people universities train, how, and for whom, the article argues that Mao made a series of creative adjustments and reinforcements. In Luo's reading, these still hold lessons for cultivating a new generation capable of shouldering national rejuvenation.

The article is organised chronologically and then thematically. The first part covers 1949–1956, when Mao adjusted university work in the transition from new-democratic to socialist construction. The second covers 1956–1966, the period of comprehensive socialist construction, when Mao strengthened it. The third draws three present-day implications for the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The evidence is mainly Party directives, instructions Mao reviewed or approved, and the Sixty Articles on Higher Education (1961).

For 1949–1956, Luo describes three measures. Party leadership was extended through Party organisations, with Party cadres installed in university leadership. The content of teaching was revised to counter 'feudal, comprador and fascist' ideas among staff and students. Teachers of political theory were trained through Party schools and Marxism-Leninism classes. For 1956–1966, Luo identifies three developments. Party secretaries were made first-responsible persons for ideological work. Courses were reshaped around the 'three educations, two haves' guideline (moral, intellectual and physical education, producing cultured workers with socialist consciousness), with growing emphasis on opposing revisionism. Education was also to serve proletarian politics and be combined with productive labour, through the Socialist Education Movement and farm and factory work. By the end of 1965, the article says, about 395 universities and over 220,000 staff and students had taken part.

Luo concludes that Party leadership produced many 'both red and expert' intellectuals, while acknowledging deviations. These included leftist tendencies after the expanded anti-Rightist campaign, with politics prioritised over academic study, and labour time that sometimes exceeded study time. For the present, Luo calls for upholding Party leadership with Party secretaries as first responsible persons, and for keeping the right political direction under Xi's 'four services' formulation to cultivate a new generation. Luo also calls for strengthening both dedicated political theory courses and 'ideological and political education across the curriculum'. Read the original if you want a documented account of Party directives on university political education in the Mao era, and of how a Chinese scholar draws on it to support current policy.
quoteEn: The correctness of Mao Zedong's "two musts" guideline for education is beyond question.
quoteZh: 毛泽东关于教育“两必须”的方针,其中的正确性不容置疑。

glossary.en: ideological and political education across the curriculum
glossary.literal: curriculum ideology and politics (课程思政)
glossary.explanation: The policy of integrating ideological and political education, including ideals and convictions, into professional and general courses beyond the dedicated political theory classes. It is promoted in Chinese higher education under Xi Jinping.
A Maoist-era slogan calling for intellectuals and cadres to combine political loyalty to socialism (red) with professional competence (expert).
Provisional regulations for universities directly under the Ministry of Education, adopted in 1961. They set out the Party committee's leading role and the place of political work in universities.
A campaign of the early 1960s, launched first in the countryside, aimed at ideological education and class-struggle awareness. It later drew in university staff and students.

t: Mao Zedong's creative use and development of the traditional concept of "tianxia" (all under heaven)
zh: 毛泽东对传统天下观的创造性运用和发展
paras: Ding Junping and Jia Shuheng ask how Mao Zedong drew on the traditional Chinese concept of tianxia ('all under heaven') and what he made of it. They argue that Mao creatively used and developed the tianxia outlook of China's fine traditional culture, and that this shows the way Mao Zedong Thought combines the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities.

The article first sets out four value components of the traditional tianxia view: tianxia as a personal responsibility, as an ideal of great harmony (datong), as an account of rise and fall tied to popular support, and as one family. It then examines Mao's handling of each in turn, from his youth to the post-1949 period, drawing on his writings and speeches. A final section assesses the significance of this development, and a short conclusion links it to the thought of Xi Jinping.

The authors' central claim is that Mao kept the emotional and ethical core of each idea but replaced its philosophical content with Marxism. In their account, the duty to bear responsibility for tianxia acquired concrete goals once Mao used class analysis and the theory of contradiction. His datong ideal was purged of absolute egalitarianism, identified with communism, and given a practical route: new-democratic revolution, socialist revolution, then gradual transition to communism. On winning popular support, Mao grounded it in historical materialism, in which the people are the driving force of history, rather than in imperial favour, and he answered Huang Yanpei's question about the 'historical cycle' of dynasties with democracy and popular supervision. For the 'one family' view, the authors cite Mao's treatment of the Chinese revolution as part of world revolution, his call for peaceful coexistence of different systems, and his stress on learning from all nations.

The authors conclude that this adaptation helped Marxism take root in China, renewed the content of the old tianxia view, produced correct policies for revolution and construction, and shaped the Communist spirit of serving country, nation and people. They add that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping has carried the line forward, including through a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Mao is presented as drawing on classical Chinese ideas of responsibility, utopia, popular support and world order.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong replaced the philosophical core of the old view of the rise and fall of tianxia, which ran counter to history and reality.
quoteZh: 毛泽东替换了旧式天下兴亡观与历史和现实相违背的哲学内核。

glossary.explanation: A classical Chinese concept with geographical, political and cultural senses, referring to the whole world or realm under a ruler and to an ordered human community.
The ideal society described in the Book of Rites, in which the world is shared by all and governed by the capable. Modern thinkers, including Kang Youwei and Sun Yat-sen, reused it.
The pattern of dynasties rising and then collapsing. Huang Yanpei raised it with Mao in Yan'an in 1945, and Mao's answer, democracy, is often cited in Party discourse.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s, stressing shared interests and joint global governance.

t: The Guide weekly and the early spread of Marxism in China
zh: 《向导》周报与马克思主义在中国的早期传播
paras: The article examines the Guide (Xiangdao) weekly, the first political organ of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party, and asks what it contributed to the early spread of Marxism in China. Liang and Ru argue that, from its launch in September 1922 to its forced closure in July 1927, the paper spread Marxism-Leninism, explained Party policy and guided the workers' movement. They describe it as a faithful and courageous 'guide' to the Chinese revolution.

Drawing on press sources and related documents, the authors place the paper in the historical setting of early Marxist dissemination. They note that it ran for 201 issues, moved between Shanghai, Beijing, Guangzhou and Wuhan, and grew from several thousand copies to more than 100,000. The article has three main parts: the exposition of Marxism-Leninism and the Party's revolutionary programme; the rebuttal of 'Dai Jitao-ism' and the 'statist faction'; and the class analysis of the revolution's forces.

In the first part, the authors count the paper's 1,474 articles. They report that 171 dealt with the relation between economic base and superstructure, and they cite special issues on Lenin, the October Revolution and the national-colonial question. In the second part, they argue that Chen Duxiu, Qu Qiubai and the short-commentary column 'Cunthie' defended the Marxist theory of the state, class struggle and historical materialism against Dai Jitao's appeal to benevolence and the statists' supra-class 'all-people revolution'. In the third part, the Guide stressed that the proletariat must hold leadership, treated the peasantry as its most reliable ally, and described the national bourgeoisie as politically dual: revolutionary at times, vacillating and compromising at others. The paper also helped shape opinion in favour of the first KMT–CPC cooperation.

The authors conclude that the Guide recorded the Party's early search for a revolutionary path and prepared rich ideological material for it. They say the paper's Fourth Congress (1925) assessment gave it a 'leading position in public opinion'. They also treat its practices as part of the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context, and as useful today: holding to the Marxist standpoint, strengthening positive propaganda and confronting erroneous ideas firmly. Read the original if you want a detailed, sourced account of how a Party newspaper of the 1920s presented Marxism, class analysis and polemics, as the Party's official historiography now tells it.
quoteEn: The Guide made clear that the Chinese revolution is part of the world proletarian revolution, and pointed out that it must give and receive mutual aid with that revolution and with national liberation movements.
quoteZh: 《向导》阐明了中国革命是世界无产阶级革命的一部分，指明中国革命必须与世界无产阶级革命、民族解放运动互相援助

glossary.en: adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context
glossary.explanation: The Party's official term for applying Marxism to China's concrete conditions and developing it in the process. The current formula is 'adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times'.

The alliance between the Kuomintang (Nationalist Party) and the Chinese Communist Party in 1924–1927, in which Communists joined the KMT to fight warlords and imperialism. It ended in 1927 when the KMT broke with the Communists.
