It also refers to the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which treated the advance of people's democracy as part of the Party's historical significance.

Zhu holds that each stage supplied conditions for the next. Examples include the Soviet governments and the \"three-thirds\" system in the base areas, the People's Political Consultative Conference and the people's congress system after 1949, and regional ethnic autonomy. Later come grassroots self-governance, consultative democracy and democratic centralism. Zhu says the Party combines Marxist people's democracy theory with Chinese practice and traditional culture. Since 2012, in Zhu's account, whole-process people's democracy has covered electoral, consultative, social and grassroots democracy, and every stage from election to supervision.

Zhu concludes that the Party's century of struggle made the people masters of the country and gave democracy \"real meaning\". The article predicts that the Party will write a more splendid chapter in the history of human political civilization. Read the original if you want a concise official-aligned periodisation of how Party scholars present the history of people's democracy.
quoteEn: Without democracy, there is no socialism and no socialist modernization.
quoteZh: 没有民主，就没有社会主义，就没有社会主义的现代化。

glossary.explanation: A concept in official Chinese political discourse, prominent since 2019, describing the Party's model of democracy as covering every stage of political life, not only elections. The 2021 white paper presented it as the core of China's democratic claims.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution from roughly 1919 to 1949, led by the proletariat and directed against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism.
A Leninist organisational principle, held in China to be the Party's basic organisational principle, combining discussion with unified decision-making and discipline.
China's fundamental political institution, a system of congresses from local level to the National People's Congress, established by the 1954 Constitution.

t: The major influence of "On Practice" and "On Contradiction" on China's scientific and technological development
zh: 《实践论》《矛盾论》推动我国科技发展的重大影响
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2021 no. 7
paras: Cui Haiying asks how Mao Zedong's philosophical essays "On Practice" and "On Contradiction" (the "two essays") have shaped science and technology in China, and what they offer to the present drive for high-level scientific and technological self-reliance. The article argues that the essays have guided science policy, scientists' thinking and shop-floor production since the 1950s, and that they remain a worldview and a method for the Party's technology work in the new era.

The article has three parts. The first surveys how the essays were studied and applied: in science planning and management, in the thinking of leading scientists, among grassroots technicians and workers, and among foreign physicists. The second analyses the internal link between the essays and technological development at three levels: textual, theoretical and practical. The third draws three lessons for self-reliance in science and technology.

In the historical survey, Cui cites the 1956–1967 and 1963–1972 science plans, the Daqing oilfield campaign's 1960 decision to study the essays, and testimony from Qian Xuesen, Li Siguang, Zhu Kezhen and Yuan Longping on how the essays informed their work. Cui also cites Japanese physicists such as Sakata Shoichi, and Sheldon Glashow's proposal to name possible deeper constituents of quarks "Mao particles". The author then shows that Mao drew on natural science to build his arguments, and claims that the essays underpin the Party's technology worldview through three habits of thought: seeking truth from facts, dialectical development and a people-centred orientation. The author contrasts the last with Western technology driven by capital and the pursuit of surplus value. In method, the essays are said to yield a hard-working practical spirit and a strong problem-orientation.

Cui proposes three lessons. The first is to keep Party leadership unchanged while speeding up institutional adjustment, including a new type of whole-nation system. The second is to rely on internal factors, meaning self-reliance, while using external factors through open cooperation. The third is to unify the subjective and objective worlds by advancing technical innovation, from basic research to core technologies, while holding to a people's standpoint. Read the original if you want a detailed, Party-theoretical account of how Mao's philosophy has been applied to science policy and scientific practice, with many cited cases.
quoteEn: Party leadership is the greatest political advantage of China's scientific and technological innovation, and advancing scientific and technological self-reliance requires keeping Party leadership "unchanged".
quoteZh: 党的领导是我国科技创新的最大政治优势，推进科技自立自强必须保证党的领导“不变”。

glossary.explanation: A 1937 philosophical essay by Mao Zedong on the relation between knowledge and practice, holding that practice is the criterion of truth. It is paired with "On Contradiction" as the "two essays".
A 1937 essay by Mao Zedong on dialectical materialism, discussing the universality and particularity of contradiction and the principal contradiction.

glossary.literal: science and technology standing on its own and strengthening itself
glossary.explanation: A policy goal stressed in Party documents of the early 2020s, aiming at independent mastery of core technologies and reduced dependence on foreign supply.
A principle taken as the core of the Party's ideological line, requiring that policy start from actual conditions and be tested in practice.

A model of mobilising state, market and research resources nationwide for major scientific and technological goals, presented as adapting the "concentrating resources to accomplish major tasks" approach to a socialist market economy.

t: The classical Marxist writers on the authority of the proletarian party
zh: 经典作家关于无产阶级政党权威的思想
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 30 June 2021
paras: Published in the centenary year of the Chinese Communist Party, this short commentary asks what Marx, Engels and Lenin said about authority in the proletarian party and why it still matters. Lü Yao argues that authority has been a constant issue in the history of the international communist movement, and that the classical writers' arguments give theoretical support for strengthening and upholding the centralised and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee in the new era.

The article is organised around two figures. The first part covers Marx and Engels: the 1847 reorganisation of the League of the Just into the Communist League, their dispute with Bakunin's anti-authoritarianism, and Engels's reflections after the Paris Commune. The second part turns to Lenin's work building a new-type party in Russia, drawing on What Is to Be Done?, One Step Forward, Two Steps Back and his later remarks on factionalism. A brief closing section links these ideas to current Party building.

Lü presents Marx and Engels as defending authority on three grounds. Revolution needs it, because united action against the bourgeoisie is impossible without it. The dictatorship of the proletariat needs it to consolidate, organise and build the new state power, as the Commune's lessons showed. And authority and autonomy are dialectically united and relative, so absolutising either is, in Engels's words, absurd. For Lenin, the author reports, a centralised party rests on democratic centralism, on upholding the authority of the Central Committee and of leaders, on discipline and statutes, and on banning factional activity, which Lenin held to be harmful and impermissible, as with the 'Workers' Opposition' after the civil war.

Lü concludes that this body of thought has informed the Party's organisational discipline and its institutional system, and that the Party in the new era has put forward the Two Upholds and raised them to the institutional level. Facing great changes unseen in a century, the author calls for placing Party leadership first, firmly upholding the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee, and advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned overview of how Chinese commentators draw on Marx, Engels and Lenin to justify central authority in the Party.
quoteEn: Authority and autonomy are dialectically united.
quoteZh: 权威和自治是辩证统一的。

glossary.explanation: A Party formula, prominent since 2018, calling on members to firmly uphold General Secretary Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the whole Party, and the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee.

The organisational principle of Leninist parties, combining democratic discussion and election with binding unity of action. In the article's formulation it means the individual obeys the organisation, the minority the majority, lower levels higher levels, and the whole Party the Central Committee.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's discipline and anti-corruption drive, promoted under Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

t: Implications of Marx's humanist theory for rural health-based poverty alleviation in China
zh: 马克思人本理论对我国农村健康扶贫的启示
source: Journal of Shanxi University of Finance and Economics, 2021, no. S2
paras: Writing in 2021, Li Xiaoqin asks what Marx's theory of the human being (renben lilun) can contribute to China's rural health-based poverty alleviation. The article opens by noting that the number of people lifted out of poverty in China since 1949 exceeds the combined populations of the United States, Russia, Japan and Germany, which it calls a "Chinese miracle". Li argues that Marx's humanist theory, read together with the Communist Party's poverty-relief experience, helps identify the internal laws of anti-poverty work and has both theoretical and practical significance for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

The article has three parts. The first summarises Marx's view of the human being under three headings: the essence of the human being, human subjectivity, and the free and all-round development of the person. The second identifies three problems in current rural health-based poverty alleviation. The third draws three lessons from Marx's theory and ends with a short conclusion that links Xi Jinping's statements on rural health poverty relief to this theoretical basis.

Li presents Marx's account as follows: human generic essence is free, conscious activity, that is, labour, while the real essence of a person is the ensemble of social relations. People are the subjects of history, with initiative, autonomy and purposiveness. Against this background Li names three problems: poor coordination among policy actors, with fragmented measures and no long-term mechanism beyond the 2020 deadline; weak classified and tiered assistance, leaving heavy costs for serious illness and formalistic chronic-disease management; and weak primary-care capacity, which forces poor patients to seek treatment elsewhere. The lessons follow Marx's formulations. Because poverty stems from alienation under capitalist private property, the author holds that socialism gives anti-poverty work a firm basis. Because people are concrete and historical, policy must meet real needs through targeted measures, big-data registration and dynamic monitoring. Because people exist in social relations, Li calls for mobilising all forces, strengthening primary-care professionals and expanding health education so that rural residents have easier access to treatment and fall ill less often.

Li concludes that great practice needs correct understanding to guide it, and that Xi Jinping's statements on rural health poverty relief grow out of his fieldwork in poor areas and are guided by Marx's humanist theory. In Li's view, they inherit earlier thought and open new paths for China's poverty alleviation. Read the original if you want a short example of how Chinese scholars apply Marx's anthropology to a concrete welfare policy field, rural health poverty relief.
quoteEn: Under the guidance of Marx's humanist theory, China draws lessons from the significance of the rural health poverty-eradication campaign.
quoteZh: 我国在马克思人本理论指导下对农村健康脱贫攻坚战的重要意义中获得启示

glossary.explanation: A term Chinese scholars use for Marx's theory of the human being, covering human essence, subjectivity and all-round development. In this article it is used to ground policy in a concern for the concrete person.
A strand of China's poverty-alleviation campaign that targets illness-related poverty, through medical insurance, medical assistance and better rural health services.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: An official goal of national revival, closely associated with Xi Jinping's leadership, which is often presented as the overarching aim of Party policy.

t: The ethical essence of China's new-type party system
zh: 中国新型政党制度的伦理本质
paras: This newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, 16 August 2021) asks why the system of multi-party cooperation and political consultation led by the Communist Party of China has lasted and grown more resilient. Li Yitian argues that, beyond its historical circumstances, the answer lies in the ethical principles the system has consistently upheld. Solidarity, democracy and harmony are said to constrain its development and to form its ethical essence, which distinguishes it from other party systems.

The piece opens by presenting the system as a new type of party system rooted in Chinese conditions and in traditional culture. It then takes the three values in turn, in three numbered sections: solidarity, democracy and harmony.

On solidarity, Li holds that the system reflects the diversity of interests among Chinese parties and social groups and confirms it institutionally. Recognising differing interests is only a basis, however. Real unity, in Li's account, comes from a shared aim of national independence, people's liberation, national prosperity and the people's wellbeing, which led the democratic parties to choose to work with the Communist Party. On democracy, Li, citing Xi Jinping, says the system seeks the "greatest common denominator" through broad participation and consultation. This, the author argues, gives it ethical legitimacy and makes decisions more scientific. On harmony, Li points to the constitutional leadership of the Communist Party, the participation of democratic parties in state affairs and mutual supervision. Li adds that consultation takes place before, during and after decisions, through meetings, interviews and written exchanges.

Li concludes that solidarity, democracy and harmony are built into the system's nature and let it solve Chinese problems as a distinctively Chinese approach. Li presents it as a contribution to modern political civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise official-line account of how Chinese scholars frame the ethical justification of the multi-party cooperation system.
quoteEn: That it has continued to the present and plays an ever more resilient role in political life is closely tied to the ethical principles and value commitments the system has consistently upheld.
quoteZh: 它延续至今并在政治生活中发挥日益强韧的作用，却跟这项制度一贯秉持的伦理原则或价值诉求密切相关。

glossary.zh: 多党合作和政治协商制度
glossary.pinyin: duōdǎng hézuò hé zhèngzhì xiéshāng zhìdù
glossary.explanation: The official name for China's party system, in which the Communist Party governs and eight non-ruling "democratic parties" take part in consultation and state affairs. It is officially described as a new-type party system.
The eight non-ruling parties legally recognised in China. They accept Communist Party leadership and are described as parties participating in government.

t: The mission and tasks of building the disciplinary, academic and discourse systems
zh: 学科体系学术体系话语体系建设的使命任务
paras: Writing in the People's Daily on 2 August 2021, historian Qu Lindong takes up the call to build a disciplinary system, an academic system and a discourse system with Chinese characteristics, Chinese style and Chinese manner (the "three systems"). Qu argues that this is a major task for philosophy and social sciences workers in the new era, and that the three systems form an inseparable whole.

The commentary opens with the historical roots of the idea, tracing it to Mao Zedong's 1938 call to give Marxism a Chinese form, and to Xi Jinping's formulation of the task. It then takes each system in turn, using history as the main illustration and drawing on works by Li Dazhao and Bai Shouyi.

Qu presents the disciplinary system as the strategic, overall framework, which should be assessed and coordinated to encourage a "large-discipline" awareness and cross-disciplinary work. The academic system is the middle link: it defines each discipline's object, aims, guiding thought, methods and place in society. In Qu's view, combining historical materialism with China's historical reality is the correct path for historiography, and Bai Shouyi's General History of China shows how such a system can be built. The discourse system is the most concrete and complex link. Qu holds that it carries research results to society, and that traditional concepts such as "min ben" (people as the root) and "cai, xue, shi" (talent, learning, insight) can be creatively transformed and joined with Marxist historiography.

Qu concludes that discourse-building requires stronger awareness and confidence in national character and continuity, and that the whole undertaking calls for both grand vision and painstaking work. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese historian links the "three systems" agenda to Marxist historiography and to China's traditional historical concepts.
quoteEn: Combining historical materialism with China's historical reality is the correct path for building the theoretical system of historiography.
quoteZh: 唯物史观与中国历史实际相结合，是历史学理论体系建设的正确路径。

t: The early critical turn in Marx's critical research
st: An understanding based on Marx's thought in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher period
zh: 马克思批判性研究中的早期批判转向分析
zhSub: 基于《德法年鉴》时期马克思思想的理解
source: Journal of Xi'an Shiyou University (Social Sciences Edition), 2021 no. 4
paras: He Zhendong asks how Marx's mode of critical research changed in the period of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (German-French Annals, 1844), and what that change shows. The article argues that the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and On the Jewish Question mark an early "critical turn". In this turn Marx moved to a materialist, Feuerbachian standpoint, raised the level of his critique and went beyond his predecessors.

The article has four parts. It first examines the theoretical precondition of Marx's critical research, then its practical basis, then the standpoint and form of the early turn. It ends with lessons for present-day Marxist theoretical research. It draws on Marx's doctoral dissertation, his ties to the Berlin Doctors' Club and the Young Hegelians, his Rheinische Zeitung experience, and the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy.

He first rejects the view that the critique of religion was the starting point of Marx's critical research. In He's account, criticality is an inner way of thinking that Marx already had before he applied it to religion. The German critique of religion was a collective effort by Strauss, Bauer and Feuerbach, and Marx affirmed it only as a stage to be passed through. His own move was from criticising heaven to criticising earth, law and politics. He did this by taking German state philosophy and legal philosophy, as the "copy", as his target, in place of German reality, the "original". On the practical side, He traces the turn to Marx's early intellectual formation and to a four-stage relation with the Young Hegelians: agreement, participation, rupture, transcendence. He also points to the gap between Hegelian philosophy and the material-interest questions Marx met in practice.

He concludes that the turn amounted to a shift from idealism to materialism and from revolutionary democracy to communism. He draws three lessons for current research. Scholars should uncover the criticality implicit in the classic texts, since critical theories are plentiful but studies of criticality itself are few. They should absorb "source" theories before examining their own knowledge critically. They should also ask why a given "leaf" comes to block the view of the mountain. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language reading of the early Marx's break with Hegel and the Young Hegelians that centres on method and "criticality" rather than on religion.
quoteEn: The critique of religion can hardly be the theoretical precondition of Marx's critical research, because it is an instance of Marx applying his criticality to a real problem, religion, and not the inner driving force of his critical research.
quoteZh: 宗教批判难以成为马克思批判性研究的理论前提，因其是马克思批判性运用到宗教现实问题的表现，并不是作为马克思批判性研究的内在驱动。
keywords: Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right

t: Marx's political philosophy and the essence of communist party organisation
zh: 马克思政治哲学与共产党组织的本质
paras: Zhang Wenxi asks what Marx meant by the "communist party" and why the question of party organisation has so often been read as a gap in his work. The article argues that Marx's concept cannot be grasped through ideology, class consciousness, special interests or sectarian programmes. In Zhang's reading, it has to be understood ontologically, as a "community of revolutionary proletarians" rooted in material conditions and historical law.

The article has two main parts and a short conclusion. The first part, on Marx's supposed "blank space" (liubai), criticises Blanchot, Althusser, Gramsci, Lukács, Badiou and other Western left thinkers who try to fill that gap. It then turns to Lenin as the thinker who revived Marx's concept. The second part offers an "ontological critique" of the concept of the communist party. It draws on the Communist Manifesto, the Marx–Proudhon dispute, the translation of "communisme" and the Paris Commune.

Zhang contends that Western Marxists misread Marx by treating the party through transparency of human nature, mystical "community" or the maturity of class consciousness. Lukács, in this account, falls back into a Platonist and subjectivist position. Against this, Zhang says the party's difference from other parties is ontological, not formal. It lies in the relation of domination and being dominated, which the proletarian community aims to abolish. Zhang adds that "communisme" is better rendered as "commonism" (gongtongzhuyi), since the Chinese character for "property" is absent from the French word. The article says this points to a "common" prior to any shared property, interest or value, and that Marx's own definition of the revolutionary party remains open.

In the conclusion, Zhang holds that party organisation is not a technical matter and cannot be settled by a rigid, unified theory. Traditional ideas of organisation, in Zhang's account, wrongly set the "backward masses" against the vanguard and ignore Marx's point that changing circumstances and self-change coincide in revolutionary practice. Zhang promises a follow-up article on how the Communist Party of China developed its political form. Read the original if you want a Chinese philosophical engagement with Western Marxist theories of the party, and with the idea of communism as \"commonism\".
quoteEn: In fact, the history of thought shows that the concept of the communist party as action should be understood from revolutionary practice, not as an academic theoretical dispute or as a ready-made instruction sheet drawn from the Communist Manifesto.
quoteZh: 事实上，思想史表明，作为行动的共产党概念应从革命实践活动上，而非作为学院式理论争论或依《共产党宣言》既定的内容说明书来理解。

t: Solidly advancing common prosperity through high-quality development
zh: 在高质量发展中扎实推进共同富裕
paras: This commentary in Guangming Daily argues that, in the new stage of development, common prosperity must be advanced through high-quality development. Shi and Cheng hold that the two are highly consistent: each serves as a condition and requirement of the other.

The piece begins with the Party's record since the 18th Party Congress (2012), including poverty alleviation and a moderately prosperous society. It then has three parts: why common prosperity is inherent in high-quality development, why high-quality development is the base of common prosperity, and what policies should follow.

The authors say high-quality development shifts attention from total output to structural problems, and from "having" to "having well". On this reading, common prosperity is its fundamental purpose and part of its content, through the new development philosophy's principle of sharing. In reverse, high-quality development both "makes the cake bigger", by raising productivity and building a modern economic system, and "divides the cake better", by improving income distribution and narrowing urban–rural and regional gaps. The authors reject both wealth for a few and egalitarianism.

The authors propose improving the quality and efficiency of development, with supply-side structural reform and innovation. They also call for upholding the basic economic system and the Two Unwaverings, and for combining distribution according to work with distribution by factors of production. Further proposals include equalising basic public services, advancing ecological civilisation, and enriching cultural life. They tie these to the 2035 and 2050 targets. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of how Party theorists linked common prosperity to high-quality development in 2021.
quoteEn: Common prosperity is not prosperity for a few, nor is it uniform egalitarianism.
quoteZh: 共同富裕不是少数人的富裕，也不是整齐划一的平均主义。

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal that Party leaders stressed from 2021. It is described as prosperity shared by all, not egalitarianism.
The official formulation since the 19th Party Congress (2017) for shifting from rapid growth to growth stressing quality, structure and efficiency.
Five principles set out in 2015: innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared development.
The policy of unwaveringly consolidating the public sector and unwaveringly supporting the non-public sector.

t: The formation of Mao Zedong's historical materialism
zh: 毛泽东唯物史观的形成
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 19 July 2021
paras: How did Mao Zedong come to adopt the materialist conception of history? Tao Jialing, in a short piece for China Social Sciences Today, holds that studying the formation of Mao's early historical materialism helps trace how Chinese communists' view of history took shape. The article argues that it developed through three stages between 1918 and 1921 and ended in a break with reformism.

The article follows Mao's writings, letters and activities in chronological order. It treats a germination stage (April 1918 to August 1919), a formation stage (September 1919 to December 1920) and an establishment stage (January to July 1921). Its sources include Mao's essays in Xiangjiang Review, his commentary on the Zhao Wuzhen suicide, letters to Cai Hesen and other friends, and the New People's Study Society meetings.

In Tao's account, the first stage began with Mao's remark that the "food problem" is the greatest, and with his essay "The Great Union of the Popular Masses". Tao reads these as early signs of the idea that social being determines consciousness, of class analysis, and of the masses as makers of history. The second stage is the core of the argument. Tao lists seven developments: an economic-analysis logic, attention to material production, sorting out a jumble of doctrines through reading Marxist works, spreading Marxism through the Cultural Book Society, a plan to found a party after Cai Hesen's letters, abandonment of reform after the failure of the Hunan self-rule movement, and a turn to violent revolution. In this last turn Mao rejected Russell's reformism, Kropotkin's anarchism and education-based change. In the third stage Mao told the New People's Study Society that it should adopt Russian-style communism. He then called historical materialism the "philosophical basis of our party" and attended the First Party Congress in July 1921.

Tao concludes that Mao's historical materialism resulted from his "challenging yesterday's self", and that it was a dynamic, constructed process. In this reading it mirrors China's wider intellectual change and marks Mao's move from revolutionary democracy to communism, driven by patriotism. Read the original if you want a concise, chronological Chinese account of how Mao's early thought is periodised and tied to specific texts from 1918–1921.
quoteEn: The formation of Mao Zedong's historical materialism was the result of his \"challenging yesterday's self with today's self\"; it was a dynamic, continuously constructed process.
quoteZh: 毛泽东唯物史观的形成乃其“今日之我与昨日之我挑战”的结果，其形成是一个动态的、不断构建的过程。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory that material production and economic relations shape social structure, politics and consciousness. The article traces how Mao came to adopt it.
A study society Mao Zedong and friends founded in Changsha, Hunan, in April 1918. Its stated aim was to renew learning and improve morals and customs, and it later took a political direction.
A weekly journal Mao edited in Changsha in 1919, in which he published "The Great Union of the Popular Masses".
A bookshop Mao helped set up in Changsha in 1920 to distribute new publications, including Marxist works.

t: Re-examining the young Marx's method of critiquing capitalism
zh: 青年马克思资本主义批判方法的再检视
source: Journal of Xiamen University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2021 no. 4
paras: Li Meng asks how the young Marx criticised capitalism while pursuing human emancipation, and what method that criticism used. The article, published in the Journal of Xiamen University (Philosophy and Social Sciences) in 2021, argues that the standard reading is incomplete. That reading places the young Marx within Feuerbach's humanist materialism and so sees only an external, a priori critique. Li contends that an internal socio-historical critique also emerged and supplemented the external one, and that the two intertwined.

The article covers the period from the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher (1843–44) to the 1844 Paris Manuscripts, with a glance ahead to The Holy Family. It opens with the external critique in Marx's letter to Ruge, the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right, On the Jewish Question and Notebook I. It then takes Moses Hess's On the Essence of Money as a case for the political-economic basis of internal critique, using the "Comments on James Mill". The third section turns to Notebook III and Marx's critique of Hegel's dialectic and of Feuerbach.

Li's central claim is that external critique measures capitalism against a normative standard, the return of the human essence, and so cannot grasp capitalism's historicity. Marx's departure from Hess is the first key move. Hess condemned bourgeois society morally and almost wholly negatively. Marx, drawing on Smith, Say, Ricardo and Mill, and on Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy, recognised the positive side of exchange and civil society and treated capitalism as containing the factors of its own negation. The second move is Marx's shift from Feuerbach's problematic to Hegel's. Marx found in Hegel's Phenomenology the idea of negativity as a moving and creating principle, and with it the rational core of the dialectic. Li says this let Marx push Feuerbach's humanism into the social sphere of real human activity. Li describes the Paris Manuscripts as a polyphony: the external critique stays dominant in form, while internal critique takes over in more and more specific analyses.

Li concludes that the two methods are unified under historical materialism. Internal critique allows the external standard to be historically "reconstructed" rather than procedurally "constructed", and it supports a more dialectical view of private property and capitalism. The author adds that in the Paris Manuscripts Marx had not yet reached historical materialism proper, because his attention to reality did not yet cover the production and reproduction of social relations. Read the original if you study the young Marx, the debates over a break between early and mature Marx, or the roles of Hess, Hegel and Feuerbach in the formation of Marx's critical method.
quoteEn: Therefore, from the standpoint of historical materialism, external critique and internal critique are in fact unified.
quoteZh: 因此，在历史唯物主义视域下的外在批判与内在批判又是统一的。

t: Marx's Brussels Notebooks in China
zh: 马克思《布鲁塞尔笔记》在中国
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 30 June 2021
paras: This short commentary was prompted by the June 2021 exhibition of the original manuscript of the fourth Brussels Notebook of Marx at the Museum of the History of the Communist Party of China. According to Kong, it is the only relatively complete Marx notebook preserved in China, bought in Europe by a Chinese entrepreneur and donated to the state. Kong notes that the notebooks were published in Germany in 1998 and first shown in China in 2018, yet Chinese scholarship has paid them little attention. The article asks what the notebooks are, why they matter and why they have been neglected.

Kong first describes the notebooks, citing the editors of MEGA2: they are Marx's 1845 economic notes from Brussels, his second systematic study of economics, written in French, German and English. The exhibited manuscript has 27 sheets (54 pages, 49 written on) and excerpts Storch, Saint-Maur, Pinto, Child and Bell, with other notes covering Say, Sismondi, Rossi, MacCulloch, Gasparin, Babbage and Ure. The article then turns to their scholarly value, the reasons for domestic neglect, and what the manuscripts mean for Marxist textual research.

Kong's central claim is that the notebooks show how the productive discourse of historical materialism took shape in an economic context, just before The German Ideology. Storch, Kong argues, supplied a view of material production as primary and moved Marx's interest from individual labour to material production. Rossi supplied a relational way of seeing production as creating relations of use and of supply and demand, which Kong links to the critique of older 'intuitive' materialism. The technologists Babbage and Ure offered a view of machine production as possibly easing labour and a micro-level analysis of how production works. Kong attributes the neglect to three difficulties: the multilingual text, which requires going back beyond the Chinese Complete Works; the fusion of philosophy and economics in Marx's study; and a research habit of explaining what a theory is rather than how it arose.

Kong concludes that research on Marxist texts needs to move from asking what a theory is to asking how it came about, and that scholars should engage more deeply with manuscripts, notes and the MEGA2 materials. Comparing Marx's excerpts and comments with the original works, Kong holds, gives a new perspective on the historical logic of Marxism's formation. Read the original if you want a brief account of the Brussels Notebooks, their contents and their place in Chinese Marx-text scholarship.
quoteEn: The research paradigm must shift from one of "what is so" to one of "why it is so".
quoteZh: 要推动“然”的研究范式向“所以然”的研究范式转变。

glossary.explanation: The second Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe, the scholarly historical-critical edition of the complete works of Marx and Engels, including notebooks and manuscripts. Its Part IV covers excerpt notebooks.
Marx and Engels's theory of history, which the article sees as founded in The German Ideology (1845).

t: The emergence and development of Marx's concept of ideology
zh: 马克思意识形态概念的出场及其展开
paras: Duan Guangpeng, in a short piece first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today (2021), asks where Marx's concept of ideology came from and how it developed. The author argues that the concept emerged under the influence of French Enlightenment thinkers and the French Revolution, and also of the German Enlightenment and German classical philosophy. Its unfolding, Duan holds, was tied both to Marx's shifts in philosophical and political standpoint and to his work on historical materialism and on proletarian emancipation.

The article has three sections. The first traces the French and German sources, from Napoleon's treatment of the "ideologists" to Marx's reading of Destutt de Tracy's Elements of Ideology in Paris in 1844, and to Kant and Hegel. The second follows Marx's early uses of the term, from the doctoral-dissertation notebooks through the Rheinische Zeitung years to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. The third turns to The German Ideology and Capital.

Duan's central claim is that Marx moved from a loose, general use of "ideology" to a critical theory of it. In 1842, in the debate on thefts of wood, Marx first applied the term to a concrete political problem. In the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, the idea that civil society determines the state led him to trace the falsity of ideology to real social life. In The German Ideology, Duan reads ideology first as "false ideas": the ruling class's ideas present its particular interests in a universal form and conceal the true nature of society. Duan adds that Marx did not treat ideology as simply false. It is inherent in a complete social structure, as the "ideological superstructure", and it reflects real common interests. In Capital, Marx criticised commodity fetishism as the core of bourgeois ideology.

Duan concludes that Marx turned ideology research into something more than a question of logical or epistemic truth and falsity. Its central task became exposing the real nature of society behind ideological illusion, and Marx's analysis of the concealed discursive strategies of ideology became the core of ideology critique. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the intellectual sources and stages of Marx's concept of ideology, as presented in Chinese scholarship.
quoteEn: In his view, ideology is not merely a question of logical or epistemic truth and falsity; more important is the exposure of the true nature of society concealed beneath ideological illusion.
quoteZh: 在他看来,意识形态不仅仅是一个逻辑上或认识上的真假问题,更重要的是对意识形态幻象掩盖下的社会真正本质的揭露。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory of history, which explains social change through material production and class relations. Chinese scholarship usually calls it by this term, literally the materialist conception of history.
In Marxist theory, the political, legal and ideological forms that rest on the economic base of society.

t: Interpretive perspectives on the concept of ideology in Marx and Engels
zh: 马克思恩格斯意识形态概念的阐释视角
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 6 July 2021
paras: Xu Douedou and Yi Zhengxuan ask how Marx and Engels' concept of ideology should be characterised. They distinguish three ways of defining it in the Marxist tradition: negative, descriptive (neutral) and positive. The authors argue that the positive and descriptive readings lack textual basis in Marx and Engels and create interpretive difficulties, so that their stance is, in the end, negative. In their account this negativity stresses the critical element in ideology and supplies a standard for rationalising thought.

The article has three sections. The first explains the logical difficulty of a positive concept of ideology. The second examines the textual grounds claimed for a descriptive concept, mainly the base–superstructure passage in the 1859 Preface. The third defends the negative reading by setting Lenin's epistemological emphasis beside the early Althusser's sociological one.

On the positive reading, the authors argue that Marx and Engels treat science as an affirmative force, while ideology is an inverted, illusory form of thought outside science. Ideology could become scientific only under historical conditions, namely the proletariat, whose class interest coincides with the broadest human interest and which needs no illusory principles. Ideology would then disappear in communism. On the descriptive reading, they note that scholars have found different German terms for "forms of social consciousness" and "ideological forms". The former is described neutrally; the latter is presented as distorted reflection of real conflicts. A neutral reading, they warn, risks stretching ideology to mean culture or consciousness in general and dissolving its critical force. The authors then claim that the negativity is dialectical: an internal critique in the epistemological sense, which also sees a transcendent, future-pointing force in bourgeois ideals, and a principle of sublation in the sociological sense. Examples of the latter are Marxism's sublation of German classical philosophy, of utopian socialism, and the late Engels' self-correction on the relative independence of the ideological superstructure.

The authors conclude that, whatever partial validity the three modes have in different textual settings, only the negative reading fits the "internal critical" meaning of ideology in Marx and Engels. They also note that Lenin's construction of proletarian ideology showed an initial real transition from illusory to scientific ideology. Read the original if you want a compact argument about the textual basis of Marxist theories of ideology and the debate over neutral versus critical concepts.
quoteEn: Only the "negative" mode of interpretation is the most reasonable way of reading Marx and Engels' view of ideology.
quoteZh: 只有“否定性”这一阐释方式才是马克思恩格斯意识形态观最合理的解读方式。

t: Assessing the contextual differences in Western Marxist spatial critique
zh: 研判西方马克思主义空间批判的语境差异
paras: Spatial critique grounded in capitalist urbanization has become an important part of Marxism outside China, but its relation to historical materialism remains unsettled. Zhang opens with a dispute: Manuel Castells accused Henri Lefebvre's theory of the production of space of drifting from Marxism towards humanism, while Edward W. Soja credited Lefebvre's "provocative inversion" with the shift from Marxist analysis of space to the spatialization of Marxism. The article argues that urban Marxism and historical materialism form two different contexts of spatial critique, differing in concepts, critical paradigms and practical paths.

This is a short newspaper commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in June 2021. It is organised in three sections: the definition of the city, the paradigm of spatial critique, and the path of spatial practice. It draws on Marx's Grundrisse and Capital and on Lefebvre, Castells, David Harvey and Soja.

On concepts, Zhang says Lefebvre's city is the modern urban form of a third, "urban" age and a commercialised, fragmented space tied to power. Marx's city rests on large European industry, with concentrated production and capital and a proletariat gathered in one place. On paradigm, historical materialism ties space to the mode of production and forms of ownership, whereas urban Marxism presumes historical materialism to be "absent" on space. Lefebvre and Castells took a urban-sociology route, Harvey and Soja a human-geography route, and each expanded dialectics: Lefebvre with a conceptual triad, Harvey with geographical unevenness, Soja with a socio-temporal-spatial trialectic.

On practice, Zhang argues that Marx saw spatial alienation as ending only through transforming the mode of production, with the proletariat as the subject. Urban Marxism, in this account, no longer treats the proletariat as that subject or class revolution as the way to sublate alienation. Harvey's "dialectical utopia" and "rebel architects" replace communism and the proletariat. Zhang concludes that urban Marxism offers no workable strategy and never reaches the level of ownership, but that the differences make Marxist spatial research interactive, open and plural. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese account of how Lefebvre, Harvey and Soja are positioned against Marx's historical materialism.
quoteEn: Urban Marxism has failed to offer a workable strategy for spatial action and has not treated the transformation of the mode of production as the necessary road to spatial liberation, so its critique of capitalist space has never reached the level of ownership.
quoteZh: 都市马克思主义未能给出切实可行的空间行动策略，也没有将生产方式变革视为空间解放的必由之路，因而其对资本主义空间的批判始终未能深入至所有制层面。

glossary.explanation: A label for the strand of Western Marxist thought, associated with Lefebvre, Castells, Harvey and Soja, that analyses capitalist urbanization and space.
Marx and Engels's theory of history, which explains social change through the mode of production and class relations.

t: Rethinking the Marxist view of progress
zh: 重新认识马克思主义进步观
paras: This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in May 2021, takes up the claim by some Western scholars that Marx was a "progressivist" whose view of history rests on a metaphysical belief in progress. Zhao argues that this reading distorts Marxism and that the Marxist view of progress must be understood from the standpoint of real human beings.

The piece first sets out two Western charges. One, associated with Francis Fukuyama, treats Marx like Hegel as holding an end-of-history eschatology. The other, represented by Sean Sayers, treats Marx's theory as a linear conception of progress. Zhao then answers each in turn.

On the first, Zhao concedes that Marx's accounts of a "community of free individuals" and the "true realm of freedom" suggest a goal, but denies that this amounts to historical teleology. In Zhao's reading, history has no preset purpose; it is made by the activity of real people, so history cannot end while people exist. Communism is presented as the start of a new history, and Zhao cites Fredric Jameson's remark that it ends prehistory, not history. On the second, Zhao argues that Marx's late study of "Eastern society" and his reply to Mikhailovsky rejected a single path for all nations. Linear progress, Zhao adds, needs a superhistorical subject such as Hegel's spirit, whereas Marx made human practice the subject. Zhao describes history as spiral, uniting diversity with general laws through the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production.

Zhao concludes that equating Marxism with end-of-history or linear progressivism contradicts its humanistic starting point. A correct understanding, Zhao says, must proceed from real human beings and their irreplaceable place in historical progress. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language rebuttal of Fukuyama-style and linear readings of Marx.
quoteEn: To understand the Marxist view of progress correctly, one must start from the dimension of the "human being" and fully recognise the irreplaceable position of real people in historical progress.
quoteZh: 要正确认识马克思主义进步观，必须从“人”这个向度着手，全面认识现实的人在历史进步中的不可替代的地位。

t: Leading the innovation of Chinese Marxist philosophy with the problems of the age
zh: 以时代问题引领中国马克思主义哲学创新
paras: Wang Zhiqiang, in a commentary for the Chinese Social Sciences Today (July 2021), asks where innovation in Chinese Marxist philosophy should come from. The answer is that real philosophy distils the spirit of its own age, so innovation must be rooted in the problems of the age. For contemporary China, the author names the country's social reality and the historical practice of modernization as the starting point and driving force.

The piece begins with a critique of current research habits. It then looks back at how Marx made his philosophical revolution out of the problems of 1830s–40s Germany. Finally, it traces the sinicization of Marxist philosophy from the late Qing crisis through the Chinese Communist Party's revolutionary period to the post-1978 debates, before returning to the present.

Wang describes a widespread routine. A scholar introduces a concept from a modern Western thinker, searches Marx's texts for similar statements and rebuilds a new Marxist narrative. The ending then declares that Marx had already surpassed the Western thinker. Wang sees two basic defects: it shows an inability to grasp the problems of the age or to produce original concepts, and it dissolves the determinate content and philosophical character of Marxism. Against this, Wang reads Marx's critique of German classical philosophy as a way of grasping modernity from within a backward country. The same pattern is traced in China, where Mao Zedong's On Practice, On Contradiction and On New Democracy, and later the debate on practice as the criterion of truth, are presented as answers to the pressing questions of their moments.

Wang concludes that grafting Western concepts onto Marxism is appropriate at most in the early stage of modernization, and that China's modernization is not a repeat of the Western philosophical process. Contemporary China is undergoing the largest modernization in human history, and Wang calls it a pioneering practice, the unfolding of the new path of Chinese modernization. Wang poses questions that philosophy must answer, including the standard of Chinese modernization, the new "principled height" of the new path and era, and how to supply universal norms of world-historical significance. Read the original if you want a short statement of the argument, in the official Chinese discourse, against derivative Western-concept scholarship in Marxist philosophy.
quoteEn: This prosperity is no more than marking time with great enthusiasm in the empty cycle of a formula.
quoteZh: 这种繁荣不过是在“套路”的空洞循环里热烈地原地踏步。

glossary.explanation: An official Party concept describing China's own path of modernization, presented as distinct from the Western model. It was elaborated especially after the 19th and 20th Party Congresses.
The process of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions and history. It is an established Party formula, usually rendered in official texts as adapting Marxism to the Chinese context.

glossary.zh: 实践是检验真理的唯一标准
glossary.pinyin: shíjiàn shì jiǎnyàn zhēnlǐ de wéiyī biāozhǔn
glossary.en: practice as the criterion of truth
glossary.literal: practice is the sole criterion for testing truth
glossary.explanation: A philosophical debate launched in 1978 that challenged dogmatic adherence to Mao-era orthodoxy. It gave ideological support to the reform and opening up policy.

t: A brief analysis of the theoretical limits of Western Marxism through the problem of "discourse"
zh: 以“话语”问题浅析西方马克思主义的理论局限
paras: Zhang Dan asks what the Western Marxist treatment of "discourse" reveals about the limits of that tradition. The short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in 2021, grants that Western Marxism placed discourse in real social history and responded critically to doubts about classical Marxism. Zhang's thesis is that its accounts of discourse depart from Marxism's basic tenets and carry an idealist, quasi-utopian colouring.

The piece looks at three thinkers: Louis Althusser's theory of ideology, Jürgen Habermas's theory of communicative action and "discourse democracy", and Ernesto Laclau and Chantal Mouffe's theory of hegemony. It then widens the point to Western Marxism as a whole, comparing it with traditional Marxism on basic theory, revolutionary subject, method of revolution and choice of path.

Zhang argues that all three exaggerate the status of discourse. Althusser stresses ideology so heavily that he neglects the subject's initiative. Habermas treats communication, not productive labour, as decisive. Laclau and Mouffe let discourse generate subjects and reject the determining role of the economic base. For Zhang, this reverses Marx's view that social being determines social consciousness, and it leads to misjudging class contradictions and revolutionary forces. Zhang also finds these schemes unworkable. Habermas's procedures demand much of citizens' culture, willingness and institutions, and Laclau and Mouffe lack concrete analysis of the state. More broadly, Western Marxism is said to weaken the proletariat's role and to favour cultural critique without overthrowing the capitalist mode of production.

Zhang concludes that theoretical innovation must keep to Marxism's basic stance and views, since abandoning Marxism solves nothing. The author holds that the tests of the present era should deepen understanding of Marxism's scientific character, in a context of changing domestic and international conditions and competition over ideological discourse. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary criticises Western Marxism from an orthodox historical-materialist standpoint.
quoteEn: Exaggerating the status of discourse while neglecting social practice ultimately leads to a distorted understanding of class contradictions in capitalist society, and so to errors in judging revolutionary forces and strategy.
quoteZh: 对话语地位的夸大和对社会实践的忽略最终导致的就是对资本主义社会阶级矛盾认识的偏差，从而对革命力量和革命策略的判断产生失误。

t: The ethical dimension of East European neo-Marxism
zh: 东欧新马克思主义的伦理之维
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 24 June 2021
paras: Why did so many East European neo-Marxist schools turn to ethics after the Second World War? Xia argues that the moral problems of the region's socialist states, together with the suppression of individuality and freedom, pushed thinkers to build their own moral theories. In Xia's account, these theories inherited Marx's ethical thought and helped develop Marxist ethics in the contemporary period.

The short piece, a newspaper commentary, surveys several currents: Kangrga's metaethics and Stojanović's 'ethics of the revolutionary movement' in the Yugoslav Praxis school, Zygmunt Bauman's morality of the 'Other' in Poland, and Ágnes Heller's 'ethics of personality' in the Hungarian Budapest School. It gives most attention to Heller.

Xia's central claim is that East European neo-Marxist ethics was practical and rooted in lived socialist experience. It was also concerned with the rationality of morality, unlike Western Marxist ethics. Heller, in this reading, joins a dimension of personality (individuality, freedom) with a dimension of virtue, so that the good person can both follow social norms and act as an autonomous moral subject. Xia contrasts this with MacIntyre, whose communitarianism is said to neglect individuality, and with Bauman, who is said to stress responsibility to the Other but pay little attention to virtue.

Xia concludes that these thinkers extended Marxist ethics creatively, but notes a split. Heller, Fehér and Kołakowski are described as favouring moral individualism over collective requirements, while Kosík, Schaff and Svitak hold that individuals bear moral responsibility to society as a whole. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese overview of how Heller, Bauman and the Praxis school have been situated in debates on Marxist ethics.
quoteEn: The unity of the personality dimension and the virtue dimension is the basic feature of Heller's ethical thought, and it is precisely what Western ethics and other East European neo-Marxists overlooked.
quoteZh: 个性维度和德性维度的统一是赫勒伦理思想的基本特点，而这正是西方伦理学和其他东欧新马克思主义者忽视的地方。

t: The dialectic of objects: the essence of machines and of humans
zh: 对象辩证法：机器与人的本质
paras: This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in June 2021, asks how technology changes the definition of the human being. Liu sets two materialist claims against each other: Marx's view that free, conscious activity is the species-characteristic of humans, and La Mettrie's "man is a machine". Liu argues that under capital and advancing technology, humans are alienated into machines, and that "the machine is human" may also become possible.

The article is organised in three stages: technology as a tool, the human as a machine, and the machine as a human. It draws mainly on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Communist Manifesto, and also refers to Heidegger, Marcuse, Descartes, Baudrillard-style notions of hyperreality and the Chinese philosopher Zhao Tingyang.

Liu holds that technology begins as an externalisation of human essential powers, with humans as subjects and machines as objects. With large-scale industry, technology becomes bound up with capital and turns into an autonomous force that dominates producers. In Liu's account this produces one-dimensional people, a blurring of the virtual and the real, and dependence on smartphones, networks and algorithms. Liu contrasts Marx, who starts from practice, with Marcuse, who criticises technology from an abstract human essence. Drawing on Zhao Tingyang's "I act, therefore I am", Liu argues that if machines or cyborgs take over all material production, human action shrinks and human existence loses meaning.

Liu concludes that one-sided technological development may lead to the "dissolution of the human" rather than human liberation, and cannot by itself reach Marx's association of free individuals. The nature of technology depends on the social system and its application, so social adaptability is the key question. Read the original if you want a brief Marxist-humanist argument about alienation, artificial intelligence and the essence of the human.
quoteEn: The essence of technological alienation is in fact the domination of humans by capital, and therefore technology dehumanises people.
quoteZh: 技术异化的本质其实是资本对人的统治，因此技术使人非人化。

t: The theoretical foundations of the common values of all humanity
zh: 全人类共同价值的理论底蕴
paras: This short commentary, published in Guangming Daily in October 2021, takes up Xi Jinping's pledge at the Party's centenary celebration to promote the "common values of all humanity": peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom. Wen argues that the concept rests on three theoretical sources: Marxism, traditional Chinese culture and long-standing value consensus in the international community.

The article is organised in three sections, one for each source. It draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, on classical Chinese texts such as the Book of Rites and the Book of Documents, and on international instruments from the Peace of Westphalia to the UN Charter and the Bandung principles.

On the Marxist side, Wen reads the concept as confirming world-history theory: deeper global interconnection raises the need for shared values. It also expresses Marx's concern for humanity and his opposition to exploitation and oppression, which Wen contrasts with unilateralism and hegemonism in some Western states. Wen then links it to the ideal of "great harmony under heaven" and the principle of harmony without uniformity, which allow both particularity and commonality. In the international section, Wen presents peace and development as the themes of the age, and fairness and justice as a rejection of power politics. Democracy, in Wen's account, takes different forms according to national conditions and economic base.

Wen concludes that the concept has deep theoretical roots and practical relevance, and offers a value basis for peaceful development and for reform of global governance. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press grounded this concept in Marxism, Chinese tradition and international norms in 2021.
quoteEn: The "common values of all humanity" recognise the particularity and difference of individuals, nations, states and social forms, while also recognising commonality, universality and similarity; at root this upholds the inclusive spirit of harmony without uniformity.
quoteZh: 全人类共同价值”承认不同个体、不同民族、不同国家、不同社会形态的特殊性、差异性，同时还承认存在共性、普遍性和相似性，从根本上是坚持了和而不同的包容精神。

t: Chinese democratic discourse as a critique and transcendence of Western democratic discourse
zh: 论中国民主话语对西方民主话语的批判与超越
paras: Li Haiqing takes up the building of a Chinese discourse system, arguing that democracy is one of its priority areas because Western democratic discourse has long been exported to China and, in the author's account, has shaped Chinese thinking and even produced a partial 'colonisation of the mind'. The article contends that Chinese democratic discourse has been constructed through a critique of Western liberal democracy and that it now goes beyond it. Li links the task to Xi Jinping's concern with China's 'spiritual independence'.

The article has five parts. It first dissects Western democratic discourse in terms of content, mode of thinking and interests. It then sets out a five-part framework for Chinese democratic discourse, identifies five of its features, and discusses its value. It closes with a note on remaining challenges. Li draws on Marx's early writings, Schumpeter, Thomas Dye, Huntington, Wang Shaoguang and speeches by Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping.

In Li's reading, Western 'liberal democracy' (natural rights, competitive elections, civil society, separation of powers) serves capital and elites. It rests on a hierarchy of civilisations, universalism and an 'end of history' outlook, and it hides the interests of powerful capital. Against this, Li sets a 'five-in-one' Chinese framework: democracy must fit specific national conditions; it operates under the Party's leadership; it depends on state capacity; it spans many fields and the whole process rather than elections alone; and it is judged by its practical function in development and governance. Li presents these features as endogenous, people-centred, complete, absorptive and attuned to the times. Li also stresses that criticising Western discourse does not mean rejecting it wholesale, citing the borrowing and adaptation of 'governance'.

Li concludes that Chinese democratic discourse solves China's own problems, deconstructs Western claims to universality, and offers developing countries an alternative path, which Li calls a higher form of human democratic discourse. Li cautions that Western discourse remains strong and that China's own democratic practice, conceptual refinement and international discursive power still need work. Li expects Chinese discourse to gain greater influence over time. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a Party School scholar frames the contrast between Chinese and Western democracy in the discourse-building campaign.
quoteEn: The fruit of democracy grows to a large extent from the root of state capacity, and a state power with central authority and governing capacity is the reliable guarantee for building up democratic institutions step by step and for democracy to keep working effectively.
quoteZh: 民主之果很大程度上是结在国家能力这个根上的，一个具有中央权威与治理能力的国家权力是民主制度逐步建立健全、民主作用持续有效发挥的可靠保障。

t: The great changes unseen in a century in the world, seen from the perspective of Marxist philosophy
zh: 马克思主义哲学视野中的世界百年未有之大变局
paras: Writing in 2021, Liu Rui takes up the widely used claim that the world is undergoing great changes unseen in a century, whose core the author describes as a shift in the balance of forces from 'the West strong, the East weak' to 'the East rising, the West declining'. Liu argues that many ordinary Chinese hold superficial or one-sided views of this change, and that Marxist dialectical and historical materialism offers a fuller reading. The thesis is that the change is dialectical in nature: its origins combine chance with necessity, its present form combines change with the unchanged, and its future course combines certainty with uncertainty.

The article follows a past–present–future sequence in three parts: origins, present condition, and development trend. Each part reviews Chinese scholarly views (for example Guo Shuyong and Ding Weihang, and Quan Heng, on event-driven accounts of origins; Wang Shaoquan, Jin Canrong, Teng Wensheng on manifestations of change) and then draws practical lessons. Each part is tied to a named error that Liu sees in popular thinking: accidental-cause determinism, subjective fantasy of change, and linear historicism.

In the first part Liu contends that Western relative decline is the necessary outcome of universal connection and eternal development, and of the basic contradiction of capitalist society. Liu also lists crises in Western economies, politics, society, culture and diplomacy. The rise of emerging-market and developing countries is presented as the rise of a new phenomenon, helped by technology diffusion, 'parallel' modernization and the new technological revolution. The second part stresses what has not changed: using the author's figures, the West keeps its economic, technological and military lead, and China remains the largest developing country, with gaps in manufacturing, services and overall strength relative to the United States. The third part holds that the long-run direction is certain, while the timing, form and outcome of great-power rivalry are not, so both complacent and pessimistic forecasts of China overtaking the United States are rejected.

Liu concludes that accurate understanding of the change is the epistemological basis for responding to it and shaping it. The practical proposals include focusing on development and technological self-reliance, strengthening Party leadership, opening up further, avoiding a new Cold War and over-extension abroad, and guarding against 'strategic rashness'. Liu calls for further research on the laws governing great-power rise and decline in periods of world transition. Read the original if you want a systematic example of how a Chinese Marxist philosopher turns official judgements about the global situation into a dialectical framework and policy advice.
quoteEn: The origins of the great changes unseen in a century contain necessity within chance; their present form contains the unchanged within change; their development trend contains uncertainty within certainty.
quoteZh: 世界百年未有之大变局的由来偶然性中有必然性，样态变中有未变，发展趋势确定性中有不确定性。

glossary.zh: 世界百年未有之大变局
glossary.pinyin: shìjiè bǎinián wèiyǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.en: great changes unseen in a century
glossary.explanation: A formula used by Xi Jinping since around 2017–2018 to describe the shifting international order, especially the rise of China and other emerging economies relative to the West.

keywords: great changes unseen in a century

t: The theoretical implications and intellectual wisdom of the "new form of human civilization"
zh: “人类文明新形态”的理论意蕴和思想智慧
source: China Party and Government Cadres Forum (Zhongguo dangzheng ganbu luntan), 2021
paras: Writing in October 2021, Gu Hailiang takes up the concept of the "new form of human civilization", which Xi Jinping advanced in his speech at the centenary of the Communist Party of China. Gu asks what theoretical basis and intellectual content the concept carries. The article argues that it rests on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, takes the coordinated progress of five civilizations (material, political, spiritual, social and ecological) as its substance, and is realised through Chinese modernization. In Gu's view it enriches Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and expresses the wisdom of Marxism adapted to China in the new era.

The article is organised in four sections. It first links the concept to the change in the principal contradiction of society since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then places it in the history of the Party's modernization goals, from the Four Modernizations to Deng Xiaoping's "Chinese-style modernization" and the completion of a moderately prosperous society. The third section treats it as part of the movement from quantitative change to partial qualitative change in the new stage of development. The last section connects it to a community with a shared future for mankind.

Gu's central moves are historical and dialectical. He compares the principal contradictions set out at the Eighth Party Congress, the Sixth Plenum of the 11th Central Committee and the 19th Party Congress. He reads the current one, between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development, as defining the new form: the "needs" now span eight areas, and the five-sphere construction is the system that supplies them. Drawing on Mao Zedong's 1959 remarks on underdeveloped and more developed socialism, and on Deng Xiaoping and Xi, Gu presents the primary stage of socialism as a dynamic process of accumulation approaching qualitative leaps. The new development stage, he says, is the setting for understanding the concept's direction.

Gu concludes that the concept is not specific to China. He argues that it has universal significance through the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, which he presents as the contemporary continuation of Marx and Engels's theory of world history. The concept embodies scientific socialism's theory of civilizational forms, draws on fine traditional Chinese culture and absorbs the achievements of other civilizations. Gu calls it an important result of twenty-first-century Marxism. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's systematic account of how the concept is derived from the principal contradiction, the primary stage of socialism and the idea of a shared future for mankind.
quoteEn: The new development stage, characterised as a process of "quantitative accumulation and change drawing ever closer to a qualitative leap", is the basic standpoint for understanding the inherent requirements of the "new form of human civilization" and the basic marker of its direction of development.
quoteZh: 新发展阶段所具有的“日益接近质的飞跃的量的积累和发展变化的过程”的特征，成为理解“人类文明新形态”内在规定的基本立场，成为理解“人类文明新形态”发展路向的基本标识。

glossary.explanation: A phrase Xi Jinping used in his 1 July 2021 speech to describe the outcome of Chinese modernization. Party theorists present it as the coordinated advance of five civilizations (material, political, spiritual, social, ecological).
The official name for China's path to modernization. The phrase goes back to Deng Xiaoping's 1979 "Chinese-style modernization" and was elaborated under Xi Jinping.
The official judgement that China, though socialist, is still at an early and underdeveloped phase of socialism. It was formalised in the 1980s and is expected to last a long time.

A Marxist-Maoist category for the central tension that shapes a period and guides Party policy. The 19th Party Congress (2017) redefined it as the contradiction between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's official concept for international relations, calling for joint governance, shared security and mutually beneficial cooperation.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Re-examining Marx's labour theory of value in the context of artificial intelligence
zh: 人工智能背景下马克思劳动价值论的再审视
paras: Jia Shupin asks whether the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has changed Marx's labour theory of value, and how labour creates happiness under AI. The article answers that AI creates no value itself and that human labour remains the sole source of value. It also argues that AI's effects depend on the social system, and that labour and happiness are only reunited under socialism.

The article opens by noting that bourgeois economists are reviving a 'factor theory of value', which Jia reads as an attempt to undermine Marx's theory of surplus value. It then proceeds in three parts: whether labour still creates value under AI; the contrasting outcomes under capitalism and socialism; and how labour produces happiness, with a closing turn to labour education for young people.

Jia's central move is to place AI within the productive forces. Drawing on Marx's three elements of the labour process, the author treats AI as a science-and-technology factor that permeates the means of labour, the objects of labour and labourers themselves. Engineers still programme and debug the systems behind 'unmanned factories', so AI is an extension of human labour rather than a replacement. The second move is institutional. Under capitalism, Jia argues, AI raises the organic composition of capital, displaces workers, deepens polarisation and hastens capitalism's crisis, without ending alienated labour. Under socialism, with public ownership and equal labour relations, AI can be steered towards liberating labour, although Jia concedes that wage labour and some alienation persist in the non-public sector.

Jia concludes that AI confirms rather than refutes the claims that labour creates value and that labour creates happiness. Short-term job displacement is acknowledged, but the author expects people to adapt and AI to relieve them of heavy toil. Citing Xi Jinping's remark that happiness comes from striving, Jia warns that some young people are over-reliant on AI and averse to labour, and calls for stronger labour education and a social atmosphere that respects labour. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends the labour theory of value against AI-related challenges and links the debate to labour education policy.
quoteEn: AI itself does not create value; it is merely a further extension of the human essence.
quoteZh: 人工智能本身是不创造价值的，它只是人的本质的进一步延展。

glossary.explanation: The theory, developed by classical political economy and by Marx, that the value of commodities derives from socially necessary human labour. Chinese Marxist scholars treat it as the foundation of Marx's theory of surplus value.
The view that land, capital, machinery and other non-labour factors also create value. Chinese Marxist writers typically present it as a bourgeois rival to the labour theory of value.
An area of Chinese schooling, strengthened by a 2020 Party and State Council opinion, that aims to cultivate respect for labour and practical labour skills among students at all levels.

t: Transcending the logic of capital: innovation and development of the basic socialist economic system
zh: 超越资本逻辑：社会主义基本经济制度的创新与发展
paras: Writing in 2021, Dai Jinping asks how the basic socialist economic system, as expanded by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), can sublate and transcend the logic of capital. The article argues that the shift from a single ownership-based system to a three-part system of ownership, distribution and economic institutions marks a major theoretical innovation. In Dai's reading, it also marks the point at which socialism with Chinese characteristics has largely taken definitive shape after more than forty years of reform.

The article has three sections. The first presents Marx's critique of the logic of capital as the key to analysing capitalist society, and notes that Marx himself spoke of capital's "laws" and "tendencies" rather than a "logic of capital". The second traces how contemporary capital has changed, using the three dimensions of valorisation, expansion and reification. The third examines in turn the ownership structure, the distribution system and the socialist market economy.

Dai argues that monopolisation, financialisation and globalisation have strengthened capital's logic of valorisation. Financial capital, in this account, is largely fictitious and speculative. Dai cites US data on financial firms' share of corporate profits and the 2008 crisis as evidence that Marx's laws still apply. Rising wealth polarisation, in Dai's view, shows that welfare-state measures cannot touch private ownership of the means of production. Against this, the article holds that public ownership as the mainstay, together with the Two Unwaverings, advances a public "logic of capital" and curbs the excesses of the private one while still using capital to develop the productive forces. Distribution according to labour as the mainstay, with other modes alongside it, is presented as protecting labour income and supporting common prosperity. The socialist market economy is said to reject the opposition between market and state and to combine the "invisible hand" with the "visible hand".

Dai concludes that these three institutions together sublate and transcend the logic of capital, and that they supply an institutional base for sustained economic growth, common prosperity and high-quality development. The article also points to the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee, which restated the Two Unwaverings, distribution according to labour and the aim of a high-level socialist market economy. Dai presents this as strengthening institutional confidence. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar applies Marx's critique of capital to justify the current Chinese ownership, distribution and market arrangements.
quoteEn: The basic socialist economic system is a sublation and transcendence of the logic of capital.
quoteZh: 社会主义基本经济制度是对资本逻辑的扬弃和超越

glossary.zh: 社会主义基本经济制度
glossary.explanation: The core institutional framework of China's economy. The Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) defined it as public ownership as the mainstay, distribution according to labour as the mainstay, and the socialist market economy.
A term in Chinese Marxist scholarship for the inherent laws and tendencies of capital's movement, chiefly valorisation. Dai notes that Marx did not use the phrase himself.
The official policy of unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector while unwaveringly encouraging, supporting and guiding the non-public sector.
A long-standing socialist goal of shared prosperity for all, stressed in Chinese policy as the aim of development and as a counter to wealth polarisation.

t: An analysis of Marx's thought on economic justice: a study of Capital
zh: 马克思经济正义思想探析——以《资本论》为研究对象
source: Journal of North University of China (Social Science Edition), 2021 no. 5
paras: Marx never treated economic justice systematically, and the long-running dispute over Marx and justice has produced divergent and one-sided readings. Zhu Xinyuan takes up the question by reading Capital, and argues that Marx's economic justice thought can be understood in a broad sense, covering economic institutions, activities and ideas, and in a narrow sense, covering justice in production, exchange, distribution and consumption. The article was published in a university journal in 2021.

The article has three parts. The first sets out three layers of meaning: justice in economic theory, based on equal rights; justice in economic activity; and justice in economic institutions, meaning communist society. The second identifies two features of the thought: the theoretical character of historical materialism and an ethical character of humanistic concern. The third turns to its contemporary value for China's socialist market economy, at the levels of theory and practice.

Zhu argues that, for Marx, the equal rights of the market are formal. Labour-power is sold in the sphere of circulation, which Marx calls the true Eden of the innate rights of man. Beyond that sphere the apparent fair exchange between worker and capitalist is, in Zhu's reading, unfair, because the capitalist appropriates unpaid labour.
