Second, practice: Hess's philosophy of action, resting on Fichte and Cieszkowski, remained idealist, abstract and moralistic, while Marx's concept of practice joins transforming the world with understanding it. Marx also made the proletariat the historical subject, whereas Hess's nationalism, later Zionism, and his petty-bourgeois intellectual radicalism are said to link him to anarchism and Blanquism. Third, Zou argues that Marx deliberately stopped at radical democracy to avoid being confused with such left radicalism, and that the German Ideology's critique of Stirner and of "true" socialism was aimed at obstacles to historical materialism.

Zou concludes that Hess was an intermediate link from the Young Hegelians through Feuerbach to Marx and an important figure in the pre-history of Marxism. Marx's critique of Hess's philosophy of action and "true" socialism was completed before his thought matured, and Hess cannot be counted among its founders. Zou adds that the Althusserian Spinoza revival seems intended to raise Hess and lower Marx, and leaves its assessment to a later article. Read the original if you study the Marx–Hess relationship, the Young Hegelian dissolution, or Chinese scholarly responses to Western debates on Marx's origins.
quoteEn: To regard Hess as a founder of Marxism is clearly an overreach.
quoteZh: 将赫斯看成是马克思主义的创始人，显然是一种越位。

t: Ellen Meiksins Wood's "Political Marxism" and its general critique of capitalism: a textual reading based on the Communist Manifesto
zh: 艾伦·伍德“政治马克思主义”的资本主义总体批判探析——基于《共产党宣言》的文本学解读
paras: Feng Wangzhou examines how Ellen Meiksins Wood, together with Robert Brenner a leading figure of "Political Marxism", reads the Communist Manifesto as a general critique of capitalism. The article argues that Wood develops this critique along four lines: the bourgeoisie, historical materialism, the nation-state and socialism. Feng contends that her reading helps readers grasp the nature of contemporary capitalism and the prospects for a revival of socialism.

The article first introduces Political Marxism, which emerged in the 1970s and has three generations of scholars. Feng describes its method as clarifying the basic concepts of historical materialism and giving prominence to social property relations. It also stresses the historical specificity of capitalism and the separation of the "economic" from the "political". The main section then sets out Wood's four dimensions in turn. A closing section assesses her work, names theoretical gaps, and draws lessons for China and for socialism in the twenty-first century.

On the bourgeoisie, Feng reports Wood's claim that capitalism and the bourgeoisie must not be equated. In her view the bourgeoisie is both revolutionary and destructive. Feng adds that, on Wood's account, English capitalism arose from competitive pressures on agrarian producers, not from a rising bourgeois class, and that the French Revolution was led largely by officials and professionals. On historical materialism, capitalism's compulsion to accumulate and maximise profit yields enormous productive capacity alongside a persistent gap with quality of life. Its separation of politics from economics allows it to tolerate formal democracy while leaving economic inequality untouched. On the nation-state, Wood rejects the thesis that globalisation dissolves it, arguing that global capital increasingly depends on territorial states. On socialism, she holds that the working class remains the only force able to transform capitalism, and that socialism requires real democracy.

Feng judges Wood's critique comprehensive and profound, and credits her with exposing the fallacy of the "bourgeois paradigm". Feng also identifies three gaps: the shift to post-Fordist and automated production, the contradictory tide of globalisation and "anti-globalisation", and the position of the nation-state, especially in developing countries. Feng draws two lessons: the working class retains its revolutionary role against post-Marxist claims, and capitalism's contradictions are intensifying in an era of neoliberalism and new imperialism. The article presents socialism with Chinese characteristics as evidence of socialism's renewed vitality. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's systematic account of Political Marxism and how it is received and evaluated in Chinese academic debate.
quoteEn: Wood holds that capitalism and the bourgeoisie cannot be equated, but differ markedly.
quoteZh: 伍德认为，资本主义与资产阶级不能等同，而是具有显著差异

glossary.explanation: A school of Anglo-American Marxism associated with Robert Brenner and Ellen Meiksins Wood, which centres on social property relations and the historical specificity of capitalism. The label was coined by Guy Bois as a criticism and later accepted by the school's members.
Political Marxism's key concept, meaning the way ownership and control of resources is socially organised. The school uses it to distinguish social formations and to explain historical change.
The official name for China's current path and system, presented by the Party as an adaptation of scientific socialism to Chinese conditions.

t: The Marxist basic principles discipline after fifteen years: a review of theoretical research and outlook
zh: 马克思主义基本原理学科15年来理论研究的回顾与展望
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2020 no. 10
paras: Zhang Jianyun takes stock of theoretical research in the discipline of the basic principles of Marxism, which was established in 2005 as a second-level discipline within the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. Zhang argues that fifteen years of work produced solid results on foundational questions, but that since about 2016 research has hit a bottleneck. In Zhang's view the discipline still lacks a distinctive problem domain and research paradigm, and the way out lies in genuinely holistic research tied to new productive forces.

The article has three parts. The first surveys 2005–2015, when scholars worked on the discipline's nature and status, the definition and content of basic principles, the wholeness of Marxism, the structure of the principles system, practical application, study of the classics, and staffing and teaching. The second diagnoses the current bottleneck, citing a sharp fall in China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) results for topics such as basic principles and the wholeness of Marxism. The third sets out principles and a direction for future work.

Zhang reports consensus on the discipline's foundational status and on teacher training, but no agreement on how to list the principles. The author contends that research on wholeness stays at the level of theory, because the unity of Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism is a relation of theory and practice that only practice can explain. Zhang faults current work for neglecting the internet-based new productive forces (big data, cloud computing, blockchain, artificial intelligence), for lagging behind socialist construction, and for lacking comprehensive analysis of practice. Zhang argues that these technologies differ in kind from the large machines Marx analysed, and that they exceed the limits of capitalist relations of production. Treating them as wholly controlled by capital would, in this reading, be a mechanical reading of Marx.

Zhang concludes that future research should hold to a principle of wholeness and a direction centred on the new productive forces of the internet technology system. This means broad knowledge across philosophy, political economy, scientific socialism and natural science, and synthesis built on concrete analysis of new practice. Zhang holds that doing so would test the truth of Marxist principles and show the inner unity of Marxism's three component parts concretely rather than abstractly. Read the original if you want an insider's account of the field's agenda, with a CNKI-based periodisation and a techno-determinist argument about internet productive forces.
quoteEn: The basic principles of Marxism are not a philosophy of the study, and the inner unity of its three component parts is not a purely theoretical unity; it must be combined with the development of the times and the practice of socialist construction, offering ways of solving problems, and on that basis advance research on the wholeness of Marxism.
quoteZh: 马克思主义基本原理不是书斋哲学，三大组成部分的内在统一也不是单纯理论上的统一，需要与时代发展和社会主义建设实践相结合，提出解决问题的思路和方法，在此基础上推进马克思主义整体性研究。

glossary.explanation: A second-level discipline created in 2005 within the first-level discipline of Marxist theory. It aims to study the main classic works and treat the Marxist system as a whole. The same name is used for a compulsory university course.
The idea that Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism form an organic unity. The 2005 official notice makes studying it the discipline's central task.
The top tier of China's official academic classification, set by the Academic Degrees Committee of the State Council and the Ministry of Education. It is divided into second-level disciplines.

t: Revisiting Marx's theory of "planned production" in the Internet age
zh: 互联网时代马克思“计划生产”理论再探
source: Observation and Thinking (观察与思考), 2020 no. 7
paras: Zhang Jianyun asks how Marx's idea of planned production, long associated with the Soviet command economy, should be understood once big data, the Internet, cloud computing, blockchain and artificial intelligence reshape production. The article, published in 2020, argues that these technologies supply the technical conditions for the consumer-centred, self-conscious planned production that Marx and Engels envisaged for a future society.

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the essence of planned production in Marx and Engels and separates it from its concrete forms. The second argues that Internet-era productive forces demand consumer-centred planning, citing overproduction, rising demand for personalised goods, accumulated wealth and the merging of production and consumption. The third uses present-day Internet practice, such as crowdsourcing and mass customisation, to sketch how planning might work, and ends with the social conditions required.

Zhang's core move is to distinguish the essence of planned production from its form of realisation. The essence, in the author's reading, is conscious production according to need and a rational plan by an association of freely united producers, meaning all members of society. Concrete forms depend on the level of productive forces: Lenin's state organisation and Stalin's highly centralised, mandatory planning suited backward, pre-Internet conditions, but are said to have failed to collect timely information or motivate workers. Equating the two, Zhang says, produced doctrinal confusion and fear that market reform betrays Marxism. Zhang then holds that digital, online information removes intermediaries and hierarchy, so consumers become co-producers ("prosumers"), firms can match supply to demand and avoid waste, and "self-organising" platforms such as crowdsourcing realise the free association of producers.

Zhang concludes that technology alone is not enough. Universal, conscious planned production also requires a fundamental change in relations of production, namely common social ownership of the means of production, which the author considers impossible under private ownership and competition. Zhang adds that the rapid growth of Internet productive forces is already creating the conditions for this change. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar uses digital-economy examples, such as Haier, Xiaomi and crowdsourcing platforms, to revive and reinterpret the Marxist theory of planning.
quoteEn: The essence of "planned production" is an economic form in which all members of society, that is, an association of freely united producers, produce consciously according to need and in line with a rational plan.
quoteZh: “计划生产”本质内涵是：由全体社会成员即自由结合起来的生产者联合体根据需要、按照合理计划自觉地进行生产的经济形式。

glossary.explanation: Marx and Engels's idea that in a future society associated producers organise production consciously according to need, in contrast to capitalism's anarchy of production. The article distinguishes it from Soviet-style state planning.
The collective subject of planning in the article's reading of Marx: all members of society freely joined as producers, rather than a government body or particular organisations.

t: "Appropriation and enjoyment": an inner moment of holistic practice
zh: “占有和享受”：整体性实践的内在环节
paras: Zhang Jianyun takes up a gap in the usual account of practice. Practice is generally understood as humans' objectifying activity, comprising two linked processes: knowing and transforming the object, and testing and evaluating the results. The article argues that a third process belongs to it: the experience, savouring and appreciation that arise when people appropriate and enjoy the products of objectification. In Zhang's view, this experiential activity is an inner moment of practice as an organic whole, not a mere afterthought.

The article, published in 2020 in Academic Exploration, has three parts. The first reconstructs the concept of objectification (duixianghua) through Hegel, Feuerbach and Marx, drawing on the Theses on Feuerbach, the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and Capital. The second turns to appropriation and enjoyment as the deeper content of objectification. The third discusses what appropriation and enjoyment mean for practice, covering comprehensiveness, the distinction between kinds of luxury, and shared development.

Zhang argues that objectification has two sides: human essential powers are realised in the object, and the object's properties and laws enter the subject's knowledge. Using Marx's remark that in consumption the thing becomes subject, Zhang holds that only through enjoying human-made products do people "intuit themselves" in a world of their own making. They confirm their own capacities, assess how far needs are met, and form ideals. Once basic needs are satisfied, the relation to the product shifts from possession to aesthetic appreciation. The resulting spiritual world is, for Zhang, the source of creativity and the driving force of further practice.

Zhang draws three implications. Appropriation must be comprehensive, using all the senses, rather than mere bodily gratification. Consumption should aim at "means of development": Zhang distinguishes luxuries that will become tomorrow's necessities from ostentatious, pathological consumption, which should be curbed. Under capitalism, Zhang says, workers cannot enjoy their products, so wealth brings them "stupidity and cretinism". Citing the 19th Party Congress (2017), Zhang argues that under socialism development results must be shared by all the people, which Zhang links to common prosperity. Read the original if you are interested in how Chinese Marxist philosophers use Marx's early texts to ground consumption, aesthetics and shared development in a theory of practice.
quoteEn: The experiential activity brought about by appropriation and enjoyment is an inner moment of practice as an organic whole.
quoteZh: 由占有和享受带来的体验活动是整体性实践的内在环节。

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal in China, stressed in Party documents, that the fruits of development be shared by all the people rather than concentrated among a few.

A concept from Hegel and Feuerbach that Marx reworked to mean the realisation of human essential powers in the products of labour. It is distinguished from alienation, which Marx ties to specific historical conditions.

t: Marx and Engels on the historical direction of modern China
zh: 马克思恩格斯论近代中国的历史走向问题
paras: Si Shuyan asks how Marx and Engels, over the five decades from the first Opium War to the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95, understood the future course of modern China. The article argues that, applying historical materialism, they judged that China's monarchical autocracy would collapse, that China would first move towards European-style capitalist civilisation, and that it would eventually reach socialism, with a theoretical possibility of shortening the road.

The article has three sections. The first treats the collapse of imperial autocracy under capitalist impact, covering the bureaucracy, the military, the economic base and the Taiping revolution. The second examines how large-scale industry transformed China's old civilisation and why Marx and Engels expected a bourgeois republic. The third turns to socialism, drawing on Marx's letter to Vera Zasulich and Engels's 1894 afterword on Russia, and closes with a short assessment of how history bore out these judgements.

Si's central move is to show that Marx and Engels saw capitalism as the historical and logical precondition of socialism, so modern China, which the author classes as an "Asiatic" formation, could not reach socialism directly. Large industry, railways and the destruction of peasant handicrafts would drive China towards a capitalist, Europeanised order. The author then sets against this the theory of leaping over a social formation. Marx and Engels, in the author's reading, always allowed the "theoretical possibility" of bypassing the capitalist system in countries retaining communal property, and Engels called Russia the "China of Europe". Si presents the two positions as the dialectical unity of sequential and leapfrogging development, and notes that Engels cautioned that only "rather vague hypotheses" were possible about the stages involved.

Si concludes that Marx and Engels's judgements were scientific because later history confirmed them: the monarchy fell, and China attempted capitalist state forms despite its semi-colonial, semi-feudal character. Within about a century China moved from autocracy to a socialist society, which in the author's view confirms the leap theory and opens a new path beyond Lenin. The author adds that the road had to be found by the Chinese people themselves, by integrating Marxism with Chinese reality. Read the original if you want a systematic Chinese account of Marx and Engels's China texts and of how they are linked to the theory of skipping the capitalist stage.
quoteEn: Marx and Engels did not state directly that modern China could achieve socialism; they only raised, in theory, the possibility that backward countries might make such a leap.
quoteZh: 马克思恩格斯并没有直接说明近代中国能够实现社会主义，只是在理论上提出了落后国家实现这种跨越的可能性

t: When did Chen Duxiu become a Marxist? A dating study
zh: 陈独秀转变为马克思主义者时间考
source: Journal of Chengdu University of Technology (Social Sciences Edition), 2020 no. 5
paras: This research article asks when Chen Duxiu, the founding Party leader and editor of New Youth, became a Marxist. Ren and Huang note that existing scholarship offers several dates: during the founding of the Communist Party, before May 1920, September 1920 (the essay "On Politics"), June–July 1920, or 1921. They argue instead that the conversion began in January 1919 with the essay "Eliminate the Three Evils" and was complete by December 1919, with the New Youth manifesto.

The article is organised in five parts. It first reconstructs Chen's 1919 writings and then examines his popularisation of Marxist theory among workers as preparation for Party-building. A third part uses Chen's 1920 activities and the testimony of others (Mao Zedong, Zhang Guotao, Voitinsky) as corroboration. A fourth part compares Chen's route with that of Li Dazhao, and a short conclusion follows.

The authors' central move is to reject the common view that a person counts as a Marxist only after mastering a systematic theory, which they call judging the past by present standards. In their account, Chen's turn was practical and gradual. Disillusioned by warlordism and the corruption of republican politics, he called in January 1919 for a people's party, which the authors read as the start of his Party-building thought and of his conversion. They then trace his endorsement of proletarian dictatorship, his use of surplus-value theory in essays on workers' wages and conditions, and his 1920 contacts with Mao, Zhang Guotao and Voitinsky. On this reading, "On Politics" (1920) merely summarised a position already held.

The authors conclude that Li Dazhao became a Marxist by internalising theory and publicly declaring his stance, whereas Chen followed a route led by practice, with theory secondary, shaped by his earlier radicalism. They acknowledge that Chen's grasp of Marxist theory was shallower and that his understanding contained errors, which they say were corrected as the Party developed and contact with the Comintern grew. They present this uneven, fragmentary path as an early instance of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Read the original if you study the early history of Marxism in China, the debates over Chen Duxiu's intellectual development, or the founding of the Chinese Communist Party.
quoteEn: The time of Chen Duxiu's conversion to Marxism should be marked at its start by the publication of \"Eliminate the Three Evils\" in January 1919, and its completion by the New Youth manifesto of December 1919.
quoteZh: 陈独秀转变为马克思主义者的时间应该是1919年1月《除三害》的提出为开始转变的标志，1919年12月《新青年》宣言发表则是其转变为马克思主义者的完成。

glossary.explanation: The influential journal founded by Chen Duxiu in 1915, central to the New Culture Movement. It later became an organ of the early Communist organisation.

t: A review of research on the Marxist study movement in the Yan'an period
zh: 延安时期马克思主义学习运动研究述论
source: Marxism Studies Journal (马克思主义学刊), 2020 no. 1
paras: This literature review, published in Marxism Studies Journal in 2020, surveys scholarship on the Marxist study movement that the Communist Party of China led at Yan'an. Cheng Linping treats the movement as one of the most significant and far-reaching of the Party's many mass study campaigns. The review argues that domestic research is broad but shallow, and that foreign research is partial and sometimes biased.

The article has two main parts. The first covers Chinese scholarship, from books and journal articles on Yan'an cadre education, the rectification movement and Party theory-building, to contemporary assessments such as Liang Shuming's 1938 impressions of Yan'an. The second covers foreign work, drawing on early eyewitnesses and later scholars, including John King Fairbank, the Japanese scholars Tokuda Noriyuki and Nomura Koichi, the Australian Nick Knight and Stuart Schram.

Cheng groups Chinese research into seven themes: the reasons the movement was launched; its content and features; study methods and mechanisms; its agents (leaders and intellectuals); lessons and implications; comprehensive studies; and its effect on adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. Most scholars, the review says, take a favourable view. Cheng criticises foreign readings: Fairbank's claim that rectification purged Moscow-trained opponents of Mao is called subjective; Tokuda's view that the Sinification of Marxism resisted Moscow is called one-sided; and Schram's 'heterodoxy' thesis is rejected. Knight's emphasis on applying universal laws to Chinese particularities is judged close to the official formulation, and Nomura's description of rectification as an educational movement is judged accurate.

Cheng's conclusion is that domestic work needs more depth. The review suggests comparing different learners (senior cadres and ordinary members, military schools and Party schools, serving and non-serving cadres), assessing learning outcomes, and examining the link to the adaptation of Marxism in China. It also suggests drawing lessons for building a learning-oriented Party. Cheng considers that foreign studies are held back by language barriers and ideological limits, and that none yet focuses specifically on the movement. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese-language scholarship on Yan'an-era Party study and an example of how Chinese researchers assess foreign interpretations of the rectification movement.
quoteEn: The Marxist study movement of the Yan'an period was a pioneering undertaking in the Communist Party of China's theoretical study, achieved great success and accumulated rich experience in study.
quoteZh: 延安时期马克思主义学习运动是中国共产党理论学习的一次创举，取得重大成功，并积累了丰富的学习经验。

glossary.explanation: A Party-wide campaign of 1942–45 under Mao Zedong, aimed at ideological education and at criticising dogmatism, sectarianism and formalism. It is officially presented as establishing the seeking-truth-from-facts line.
The Party's term for combining Marxism's universal principles with China's concrete conditions. It was put forward by Mao Zedong at the Sixth Plenum in 1938.

t: The circulation and rediscovery of Marx's Grundrisse in the West
zh: 马克思《大纲》在西方的流传与再发现
paras: Marx's Grundrisse (the 1857–58 manuscripts) has become an indispensable classic in Marxist research, yet Kong Zhijian argues that Western scholars' reception of it is a historical construction. Although written before Capital, it reached readers after Capital. Kong holds that tracing this transmission history helps Chinese readers cite Western interpretations critically and grasp Marx's critique of political economy more accurately.

The article follows the text through four stages. The first is the 'hundred years of solitude' from 1857 to 1953: neglect after Marx, Ryazanov's 1923 announcement, the Moscow edition of 1939–41, and the East Berlin reprint of 1953 taken up by Frankfurt School figures such as Marcuse and Alfred Schmidt. The second is the 1960s and early 1970s, when fragments gave way to whole-text readings. The third is the peak of research from the 1970s to the late 1980s, and the fourth is the calmer period after the Soviet collapse.

Kong's central claim is that each phase of reception was shaped by the theoretical and political conditions of the time. Full translations into French, Italian and English came from non-Communist publishers, driven by young leftists seeking a path beyond Soviet orthodoxy, as in Italian workerism and the British New Left. Althusser's structuralist debates, Rosdolsky's 1968 book and Martin Nicolaus's 'The Unknown Marx' turned the manuscript into an independent object of study. In the peak period the draft's open, experimental character produced rival readings, such as McLellan's view of it as Marx's most complete work, Nicolaus's critique of its Hegelian method, and Negri's 'Marx beyond Marx'. Kong concludes that the hoped-for 'unknown Marx' became a 'many-faced Marx'.

After 1990, Kong notes, ideological pressure eased and philological work based on MEGA2 grew, alongside revisiting studies. Kong credits Western scholars with discovering and publishing the text, but sees fragmentation, extremism and politicisation, and even 'creative misreadings'. Kong proposes three principles: return to the facts and read the work in the context of Marx's development; put China's own practice first while borrowing critically from the West; and keep to the practical orientation of the critique of political economy, including its treatment of machinery, ecology and the world market. Read the original if you want a concise account of how the Grundrisse was published and interpreted in the West, and how a Chinese scholar assesses that history.
quoteEn: Between the Grundrisse and Capital there are indeed theoretical gaps and differences, and ignoring or exaggerating them will both lead to theoretical deviation.
quoteZh: 从《大纲》到《资本论》，在理论上确实存在着差距和差异，无视或夸大这种差异都会造成理论的偏差

t: Production justice: the logical starting point of Marx's theory of justice
zh: 生产正义：马克思正义理论的逻辑起点
source: Gansu Theory Journal (Gansu Lilun Xuekan), 2020 no. 6
paras: Debate over "what is Marx's justice" has run for decades since the Tucker–Wood thesis, and current scholarship on how justice is to be achieved concentrates on distributive justice. Zhang Tingting argues that this focus, driven by dialogue with Rawls's A Theory of Justice and by domestic concern over the wealth gap, misses Marx's own emphasis. In Zhang's reading, Marx's theory begins from "production justice", and distributive justice is subordinate to it.

The article has five parts: the contrast between distributive and production justice; the core content of production justice; the conditions that make it possible; its final orientation; and a short conclusion. Zhang draws mainly on Marx's Introduction to the Critique of Political Economy (the 1857 Introduction) and Critique of the Gotha Programme, and also on Capital, the Communist Manifesto and the Circular Letter of the Communist League. Aristotle, Hegel and Proudhon appear as foils.

Zhang argues that, for Marx, production determines distribution: the structure of distribution is fixed by the structure of production, so a theory that only redistributes outcomes endorses the existing mode of production. Justice, Zhang says, is not a virtue or an eternal principle but is measured by its fit with a given mode of production, citing Capital on the justice of transactions. Capitalism is described as dual: progressive in its time, yet unjust because it rests on exploitation and the separation of labourers from the means of production. Hence private ownership of the means of production is held to be the root of social injustice, and production justice means replacing it with public ownership. Zhang grounds this in objective conditions (recurrent crises from the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation) and subjective ones (the alienated proletariat as the gravedigger of capitalism).

Zhang concludes that production justice points to human emancipation, in four senses: beyond political emancipation, beyond alienated labour, beyond "dependence on things", and beyond the principle of right, towards distribution according to need. Justice itself, Zhang adds, is a historical product with no content of its own, and it will disappear, like religion, when the conditions that produce it disappear. Read the original if you want a Chinese reading that places Marx's critique of distributive justice within his account of the mode of production and ownership.
quoteEn: Private appropriation of the means of production is the root of all social injustice; achieving production justice means abolishing private ownership of the means of production and establishing public ownership.
quoteZh: 生产资料私人占有是一切社会非正义的根源，实现生产正义就是要废除生产资料私有制，实现生产资料公有制。

t: Rethinking the intellectual relationship between the young Marx and Engels
zh: 青年时期马克思和恩格斯学术关系再思考
source: Journal of South-Central Minzu University (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2021 no. 4
paras: Debate over the intellectual relationship between Marx and Engels, which Sartre's charge that Engels distorted Marx exemplifies, has never produced a consensus. Zhang and Li argue that the disagreement stems partly from scholars choosing different time spans and different topics. They narrow the question to the years 1839–1846 and to one theme, the thinking on social development. Their answer is that, on this theme, the young Engels was the inspirer of the new ideas.

The article first sorts recent scholarship into three camps. The "opposition" camp includes Norman Levine and David McLellan. The "unity" camp includes Zhu Chuanqi and Henry. The "difference" camp includes Terrell Carver and Yu Wujin. It then follows the two men chronologically in three sections: their early journalism and their attention to the industrial worker; Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy and its effect on Marx; and the period of the Holy Family, The Condition of the Working Class in England and The German Ideology.

Zhang and Li make three main moves. First, they say that Engels, who came from a commercial background, noticed the industrial worker as a key part of modern class structure earlier than Marx, whose early attention went to peasants and small artisans. Second, they argue that Engels's critique in the Outlines, which located the root of competition in private property, helped to turn Marx from critique of Hegelian philosophy to critique of political economy. Marx later cited the work in the 1844 Manuscripts and in Capital. Third, they hold that The Condition of the Working Class in England supplied empirical material that Marx drew on, and that Engels's invitation to Manchester strengthened Marx's path towards a critique of capital. The authors note that Engels's value theory centred on price, not on Marx's labour–value relation. They add that The German Ideology (1845–46) is where the two first jointly set out their shared starting point in real individuals and their material conditions.

The authors conclude that, for 1839–1846 and for social-development theory, the evidence points to Engels as the inspirer of Marx's new thinking. They say they do not mean only to stress Engels's role. Their aim is to make the question of Marx and Engels's relationship more specific, so that it is no longer handled through empty abstract commentary. Read the original if you are interested in the Marx–Engels question, the history of Marxism, or the early Engels's influence on Marx's turn to political economy.
quoteEn: It was precisely the young Engels's critique of private property that firmed up the young Marx's research path of dismantling the problems of bourgeois society through the critique of political economy.
quoteZh: 正是青年恩格斯对私有制的批判，才坚定青年马克思以政治经济学批判解构资产阶级社会问题的研究路径
keywords: Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy
The Condition of the Working Class in England

t: On the logical starting point of historical materialism
zh: 论历史唯物主义的逻辑起点
source: Collected Papers on Marxist Philosophy, 2020, vol. 2
paras: Lu Sixi asks what the logical starting point of historical materialism is, and treats this as the first problem in building a Marxist philosophical system. The article rejects the view that Marx's eleventh thesis on Feuerbach aims to abolish philosophy. In Lu's reading, the thesis stresses the practical character of the new materialism without dropping theoretical explanation. Lu's answer is that the starting point is practical activity, which unites transcendence and reality, whereas philosophies that start from things or from thought remain abstract.

The article has three main sections. The first examines the standpoint of 'things' in ancient naive materialism, early modern mechanical materialism and Feuerbach's intuitive materialism, with most attention to Feuerbach. The second examines the standpoint of 'thought' in Descartes, Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre and later attempts to escape solipsism, including Zhao Tingyang's idea of 'co-existence'. The third sets out the practical standpoint, followed by a short conclusion.

On the first standpoint, Lu argues that things lack transcendence. Mechanical materialism reduces humans to links in a causal chain, and Feuerbach turns to the human viewpoint but treats production and commerce as animal instinct. In Lu's account he locates the human essence only in orientation towards the infinite, which splits his materialist view of nature from his idealist view of history. On the second, Lu argues that thought-based philosophy lacks reality. Its two ways out of solipsism, 'from one to none' (Sartre's pre-reflective self-consciousness, compared to the Buddhist storehouse consciousness) and 'from one to many' (intersubjectivity and co-existence), are said to fail. The first dissolves the self, and the second cannot establish that shared existence is real rather than a 'game'.

Lu then argues that practice keeps materialism's basic standpoint, because successful practice presupposes that nature exists. It also grounds human agency in objectifying activity, in which self-consciousness is always present. Practice creates a 'humanized world' that unifies nature, society and thought. Human transcendence is therefore achieved through the transcendence of that world as a whole, not through bodily 'superhumans' or self-cultivation. Lu concludes that historical materialism unites ontology, epistemology and axiology, and that practice is the fulcrum of 'first philosophy'. Read the original if you want a Chinese account of Marx's break with Feuerbach, phenomenology and idealism that argues for practice as the foundation of Marxist philosophy.
quoteEn: Practical activity is the fulcrum of first philosophy in the true sense.
quoteZh: 实践活动是真正意义上的第一哲学的支点。

t: Research on Marx's concept of civil society: achievements, problems and prospects
zh: 马克思市民社会概念研究的成果、问题与展望
source: Social Sciences Trends (Shehui kexue dongtai), 2020 no. 12
paras: This literature review surveys roughly half a century of scholarship on Marx's concept of civil society (bürgerliche Gesellschaft), which Chen Ke describes as the conceptual cornerstone of Marx's critique of capitalist society. The article asks how existing studies have settled the concept's "positioning and naming" within Marxist theory. Chen's thesis is that Chinese and foreign research has been productive, but that its habit of reducing the concept to the economic base rests on a methodological flaw.

The review has three parts. The first covers Chinese scholarship along a vertical axis (the stages of the concept's formation and the claim that it "disappears" in Marx's later work) and a horizontal axis (what the concept means and whether it is "equated" with other terms), and then looks at the significance scholars draw from it. The second covers foreign work in three tendencies: defence by the Japanese civil-society school (Mochizuki Seiji, Hirata Kiyoaki), reinterpretation by Western Marxists (Gramsci, Habermas, Cohen and Arato), and criticism by Western scholars (Shils, Taylor, Keane) of Marx's "economism". The third part assesses the field.

Chen reports that two-stage accounts treat the concept as an immature early notion replaced by the economic base, whereas three-stage accounts trace it into Capital and explain its lower frequency in the text as a "reconstruction". The article favours the three-stage view. On meaning, it sorts four positions into two models: one-dimensional readings that equate civil society with the economic base or with bourgeois society, and readings that find two or three senses in Marx's usage. Chen judges the first model dialectically deficient and the second more complete. Chen faults foreign scholars for downplaying class and for treating civil society as an independent sphere opposed to state power. Chen also sees their work as having enriched the concept's cultural and communicative dimensions.

Chen identifies two weaknesses in Chinese research: it neglects conceptual history, and it relies on abstract, word-to-word debate that reduces the concept to "material relations" in every era. This, Chen argues, departs from Marx's method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete. The article proposes combining static comparison of civil society, economic base and bourgeois society with a dynamic study of how the concept changes. It stresses tracing how Marx lifts civil society up into capitalist society. Read the original if you want a map of Chinese and foreign debates on Marx's civil society, including the Japanese school and the "disappearance" and "equation" controversies.
quoteEn: In Marx's intellectual development the concept of civil society went through a process of change, and its different meanings are interrelated; a static, abstract definition can hardly reflect how these changes interweave.
quoteZh: 市民社会概念在马克思的思想演进中有一个变化发展的过程，不同含义之间也是相互联系的，静态的抽象化定义难以反映这种变化之间的相互交织。

glossary.explanation: Chinese rendering of bürgerliche Gesellschaft, which in German also means bourgeois society. Chinese scholars debate whether Marx used it for the economic base, for bourgeois society, or in several senses.
The relations of production that, in the Marxist base–superstructure model, underlie a society's political and ideological superstructure.
The society dominated by the bourgeoisie. The review discusses whether it can be distinguished from civil society and from capitalist society.

t: A preliminary discussion of Marx's "historical determinism"
zh: 马克思的“历史决定论”刍议
source: Journal of Shanxi Normal University (Social Science Edition), 2021 no. 1
paras: Is Marx a determinist? Wang Fengming takes up a question that, since the 1970s, has been central to Western Marxist debate. The article argues that historical materialism is in essence a form of historical determinism, and that the real issue is not whether Marx was a determinist but how his determinism should be understood.

The article moves in five steps. It first collects determinist passages from The German Ideology, the 1859 Preface and Capital with its manuscripts. It then surveys criticism of historical determinism, from Karl Popper's attack on historicism to Chinese scholars who set determinism against agency and moral norms. Next it reviews defences by Herbert Marcuse and Adam Schaff, followed by a conceptual history of "determine" drawn from Raymond Williams, and finally it proposes principles of interpretation.

Wang's central move is to reject the opposition of historical law to human agency and of determinism to normative judgement. Citing Marx on the labour process and on social relations that appear as an alien power, Wang holds that purposes and wills are internal elements of objective law, and that law is the overall result of purposeful human activity. Moral conduct and value judgements are then the outward forms through which law is realised, as a falling apple with its contingencies realises gravitation. Wang adds that critics often attack one meaning of determinism with another. Marx's version is read as "tendency determination" in the sense of practical philosophy, and as a scientific abstraction. It is not Plekhanov's genetic "origin determination", nor a statistical "big-data" determination. Wang gives the example that clothes must fit the person, not the person the clothes, and says the principle that productive forces determine relations of production is equally commonplace.

Wang endorses Schaff's view that determinism is the core of historical materialism, and Bertell Ollman's view that debate should ask where Marx is and is not a determinist. Wang proposes four principles of interpretation. These are to read Marx through Capital and its manuscripts, to analyse concrete problems rather than abstract concepts, to absorb research from economics, sociology, history and political science, and to interpret determinism within the integrated whole of Marxist philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist defence of determinism that engages Popper, Williams, Marcuse and Schaff, or if you follow debates on Marx's philosophy of history.
quoteEn: It follows that the crux is not whether historical materialism is a determinism or historical determinism, but how this determinism is to be understood and interpreted.
quoteZh: 由此可见,问题的关键并不在于唯物史观是否是一种决定论或历史决定论,而在于究竟如何理解和阐释这种决定论或历史决定论。

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory that material production and social relations shape political and intellectual life. Chinese texts use the term for Marx's and Engels's theory of history.
The view that history develops according to objective laws. Critics read it as mechanistic or fatalist; the article defends a non-fatalist reading.

t: The inner logic of the epic struggle of New China over more than 70 years
zh: 新中国70多年感天动地奋斗史诗的内在逻辑
source: Study and Research (学习与研究), 2021 no. 4
paras: Writing in 2021, the centenary year of the Communist Party, Gong Yun asks how the history of New China should be understood as a whole, given its division into the periods before and after the reform and opening up that began in 1978. The article answers that the two periods are an inseparable, unified whole that is consistent in essence. It follows Xi Jinping's formula that neither period may be used to negate the other, and it presents this as a guard against historical nihilism.

The article has three parts. The first sets out four forms of consistency between the periods: the nature of society, the social system, Party leadership, and the Party's founding mission. The second argues that the periods are continuous and that the earlier one supplied the later one with its foundations. The third explains why handling the relationship correctly matters for upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Gong draws throughout on statements by Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping and on the 1981 Party resolution on history.

Gong holds that the pre-1978 period gave the later one its political premise and institutional base, its material and technological base, its theoretical preparation, positive and negative experience, and a favourable international environment. As evidence the article cites industrial and output growth figures for 1949–1978 and the policy ideas of the Mao era, including the "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese conditions. Reform and opening up, in this reading, continued, reformed and developed earlier socialist exploration. Gong also states that the two periods differ markedly in guiding thought, policy and conditions. He describes the relationship as a spiral ascent and as a sublation that keeps the basic socialist system while overturning ideas and institutions unsuited to the productive forces.

Gong concludes that the relationship between the two periods is above all a political question. Handling it properly, he argues, helps people grasp the theme, main line and mainstream of New China's history, and it does not require ignoring past errors. It also deepens understanding of the laws of Party governance and of socialist construction, strengthens the Four-sphere Confidence, and builds consensus around the second centenary goal. He warns that hostile forces attack the history of the revolution and of New China in order to confuse people. Read the original if you want a representative statement of the official Party-history line on the "two periods" question, with the main supporting quotations from Mao, Deng and Xi.
quoteEn: The new period of reform and opening up was a great revolution against certain ideas, systems and mechanisms of the earlier period that no longer suited the needs of productive forces. It was a "sublation" carried out on the basis of upholding the basic socialist system, and a process of spiral ascent.
quoteZh: 改革开放新时期是对改革开放前时期一些不适应生产力发展需要的观念、体制、机制的巨大革命，是在坚持社会主义基本制度基础上的“扬弃”，是一种螺旋式上升过程。

glossary.explanation: In Party usage, a label for views that negate the Party's revolutionary and socialist history or set its periods against each other. It is a frequent target of official campaigns, especially since the 2010s.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
Official slogan calling for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The Party's official name for its path of socialist development since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, public ownership and a socialist market economy.
The goal of building a modern socialist country that is prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced and harmonious by 2049, the centenary of the People's Republic.

t: Fully, accurately and comprehensively implementing the new development philosophy
zh: 王舒傲、古梁;完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念
paras: Writing in the PLA Daily in March 2021, Wang Shu'ao and Gu Liang take up Xi Jinping's repeated instruction to implement the new development philosophy fully, accurately and comprehensively, so that the 14th Five-Year Plan period gets off to a good start. The commentary argues that this requires three points of emphasis: the fundamental purpose, a problem-oriented approach and a sense of potential danger. Together they are meant to turn the Party's institutional advantages in leading economic work into governance effectiveness.

The piece is organised in three sections, one for each point of emphasis. Each section sets out how the five elements of the philosophy (innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing) should be read from that angle. It draws on Xi's speeches, a 1950s remark by Mao Zedong on common wealth and the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020).

The authors first present service to the people as the "root and soul" of the philosophy. They link it to meeting the people's needs for a better life and to a stronger emphasis on common prosperity, which they describe as a major political question bearing on the Party's basis for governing. They then argue that the principal contradiction of the new era, between growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development, should guide targeted measures, such as work on core technologies and supply-chain security. Finally, they call for balancing development with security, with each of the five elements tied to a security task, and for self-reliance whatever the external environment.

The authors conclude that the philosophy should run through all development and fields, with innovation as the primary driving force and sharing as the fundamental goal. This, they say, will guide the building of a new development paradigm. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-army press commentary presents the new development philosophy at the start of the 14th Five-Year Plan.
quoteEn: The Chinese economy is a vast sea, not a small pond.
quoteZh: 中国经济是一片大海，而不是一个小池塘。

glossary.explanation: A framework put forward by Xi Jinping in 2015 and built on five elements: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing. It is presented as the guide for China's economic and social planning.
A long-standing socialist goal of prosperity shared by all, stressed again in Party documents of the 2020s. It is tied to reducing regional, urban–rural and income gaps.

The Party's formulation of the main tension in Chinese society. Since the 19th Party Congress (2017) it has been defined as the one between the people's growing needs for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development.

t: Strategic guidance for building a modern socialist country in all respects
zh: 全面建设社会主义现代化国家的战略引领
paras: Writing in Dongyue Tribune in 2021, Hao Xianyin interprets the Proposal on the 14th Five-Year Plan and the Long-Range Objectives for 2035, adopted at the Fifth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2020). Hao argues that the Proposal is the programmatic document for building a modern socialist country in all respects, and that it rests on a long Party tradition of medium- and long-term planning.

The article has four parts. The first reviews planning since 1951, from the "step-by-step" modernization goals (the Four Modernizations, the "three-step" and "new three-step" strategies, and the two-stage plan to 2035 and mid-century) through the thirteen Five-Year Plans. The second sets out the Proposal's blueprint, its guiding principles and its key themes. The third and fourth treat the principles to be followed and the major relationships to be handled in implementation.

In Hao's account, the planning record yields five lessons: planning must start from the primary stage of socialism, put the people at the centre, follow a sound development philosophy, reflect the shift from a planned to a market economy, and uphold the Party's overall leadership. Hao presents high-quality development, supply-side structural reform, the "dual circulation" development pattern and common prosperity as the main lines of the new stage. The Proposal's lack of quantified targets is explained as a matter of setting direction, with figures to follow in the outline plan, and as a choice to stress quality over doubling of output.

Hao concludes that implementation requires the Party's overall leadership, a people-centred approach, the new development philosophy, deeper reform and opening up, and systems thinking. Five relationships must also be handled: inheritance and innovation, government and market, openness and self-reliance, development and security, and strategy and tactics. The article closely follows official texts and cites Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping throughout. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned reading of the 14th Five-Year Plan Proposal and a historical account of Chinese national planning from 1953 to 2020.
quoteEn: The formulation and implementation of plans for national economic and social development must be grounded in the basic national condition of the primary stage of socialism.
quoteZh: 制定和实施国民经济和社会发展规划(计划)必须立足社会主义初级阶段的基本国情。

glossary.explanation: An official thesis, formalised in 1987, that China is in an underdeveloped phase of socialism lasting a long historical period. The article treats it as the basic national condition for all planning.
Xi Jinping's five-part framework of innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared development, put forward in 2015 to guide the 13th Five-Year Plan and later plans.
The official goal, adopted around 2017, of shifting from high-speed growth to growth stressing quality, efficiency and innovation.
A long-standing socialist goal of prosperity shared by all, which the article says the Proposal elevated as a stated aim for 2035.

t: The capitalist economic cycle and the hundred-year cycle of world politics
zh: 资本主义经济周期与世界政治的百年轮回
paras: Wang Lixin asks how the recurring crises of capitalism shape world politics, and argues that the world has in effect returned to the 1930s after roughly a century. In the article's account, the deepest root of this "hundred-year cycle" is the capitalist business cycle: each worldwide economic crisis brings profound political change, after which humanity gradually leaves the crisis and returns to the "normal track". Wang names four types of political consequence: domestic social and political crisis with policy shifts, damage to the prestige of liberal democratic capitalism, a changed balance among great powers, and shocks to international norms and order.

The article compares the three worldwide crises of the past century: the Great Depression of the 1930s, the stagflation of the 1970s and the financial crisis of 2008. It treats the first and third as having by far the greatest political impact. Its sections follow these cases in turn, drawing on GDP comparisons for Britain, France, the United States, Germany, Japan and the Soviet Union, and on scholarship by Huntington, Przeworski and Larry Diamond.

For the 1930s, Wang describes the fall of the Weimar Republic, Japanese militarism and Roosevelt's turn to state intervention and isolationism. The author also notes the rise of fascism as an alternative to liberal democracy, the Soviet Union's growth outside the capitalist system, the weakening of Britain, France and the United States, and the collapse of the internationalist basis of the post-1918 order. The 1970s are presented as a milder case, marked by American retrenchment, a narrowing gap with the Soviet Union and the end of dollar convertibility into gold. For 2008, Wang identifies populism, inequality and social polarisation, a "democratic recession", the relative rise of China, India and other non-Western states, the return of great-power competition, and a crisis of the liberal international order that Trump's protectionism and unilateralism made worse.

Wang concludes that populism, extreme nationalism, weakening democracy, power politics and the breakdown of international norms make today's world resemble the 1930s. Seen through this cyclical lens, the "great changes unseen in a century" may be understood more fully, and, the author adds, with more calm and composure. Read the original if you want a historical-comparative account, from a Chinese scholar, of how the Great Depression and the 2008 crisis reshaped domestic politics and the international order.
quoteEn: The deepest root of this hundred-year cycle lies in the cycle of capitalist development: every worldwide economic crisis brings profound change to world politics, after which humanity gradually emerges from the crisis and returns to the "normal track".
quoteZh: 这一百年轮回的最深刻根源在于资本主义发展周期，每次世界性经济危机都会给世界政治带来深刻变化，然后人类又逐渐走出危机，重回“正轨”。

glossary.en: great changes unseen in a century
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Chinese leaders since about 2017–2018 to describe the shifting global balance of power and order. The article uses it to frame the current international situation.

t: Learning from Party history to understand why Marxism works
st: Grasping the historical, theoretical and practical logic of "why Marxism is effective"
zh: 学史明理深刻领悟马克思主义为什么行
paras: Writing in Chengdu Daily on 31 March 2021, during the Party History Study and Education campaign, Jing takes up Xi Jinping's call to "learn from history to understand principle" (xue shi ming li). The commentary asks why Marxism "works" (xing) in China and answers that this can be grasped through three logics Xi names: historical, theoretical and practical. Jing presents the campaign as a way to reinforce the faith, ideals and original mission of Party members through study of the Party's hundred-year history.

The piece is organised under three headings, one for each logic. It begins with Xi's remarks in Fujian, then traces the introduction of Marxism to China after the October Revolution and the founding of the Communist Party. It goes on to compare Marxism with other responses to national crisis since the Opium War, and ends by linking Marxism to the needs of successive historical periods. Jing relies heavily on quotations from Engels, Marx, Mao Zedong and Xi.

On the historical logic, Jing argues that the red thread through the Party's history, from its founding through the establishment of the People's Republic and reform and opening up to the new era, is the effort to combine Marxism's universal principles with China's concrete conditions. On the theoretical logic, Jing says that other options, from "Chinese learning as the essence" to bourgeois democracy and wholesale Westernisation, all failed, while Marxism succeeded because of four traits: a thoroughly materialist philosophy, a people-first political stance, a method of seeking truth from facts rather than a creed, and openness to development. On the practical logic, Jing holds that theory is realised in a country in proportion to how far it meets that country's needs, so Marxism has taken root by answering the problems of each era.

Jing concludes that Marxism has developed in stages: Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. In contemporary China, the author says, upholding Marxism means upholding that last body of thought. Jing calls on every Party member to become a firm believer in and faithful practitioner of this thought, using the campaign's slogan to study history, grasp the thought, do practical work and open new horizons. Read the original if you want a compact example of how the 2021 Party history campaign framed the claim that Marxism "works" in China.
quoteEn: Marxism is not a creed but a method; it supplies no ready-made answers, but offers people a scientific method to follow in exploring solutions to real problems.
quoteZh: 马克思主义不是教义，而是方法，它不提供任何现成的答案，而是为人们探索解决现实问题出具可资遵循的科学方法。

glossary.en: Party History Study and Education campaign
glossary.explanation: A nationwide Party-wide campaign launched in early 2021 ahead of the centenary of the Party's founding, centred on study of the Party's hundred-year history.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
A guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao, adopted by the Party in the early 2000s, stressing people-centred, comprehensive and sustainable development.
Jiang Zemin's theory that the Party should represent advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the majority.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: On the historical evolution of Marx's concept of alienation
zh: 论马克思异化概念的历史演进
source: Journal of Social Sciences of Shanxi Higher Education Institutions, 2020 no. 12
paras: Wang Guangye asks how Marx's concept of alienation took shape, and why it differs from the versions held by Hegel and Feuerbach. The article argues that alienation, a central concept running through Marx's whole career, was not conceived suddenly. In Wang's account it developed historically, from Hegel's absolute idealism through Feuerbach's intuitive materialism to the analysis of social reality, ending in an economic critique of capital's enslavement of modern people.

The article is a work of intellectual history in three stages. It first treats speculative and religious alienation, covering Marx's doctoral dissertation, Bruno Bauer and Feuerbach. It then turns to political alienation, drawing on Marx's writings on the Jewish question and his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right. Finally it takes up alienation in civil society, looking at The German Ideology, Marx's 1844 study of classical political economy and the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844.

Wang's central claim is a sequence of reversals. Marx first used Hegel's idea that appearance is the alienation of essence. He then moved towards the religious critique of Feuerbach and the Young Hegelians, but rejected Bauer's view that religious alienation underlies political alienation. For Marx, Wang says, religious alienation arises from the split between the political state and civil society, in which people live a double life, as citizens in a heavenly state and as egoistic private individuals. Against Hegel, Marx then held that civil society determines the state. Political alienation is therefore only a 'copy', and the 'original' is the division within civil society, which must be examined through political economy. Wang reads Marx's analysis of money, the Jewish spirit and the worker's loss of his product to capital as marking this shift.

Wang concludes that Marx took over Hegel's and Feuerbach's concept but found it unable to analyse modern capitalist society concretely. Marx therefore turned to the economic level of civil society, where alienation acquires material content and a meaning distinct from earlier abstract notions such as externalisation, objectification and transfer. The article supports its case by citing Hyppolite, who calls alienation the basic concept and source of all Marxist thought. Read the original if you want a compact, text-based outline of how Marx moved from the Young Hegelian critique of religion to the economic theory of alienation.
quoteEn: Political alienation is derived from civil society; the divided state of civil society is the 'original' of the whole phenomenon of alienation.
quoteZh: 政治异化是由市民社会派生出来的，市民社会的分裂状态才是整个异化现象的“原本”。

t: Refuting the "amoralist" reading with Marx's philosophy
zh: 以马克思哲学批驳“非道德论”观点
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary of October 2020, Wang Kunpeng takes up a long-standing Western doubt about whether morality has any proper place in Marx's philosophy. The author argues that this "amoralist" view contradicts the core socialist values and undermines the legitimacy of building Marxist ethics and political philosophy in the primary stage of socialism and the new era. Wang's answer is that morality is one of the basic dimensions of Marx's philosophy.

The piece first sets out the position of Allen Wood and like-minded scholars, including Derek Allen, Sean Sayers, Robert Tucker and Richard Miller. It then offers two lines of criticism and closes with a reading of Marx's early and mature texts, from the doctoral dissertation on Epicurus to "On the Jewish Question" and the introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right.

Wang reports that Wood separates "moral goods" such as virtue and rights from "non-moral goods" such as self-realisation and community. On this reading Marx criticised capitalism by non-moral standards, and capitalist exploitation counts as just because it matches the relations of production. Wang first replies that Wood's treatment of modern right-based justice is metaphysical: ancient and modern justice are connected, and lawfulness cannot simply be non-moral. Wang's second and weightier reply is that Marx's critique of class morality as ideology does not make his thought value-neutral. Historical materialism, in Wang's account, is bound up with human freedom, dignity and emancipation, and with a justice and morality that go beyond class society.

Wang concludes that Marx's philosophy contained a morality beyond the bourgeois one from its beginnings. Later notions such as "human society", the "true community" and the "association of free individuals" give it a scientific basis. The author calls for drawing out the premises, ultimate aim and field of realisation of this moral appeal, for contemporary Marxist ethics and political philosophy and for the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese rebuttal of Wood's amoralist reading of Marx.
quoteEn: In this sense, we stress that the moral appeal is one of the basic dimensions of Marx's philosophy.
quoteZh: 在此意义上，我们强调，道德诉求是马克思哲学的基本维度之一。

glossary.explanation: Official characterisation of China's present historical stage, formalised in the 1980s, in which socialism is established but still underdeveloped.
Slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, referring to national rejuvenation and the people's aspiration for a better life.
A set of twenty-four characters in twelve values (such as prosperity, democracy, freedom, justice) promoted officially since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

t: Marx's concept of social being and its foundational significance
zh: 马克思的社会存在概念及其基础性意义
source: Social Sciences in China (Zhongguo shehui kexue), 2019 no. 7
paras: Zou Shipeng argues that "social being" is the pivotal concept of Marx's philosophy and social theory, yet has never been fully grasped in China or abroad. The article contends that it is the foundational concept of both the new materialism and the materialist conception of history, so that understanding it reveals their inner unity. Lukács, Western Marxism, Gould and Chinese research on Marx's ontology are all said to stop short of it.

The article has five sections. It first treats Marx's ontological revolution and his break with German classical philosophy and Feuerbach. It then traces the historical formation of social being, its value-theoretical (philosophical-anthropological) content, and its link to the thesis that the human essence is the "ensemble of social relations". It ends with the relation between social being and social consciousness, and with implications for scholarship.

Zou's core move is that Marx rejected the transcendent, substantial Western concept of being, so social being is a distinct term. It comprises material production, mental production, the production of population and of social relations, with material production as its "ontology". It is historically formed, moving from existing bourgeois society to a future human society, and it is practical, sensuous and relational. Labour, communication and sensuousness give it a value content that Zou says Lukács (who over-weights labour) and Habermas miss. Zou also argues that Marx's formulation turns the basic question of philosophy into social being and social consciousness. Consciousness becomes knowledge, ideology critique follows, and speculation gives way to a positive science. Zou argues that Comte, Spencer, Durkheim and Weber lack this concept.

Zou concludes that clarifying this core concept can bring together the practice-centred new materialism, the historical-materialist paradigm and dialectical materialism, serving socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zou also urges scholars to move beyond Western ontological frameworks, including Heidegger, and calls for social being to be a basic concept of modern social science and of Chinese philosophy and social science. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based argument on Marx's ontology, set against Lukács, Gould, Habermas and classical sociology.
quoteEn: Social being is the foundational concept of the new materialism and the materialist conception of history; to understand it is to understand the inner unity of Marx's new materialism and historical materialism.
quoteZh: 社会存在乃是新唯物主义与唯物史观的基础概念，理解了这一概念也就意味着理解了马克思的新唯物主义与唯物史观的内在统一。

glossary.explanation: Marx's term for the totality of human social life, formed through production and social relations. It is the basis that determines social consciousness.
Chinese scholars' label for the materialism of Marx's 1845 Theses on Feuerbach, centred on practice. It is usually set against old, contemplative materialism.
Marx and Engels' theory that material production and social relations shape political life and consciousness. It is often rendered as historical materialism.
The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

t: Rebuilding the normativity of the concept of reification through recognition theory
zh: 以承认理论重建物化概念的规范性
paras: This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, asks how Axel Honneth revives Lukács's concept of reification in contemporary social philosophy. The authors argue that Honneth gives the concept a normative reconstruction through recognition theory, which widens the study of reification but leaves it less critical of capitalism than Lukács.

The article begins with Western Marxist treatments of reification: Marcuse on false needs and the one-dimensional person, and Baudrillard on abundant objects that turn people into sign-beings defined by consumer goods. It then follows Honneth's reading in three steps: the shift from economic rationality to value rationality, the normative presupposition of an original practice of mutual recognition, and the move from a subject–object paradigm to an intersubjective one.

In the authors' account, Lukács located reification in the profit-maximising attitude of commodity exchange, where each party treats the other, and themselves, as calculable instruments. Honneth defines reification as the forgetting of recognition. Drawing on developmental psychology, Adorno and Stanley Cavell, he holds that recognition and empathic participation take priority over neutral cognition. He treats this original relation as the basis of three forms of recognition: love, rights and solidarity. Honneth's intersubjective paradigm, the authors say, lets people be seen as many-sided totalities rather than instruments.

The authors conclude that Honneth supplies what Lukács lacked: a social-ontological proof of original recognition and concrete mechanisms for restoring it. They add that Honneth stays within capitalist production and exchange and seeks only reform. In their judgement this makes his critique cautious and inferior to Lukács's, since it accepts the rationality of the capitalist mode of production. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language assessment of Honneth's reconstruction of reification from a Marxist standpoint.
quoteEn: Honneth holds that the essence of reification is the forgetting of recognition.
quoteZh: 霍耐特认为，物化的本质是对承认的遗忘。

t: A historical-materialist assessment of economic determinism
zh: 经济决定论的历史唯物主义评判
source: Social Sciences in China (Zhongguo shehui kexue), 2020 no. 7
paras: Historical materialism has long been read, by bourgeois scholars and by some self-described Marxists alike, as 'economic determinism'. Shen argues that this reading is a misreading rooted in mechanical, reductionist thinking, and that historical materialism is properly a historical dialectic in which the economy is decisive only 'in the last instance' (guī gēn dào dǐ). Economic determinism, in Shen's view, is therefore not the 'original sin' of historical materialism.

The article has four parts. It first traces economic determinism from the Second International (Kautsky, Bernstein, Lafargue) and the Russian 'Economists' to Russell, Popper, Collingwood and Habermas. It then reviews critiques by Marx, Engels and Lenin and by Western Marxists: Gramsci, Lukács, Korsch, Althusser, Kosík, Sartre and Poulantzas. The third part sets out the dialectical reading, and the fourth draws implications for contemporary China.

Shen contends that economic determinism takes 'the economy' as an absolute starting point to which politics, morality and religion can be reduced, so that society is cut into abstract factors linked only mechanically. Marx and Engels, by contrast, stressed production in their early polemics against idealism, a one-sidedness Engels later acknowledged as a limit of the period. They never made the economic factor the sole one. Shen faults the Western Marxist corrections too: the subjectivist line (Gramsci, Lukács) over-stressed human will, and Althusser's 'overdetermination' lost the distinction between principal and secondary contradictions. Shen's own position is that history is law-governed yet leaves room for contingency and agency, and that the economy is the 'central axis' but not the whole.

Shen concludes that the debate shows the need to apply Marxist method to new phenomena rather than discard Marxism. The article links this to China: the Party's post-reform shift to economic construction, a socialist mode of production with Chinese characteristics said to carry an innovation-driven mechanism, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. It presents Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as a concrete application of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a detailed Chinese survey of the economic-determinism debate from the Second International to Althusser, and of how it is used to support current Party theory.
quoteEn: Historical materialism is not a theory of multiple factors, because among the many factors it grasps the one that plays the foundational or decisive role, namely the economic factor.
quoteZh: 历史唯物主义不是多因素论，因为它在多种因素中抓住其中起基础性作用或言决定作用的因素即经济因素。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It stresses joint consultation, contribution and shared benefits among states.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
The official name for China's path since reform and opening up. It combines Party leadership and public ownership with a socialist market economy.
Engels' qualifier in his late letters: the economy is ultimately decisive in history, but not the only factor. Shen uses it against the charge of economic determinism.
Shen's term for the dialectical method he sees as inseparable from historical materialism. It stresses interaction among factors, practice and human agency.

t: Marx's anthropological philosophy and the fate of humanity as a theme of our age
zh: 马克思人类学哲学以人类命运为时代课题
paras: Liu Qionghao and Miao Qiming ask what theoretical foundation underlies the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. Their answer, in this short piece first published in the China Social Sciences Today in December 2019, is that the idea rests on what they call Marx's anthropological philosophy, a philosophy that understands the world from the standpoint of humanity's anthropological characteristics.

The authors first define Marx's anthropological philosophy and argue that Marxist philosophy can legitimately be read in this way. They then set out seven foundations of the community-with-a-shared-future idea in Marx's thought: an anthropological standpoint, an anthropological horizon, anthropological value principles, the height of world history, the "world-historical individual", the "true community", and the reconciliation of humans with nature and with each other.

The authors contend that Marx took on a double historical mission: human emancipation, and the survival and liberation of the proletariat. From this they derive a double problem field. After 1847, they say, Marx turned mainly to economic questions without abandoning anthropological ones. In their reading, anthropological philosophy is the overall outline of Marx's lifelong thought, and his economic philosophy is its application to pressing problems of his day. Each of the seven foundations is then matched to the community-with-a-shared-future idea, which they say embodies a standpoint beyond class, nation and state.

They conclude that the proposal for a community with a shared future for mankind can be seen as the anthropological task of world history in the present era. They present it as a product of combining Marx's thought with contemporary world-historical development. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese scholars ground this foreign-policy concept in Marx's early writings and in a reading of Marxism as anthropological philosophy.
quoteEn: Anthropological philosophy is the general outline of Marx's lifelong philosophical thought, and his economic philosophy is merely the theoretical expression of that anthropological philosophy applied to the pressing problems of his time.
quoteZh: 人类学哲学思想是马克思一生哲学思想的总纲，经济学哲学思想不过是他的人类学哲学思想针对当时的现实迫切问题的理论体现。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s. It calls for countries to cooperate on shared global problems and development.

Here it means a philosophy that understands the world from humanity's anthropological characteristics. The authors treat it as the basis of Marx's thought, in contrast to a reading centred on economics.
A term from Marx's The German Ideology for individuals whose existence is tied to world history rather than local limits. The authors read it as a demand for a worldwide, humanity-wide outlook.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Main experiences in building the discipline of Marxist theory
zh: 马克思主义理论学科建设的主要经验
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in October 2020, Mo Yueyun asks what experience has accumulated in building the discipline of Marxist theory in China since 1949. The author describes the discipline as one that studies the basic principles and scientific system of Marxism as a whole. Mo's thesis is that its development, from early groundwork through systematic construction to rapid growth, has produced a complete disciplinary system and raised the discipline's standing and influence.

The short commentary is organised around four "experiences". It first traces the step-by-step construction of the disciplinary system, from ideological-political courses to degree programmes. It then covers Party leadership, the scientific advancement of the discipline, and the discipline's "navigating" role for philosophy and the social sciences. Mo supports the account with the dates of curriculum reforms, the creation of degree programmes and central policy documents.
