On construction, Mo reports that Marxism-Leninism courses were adjusted three times before 1978 (the "53", "56" and "61" plans) and three more times after reform and opening up (the "85", "98" and "05" plans). Marxist theory became an independent first-level discipline in 2006, and by the end of 2018 it had 81 first-level doctoral programmes and 407 first-level master's programmes, which the author says is more than any other discipline. On leadership, Mo stresses that central bodies decided the course plans and that the Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project, launched in 2004, produced more than 150 textbooks. On method, Mo names three principles: studying Marxism as an integrated whole, taking the adapting of Marxism to Chinese conditions as the main line, and combining political orientation with scholarly rigour.

Mo concludes that the discipline has moved from "setting sail" to "navigating", guiding the whole of philosophy and the social sciences. The author says it has done so by embedding Marxist standpoint and method in every field, in line with Xi Jinping's 2016 call to uphold Marxism's guiding position. Read the original if you want a concise official-style account of the milestones, policy documents and statistics behind the institutional growth of Marxist theory as an academic discipline in China.
quoteEn: The gradual progression from course construction to discipline construction reflects both the concrete path of building the Marxist theory discipline and the process by which contemporary Chinese Marxist theory has gradually formed, developed and matured.
quoteZh: 从课程建设到学科建设的渐进式发展，既反映了马克思主义理论学科建设的具体路径，也反映了当代中国马克思主义理论逐步形成、发展和成熟的过程。

glossary.explanation: Compulsory courses on Marxism, Party theory and moral education taught in Chinese universities, usually abbreviated as sizheng ke. Their content has been revised several times since 1949.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义理论研究和建设工程
glossary.pinyin: Mǎkèsī zhǔyì lǐlùn yánjiū hé jiànshè gōngchéng
glossary.en: Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project
glossary.explanation: A programme launched by the Party Central Committee in 2004 to research Marxist theory and to compile standard textbooks for philosophy and the social sciences. It is commonly abbreviated as the "Ma Gongcheng".
The top tier of China's official academic classification, under which several second-level disciplines are grouped. Its status determines the right to award degrees and the allocation of resources.

keywords: Marxist Theory Research and Construction Project
adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: Rethinking the "Korsch problem"
zh: 重思“柯尔施问题”
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 30 April 2020
paras: Qi Tao asks what Karl Korsch's response to the "crisis of Marxism" in the 1920s can teach current debates in Chinese Marxist philosophy. Recent topics, such as the legitimacy of Marx's political philosophy and whether Capital is philosophy or economics, have in Qi's view widened research but also produced confusion. Qi argues that the situation resembles Korsch's: an anti-philosophical scientific positivism is spreading, and a return to Marxism's philosophical foundations and its wholeness has become urgent.

This short commentary has three parts: holding to Marxism as a whole, holding to the philosophical character of Marx's thought, and returning to Marxism's philosophical foundations. It draws on Korsch's Marxism and Philosophy, Hegel's Logic and Philosophy of Right, and the Japanese philosopher Hiromatsu Wataru's The Original Image of the Materialist Conception of History.

Qi reads the Second International's extraction of economic, political and cultural elements as partly reflecting capitalist society's own separation of spheres. Korsch conceded this, Qi notes, but insisted that separate elements never replace the whole, and Marx's return to Hegel's Logic in 1858 shows his commitment to a systematic science. Qi then criticises Hiromatsu for overstating Adam Smith's role and treating Hegel's Philosophy of Right as a branch philosophy rather than metaphysics, which in Qi's view strips Marx's critique of its philosophical base. For Qi, Marx's critique of Hegel's legal philosophy is also a critique of metaphysics, and it led to a double break with Hegel and Feuerbach.

Qi concludes that Marxist philosophy today must answer major questions of the age, which requires basic research and a grasp of Marx's philosophy as a whole, so that philosophy can grasp the essence of social reality and intervene in it. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language argument, framed through Korsch, against fragmenting or de-philosophising Marx, and a critical response to Hiromatsu's reading.
quoteEn: Today's study of Marxist philosophy calls for responses to the major questions of the age. It must attend to foundational research and a holistic grasp of Marx's philosophy, so that philosophy can understand the essential dimension of social reality and thus be able to intervene in it.
quoteZh: 今天马克思主义哲学的研究，呼唤着回应时代的重大问题，必须重视马克思哲学中的基础研究和整体把握，让哲学理解社会现实的本质维度，从而有能力介入现实。

t: Two uses of the concept of justice in Marx and Engels: with a critique of two misunderstandings by Allen Wood
zh: 马克思和恩格斯对正义概念的两种用法——兼评伍德的两个误解
paras: Duan Zhongqiao takes up the 1970s–80s Anglo-American debate on "Marx and justice" and Allen Wood's claim that Marx did not regard capitalism as unjust. Duan argues that Wood misreads the concept of justice in Marx and Engels because he does not see that they use it in two different ways. The article, published in Social Sciences in China in 2020, aims to correct two resulting misunderstandings that Duan says have also influenced Chinese scholars.

The article first sets out the two uses, which Duan reconstructs from Marx's and Engels's remarks on distribution under capitalism, since neither ever defines justice. It then examines Wood's three papers (1972, 1979 and his 2018 reply to Duan), showing how each use appears in Wood's own interpretation. It closes with a point-by-point reply to Wood's objections to Duan's earlier article, which is cited as "Bianxi", with close readings of passages from Marx and Engels.

Duan holds that justice means "giving each person their due" and is a moral evaluation. In the first, historical-materialist use, it belongs to the ideological superstructure and is determined by relations of production. For this reason Marx and Engels refused to ground criticism of capitalism or the proletarian cause in justice, and attacked Proudhon, Dühring and Lassalle. In the second use, different classes each call their own distributive demands "just". Wood's first error, in Duan's view, is to treat justice in the first use as a juridical concept that serves the dominant mode of production, when it is a moral concept that can also express the dominated class's demands. His second error is to claim that Marx never judged capitalism unjust. Duan cites Marx's Grundrisse remark about workers' "tremendous consciousness" and Engels's 1884 preface, which he reads as showing that they shared the workers' moral judgement. He also argues that Wood omitted a key part of Marx's reply to Adolph Wagner and confused two separate questions.

Duan concludes that Marx and Engels did regard capitalist exploitation as unjust, because surplus product belongs to the worker as its true producer. They said little on the point because earlier socialists had already made it and because they rested communism on historical necessity rather than morality. Duan stresses the need to clear up Wood's misunderstandings given his influence in China. Read the original if you follow the Marx-and-justice debate and want a detailed Chinese philosophical rebuttal of Wood, with close textual argument.
quoteEn: In my view, a deeper cause of our disagreement is that Wood has not grasped the two uses of the concept of justice (or fairness) in the relevant passages of Marx and Engels.
quoteZh: 在笔者看来，导致我们分歧的一个深层原因，是伍德没有弄清马克思和恩格斯在相关论述中对正义(或公平)概念的两种用法。

t: The socialist system with Chinese characteristics shows its strengths in practice
zh: 中国特色社会主义制度在实践中彰显优势
paras: Writing in Economic Daily in October 2020, Liang takes up the question of why the socialist system with Chinese characteristics is a good one. Taking Xi Jinping's remarks at the national commendation meeting for the fight against COVID-19 as a starting point, Liang argues that the system's distinctive strengths can be explained in theory and have also been verified and demonstrated in practice.

The commentary has three parts. It first traces how the system's strengths came out of practical exploration, from the founding of the People's Republic through reform and opening up to the period after the 18th Party Congress (2012). It then points to practical results, namely economic development, social stability, reform and the epidemic response. Finally it considers how to strengthen these advantages further.

Liang's core claim is that the strengths follow from persisting in the Party's centralised and unified leadership, a people-centred approach, and reform and innovation. As evidence the author cites rapid industrialisation, the rise to the world's second-largest economy and long-term social stability. The epidemic response, in the author's account, showed an exceptional capacity for organisation, mobilisation and coordination, and the ability to concentrate resources on major, difficult and urgent tasks.

Liang calls for upholding the system while improving it through reform, so that it becomes more mature and more fully defined. In a period of global upheaval and with uneven development at home, the author urges using the system's capacity to concentrate efforts on key technologies, removing deep institutional obstacles and energising market players. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official 2020 line on institutional confidence and the lessons drawn from the pandemic.
quoteEn: In judging whether a system works, is efficient and is truly useful, practice is the most persuasive test.
quoteZh: 评判一种制度是否行得通、有效率、真管用，实践最有说服力。

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义制度
glossary.explanation: The set of basic institutions of the Chinese state, including the Party's leadership, the people's congress system and the socialist market economy. Official texts present it as the institutional form of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

t: Attempt and bankruptcy: rethinking Heideggerian Marxism
zh: 尝试与破产：反思海德格尔式的马克思主义
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 28 May 2020
paras: Scholars of Western Marxism have long attended to Herbert Marcuse's "Hegelian Marxism" and "Freudian Marxism", but Deng argues that his early attempt to build a "Heideggerian Marxism" has received far less notice. This short commentary, published in 2020, asks two questions: why dialectics must be combined with historical materialism, and how a phenomenological materialist dialectic is possible. Deng's answer is that Marcuse showed such a combination to be possible and even necessary in method, but that his project ultimately failed because he lacked a grounding in concrete history.

The article reconstructs Marcuse's argument in three steps. It first traces his account of dialectics from Plato's logos through Hegel to Marx. It then turns to his case for joining phenomenology with materialist dialectics. It ends with the event that Deng treats as a turning point: the 1932 publication of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, after which Marcuse abandoned the Heidegger–Marx synthesis and returned to Marx from 1933.

On Deng's reading, Marcuse held that dialectics is first a feature of how things come to be, and only secondarily a logical tool. Hegel united these two aspects but reduced real movement to the movement of spirit, whereas Marx turned dialectics into a materialist one. Because only human beings are historical, Marcuse concluded that dialectical materialism must also be historical materialism. Human historical movement is both a process of becoming, which needs dialectics, and a repeated disclosure of the meaning of being, which needs phenomology. Marcuse therefore judged phenomenology and materialist dialectics compatible, despite Heidegger's remark that phenomenology and dialectics are as incompatible as fire and water, a remark Deng says was aimed at idealist dialectics. Deng adds that after reading the 1844 Manuscripts Marcuse saw that Marx already offered an account of alienation, and that Heidegger stayed at the existential level and lacked a "concrete philosophy".

Deng grants that the attempt is worth reflection, since phenomenological elements might help clarify the historical meaning of concepts such as "worker", "commodity" and "capitalist" in Marx's work. Yet the author sees a basic methodological limit in Marcuse's effort to redefine materialism and dialectics on a phenomenological base. In Deng's view, social reality can be grasped only from historical materialism, looking at historical, concrete and sensuous objects. Phenomenology and existentialism, Deng says, still only interpret the world, while the power to change it lies in countries and peoples that have inherited and developed Marxism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese assessment of Marcuse's early Heideggerian phase and its relation to the 1844 Manuscripts.
quoteEn: However, Marcuse's attempt to redefine materialism and dialectics on the basis of phenomenology shows his main methodological limitation.
quoteZh: 但是，马尔库塞尝试以现象学为基础重新界定唯物主义和辩证法，这表明了他在方法论上的主要局限。

t: The three dimensions of Marx's critique of egoism
zh: 马克思批判利己主义的三重维度
paras: Li and Liu ask how Marx criticised egoism and whether civil society's "private person" can become a human society. Their short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, argues that Marx's critique ran through his whole intellectual career and accompanied his critique of modern civil society. Egoism, in their account, is a product of private property and the social division of labour, and it peaks under capitalism.

The authors distinguish Marx's "superstitious egoism" of pre-capitalist society from the "enlightened egoism" of capitalism. They then organise the critique along three lines: philosophical, political-economic and scientific-socialist. The philosophical line takes in Stirner, Hegel, Bauer and Feuerbach; the economic line draws on the Critique of Political Economy and The German Ideology; the political line draws on the Paris Commune and the proletariat.

In the first dimension, Marx is said to treat Stirner's materialist egoism as one more abstraction replacing an older idealist one. Its end requires abolishing real egoistic life, following a historical-materialist "dialectic of labour". In the second, egoism appears as the economic form in which individuals serve one another only as means to their own ends, so that "common interest" becomes an exchange of selfish interests. Private property and the division of labour, the authors report, are the source of this split, and overcoming it depends on developing the productive forces and new relations of production. In the third, only the propertyless proletariat can generalise non-ownership and win human emancipation, by transforming itself and its circumstances through long struggle.

The authors conclude that egoism is the practical motive force of competition-based capitalist relations of production. It is also what the proletariat must sublate in order to carry out its mission. They present Marx's critique as a historical-materialist route to answering whether and how civil society becomes human society. Read the original if you want a compact overview of how Marx's critique of egoism links his early philosophy, his political economy and his political writings.
quoteEn: Marx's critique of egoism offers a solution, grounded in historical-materialist principles, to the scientific question of whether and how civil society and its "private persons" can develop into human society and its socialised humanity.
quoteZh: 马克思对利己主义的批判为科学地回答市民社会及其“私人”能否以及如何发展为人类社会及其社会的人类，提供了具有历史唯物主义原则的解决思路。

t: Dimensions of interpretation in the theoretical orientation of Capital
zh: 《资本论》理论定向的阐释维度
source: Social Sciences in China (Zhongguo shehui kexue), 2020 no. 8
paras: Bu Xiangji asks how Capital should be read if one accepts, as a premise most scholars can share, that the work is oriented by the materialist conception of history. The article argues that the economic and philosophical readings each have a limited field of vision. It holds that the decisive issues are how to understand the basic character of Marx's philosophy and its link to Capital, and how to treat the Hegelian moment in Marx's development and the Hegelian element in Capital.

The first part surveys interpretive routes: the economic one (the Second International, analytical Marxism, the mathematical Marxist school) and the philosophical ones (Lukács's Hegelianism, Althusser's dialectical materialism, the 'new Hegelian Marxism' of Arthur and others, and the domestic 'extension, application and proof' view of historical materialism). The second part traces how the materialist conception of history arose from Marx's early work and from Hegel. The third part examines Capital's structure, categories and method of value-form analysis.

Bu contends that historical materialism was not created independently of Capital and then applied to it. In Bu's account, the 1844 Manuscripts already set the research programme of Capital, and The German Ideology, with its 'spontaneous division of labour', answered the two preliminary tasks that programme required. Hegel's dialectic of labour is held to be the source of the practical-materialist paradigm and of the totality, difference and historicity of the materialist conception of history. Bu faults Lukács for misreading this Hegelian inheritance and Althusser for discarding it, and faults the new dialectic school for turning Capital into a copy of Hegel's Logic. Against these, Bu argues that Capital's order of categories reflects the objective logic of capitalist relations, that each category expresses definite social relations, and that mediation and retrospective tracing to origins mark a method that surpasses Hegel.

Bu concludes that Hegel's influence on Marx should be neither erased nor exaggerated. Only by seeing both the necessity of the Hegelian moment and Marx's break with speculative philosophy can an internal link between the materialist conception of history and Capital be rebuilt. Read the original if you work on Marx's relation to Hegel, Western Marxist readings of Capital, or the debate over the value-form and the 'new dialectic', and want a Chinese critical map of those schools.
quoteEn: The true materialist conception of history exists in Capital.
quoteZh: 真正的唯物史观就存在于《资本论》中。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese term for Marx's theory of history, also rendered historical materialism. Bu treats it as the theoretical orientation of Capital and as distinct from a general dialectical materialism.
The analysis of the forms taken by value (commodity, money, capital) in Capital. It is a central battleground between the 'new dialectic' school and Bu's reading.
A Western current, associated with Christopher Arthur, that reads Capital's structure through Hegel's Logic. Bu criticises it as an ontologising of Capital's logical form.
The general philosophical doctrine of Marxism, as systematised in the Soviet tradition. Bu discusses it chiefly through Althusser's reading of Capital.

t: Research on British Marxist class theory
zh: 英国马克思主义阶级理论研究
paras: Fang Jue's short review, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2020, asks how British Marxist theories of class have developed since the 1950s. The author argues that they have passed through three research paradigms: a historical one, a political-science one, and a return to political economy. Fang presents this sequence as showing a distinctive British understanding of historical materialism.

The article places British Marxism within Western Marxism's two broad tasks, critique of contemporary capitalism and the theory of revolution. It then takes each paradigm in turn. The first rests on the work of E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm after the rise of the British New Left in 1956. The second centres on Ralph Miliband and the Miliband–Poulantzas debate. The third covers the response to neoliberalism and the 2008 financial crisis, with Alex Callinicos as the main figure.

Fang reports that the historical paradigm treats class as a relation and as inseparable from class consciousness. Experience, custom and national cultural tradition are said to shape class formation alongside capitalist production. The political paradigm uses class analysis of power, the Capital concept of the "collective worker" and a theory of the state. Miliband holds that the state has relative autonomy but remains an instrument of the bourgeoisie. Against neoliberal talk of the "end of class", analytical Marxism and post-Marxism, the third paradigm restores the labour theory of value. In Fang's account, Callinicos's Deciphering Capital uses it to defend the working class as the revolutionary subject.

Fang concludes that the return to political economy is the main trend of twenty-first-century class theory. The reason given is that capital's drive for self-valorisation is unchanged, so Marx's class-struggle analysis of capitalism remains valid. British Marxists, in this reading, treat historical materialism as grounded in modern socialist movements, not as an abstract formula. Read the original if you want a compact overview of the main phases and figures of British Marxist class theory as presented in Chinese scholarship.
quoteEn: The historical materialism they understand is not an abstract formula but takes the modern socialist movement as its content and foundation.
quoteZh: 他们所理解的历史唯物主义并非抽象的公式，而是以现代的社会主义运动作为自己的内容和基础。

t: A multidimensional exploration of contemporary research on Marxist ethical thought
zh: 当代马克思主义伦理思想研究的立体化探索
paras: This is a book review, published in Guangming Daily on 20 October 2020. Li Jianhua reviews Heritage and Coordinates: Interviews on Marxist Ethical Thought (Zhongyang bianyi chubanshe, June 2020), edited by Li Yitian and Zhang Xiao. Li argues that the volume gives a "three-dimensional" view of present-day research on Marxist ethics, at a time when building an ethics of socialism with Chinese characteristics has become a prominent concern in Chinese scholarship.

The reviewer organises the assessment around three dimensions: how the content of Marxist ethical thought is presented, how the interviewees were chosen, and how the book handles historical inheritance and the new coordinates of the new era. The book rests on interviews with 13 well-known scholars in China and abroad, including British, American, Russian and Japanese researchers.

On content, Li says Marxist ethics was once understood narrowly as the ethics of Marx and Engels alone. Drawing on Li Yitian's preface, the review distinguishes three types: the ethical thought of Marx and Engels, that of their successors, and that of those who study them. On selection, Li stresses that the interview format gathers varied voices in one book and singles out four Chinese interviewees: Song Xiren, Song Huichang, Tang Kailin and Zhang Haishan, whose works he characterises briefly. On orientation, Li holds that an ethics of socialism with Chinese characteristics is a new form distinct from traditional Chinese, Soviet-model and Western ethics, and that its internal logic lies in the deep structure of Marxist ethics, centred on human existence, development and freedom.

Li concludes that the book rightly aims at a Marxist ethics that draws on historical lineage, faces the world, answers classical questions and is grounded in Chinese reality. Read the original if you want a short Chinese assessment of this interview collection and of how Chinese scholars frame Marxist ethics and the construction of an ethics of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
quoteEn: Marxist ethics takes human development and perfection as its theoretical starting point, and takes facing real life, and striving to discover, reflect on and solve people's new problems in real life, as its guiding purpose.
quoteZh: 马克思主义伦理学把人的发展完善作为理论出发点，把面向现实生活，致力于发现、思考和解决现实生活中人的新问题作为行动主旨

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, developed since the reform era. It is used as the framework for theoretical work in many fields, including ethics.

t: Assessing the practice philosophy of East European New Marxism
zh: 研判东欧新马克思主义实践哲学
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 24 September 2020
paras: Guan Siyue asks how Marx's concept of practice can be recovered after the Soviet textbook system, which in the author's view ignored human subjectivity and turned Marxism into a rigid dogma. The article, a short newspaper commentary, argues that East European New Marxism's treatment of practice philosophy offers one direction for understanding, interpreting and applying Marx's practice philosophy.

The piece has two parts. The first outlines the practice-philosophical foundations of East European New Marxism, covering the Yugoslav Praxis group, the Budapest School and the Polish and Czechoslovak figures Adam Schaff and Karel Kosik. The second sets out the theoretical framework of the Yugoslav Praxis school, which Guan regards as the most comprehensive and profound of these currents.

Guan contrasts East European New Marxism with Western Marxism. Both build on Marx's theory of alienation and practice to criticise existing capitalism and existing socialism, but Guan holds that Western Marxist critique left existing institutions untouched and became utopian. East European thinkers, by contrast, treated practice as a stance toward changing society, and their ideas of humane and democratic socialism supported reforms by Tito, Gomulka, Nagy and Dubcek. On the Praxis school, Guan reports that its thinkers read practice through the Greek praxis, as an ontological and anthropological concept and the basic mode of human being. From this they derived a view of alienation as ineradicable in principle and of revolution as a philosophical category, a way of human existence, not only a transfer of power.

Guan concludes that this tradition returns to Marx's basic problematic by placing the human being at the centre of practice. Read the original if you want a brief overview of the Praxis school's concepts of practice, alienation and revolution, and of how Chinese scholarship in 2020 situates East European New Marxism against Western Marxism.
quoteEn: For East European New Marxism, practice philosophy was not only a theoretical position but also a real attitude toward transforming society.
quoteZh: 实践哲学在东欧新马克思主义这里不仅是一种理论立场，更是一种变革社会的现实态度。

glossary.explanation: The tradition of Lukács, Korsch, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and others, which emphasised philosophy, culture and critique of capitalism.
A group of Yugoslav Marxist philosophers who published the journal Praxis and ran the Korčula Summer School from 1963 to 1973, stressing humanist readings of Marx.

t: The origins of the discourse of ecological Marxism
zh: 生态学马克思主义话语缘起
paras: Ecological Marxism is usually said to have been systematically outlined first by the Canadian scholar William Leiss. Liu Bingjing, in this short commentary from the Chinese Social Sciences Today (30 April 2020), argues that André Gorz, Herbert Marcuse and Guy Debord had already conveyed its standpoint independently in the early 1970s, and that together they brought its discourse into being.

The piece sets out four steps: ecological questions within Marx and Engels; the maturing of the discourse as ecological crisis grew; the reading of ecological crisis as capitalism's self-produced crisis; and the emergence of a new anti-capitalist force around ecological issues.

Liu holds that Marx and Engels treated ecological damage as a by-product of capitalism but not as the key to its critique, since pollution did not yet threaten human life. For them capitalism's fall came from its mode of production and economic crises. By the 1970s, Liu argues, globalised expansion, welfare-state policies and consumerism had eased supply–demand contradictions, delayed economic crisis and softened class conflict. Gorz, Marcuse and Debord therefore saw ecological crisis as the force able to shake capitalism. They treated it as a necessary result of irrational, profit-driven production, and ecological movements as a direct negation of capitalist rule. Liu reports their view that ecological threats revive a lost class consciousness and gather a spontaneous, popular subject.

Liu concludes that, though the three thinkers had no direct contact, they jointly linked ecology to capitalist crisis, emancipation and class subject. With Leiss and Ben Agger they opened the field of Western ecological Marxism. Read the original if you want a brief account of the early-1970s sources of ecological Marxism beyond Leiss.
quoteEn: Ecological crisis is by no means merely an environmental problem such as water pollution or nuclear radiation, but a real crisis that capitalism produces for itself, with the objective effect of resisting capitalist rule.
quoteZh: 生态危机绝不只是水污染、核辐射等环境问题，而是资本主义自我生产的现实危机，具有反抗资本主义统治的客观效果。

glossary.explanation: A current of Western Marxism that combines Marxist critique of capitalism with ecological concerns. Chinese scholars often date it to the 1970s.

t: Clarifying Marx's concept of the community
zh: 马克思共同体概念的澄明
paras: Since Xi Jinping put forward the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, Chinese scholars have studied Marx's thought on the community (gongtongti) widely. Zha notes that Marx used the term often but never defined it for its different periods and contexts. This short newspaper commentary (Chinese Social Sciences Today, 2020) reads Marx's texts to extract a concept and offers a definition, intended as scholarly support for building a community with a shared future for mankind.

The piece has three sections. It treats the community as a form of human social existence, distinct from society. It then asks how the community arises through association, and finally how it relates to freedom. It ends with a proposed definition.

Zha contrasts Tönnies and Bauman, who separate community from society but do not link communities to stages of social development. Marx, in Zha's reading, ties each community to a particular social formation, citing passages from The Holy Family and Capital. On association, Zha rejects equating the association (lianheti) with the community. Only an association of free individuals counts as a community, and association rests on modern productive forces and world intercourse. Exclusive associations built on private or group interest do not qualify. Zha also argues that the "free development of each" could become a war of all against all unless association matures into a community. Communities that serve bourgeois values and exclude the majority are, following Marx, "false communities". The true community is the outward expression of the value of freedom.

Zha defines Marx's community as a dynamic system. People join through social intercourse, in response to the needs of social development, to overcome individual disorder, guarantee individual freedom and pursue common free development. Zha holds that communities remain necessary even in a perfected society, and so calls building a community with a shared future for mankind a task for a thousand years. Read the original if you want a brief, text-based attempt to define Marx's community concept in connection with that Chinese political idea.
quoteEn: The community is a dynamic system in which people, adapting to the needs of social development, are linked through social intercourse, so as to overcome individual disorder, guarantee individual freedom and seek common free development.
quoteZh: 共同体是人适应社会发展的需要，通过社会交往而联结起来，以克服个体无序与保障个体自由来谋求共同自由发展的动态体系。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny for humanity
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13. It calls for countries to cooperate on shared interests and global challenges.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Marx's critique of fetishism and the semantics of capital
zh: 马克思拜物教批判与资本语义学
paras: Yao Manlin asks how Marx's critique of fetishism dismantles the mystery surrounding commodities, money and capital. The short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in 2020, argues that Marx's layered critique amounts to a method of demystification, which Yao calls a "semantics of capital".

Yao begins with the religious origin of the term fetishism and its adoption by de Brosses, Comte and Tylor. Yao notes that Marx drew on de Brosses as early as 1841 but turned to economic life, chiefly in Capital. The article then takes commodity, money and capital fetishism in turn.

For Yao, Marx locates the commodity's mystery in the commodity form itself, which conceals the social character of labour, and he resolves it through the dual character of labour. Money's mystery is traced back to its being a commodity serving as general equivalent. Capital's mystery, its capacity to self-expand, is explained by distinguishing labour from labour-power, the special commodity that produces surplus value outside the sphere of exchange. In each case a retrospective analysis returns from the illusion to simpler categories.

Yao concludes that commodity, money, capital, labour, labour-power, use-value, value and surplus value form the basic units of this semantics, which Yao links to a hermeneutics of demystification. Yao adds that exposing surplus value connects it to wage labour and the working class, and that human liberation depends on the awakening of that class's consciousness. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language overview of how Marx's fetishism critique is presented as a method in Capital.
quoteEn: Marx put forward a semantics of capital, whose basic units are commodity, money, capital, labour, labour-power, use-value, value, surplus value and so on.
quoteZh: 马克思提出了一种资本语义学，商品、货币、资本、劳动、劳动力、使用价值、价值、剩余价值，等等，构成了这一语义学的基本单位。

t: Habermas's "theory of communication" and its basis in the concept of labour
zh: 基于劳动概念的“交往理论”
paras: This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2020, asks how Jürgen Habermas's theory of communicative action relates to Marx's concept of labour. Zhou argues that Habermas builds on historical materialism and seeks to reconstruct it, but does not follow the logic of Marx's concept of labour. Instead, Habermas splits labour from communication.

The article first sets out how Habermas extends the concept of labour through language-mediated communication, drawing on the linguistic turn and universal pragmatics. It then covers his two-tier model of society, "system" and "lifeworld", and his idea of the colonisation of the lifeworld, which Zhou links to the first-generation Frankfurt School critique of instrumental reason. It closes with an assessment of the theory's merits and limits.

Zhou reports that Habermas applies Piaget's genetic epistemology to the lifeworld. He starts from individual learning in moral practice rather than from Marx's species-subject, and so gives moral-practical progress priority over productive forces. Zhou sees a residue of Kantian "nature–freedom" dualism in this scheme. In Zhou's reading, Marx already holds that labour contains two relations: the subject–object relation to nature and the intersubjective relation of communication. Habermas, by separating the two, fails to reunite them.

Zhou rejects the view that Marx and Habermas differ over whether material production or communication is fundamental. The real difference, in the article's account, is that Marx understands labour comprehensively and dialectically, while Habermas stresses its social side. Zhou nonetheless credits Habermas with trying to help historical materialism address modern crises. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese assessment of Habermas as a reconstructor of historical materialism.
quoteEn: In fact, the fundamental difference between Marx and Habermas lies not in this choice, but in the fact that Marx's understanding of labour is comprehensive and dialectical, whereas Habermas places more emphasis on the social side of labour.
quoteZh: 事实上，马克思和哈贝马斯的根本分歧不在于这种抉择，而在于马克思对劳动的理解是全面、辩证的，哈贝马斯则更侧重于劳动的社会性一面。

t: Three propositions in Marx's thought on education
zh: 马克思教育思想的三个命题
paras: This newspaper commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in September 2020, identifies three central propositions in Marx's thinking on education. Xia Wei and Cheng Lin argue that these concern the nature of education (its relation to class), its method (combination with productive labour) and its aim (the all-round development of the human being). They hold that the propositions once shaped Chinese educational theory and practice and remain relevant today.

The piece takes each proposition in turn. It links the class character of education to historical materialism, then discusses how combining education with productive labour has been misread, and finally places the aim of all-round development within Marx's idea of human emancipation. Mao Zedong's educational policy and the 1949 national education conference serve as Chinese reference points.

On class, the authors argue that education belongs to the superstructure and always serves a particular class, even when ruling classes present their own ideas as universal. They add that class character is not education's only or always its primary property, since education also rests on human nature and has national, historical and ethical dimensions; letting class obscure these, they warn, could have disastrous practical results. On method, they identify three deviations: reducing productive labour to heavy manual work, rejecting theory and book learning although Marx put intellectual education first, and over-emphasising employment while neglecting basic subjects.

Marx's aim, the authors conclude, was not vocational training or higher efficiency. Modern large-scale industry brings mental and manual labour closer, so that everyone could become both an educated person and a worker, narrowing or ending the gap between the two. Read the original if you want a short Chinese statement of how Marx's educational ideas are interpreted and how their past misapplication is assessed.
quoteEn: Using class character to obscure or even replace education's other characteristics does not accord with the purpose of Marx's educational thought, and may lead to disastrous consequences in practice.
quoteZh: 用阶级性遮蔽乃至取代教育的其他特性不符合马克思教育思想的宗旨，并可能在实践中导致灾难性的后果。

t: Three dimensions of Marx's critique of egoism
zh: 马克思批判利己主义的三重维度
paras: This short commentary asks how Marx criticised egoism and whether it can be overcome. Li and Liu argue that the critique ran through Marx's whole intellectual development, was bound up with his critique of modern civil society, and unfolded along philosophical, political-economic and scientific-socialist lines.

The authors begin with egoism as the outlook of the "private person" of civil society, a product of private property and the social division of labour. They note Marx's distinction between the "superstitious egoism" of pre-capitalist society and the "enlightened egoism" of capitalism. Three sections then take up Stirner and Hegel, economic egoism, and the political egoism of the propertied classes.

In the philosophical dimension, Li and Liu read Marx as holding that Stirner merely replaced an idealist abstraction with a materialist one. Marx's alternative is a dialectic of labour: people objectify private property and the "private person" through labour, and labour then sublates this objectification. In the political-economic dimension, common interest is described as an exchange of selfish interests that consolidates capitalist relations of production. Only new productive forces and relations can turn economic egoists into fully free people. In the third dimension, the proletariat, holding no private property, is the agent of change. The authors cite Marx on the Paris Commune and on workers transforming themselves while transforming circumstances.

The authors conclude that egoism, tied to individualism and liberalism, drives competitive capitalist production and must be sublated by the proletariat's self-transformation. They say Marx's critique offers a historical-materialist answer to whether and how civil society can develop into human society. Read the original if you want a compact outline of how Marx's treatment of egoism links Stirner, Hegel, political economy and the Paris Commune.
quoteEn: In the final analysis, the key to ending abstract egoism is the abolition of real egoistic life, and the logic it follows is the historical-materialist dialectic of labour.
quoteZh: 归根结底，抽象利己主义终结的关键是现实利己主义生活的消灭，其遵循的逻辑是历史唯物主义的劳动辩证法。

t: Marx's philosophical mode of expression
zh: 马克思的哲学表达方式
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 30 April 2020
paras: Against twentieth-century proclamations of the "end of philosophy", and a French-led current that places Marx beside Nietzsche and Freud as an anti-metaphysical thinker, Xia Ying asks whether "Marxist philosophy" is a legitimate concept at all. The article, a short commentary in a newspaper, argues that Marx did not abandon philosophy. In Xia's reading, he created a new way of expressing philosophy, and the materialist conception of history is itself a philosophical revolution.

The piece begins with the "Korsch question", raised in the early days of Western Marxism, over whether Marxism is a philosophy and in what sense. Xia treats its value as exposing a tension between theory and practice, not as a choice between philosophy and science. It then turns to Marx's mockery of philosophers in the Theses on Feuerbach and The German Ideology, to two features of the materialist conception of history, and to Marx's relation to Hegel, the Young Hegelians and German classical philosophy.

Xia argues that the "philosophy" Marx rejected around 1845 was speculative, Hegelian-style systems, in which constructing theory is equated with practice, together with the one-sided Young Hegelians. The materialist conception of history, by contrast, studies the material conditions of real individuals' activity, which gives it a "logical priority" of objectivity. Its sense of history also looks forward to an anticipated end of the division of labour and alienated labour, and to human freedom. For Xia, this makes it less a "scientific study" of the past than a "philosophical study" of the possibility of freedom.

Xia concludes that Marx's questions, the first causes of things and the conditions of human freedom, remain within the traditional problem field of philosophy. What changed is the mode of expression. Since Kant, German classical philosophy had added historical consciousness, and Marx pushed this furthest by attaching historical-period qualifiers to his statements and by making capitalist economic structures and material life philosophical problems. The difference between Marx and earlier Western philosophy is therefore a difference between new and old modes of philosophical expression, not between non-philosophy and philosophy. Read the original if you want a brief, clearly structured argument for treating the materialist conception of history as a philosophy, in response to the Korsch question and the "end of philosophy" thesis.
quoteEn: The difference between Marx's philosophy and all earlier Western philosophy is less a difference between non-philosophy and philosophy than one between a new mode of philosophical expression and the modes of expression of earlier ages.
quoteZh: 马克思的哲学与此前全部西方哲学的差异，与其说是非哲学与哲学的差异，不如说是新的哲学表达方式与旧有时代的哲学表达方式之间的差异。

t: An interpretation of Marx's idea of the community
zh: 马克思共同体思想诠释
paras: Hu Xiaojun's short commentary, first published in the China Social Sciences Today in September 2020, takes up Marx's concept of the community (gongtongti) as a foundational category in his account of human social development. Hu argues that the concept expresses the social essence of human beings and that common interest is the basic lens through which Marx explains how communities arise and change.

The article follows the historical sequence of three forms: the "natural community", the "illusory community" represented by the capitalist state, and the "true community" as an association of free individuals. Hu draws mainly on The German Ideology and on Marx's writings on money and capital.

Hu explains that natural communities such as clans, tribes, village communes, guilds and the Germanic "mark" rested on low productivity and personal dependence. With the division of labour and private property, the conflict between particular and common interests led to the state as an independent form that, in Hu's reading, serves only the ruling class and hides this behind constitutional equality. Under capitalism, money becomes capital and a "monetary community" that dominates individuals, so that relations between people are replaced by relations between things.

Hu concludes that Marx set the true community as a value goal, reachable only through highly developed productive forces, the abolition of private ownership, class oppression and the constraints of the division of labour. Production would then be planned according to need and aim at use value, so that all members could share in it. Read the original if you want a compact, textbook-style outline of Marx's three types of community and the link he draws between common interest, capital and communism.
quoteEn: However, the move from the \"illusory community\" to the \"true community\" is by no means a natural process.
quoteZh: 但是，从“虚幻共同体”走向“真正共同体”绝不是自然而然的过程

t: The contemporary significance of Dialectics of Nature
zh: 《自然辩证法》的当代意义
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 24 September 2020
paras: Writing for the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, Zhang Yunlong asks what Engels's Dialectics of Nature still offers a world facing what the article calls "great changes unseen in a century" and a disruptive wave of new technologies. The article argues that the classical work remains an intellectual guide for explaining a complex nature, understanding the current technological revolution and finding a way out of the ecological predicament. Zhang calls it the "living source" of contemporary philosophy of science and technology.

This is a short commentary in three parts. It first notes how the field grew from an unfinished manuscript, first published in full in 1925 and spread in China from the 1920s, into a broad discipline. Zhang worries that Western-paradigm philosophy of science and technology is eroding the classical territory and drifting from Engels's basic spirit. The sections then take up Engels's conception of nature, the relation of humans and nature in historical materialism, and technology in the service of humanity.

Zhang first presents Engels as achieving a "Copernican revolution" in the view of nature. Against a long metaphysical tradition of an unchanging world, including Newton's mechanical picture, Engels drew on cell theory, energy conservation and evolution to treat nature as in perpetual flux, without forcing dialectical laws onto it as Hegel did. Zhang then rejects the charge, made by Alfred Schmidt and Herbert Marcuse, that Engels was a mechanistic determinist who ignored human beings. In Zhang's reading, Engels insisted that humans act back on nature and change it, so that nature "is dissolved into history".

On technology, Zhang argues that Engels did not look back to pre-industrial life and located technological alienation in the capitalist mode of production and its logic of capital, not in machines themselves. Understanding the unity of humans and nature is not enough, in this account. What is needed is a complete transformation of the mode of production and the social system, ending with communism's planned and conscious social production. Zhang concludes that institutional change is the fundamental remedy for technological alienation, and that advancing the modernization of national governance in the new era follows Engels's theory. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese defence of Engels's natural dialectics against Western Marxist criticism and a view of how it is linked to ecology and technology policy.
quoteEn: In short, institutional change and social transformation are the fundamental way to eliminate technological alienation.
quoteZh: 质言之，制度变革与社会改造是消除技术异化的根本方式。

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.en: great changes unseen in a century
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping and in official discourse to describe a period of rapid shifts in the global order, technology and geopolitics.
An official goal, prominent since the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013), of improving the institutions and capacity through which the state is governed.

t: Lukács and the cultural theory of East European neo-Marxism
zh: 卢卡奇与东欧新马克思主义文化理论
paras: This short piece, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2020, asks how Georg Lukács shaped the cultural theory of post-war East European neo-Marxism. Liu argues that Lukács's reading of Marxism, set out in History and Class Consciousness (1923), not only founded Western Marxism but also fixed the basic theoretical position of the East European current, making him in a certain sense its founder.

The article covers Lukács's return to Hungary in 1945 until his death in 1971, when he trained Agnes Heller and other members of the Budapest School and exchanged views with East European theorists at venues such as the Korčula Summer School. Liu organises the influence under three dimensions: theoretical position, theoretical theme and theoretical aim. These are discussed through the critique of reification, a view of revolution centred on consciousness, and the pursuit of human value.

Liu argues that Lukács saw capitalism as a world dominated by commodity fetishism and technical rationality, in which reification also becomes an inner reified consciousness. Proletarian revolution therefore requires more than seizing power: it needs a revolution of consciousness to restore the whole human being. Liu shows these ideas recurring in Živadin Jovanović's account of reification in Yugoslavia, György Márkus's critique of modernity, Karel Kosík, Ivan Svitak, Heller, Mihailo Marković, Zygmunt Bauman and Gajo Petrović's successors in the Praxis group. All of them link culture to human essence and all-round human development.

Liu concludes that Lukács's dialogue with these thinkers gave their work depth and breadth, and left it with a distinctive East European stamp. The article holds that this body of theory is an important part of twentieth-century cultural theory and helps us understand the century's cultural anxiety, crisis and resistance. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese overview of Lukács's legacy among Praxis, Budapest School and Czech and Polish Marxists.
quoteEn: In a certain sense it can be said that Lukács was the founder of East European neo-Marxist cultural theory.
quoteZh: 在一定意义上可以说，卢卡奇是东欧新马克思主义文化理论的奠基人。

t: Four shifts to deepen the study of foreign Marxism
zh: 深化国外马克思主义研究的四个转换
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in April 2020, Wang Yuchen asks how Chinese research on foreign Marxism can be taken further. Wang notes that the field has already moved from the study of Western Marxism to the broader study of foreign Marxism, and cites Xi Jinping's call to examine new foreign findings analytically, neither rejecting nor copying them wholesale. The article's thesis is that the field will deepen only if it achieves four shifts.

The piece is a short programmatic essay organised around the four shifts. These are from introducing schools to studying basic theoretical problems, from a "materials-introduction" method to a "problematic" method, from objective introduction to a value stance serving the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, and from intellectual history to its combination with academic history. Each section diagnoses a weakness in current practice and says what should replace it.

Wang argues that introducing schools is only a first step. Understanding a thinker requires uncovering the "realistic logic" (the era, cultural tradition and questions addressed) and the "theoretical logic" (starting concepts, method and effects). Wang sees foreign Marxism as passing through a "cultural-studies turn" and a later "political-economy turn". The materials-introduction method reads texts in the abstract and weighs them against Marxist doctrine. In Wang's view it oversimplifies the history of Marxist philosophy and ignores the unity of theory and practice. The problematic method instead starts from that unity and from the idea of "one source, many streams". Wang also criticises research that merely introduces foreign theory, saying it produces arbitrary topic choice, academicism, obscure language, fragmentation and marginalisation. The author wants research to focus on schools that illuminate contemporary capitalism and modernity problems such as ecology, alienation, consumerism, gender, justice and distribution. On the fourth shift, Wang says intellectual history treats thinkers' ideas as homogeneous and neglects theoretical lineages, the interaction with Western social movements, and the history of interpretation and dissemination, including in China.

Wang concludes that Chinese study of foreign Marxism should be oriented to theory-building and modernization practice in China, and that it should combine the evolution of ideas with the study of their effects and reception. Only then, Wang holds, can the field grasp its inner logic and its influence on Marxist research and social development in both China and the West. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a Chinese scholar of foreign Marxism sees the field's methodological shortcomings and its intended role in Chinese theory-building.
quoteEn: The \"materials-introduction\" method is characterised by abstract readings of a thinker's texts, detached from the social-historical conditions and cultural tradition in which they arose, and then comparing them with specific Marxist propositions to judge their gains and losses.
quoteZh: “资料评介式”研究方法的特点是脱离理论家所处的社会历史条件和文化传统对其理论文本展开抽象的解读，然后与马克思主义的具体理论观点作对比，评价其理论得失。

glossary.explanation: The broad Chinese field covering Marxist and Marxism-related currents outside China. It is wider than Western Marxism in the narrow sense, which means Lukács, Gramsci, the Frankfurt School and similar figures.
Wang's phrase for the view that Marxist philosophy, rooted in Marx and Engels, develops into many forms and schools in different national conditions.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: The historical path of adapting the Marxist view of nationality to the Chinese context
zh: 马克思主义民族观中国化的历史进路
paras: This short piece, published in the China Social Sciences Today newspaper in August 2020, asks how the Marxist view of nationality (minzu) and national questions was formed and then Sinicised over the past century. Ning argues that the view was laid down by Marx and Engels, developed by Lenin, and carried forward by the Chinese Communist Party through revolution, construction, and reform and opening up. Understanding this path, the author says, is needed both for theoretical innovation and for ethnic work in the new era and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

The article is organised chronologically. It first summarises the foundations in Marx, Engels and Lenin. It then moves through the successive Party leaders: Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Xi Jinping. For each, Ning lists the leader's main positions, often with short quotations, on equality, unity, regional autonomy, development, cadres and Party leadership.

In Ning's account, Marx and Engels grounded nationality in labour and the development of productive forces, and treated national oppression as bound up with class struggle and capitalist private ownership. Lenin put national equality first, made national unity and the unity of the proletariat central, and developed legal protections and the principle of self-determination. Ning presents the Chinese stage as a continuous accumulation: Mao originated the Sinicisation, set out regional ethnic autonomy and wrote it into the 1954 Constitution; Deng named economic development, minority cadres and the Four Cardinal Principles as keys; Jiang stressed rule of law, opposition to separatism and Party leadership; Hu proposed theories of national development, harmony and interests.

Ning treats Xi Jinping's statements as the latest result of this process. They centre on a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation, Party leadership, equality and unity, and the continued upholding of regional ethnic autonomy as a basic political system. The author concludes that over nearly a hundred years the Marxist view of nationality has been adapted to local conditions and the times, and that new-era ethnic work should draw out the basic laws of this process and follow its path. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned overview of how Party theory on ethnic questions is presented as developing from Marx to Xi.
quoteEn: The Marxist view of nationality has undergone a process of Sinicisation, adapted to local conditions and keeping pace with the times, and has provided an important theoretical guide for China in resolving ethnic questions and handling ethnic relations.
quoteZh: 马克思主义民族观经历了因地制宜、与时俱进的“中国化”过程，为中国解决民族问题、处理民族关系提供了重要的理论指南。

glossary.explanation: The system under which areas where minority nationalities live in concentrated communities establish organs of self-government within the unitary state. It was written into the 1954 Constitution and is described as a basic political system of China.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of the Party, especially prominent since the 18th Party Congress (2012), referring to restoring China's national strength and international standing.

glossary.en: a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A concept emphasised under Xi Jinping that all ethnic groups in China belong to one national community. It is promoted as the guiding idea of ethnic work.
Principles set out by Deng Xiaoping in 1979: upholding the socialist path, the people's democratic dictatorship, the leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought.
The policy of economic reform and engagement with the outside world launched in China in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.

t: Engels and Marx's "turn to political economy"
zh: 恩格斯与马克思的“政治经济学转向”
paras: Liu Xiuping asks how Marx came to turn from law, philosophy and history to political economy, and argues that Engels played a key facilitating role. The piece, first published in Guangming Daily in July 2020 for the bicentenary of Engels's birth, presents this turn as decisive for Marx's critique of capital.

The article begins with Engels's early observation of capitalist society in Barmen, Bremen and Manchester. It then turns to Marx's own path through the Rheinische Zeitung, his Kreuznach studies and his reading of Hegel. It ends with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and their debts to Engels.

Liu argues that Engels's experience of the gulf between workers and the bourgeoisie moved him from humanitarian indignation to a structural view of economic facts as the basis of class conflict and political history. Marx, troubled by the question of how universal freedom is possible when private interest dominates the state, had concluded that civil society determines the political state but did not yet grasp its economic relations. Engels's Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy, which Marx read while preparing the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, supplied that insight and prompted the turn. Liu adds that after the ten days the two spent together in Paris in 1844, the Manuscripts reflected Engels's work in three ways: in their aim of criticising political economy, in their material on the condition of the workers, and in their historically grounded critique of private property.

Liu concludes that Engels's close attention to concrete social problems and empirical material helped answer Marx's troubling question and led Marx to pursue the problem of capital more deeply. Read the original if you want a short account of Engels's contribution to the formation of Marx's political economy.
quoteEn: Engels's careful observation of concrete social problems and his great regard for empirical material were noticed and absorbed by Marx in the period when his thought was taking shape.
quoteZh: 恩格斯对社会具体问题的细致观察、对实证材料的高度重视，为思想起源期的马克思所关注和吸收。
keywords: Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy
The Condition of the Working Class in England

t: Engels: examining environmental problems from the unity of nature and thought
zh: 恩格斯：从自然界和思维统一视角考察环境问题
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 19 May 2020
paras: Wang Wei, in a short newspaper commentary, asks what Engels offers for thinking about environmental problems. Wang contrasts Engels with Marx, who is said to have paid little attention to the environment, and argues that Engels's views contain more elements that can readily be linked to environmental questions.

The piece has three parts. The first treats Engels's idea of nature's revenge as an ecological warning. The second turns to his account of metaphysical and dialectical modes of thinking as a way of explaining the roots of environmental problems and their remedy. The third discusses his call for institutional change.

Wang reads Engels's remark that humans belong to nature "with flesh, blood and brain" as the basis for his warning against being too intoxicated by victories over nature. The examples Engels gives are deforestation in Mesopotamia and the Alps and the spread of the potato. Wang then argues that the metaphysical habit of isolating natural things and treating them as fixed turns nature into an inexhaustible stock of resources, whereas dialectical thinking sees nature as connected, changing and historical. Finally, Wang notes Engels's view that understanding natural laws is not enough. In this reading, a complete transformation of the production mode and the social system is needed, because capitalism cares only about profit, as in Engels's example of Spanish planters burning forests in Cuba.

Wang concludes that Engels's concept of nature carries rich ecological meaning, covering both the causes of environmental problems and ways to resolve them. Wang holds that it can give socialist ecological civilization construction in China a solid theoretical basis. Read the original if you want a brief, Chinese-language overview of how Engels's writings on nature are mobilised in support of ecological civilization.
quoteEn: By replacing metaphysical thinking with dialectical thinking, Engels made a positive contribution to reversing the opposition between humans and nature, abolishing habitual ideas that damage nature, and establishing an ecological outlook of unity and harmony between humans and nature.
quoteZh: 恩格斯以辩证思维取代形而上学思维，对于扭转人与自然之对立，进而取消破坏自然的习惯性观念，树立人与自然统一和谐的生态思想有着积极意义。

glossary.zh: 社会主义生态文明建设
glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy and theoretical framework, prominent since the early 2010s, that links environmental protection to socialist development and treats ecology as part of national construction.
A label Chinese scholars give to Engels's warning, in Dialectics of Nature, that every human victory over nature brings unforeseen adverse consequences.

t: Marx's transcendence of moral nihilism
zh: 马克思对道德虚无主义的超越
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 16 June 2020
paras: Zhang Shoukui takes up a long-running dispute among Anglo-American Marxists over the place of morality in Marx's thought, in which some scholars label Marx a "moral nihilist", that is, someone who denies the existence of morality. Zhang argues that this charge rests on misreadings. In the article's view, Marx rejected abstract moral speculation and preaching, but his thought carries strong value commitments and moral claims.

This short piece, first printed in a Chinese newspaper in 2020, reconstructs the three reasons Western scholars give for the charge and then answers each in turn. It closes by considering what the misreading costs, both for understanding Marx's central aims and for present-day Marxist scholarship.

The three reasons are, in Zhang's account: Marx's thoroughgoing atheism, which supposedly dissolves every suprasensible realm including moral values; the Communist Manifesto's statements that communists do not preach morality and break most radically with traditional ideas; and the historical-materialist view of morality as part of a secondary ideological superstructure, which allegedly leads to relativism. Zhang replies that Marx's critique of religion and politics always presupposed his own value commitment to the liberation of real individuals and their free and all-round development. The Manifesto's "morality" and "traditional ideas" refer, Zhang says, to ideologies defending bourgeois private property, not to all moral heritage. Western critics, Zhang contends, also confuse the relativity of morality with moral relativism, whereas Marx's practical dialectic holds relativity and absoluteness, historical continuity and consistency together.

Zhang concludes that human emancipation and each person's free and all-round development form Marx's highest aim, which is both constructive and critical or regulative, and which belongs to a "higher-order morality". On this basis Marx's critique of the capitalist mode of production is, in Zhang's reading, at once scientific analysis and moral critique, so he transcends both scientific positivism and moral nihilism. Zhang warns that denying this normative dimension reduces Marx to a purely empirical science, and calls on Marxist scholars to answer the misreading and to explain the normative foundations of Marx's thought. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language statement of how a Chinese scholar answers the Anglo-American "Marx and morality" debate.
quoteEn: Marx's critique of the capitalist mode of production and of the relations of production and exchange that correspond to it is both scientific analysis and moral critique.
quoteZh: 马克思对资本主义生产方式及其与之相适应的生产关系、交换关系的批判，既是科学分析，又是道德批判。

t: Contemporary lessons from the young Marx's turn to materialism
zh: 青年马克思唯物主义转变的时代启示
paras: Zhou Jiaxin asks how to understand the young Marx's shift from idealism to materialism, and what kind of materialism resulted. Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in 2020, the author argues that the shift was not a purely speculative event. In Zhou's account it came from Marx's deepening grasp of social reality, and later Marxist emphasis on it must be read against the intellectual context of the late nineteenth century.

The piece opens with the research background. Chinese scholars have spent over forty years on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and on the path from materialism to historical materialism. Zhou then reviews how Second International and early Soviet researchers, Western "Marxology", Alfred Schmidt and Louis Althusser treated the question, and how Chinese scholars answered with concepts such as "general materialism", "humanist materialism", "social materialism" and "legal-right materialism". Zhou next turns to Marx's relation to Feuerbach and to Engels's later retrospective writings.

Zhou makes two main moves. First, on the textual evidence, Marx used the word "materialism" in the Rheinische Zeitung, Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right and "On the Jewish Question" mainly in the sense of crude material interest. Sustained discussion appears only in The Holy Family and the Theses on Feuerbach (1845), while Engels, during his stay in England, had raised the question earlier. Marx moved from legal study and critique of religion to political history and the critique of political economy, and Feuerbach was only a temporary "fellow traveller". Second, Zhou explains why Engels later stressed Feuerbach, rejecting the Western "Marxology" myth of an Engels opposed to Marx. After 1848, vulgar or "economic" materialism spread. Zhou says Marx and Engels needed to clarify the materialist character of the method of Capital, which readers such as Kaufmann took to be idealist. Engels also needed to win over German workers, so criticising Feuerbach was a means and sublating bourgeois ideology the end.

Zhou concludes that rethinking this transition helps people grasp the formation of Marxism and the intellectual sources of its philosophical revolution. It also offers lessons for adapting Marxism to the needs of our times and making it popular. Zhou links this to Marx's spirit of exploration and self-criticism, and ends by saying that "seeking truth from facts and emancipating the mind" is the scientific understanding of materialism in twenty-first-century Marxist theory. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Chinese debates on the young Marx's materialism and on Engels's Feuerbach writings.
quoteEn: The critique of Feuerbach was only a means; the sublation of bourgeois ideology was the end.
quoteZh: 对费尔巴哈的批判只是手段，而对资产阶级意识形态的扬弃才是目的。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义时代化、大众化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the needs of our times and making it popular
glossary.literal: the epochal-isation and popularisation of Marxism
glossary.explanation: A formula in Chinese Party theory for making Marxism fit contemporary conditions and spreading it among the masses. Zhou also applies it to Marx and Engels's own efforts in the nineteenth century.

glossary.en: seeking truth from facts and emancipating the mind
glossary.explanation: Two slogans associated with Mao Zedong and, from 1978, with Deng Xiaoping's ideological line at the start of reform and opening up. They are used here as a summary of Marxist philosophical method.
The rendering of Hegel's Aufhebung: to negate something while preserving and transcending its valid content.

t: The ethical turn in Anglo-American Marxism
zh: 英美马克思主义的伦理学转向
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 30 July 2020
paras: Wei Tingxue's short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2020, asks how Anglo-American Marxism has come to treat ethics and where that turn leaves historical materialism. Wei argues that the debate has moved from a normative reading of Marxism, associated with G. A. Cohen, towards a reconstruction of Marxist ethics grounded in historical materialism and the defence of the proletariat. Wei concludes that any such reconstruction must keep historical materialism as its foundation.

The article begins with the "Marxism and justice" dispute that started in the 1970s and 1980s with Tucker, Wood and Husami, and which gradually became a discussion of Marxist ethics. It is organised in three parts: Cohen's shift from factual to normative interpretation, recent English-language work that defends the proletariat and builds a revolutionary ethics, and a closing reflection on the gap between theory and reality.

Wei reads Cohen as moving from a functionalist account of historical materialism, in which productive forces explain history, to doubt that any large group still fits the definition of the proletariat. Wei says this led him to justify socialism morally, through egalitarian arguments against Nozick and Rawls, and treats this as turning Marxism into a normative theory, at odds with Marx's critique of "principles" in The Holy Family and The German Ideology. In response, Wei reports, scholars such as Paul Blackledge and Brian Leiter argue that wage-labourers are growing in number, that inequality persists and that the conditions that create a proletariat remain. Blackledge, drawing on the early MacIntyre, holds that Marxist ethics arises from concrete struggle and centres on collective self-determination and solidarity. Jeff Noonan argues that community should be preferred to equality. Wei describes this as a methodological move from normative reasoning to a dialectical approach in which moral categories are historically specific.

Wei concludes that these scholars stress the distinctly Marxist character of their ethics, but that the tension between theory and reality remains open. In the context of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, Wei calls for flexibility and keeping pace with the times, while keeping historical materialism as the core. Wei criticises some contemporary French radical left thinkers for using Marxism's name for unrelated theories, and warns against dogmatism. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese overview of Cohen, Blackledge, Noonan and Leiter on Marxist ethics and of how Chinese scholars assess it.
quoteEn: Therefore, whether in research on Marxist political philosophy or in the reconstruction of Marxist ethics, the foundational status of historical materialism should be emphasised.
quoteZh: 因此，无论是对马克思主义政治哲学的研究还是对马克思主义伦理学的重构，都应当强调历史唯物主义的基础性地位。

glossary.explanation: The official idea that Marxism must be applied and developed in light of China's specific circumstances. The article uses it to justify flexibility alongside fidelity to historical materialism.

t: The scientific form of Marx's philosophy
zh: 马克思哲学的科学形式
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today, 30 April 2020, no. 1918
paras: Wang Shizhong asks how Marx's philosophy, read as a "philosophy of practice", can be given a scientific form. Writing in a newspaper piece of 2020, Wang starts from scholars since the early 2000s who have tried to reinterpret Marxist philosophy from a practice standpoint. Wang argues that a purely philosophical account of practice stays under the shadow of "theoretical philosophy", so practice needs a scientific theoretical form.

The piece has three parts: the demand for scientific form, the relation between nature, society and science, and a proposed structure for Marx's philosophy. It engages the Austrian economist Carl Menger, game theory in institutional economics, Hegel's dialectic and the Italian thinker Benedetto Croce.

Wang holds that natural science deals with the relation between humans and nature, while social science deals with relations between people, who are willed, purposive and free. The two cannot be collapsed into one, and the boundary between them still needs study. Wang finds that economics faces a paradox, since it loses legitimacy without history and loses scientific standing with it. The author therefore seeks the scientific form by a \"reverse forcing\" method, tracing the limits of each science in turn. Hegel's dialectic is one step, and Croce's dialectic of distincts is a further one, but Wang objects that Croce's structure is a closed circuit.

Wang proposes remodelling it as an open, \"double-layer, three-dimensional\" structure that separates theoretical from practical activity, divides practical activity into higher and lower levels, and leaves room for human freedom. Wang offers this as an interpretive framework for a workable scientific programme for Marx's philosophy. Read the original if you want a brief outline of one Chinese attempt to link practice philosophy with scientific method.
quoteEn: "Science" should be used as the theoretical form that represents "practice", rather than stopping at a "philosophical" interpretation of practice.
quoteZh: 要以“科学”作为表征“实践”的理论形式，而不能停留在关于实践的“哲学”阐释之中。

glossary.explanation: A reading of Marx's philosophy, prominent in Chinese scholarship since the early 2000s, that places practice rather than abstract theory or matter at its centre.
The author's method of finding a scientific form for Marx's philosophy by examining the internal limits of the natural and social sciences in turn.

t: The historical significance and contemporary value of Engels's "Outlines of a Critique of Political Economy"
st: In commemoration of the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth
zh: 《国民经济学批判大纲》的历史意义与当代价值——纪念恩格斯诞辰200周年
paras: Marked the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, this article asks why his early work, written in 1843–44, still matters. Yu Bin argues that the text, which Marx called a "brilliant sketch of a critique of economic categories", is a work of genius. In Yu's account it shaped Marx's lifelong study of political economy, and it remains more valuable than present-day Western economics, which Yu says still propounds positions the work already refuted.

The article first sets out the work's historical significance. It traces Marx's references to the text in the 1844 Manuscripts, in Capital and in later prefaces, and shows how it anticipated the Communist Manifesto. It then turns to contemporary value: Yu takes Engels's critiques of utility theory, of the self-interested economic agent, of the term "national wealth", of commerce, of private property and of competition and monopoly, and sets each against modern Western economics. Yu closes by noting Engels's own later verdict that the work was outdated and contained errors.

Yu's central claim is that Engels's critique of private property underpins the whole work. Engels held that competition presupposes and turns into monopoly, and that the contradictions of competition are those of private property itself. On this basis Yu argues that Western economics, which praises competition and opposes monopoly, is a "private economics" built on private ownership. It does so, Yu says, to protect the monopolies of developed countries and to hold back developing ones. Yu also reads Engels's remark that trade rests on force as describing the nature of the US trade war against China. Engels's analysis of competition in morality and crime is presented as evidence of how private property degrades people. Yu calls Marxist political economy a "compulsory course" and says it remains marginal in Chinese universities.

Yu concludes that the faults of the work were corrected by Marx in Capital, so its colours now look dimmer, but its value still exceeds that of Western economics. Yu argues that China must build its national strength and eventually renegotiate unequal treaties, and that economics with Chinese characteristics must rest on public ownership as the main body. Yu also holds that ethnic unity ultimately depends on abolishing private ownership, and presents the young Engels, who had no university education, as a model for Chinese students. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist's reading of Engels's early economic critique, applied to current debates on Western economics and the US–China trade conflict.
quoteEn: Today, the many false advertisements we have seen, are seeing and will go on seeing all prove the correctness and foresight of this critique by Engels.
quoteZh: 在今天，我们曾经、正在、还将看到的许多虚假广告，也无不证明着恩格斯的这个批判的正确性和前瞻性。
