Pang Yuehui argues that Eagleton uses historical and contemporary facts to strengthen the persuasiveness of Marxist discourse, and so confirms Marxism's scientific standing through empirical evidence. The author treats the link between theory and objective social reality as the mark of that scientific character.

The article is organised around four Marxist theses that Eagleton is said to corroborate: the nature of capital accumulation, human subjective freedom, the exploitative essence of wage labour, and the forms and paths of social change. A final section reflects critically on Eagleton's views.

On accumulation, Pang says Eagleton documents Victorian-era plunder in India, China, Brazil, Korea, Russia and parts of Africa, and late twentieth-century polarisation between rich and poor. Pang reads this as supporting Marx's line that capital comes into the world dripping with blood and dirt. On wage labour, Eagleton shows that tenants, hired labourers, white-collar staff, technical workers and service workers are all exploited, and that talk of a classless society hides this. On revolution, Eagleton notes that many Westerners who claim to oppose revolution approve of the American, Irish, Indian and Kenyan independence struggles. Pang also credits him with grounding Marx's view of human agency in the contrast between humans and animals.

Pang adds that Eagleton, as a Western Marxist, lacks a sense of social-historical totality. The author does not fully accept his six-stage periodisation of capitalism or his claim that class struggle is essentially a struggle over surplus value. Pang still values his search in Marxism for answers to alienation and commodification, and concludes that Marxism supplies a scientific epistemology and methodology for diagnosing social problems. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese commentary in 2018 read Eagleton's popular Marxism as evidence for Marxism's scientific character.
quoteEn: Stressing the unity of theory and practice, and opposing arbitrary abstraction and empty preaching, is precisely a salient expression of the scientific character of Marxism.
quoteZh: 注重理论联系实际，反对随意的抽象和空洞的说教，正是马克思主义科学性的显著体现

glossary.explanation: In Chinese scholarship, a label for Marxist thinkers in Western countries, often contrasted with the Marxism of the Soviet and Chinese traditions. Here it is used to mark the limits of Eagleton's perspective.

t: Marx's transcendence of Hegel's theory of "civil society"
zh: 马克思对黑格尔“市民社会”理论的超越
paras: Dong Xiaobo asks how Marx moved beyond Hegel's concept of "civil society" and argues that the move was central to Marx's break with idealism. The piece, a short commentary first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2018, holds that Marx turned a concept Hegel had subordinated to the state into a core category of historical materialism.

The article first sets out Hegel's account in the Elements of the Philosophy of Right, then turns to Marx's treatments in the Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and The German Ideology. It closes by considering what Marx's reversal of the relation between civil society and the state means for the relation between economic base and superstructure.

Dong credits Hegel with first separating civil society from the political state and with criticising contract theorists who conflated the two. Civil society, for Hegel, is the sphere of needs and material interests, an "external state". Dong argues that Hegel remained incomplete, since he still placed the judiciary and police inside civil society. He also treated the political state as the determining element and as the embodiment of "good", against civil society as a "battlefield of private interest", and so could not escape historical idealism. For Marx, by contrast, civil society is the sum of material relations and the real birthplace and stage of all history, to be anatomised through political economy. Dong stresses that Marx therefore reversed the relation: civil society determines the state, and a given civil society produces the political state that formally expresses it.

Dong concludes that by turning a concept Hegel had demoted into a pillar of historical materialism, Marx achieved a historical transcendence of Hegel. The author describes this as a fundamental shift from idealism to materialism and from democratism to communism. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language outline of how Marx's concept of civil society is distinguished from Hegel's, with the key passages cited.
quoteEn: It is not the state that determines civil society, but civil society that determines the state.
quoteZh: 不是国家决定市民社会，而是市民社会决定国家。

t: Research on Western Marxism in China since reform and opening up
zh: 中国改革开放以来的西方马克思主义研究
paras: Guo Yanjun asks how the translation and study of Western Marxism in China has developed since reform and opening up, and what it has meant for Chinese Marxist philosophy. The article, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in March 2018, argues that Western Marxism research and the renewal of Chinese Marxist philosophy advanced in step with each other.

Guo begins with the early 1960s, when Western Marxist thinkers were first translated but treated only as targets of criticism within the Soviet textbook system. The article then follows the period after the 1978 debate on the criterion of truth, through the 1990s, to the fields that became popular in the early twenty-first century, such as ecological Marxism, feminist Marxism and post-Marxism.

In Guo's account, two needs drove the research: the demand for knowledge of Western thought under the policy of reform and opening up, and the need to rethink the Soviet textbook system. Chinese scholars, Guo says, approached Western Marxism critically and used it as a resource, always anchored in close reading of Marx's texts. That reading brought out neglected themes, including Marx's ideas on world history and Eastern societies, and produced many interpretive approaches. Guo warns against fragmented, novelty-seeking studies of individual thinkers, and against applying Western Marxist critiques of modern society directly to China.

Guo concludes that Chinese Marxist philosophy should rest on accurate reading of Marx's texts while addressing China's real problems. Western Marxism research should stay in dialogue with the study of Marx. It should also be placed in a world-historical perspective, in which Guo sees socialism with Chinese characteristics as having world-historical significance for a new type of human civilization. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic account of how Western Marxism studies were institutionalised after 1978.
quoteEn: The translation and study of Western Marxism in China and the innovation of contemporary Chinese Marxist philosophy have unfolded in step with each other.
quoteZh: 西方马克思主义在中国的译介、研究与当代中国马克思主义哲学的创新是同步展开的。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current system and path, associated with the reform era from Deng Xiaoping onwards.
The policy of domestic economic reform and opening to the outside world adopted at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in December 1978.

glossary.en: the debate on the criterion of truth
glossary.literal: great discussion on the criterion of truth
glossary.explanation: A 1978 ideological debate asserting that practice is the sole criterion of truth, which loosened dogmatic constraints and prepared the ground for reform.

t: The value of the "marginal notes" in the Feuerbach chapter of The German Ideology for the materialist conception of history
zh: 《德意志意识形态》费尔巴哈章“边注”的唯物史观价值
paras: An Qinian takes up a neglected feature of the Feuerbach chapter of The German Ideology: the 33 short marginal notes that Marx and Engels wrote beside the text. The article, published in Philosophical Trends in 2018, argues that although most notes are only a few characters long, they carry a great deal of information about how the materialist conception of history took shape and what its core is.

The article first examines where the notes sit. They appear only in passages that Marx and Engels extracted from their earlier critique of Bruno Bauer and Max Stirner and moved into the chapter, and never in the paragraphs written specially for it. An sorts the 33 notes into five types: notes on Feuerbach (9), Marx's summaries of his own intellectual path and core ideas (4), criticisms of German idealist historical views (9), summaries of materialist ideas in the text (9), and two technical remarks by Engels. An concentrates on the first and second types.

An argues that the Feuerbach notes show the decisive difference from Feuerbach. Marx and Engels held that Feuerbach saw nature and humanity as objects of contemplation and did not grasp that nature and social ties are products of labour practice. In this reading, the notes show that the fundamental divide between materialist and idealist views of history is whether practice explains ideas or ideas explain practice. For note 2 ("philosophical and real liberation; man; the Unique; the individual; geological, hydrological conditions; the human body; needs and labour"), An reads the first half as a compressed account of Marx's path from Feuerbach's "man", through Stirner's "Unique One", to the "individual" as the ensemble of social relations. The second half, in An's view, states the core of the theory: natural conditions and bodily organisation compel labour, and needs generated by labour drive history.

An concludes that the Feuerbach-plus-Hegel account of Marx's development is untenable, because the decisive step was criticising Feuerbach's lack of a labour-based view of history. An also rejects the view that practical materialism negates the dialectical-materialist concept of matter, saying Marx and Engels stayed materialists on nature. Further, An holds that "social being determines social consciousness" does not fully capture Marx's starting point, which is labour and production, and that the theory has an inherent value dimension, as a path to human liberation. Read the original if you study the formation of historical materialism, Marx's relation to Feuerbach and Stirner, or the editorial history of The German Ideology.
quoteEn: Labour practice is the cornerstone of historical materialism as a whole.
quoteZh: 劳动实践活动是整个唯物史观的基石。

t: Marxism as the powerful ideological weapon that opened reform and opening up
zh: 马克思主义是开启改革开放的强大思想武器
paras: Writing for Qiushi in 2018, on the 40th anniversary of reform and opening up, Liu Jianhui asks what ideological force launched the policy. The article's answer is that Marxism was the 'powerful ideological weapon' that opened it, and that four decades of practice demonstrate the truth and strength of Marxism.

This is a short commentary in three parts. It traces how a 'great awakening' within the Party gave rise to reform and opening up, then discusses why emancipating the mind must both uphold and develop Marxism, and finally assesses what the reform period shows about Marxism's power.

Liu argues that the awakening began with the Party's renewed understanding of Marxist fundamentals. It started with the debate on practice as the sole criterion of truth, which broke the constraint of the 'two whatevers' and prepared the ground for the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). Drawing on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, Liu holds that emancipating the mind meant freeing thought from dogmatic readings of Marxism. This produced Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

Liu concludes that applying Marxist principles to China's circumstances carried the nation from 'standing up' to 'becoming prosperous' and, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to 'becoming strong'. The article calls for continued emancipation of the mind and seeking truth from facts in order to realise the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of the Party's 2018 official narrative linking Marxism to the origins of reform and opening up.
quoteEn: Reform and opening up was the product of a great awakening, and that awakening came first of all from the Party's ideological awakening to the basic principles of Marxism.
quoteZh: 改革开放是伟大觉醒的产物，伟大觉醒催生了改革开放，而这次伟大觉醒首先来自我们党对马克思主义基本原理的思想觉醒。

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in December 1978.

glossary.literal: emancipate the mind, seek truth from facts
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the late 1970s associated with Deng Xiaoping. It calls for breaking with dogma and basing policy on practical conditions.
A 1977 formula holding that whatever policy decisions Mao made and whatever instructions he gave must be upheld. Reformers criticised it as dogmatic.
A Party guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao that stresses comprehensive, coordinated and sustainable development.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing.
A theory associated with Jiang Zemin. It holds that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the people.

t: Stages and research orientations of twentieth-century French Marxist historiography
zh: 20世纪法国马克思主义史学的阶段特征及研究取向
paras: Liang Minsu asks how French Marxist historiography developed across the twentieth century and what its research orientations were. The article, a newspaper piece from 2018, argues that this current was an important force within a diverse French historical field. It divides the current into three stages, which in Liang's view reflect both its own theoretical tradition and the evolution of the Western "new history".

The article names figures such as Jean Jaurès, Albert Mathiez, Georges Lefebvre, Pierre Vilar, Albert Soboul and Michel Vovelle. It concentrates on Soboul and Vovelle and on the history of the French Revolution, seen through social history and the history of mentalities. It is organised chronologically: the interwar years to the 1940s, the 1950s to 1970s, and the period from the 1980s onwards.

In Liang's account, the first stage was marked by strong ideological and political-practical commitments. The founding of the French Communist Party in 1920 and figures such as Maurice Thorez supported early Marxist history-writing, and a first generation of professional Marxist historians appeared, including Jean Bruhat and Marc Piolot. The second stage established a social-history outlook. Soboul used Marxist theory together with the new history and other social sciences, and he led the Robespierre society and the study of the Revolution "from below", a path Liang traces back to Lefebvre. Institutions such as the Marxist research centre (1959) and the Maurice Thorez Institute (1966) supported this work. In the third stage, Vovelle called for historical materialism to be combined with the history of mentalities, partly to escape the dualism of economic and political explanation. Working alongside Annales-linked historians, he made collective psychology and mental states a new direction in Revolution studies.

Liang concludes that, under globalisation, French Marxist historians have joined their work to non-Marxist currents and adjusted their orientation, while staying close to social change and contemporary concerns. Dialogue and debate with other schools, the author says, have deepened understanding of the complexity of French history and of French Marxist historiography itself. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language periodisation of French Marxist historians and their links to the Annales school, and you are content with a short overview rather than detailed historiographical argument.
quoteEn: The currents of thought and the scholarly course of French Marxist historiography can be roughly divided into three stages.
quoteZh: 法国马克思主义史学思潮及学术历程大致可划分为三个阶段

glossary.explanation: The Marxist theory that material and economic conditions shape social and historical development. The article presents it as the guiding idea Vovelle and others promoted from the 1980s.

t: New developments in the Marxist thought on world history
zh: 马克思主义世界历史思想的新发展
paras: This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in August 2018, asks how the Marxist thought on world history has developed in the Chinese context. Lu Pinyue argues that Xi Jinping's idea of a community with a shared future for mankind enriches and develops that thought.

Lu starts from Marx and Engels's mid-nineteenth-century claim that national histories are turning into world history. The article then traces how the Communist Party has combined this thought with Chinese conditions, citing Mao Zedong on the Chinese revolution as part of the world revolution and Deng Xiaoping on absorbing the achievements of human civilisation. It ends with Xi's formulation after the 18th Party Congress (2012).

Lu's central argument is that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind inherits the value stance of the Marxist thought on world history: it is people-centred, seeks win-win cooperation and sets itself against power politics and zero-sum thinking. In Lu's account it also analyses new features of the present world. Lu holds that the root of current problems is not economic globalisation but three unresolved contradictions: weak global growth momentum, lagging global economic governance and unbalanced global development. Lu cites the Belt and Road Initiative as an example of building new international relations through equal consultation.

Lu concludes that the idea joins the theoretical logic of the Marxist thought on world history with the practical logic of human development, and will promote common development and lasting peace. Read the original if you want a brief, official-press statement of how Chinese commentators place Xi Jinping's idea of a shared-future community within the Marxist tradition.
quoteEn: However, the root of the world's major problems is not economic globalisation, but the failure to resolve three prominent contradictions: insufficient global growth momentum, lagging global economic governance and global developmental imbalance.
quoteZh: 然而，造成世界重大问题的根源不是经济全球化，而是全球增长动能不足、全球经济治理滞后、全球发展失衡三大突出矛盾没有得到有效解决。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as the aim of China's foreign policy. It stresses interdependence, cooperation and shared development among states.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 to build infrastructure, trade and investment links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.
The Marxist view that capitalist production and exchange break down national isolation and turn separate national histories into a single world history.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Deepening our understanding of the laws of human social development
zh: 深化对人类社会发展规律的认识
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in 2018, Zhao Jiaxiang takes up Xi Jinping's call to deepen, with a fresh perspective, understanding of the laws of Communist Party governance, of socialist construction and of human social development. Zhao treats the last of these as the foundation of the other two. The article's thesis is that social laws are products of human practice, yet objective, historical, long-term and cyclical, and not directly given as reality. The author argues that "acting in accordance with objective laws" is therefore a complex process, not a matter of copying a ready-made pattern.

The piece is organised under six headings. It begins with the origin of social laws in conscious human activity, then treats in turn their objectivity, historicity, long-term and cyclical character, and their "non-immediate reality". It closes with the correct meaning of "acting in accordance with objective laws". Zhao relies mainly on texts by Marx, Engels, Lenin and Mao Zedong, including Anti-Dühring, Capital, Engels's letters to Conrad Schmidt and Friedrich Albert Lange, and Lenin's Imperialism and Materialism and Empirio-Criticism.

Zhao first explains why laws that people make through purposeful action can still be objective. Individual aims cancel or interfere with each other and produce a resultant nobody intended. Action is also constrained by objective conditions and by the actors' own abilities, and it cannot skip the stages of history. The author then argues that laws are historical. Each social formation has its own laws, and capitalist laws are not eternal, which the author takes as a refutation of the "end of history" thesis. Even general laws differ in form across formations and across stages, and Zhao says the laws of present-day capitalism and of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era need fresh study. Drawing on Engels's letter to Schmidt, Zhao holds that a law is only an approximation, a tendency or an average. It is not immediate reality, partly because many laws operate at once and partly because concepts never coincide with the reality they abstract from. Zhao reads Karl Popper's rejection of social laws as a mechanical misunderstanding of this point.

Zhao concludes that the law that socialism will replace capitalism is still in the process of formation, since capitalism has not yet been superseded worldwide. The author criticises the common reading of "respecting objective laws" as obeying a pre-existing, fixed reality. Laws emerge only gradually, appear in changing forms, and are grasped only approximately. Understanding must therefore be revised continually, and fixed understandings risk violating the laws they claim to follow. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist philosopher in 2018 grounds the theory of social laws in classical texts and applies it to debates on capitalism, socialism and policy-making.
quoteEn: In fact, a law is only a tendency; it is neither a fiction nor a direct, ready-made reality.
quoteZh: 其实，规律只是一种趋势，它既不是虚构的，也不是直接的、既成的现实。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up. The article says it has entered a new era since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and that its laws take new forms.
A Marxist term for a historically specific type of society, defined by its economic base and superstructure, such as slave, feudal or capitalist society. Zhao argues each has its own laws.

glossary.literal: theory of the end of history
glossary.explanation: The view, associated with Francis Fukuyama, that liberal capitalism is the final stage of social development. Zhao says Marx and Engels had already refuted such ideas.

t: Mao Zedong and the original aspiration and mission
zh: 毛泽东与初心使命
paras: Published in Study Times in July 2018, this short commentary asks how Mao Zedong upheld and practised what Chinese Communists now call the original aspiration and mission of the Party. Yang Mingwei argues that seeking happiness for the people and rejuvenation for the nation was Mao's lifelong pursuit. In Yang's account, Mao's own definition of Communists as people who seek no private gain is the Party's founding purpose, and Mao lived it fully.

The article looks at Mao through three aspects. The first is his lifelong faith in Marxism and his unchanged original aspiration. The second is his wholehearted service to the people, illustrated by a series of quotations on the nature of the Communist Party. The third is his long-term strategic planning for the country and nation, with examples from the 1960s and from his final weeks in 1976.

On faith, Yang recounts Mao's 1936 remarks to Edgar Snow that the Communist Manifesto and two other works established his Marxist belief in 1920 and that it never wavered. Yang adds that Mao reread the Manifesto whenever he faced major problems, urged senior cadres to study Marx and Lenin to tell true Marxism-Leninism from false, and kept three editions of the Manifesto by his bed until death. On service, Yang says Mao's statements show the Party's fundamental nature, that history is made by the people, and that its aims coincide with theirs. Yang presents Mao's lines "stand on the side of the great majority of working people" and "take the people as teacher" as the root cause of the Party's victories in revolution, construction and reform. On foresight, Yang cites Mao's 1963 warning that China would be vulnerable to attack unless it ended its economic and technological backwardness, his stress on basic industry in the Third Five-Year Plan, and his reaction to the 1976 Tangshan earthquake.

Yang concludes that Mao died regretting that the country was not yet fully unified, the people not yet prosperous and the nation not yet rejuvenated, but believing these goals would be achieved. Yang also treats Mao's definition of the Party as a basic starting point for understanding the "new era", "new thought" and "new journey" and says the Party's purpose and character must never change. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party historian in 2018 presented Mao as a model of the Party's original aspiration and mission, with the quotations chosen for that purpose.
quoteEn: Serving the people wholeheartedly, rather than half-heartedly or with two-thirds of one's heart and mind, is the direction and attitude of work that Mao Zedong set out for the Communist Party of China.
quoteZh: 全心全意为人民服务，而不是半心半意或者三分之二的心三分之二的意为人民服务，这就是毛泽东为中国共产党指明的工作方向和工作态度。

glossary.explanation: A phrase popularised after the 19th Party Congress (2017) for the Party's founding purpose of seeking the people's happiness and the nation's rejuvenation. It was the theme of a Party-wide education campaign launched in 2019.
The term for the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012), officially proclaimed at the 19th Party Congress (2017). It is attached to Xi Jinping Thought.

t: Mao Zedong and the establishment of China's great-power status
zh: 毛泽东与中国大国地位的确立
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2013, Wang Yiqiu takes up the claim that one of Mao Zedong's historical achievements was to restore China's international standing as a great power. The article argues that three wars, led by the Communist Party under Mao, were decisive: the War of Resistance against Japan, the War of Liberation and the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea.

The article is organised chronologically in three sections, one for each war. Each section asks what that war contributed to China's status: a return to the ranks of the great powers after 1945, real sovereign independence after 1949, and international influence and a voice in world affairs after the Korean War. Wang draws on Mao's Selected Works, official Party histories, Peng Dehuai's memoir and remarks by John King Fairbank, Arnold Toynbee, Khrushchev and the US commander Mark Clark.

On the anti-Japanese war, Wang credits the Kuomintang government's frontal battlefields but says it would be unfair to give all the credit to Chiang Kai-shek. In Wang's account the Communist Party's line of protracted war and the united front made it the "mainstay" of national resistance, and the article cites figures for enemy troops killed and Party-led casualties. On the civil war, Wang describes the United States as supporting Chiang, curbing China's sovereignty through treaties and a large military presence, so that China was nominally a great power but not yet fully independent. Victory in 1949 is presented as ending imperialist domination. On Korea, Wang defines a modern great power as one with sovereignty plus global influence. The war, the article argues, secured a security buffer for the industrial Northeast, strengthened national confidence, forced Washington and Moscow to reassess China, and was followed by the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and border settlements with neighbours.

Wang concludes that Mao's name is tied to China's great-power status and that national prestige, military strength, international standing and national backbone are the legacy of the Mao era. The article holds that today's China can advance from a great power to a true world power (shijie qiangguo) only on the foundation Mao laid. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxism institute scholar, writing in 2013, framed Mao's legacy through foreign policy and war, together with the sources it relies on.
quoteEn: National prestige and military might, international reputation and national backbone are the precious wealth created and accumulated in the Mao era; only on the foundation Mao laid can China today advance from a major world power towards the goal of a true world power.
quoteZh: 国威和军威、国际声望和民族骨气，这是毛泽东时代创造和积累的宝贵财富，今日中国只有在毛泽东奠定的这一基础上，才能由一个世界大国向一个真正的世界强国目标挺进。

glossary.en: the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea
glossary.explanation: The official Chinese name for China's involvement in the Korean War (1950–53), in which Chinese People's Volunteers fought US-led UN forces.
The official Chinese term for the 1946–49 civil war between the Communist Party and the Kuomintang, which ended with the founding of the People's Republic.

glossary.en: the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence
glossary.explanation: Principles of mutual respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence, promoted by China in the 1950s.

t: Mao Zedong and economic construction in New China
zh: 毛泽东与新中国的经济建设
paras: This piece, published in Guangming Daily in January 2014, assesses Mao Zedong's role in China's socialist economic construction between 1949 and 1976. Sha Jiansun argues that Mao was the chief organiser and leader of that effort, that his correct theory of economic construction forms an important part of Mao Zedong Thought, and that the achievements of the period laid a solid material foundation for China's later development.

The article has three parts. The first sets out Mao's view of industrial or economic revolution as China's "second revolution". The second examines how Mao and his comrades fixed the direction, path and policies of economic development. The third reviews the historic progress made in these years, using statistics on output, growth and living standards.

In the second part, which carries most of the argument, Sha reports that Mao held the socialist road to be the only real way to solve China's industrialization, since the capitalist road would be slower and more painful. Sha traces the goal of the "four modernizations" and the "two-step" strategy: first an independent and fairly complete industrial and national economic system, then modernization of agriculture, industry, national defence and science and technology. Sha also lists Mao's policy principles: agriculture as the foundation and industry as the leading factor, "walking on two legs", overall balance and planned, proportionate development alongside commodity production and the law of value, "overall planning with due consideration for all", and self-reliance combined with trade and learning from abroad. Sha notes that Mao's timetable estimates were over-optimistic for a time and were revised after the Great Leap Forward.

Sha acknowledges two serious setbacks, during the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, but concludes that the overall achievements were great. The article cites an average annual growth of 8.2 per cent in gross agricultural and industrial output from 1952 to 1978, rises in China's world ranking for major products, and rising consumption and schooling. It closes with the American historian Maurice Meisner's favourable comparison of the Mao era with other late industrializers. Read the original if you want a concise Party-historian's defence of Mao-era economic policy, with its key quotations and figures, as presented in a Chinese official newspaper.
quoteEn: From the founding of New China to 1976, Mao Zedong was the main organiser and leader of socialist economic construction.
quoteZh: 在新中国成立以后到1976年这一段时期，毛泽东是社会主义经济建设的主要组织者和领导者。

glossary.explanation: A development strategy attributed to Mao and Zhou Enlai, formally stated in 1964: first build an independent industrial system, then achieve comprehensive modernization.
The goal of modernizing agriculture, industry, national defence, and science and technology, set out in the 1960s and later taken up in the reform era.
The 1958 campaign for rapid industrial and agricultural growth, which the article treats as a serious setback.
A Maoist formula for pursuing several measures simultaneously, such as central and local, large and small, modern and indigenous production.

glossary.en: overall planning with due consideration for all
glossary.literal: overall planning and taking all sides into account
glossary.explanation: A policy principle of Mao's for balancing relations among the state, collectives and individuals, and between sectors and regions.

t: Key assessments of Mao Zedong by the Party since reform and opening up
zh: 改革开放以来我们党对毛泽东同志的几个重要评价
paras: Writing in the People's Daily in December 2013, around the 120th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, Chen Jin sets out the fixed assessments of Mao that the Communist Party has gradually formed since reform and opening up. The article argues that understanding these formulations helps readers grasp Mao's specific character as a historic figure and the scale of his achievements.

The piece is organised around five official judgements, each with its own heading and each traced to a leader and a date: Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, plus the 1981 Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party since the Founding of the People's Republic of China (the Historical Resolution) and the 17th and 18th Party Congresses. They cover Mao's role in the revolution, his standing as Marxist, strategist and theorist, his place in the leadership, his status as patriot and national hero, and his relation to socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Chen's central reasoning is that the Party's verdicts form a coherent, progressively deepened line. Without Mao's leadership, the author says, the Chinese people would have groped in the dark far longer, because history chose Mao through a complex process of comparison after earlier leaders' failures and the Zunyi Meeting. Chen sets out the three rising formulas on his leadership role, and lists Mao's strategic decisions as evidence for the title of strategist, a term the Party applies to him alone among the older leaders. The author reads the Party's three great undertakings (the new-democratic revolution, the socialist revolution and construction, and reform and opening up) as continuous: the first two supplied the fundamental political premise, institutional foundation, experience, theoretical preparation and material base for the third.

Chen concludes that Mao's late-life errors do not cancel the judgement that his achievements come first, and that a Marxist party cannot demand flawlessness of great figures. Correctly assessing Mao, in this account, is a matter to be upheld permanently, and the best commemoration is confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, to realise the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. Read the original if you want a compact, authoritative-style catalogue of the Party's official formulas on Mao and their dates of origin.
quoteEn: Of these three great undertakings, the first two were accomplished under Comrade Mao Zedong's leadership, and the last was carried out after his death.
quoteZh: 这3件大事，前两件都是在毛泽东同志领导下完成的，后一件是在他逝世后进行的。

glossary.explanation: The 1981 Party resolution adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 11th Central Committee, assessing Party history since 1949 and Mao Zedong's role, affirming his achievements as primary and criticising his late-life errors.
The official name for the Party's path, theory and system since reform and opening up, which it presents as Marxism applied to China's conditions.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.

glossary.literal: great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing after the 'century of humiliation'.
A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, equated with national rejuvenation.

t: The original basic programme of Marxist philosophy
st: A systematic new reading of the Theses on Feuerbach
zh: 马克思主义哲学原生态基本纲领
zhSub: 《关于费尔巴哈的提纲》系统化新解
paras: Lu Pinyue offers a systematic re-reading of Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, which he treats as containing the basic 'ideological code' of Marxist philosophy. Drawing on Xi Jinping's description of the text as the founding statement of dialectical materialism, Lu argues that its eleven theses form a coherent programme built on two key concepts, practice and social relations. The article also takes a firm stand in a long-running dispute over how the tenth thesis should be read.

Lu divides the Theses into three parts. Theses 1–3 make practice the foundation for ontology, epistemology and the conception of history. Theses 4–7 set out the core of historical materialism through the idea that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations. Theses 8–11 state the three essential features of the 'new materialism'. Lu also reads the Theses against Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and against Engels's edited version of the text.

In Lu's account, old materialism and idealism both misread the subject–object relation, treating it as intuition or theory rather than practice. Grounding it in practice yields a thoroughgoing and dialectical materialism, in which humans are part of nature. It also yields an epistemology in which truth is tested in practice, and a view of history as the practice of the masses. Lu rejects what he calls 'practice ontology', arguing that a material world outside practice is the precondition of practice. The Theses, he says, also amount to Marx's self-criticism of the Manuscripts' abstract 'species essence'. On the tenth thesis, Lu argues that 'civil society' means the abstract aggregate of isolated individuals found in Enlightenment thought and Hegel, not capitalist society as such. He holds that 'human society' means actual society, past and present, not a future communist society. In his view the latter reading would make Marx a utopian and bring back Feuerbach's abstract human nature.

Lu concludes that the Theses identify three unified features of the new materialism. It dispels mysticism through seeking truth from facts, it takes real human society built on social relations as its standpoint, and it takes changing the world as its task. Lu links the first feature to Deng Xiaoping's remark that seeking truth from facts is the essence of Marxism. Lu suggests that the setbacks of socialism are partly tied to utopian readings of Marx. Read the original if you want a detailed, Xi Jinping-endorsed reading of the Theses on Feuerbach, especially the argument over 'civil society' and 'human society' in the tenth thesis.
quoteEn: In the tenth thesis, 'human society' and 'social humanity' (changed by Engels to 'socialised humanity'), the standpoint of the new materialism, are real human society organised by real social relations, including all real societies from ancient times to the present.
quoteZh: 《提纲》第十条中作为新唯物主义立脚点的“人类社会”和“社会的人类”（ 恩格斯改为“社会化的人类”） 就是由现实的社会关系组织起来的现实人类社会，包括从古到今的所有的现实社会。

glossary.explanation: A principle of Chinese Marxism associated with Mao Zedong and later Deng Xiaoping, who called it the essence of Marxism. It stresses starting from actual conditions and testing ideas in practice.

t: Why has China always managed to turn the tide in every major crisis?
st: An excerpt from "People's Open Class"
zh: 中国为何每次逢大危机总能力挽狂澜？
source: Utopia website (Wuyouzhixiang), reprinted from Liaowang Institute, 23 July 2017
paras: This is a book excerpt (from People's Open Class, Zhejiang People's Publishing House), republished via Liaowang Institute and Utopia, in which Wen Tiejun asks why China has survived each major crisis since the late Qing. Wen argues that, once ideological labels are set aside, the record shows a repeated pattern: foreign capital brought in to industrialise a capital-starved country produced debt or dependence and then crisis, and the crisis was absorbed by shifting its costs onto the countryside.

The article moves from the present back to the Qing and forward again. It first describes the shift from a century of shortage to what Wen calls three overlapping surpluses (industrial, financial, commercial). It then covers the Self-Strengthening Movement, the Republic's 'golden decade' and silver crisis, the early People's Republic, the Soviet-aided period, the Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution and the Fourth and Fifth Five-Year Plans. It closes by comparing China's costs with the debt crises of the United States and the eurozone.

Wen's central claim is that policy orientation follows material conditions rather than ideology. When capital is extremely scarce, any government must be pro-capital, and revolutionary ideology and collectivised labour served as a substitute for capital (labour replacing capital). Wen counts four waves of foreign capital since 1950, each followed by two crises (for example the Soviet investment, then the crises of 1960 and 1968). Wen holds that crises were softened where the cost could be passed to the 'three rural issues': about 40 million educated youths sent to the countryside were absorbed because collectives existed, and land distribution, the author says, kept 85 per cent of the population relatively insulated from monetary turmoil. Wen also reads the Republic's fall as a financial collapse and the Korean War as bringing military industry and Soviet alignment.

Wen concludes that China's path was workable and that the country, now in surplus, can invest in people's livelihood and sustainable development. Western-style institutions are presented as costly, debt-driven superstructures that even the West can no longer sustain, citing US and eurozone debt. Wen urges younger Chinese to free themselves from ideologised vocabularies, whether anti-Mao or Westward-looking. Read the original if you want a heterodox political-economy narrative of a century of Chinese crises, which draws on the author's own rural experience and defends the revolutionary era on grounds of capital accumulation.
quoteEn: The soft landings were possible fundamentally because the peasants supported Mao Zedong, since he gave them land to till.
quoteZh: 能软着陆，根本上就是因为农民支持毛泽东，因为他使耕者有其田。

glossary.explanation: A common shorthand for agriculture, the countryside and peasants, used in Chinese policy discourse as a single problem area.
The 1958–1960 mass campaign for rapid industrialisation and collectivisation, followed by severe economic crisis.
The late Qing effort, from the 1860s, to adopt Western military and industrial technology.

t: The foundation of state coercive capacity is violence, but it is also a necessary condition for reducing violence
st: A preface to Fan Peng's study of China's public security and police system
zh: 国家强制能力的基础是暴力，但它也是减少暴力的必要条件
source: Wuyouzhixiang website, reposted from 'Yali Reading' (14 November 2017)
paras: This text, dated July 2017 and circulated in November 2017 via the website Wuyouzhixiang, reads as a preface to Fan Peng's book on China's public security and police system. Wang Shaoguang argues that state coercive capacity, which rests on violence or the threat of it, is also a necessary condition for reducing violence. Wang adds that China has built this capacity in its own way, not along the single Western path.

Wang begins with the shift in political science from regime form and democratization towards state capacity. In this shift, Wang says, coercive capacity has been neglected. The text then surveys the history of violence through archaeology, ancient texts, Engels's Anti-Dühring, and work by Fukuyama, Morris, Scheidel and Pinker. It turns to Fan's evidence on policing, crime and homicide in China, and ends with Fan's closing questions about what coercive capacity really means.

Wang holds that violence is a core, universal feature of human society and should be analysed, not only condemned. Citing Engels, Arendt and others, Wang says violence has also driven institutional change, growth and, historically, lower inequality. Its greatest positive effect, Wang argues, is reducing violence: war produced ever larger political units and states, and states that monopolise legitimate force lower war deaths and homicide rates. Wang then takes up Pinker's reading of China as a 'police state'. Drawing on Fan's data, Wang says China has a very low police-to-population ratio, tight police funding and a homicide rate of 0.7 per 100,000 in 2015, among the lowest in the world. Wang concludes that capacity should be measured by outputs, not inputs.

Wang presents Fan's central point as follows. China's state monopolises legitimate force but uses it sparingly and seeks to reduce and defuse conflict, in imperial, revolutionary, Maoist and reform-era periods alike. In Wang's account, this reflects a governing tradition from Confucius's 'nurture, teach, govern' to the Communist Party's people-centred approach of 'embedding security in service', which mobilises officials, Party organisations and society. Wang rejects the assumption of one universal, linear path to a modern state. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's argument that Western accounts of coercion misread China, or if you want the crime and homicide data Wang draws on from Fan's book.
quoteEn: The foundation of state coercive capacity is violence, but it is also a necessary condition for reducing violence.
quoteZh: 国家强制能力的基础是暴力，但它也是减少暴力的必要条件。

t: China can neither plunder abroad nor pursue internal colonisation: it must build more equal urban–rural relations
st: Zhao Yuezhi on "the countryside as method"
zh: 中国既不能对外掠夺，也不能走内部殖民的路径，必须构建更平等的城乡关系
source: Originally on Wuyouzhixiang website, reprinted from "Critical Communication Studies", 6 July 2017
paras: This is a written report, reviewed by the speaker, of a keynote lecture given by Zhao Yuezhi on 2 July 2017 at the international summer school "From the Global to the Village: The Countryside as Method" in Jinyun County, Zhejiang. Zhao presents "the countryside as method" as a theoretical and practical approach, and argues that China, having been shaped by revolution and reform, faces a crossroads for its villages. In Zhao's view, China can neither plunder other countries nor colonise its own countryside, and so must build more equal urban–rural relations.

The talk has five parts: the origins of the question, drawing on three photographs Zhao took; the theoretical resources; the meanings of the approach; its methodology and practice; and its historical and present significance. Zhao draws on Mitsuhiro Mizoguchi's China as Method, Chen Kuan-Hsing's Asia as Method, C. Wright Mills's The Sociological Imagination, and the work of Canadian Indigenous scholars. The photographs show a Jinyun woman arriving at Shanghai station, an elderly villager doing outsourced plastics work for export, and a lone woman harvesting rice in a hollowed-out village.

Zhao's central move is to treat colonial relations as seen by Indigenous theorists as important as capital–labour relations, and to extend this to the urban–rural relationship. She argues that the industrialisation and urban growth of China rest on unequal exchange with, and great sacrifices by, peasants, and that Anglo-American capitalism rose on the massacre of Indigenous peoples and plunder of colonies. She distinguishes five senses of the term: rural as the counterpart of the city; the village as an intimate community; the organic diversity of villages; the subjectivity of the "three rural issues" (peasants, villages, agriculture); and the countryside as a "source of hope" for humanity amid capitalist crisis. She joins this to a framework of political economy of intercultural communication, ethnography and action research.

Zhao names three paths for the countryside: a populist rural reconstruction that avoids socialism, the view that 21st-century enclosure is inevitable (in which she sees neoliberals and Trotskyists converging), or reorganisation along socialist lines. She claims the approach explains the Chinese revolution, speaks to a world where peasants remain a major force, and carries anti-imperialist and anti-capitalist values, without implying a return to the pre-modern or to nativism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of a socialist, critical-communication scholar's case for rural China as a theoretical standpoint and for a 2017 debate on rural reconstruction.
quoteEn: Today, China can neither plunder abroad nor take the path of internal colonisation; it must build more equal urban–rural relations.
quoteZh: 今天，中国既不能对外掠夺，也不能走内部殖民的路径，必须构建更平等的城乡关系。

glossary.explanation: An approach modelled on Mizoguchi's "China as method" and Chen Kuan-Hsing's "Asia as method". It uses the countryside and urban–rural relations as a standpoint for analysing development, history and global capitalism.
A common Chinese shorthand for the problems of agriculture, villages and peasants, used in policy and scholarly debate.

Movements and projects to rebuild rural society, historically associated with 1930s figures such as Liang Shuming and revived since the 2000s. Zhao criticises some versions as populist and silent on socialism.

t: Theories of "civilization" and China in the twenty-first century
zh: “文明”论与21世纪中国
source: Wenyi lilun yu piping (Literary Theory and Criticism), 2017 no. 5; reposted by Wuyou zhi xiang from the WeChat account "Wenyi pipping", 3 October 2017
paras: He Guimei asks how Chinese intellectuals have come to interpret "China" through the category of "civilization", and argues that since the turn of the century this has become a paradigm-level shift. It has displaced earlier accounts based on the nation-state, modernization theory and the Cold War opposition of socialism and capitalism. The article, first drafted in 2013 and finalised in 2017, seeks to trace the lineage of these civilization theories and to set out their limits. It then proposes a "plural" conception of civilization as a critical alternative.

The article has four parts. It begins with the rise of the "civilization-state" idea, from Samuel Huntington's clash of civilizations through Martin Jacques and Zhang Weiwei to Gan Yang's "civilization-state" and "unifying the three traditions", and Pan Wei's "China model". It then examines how Fei Xiaotong, Wang Mingming and Wang Hui define civilization and its relation to China. A third part considers the "traditional culture fever" and the contemporary meaning of tradition. The last part reconstructs the intellectual history of the concept of civilization.

He's central move is to distinguish three conceptions: a universalist one tied to Enlightenment ideas of progress and colonial hierarchy, a nationalist one that equates civilization with culture, and a plural one that treats civilizations as overlapping social-cultural-economic totalities. The author argues that many Chinese civilization-state accounts leave "civilization" vaguely defined, often equating it with Confucian tradition, and risk sliding into nation-statism. In this reading, tradition revival is often absorbed into nationalist ideology, which the author sees as a by-product of globalization. Drawing on Marcel Mauss, Fernand Braudel and Wang Mingming's work, He holds that the plural view breaks with both Eurocentrism and nationalism, and that Huntington's version lost the critical edge of 1960s civilizational history.

He concludes that a plural conception clarifies three relations: it moves beyond both statism and cosmopolitan universalism, beyond both revivalism and modern-centrism, and it treats civilization as a non-uniform totality rather than a homogeneous whole. Traditional China can then serve as a critical resource, without implying a return to empire, for rebuilding China's subjectivity in the global order and escaping "China-centrism". Read the original if you want a detailed intellectual map of Chinese "civilization" discourse, with extensive references to Gan Yang, Wang Hui and Wang Mingming, and a critique of its nationalist tendencies.
quoteEn: Between discontinuous historical forms and discursive formations, without the link of "politicization", the continuity of a civilization does not arise naturally.
quoteZh: 在断裂性的诸历史形态与话语构成之间，缺少“政治化”这个环节，文明的连续性并不会自然生成。

glossary.explanation: A designation for China as a state defined by a long-continuous civilization rather than a Western-style nation-state. Gan Yang advanced it in 2003, and Martin Jacques and Zhang Weiwei developed related formulations.

Gan Yang's formula that the traditions of Confucius, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping form one continuous Chinese historical civilization. The phrase borrows from the Gongyang school of classical Confucian thought.
A term for the distinctive path of the People's Republic's development. Pan Wei and colleagues theorised it around 2009 as resting on the continuity of Chinese civilization.

The widespread revival of interest in classical culture, Confucianism and national studies in China since the early 2000s. The author treats it as a social, political and economic phenomenon, not only a cultural one.

t: A critical assessment of several current erroneous views
zh: 对当前几种错误观点的评析
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscript in 2015, Mei Rongzheng takes up the ideological sphere since the 18th Party Congress (2012). Mei describes its overall trend as positive and healthy, but argues that struggle remains complex and that certain erroneous views interfering with the guiding ideology of the Party and state deserve particular attention. The article assesses four such views and argues that each distorts or displaces Marxism.

The piece is a polemical commentary in four numbered sections. It deals with the claim that Soviet Marxism is not Marxism; three Confucianism-related positions (using Confucianism against, to transform, or to dilute Marxism); the use of Western Marxism to reinterpret Marxism; and the allegation that Marxists are mislabelled as non-Marxists and vice versa. It closes by citing Deng Xiaoping's 1983 call for Marxists to speak out.

On the first view, Mei says it recasts the Soviet model as 'Soviet Marxism' and so implies that the Party was never truly Marxist. Mei distinguishes universal from non-universal elements of the Soviet experience and holds that the universal ones were the origin of the Four Cardinal Principles. On Confucianism, Mei rejects the label of historical nihilism for the New Culture Movement's critique of Confucian doctrine. Citing Li Dazhao and Liu Danian, Mei describes Confucianism as the product of a small-peasant economy, lacking materialism and economics, and argues that China's strongest eras were not Confucian ones. Mei still allows that Confucianism has historical value and calls for its creative transformation. On the fourth view, Mei holds that a society's character is set by the dominant form of ownership of the means of production. Mei therefore treats the 'functional socialism' thesis, which allows private ownership to count as socialist, as in effect democratic socialism and contrary to the Constitution.

Mei contends that these views, including those that claim to be Marxist, threaten identification with the Party's guiding ideology, and warns that Western Marxism has weakened the teaching of the classics in some university programmes. The author calls on Marxist scholars to take a clear stand, as Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping have urged. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-aligned scholar framed ideological struggle over Soviet Marxism, Confucian revival and Western Marxism in 2015.
quoteEn: Confucianism must not be raised to the level of the guiding ideology of the Party and the state.
quoteZh: 不能把孔学提到党和国家的指导思想的高度

glossary.explanation: Principles formulated by Deng Xiaoping in 1979: keeping to the socialist road, the people's democratic dictatorship, the leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought.
A slogan the author attributes to critics who hold that Soviet-era Marxism, especially under Stalin, departed from Marx's thought and misled the Chinese revolution.
In Chinese Party discourse, a term for social-democratic currents, generally criticised as departing from scientific socialism.
A label in Party discourse for views seen as wrongly negating the Party's or the revolution's history and the legitimacy of its choices.

keywords: ownership of the means of production

t: Understanding Marx's thought on freedom of the press accurately
zh: 准确理解马克思的新闻出版自由思想
source: Journalism and Communication Studies (新闻与传播研究), 2017 no. 10
paras: Yuan Xiuli takes up a view that cites Marx's and Engels's statements on press freedom (for example, that without it all other freedoms become illusory, and that it is a universal right of everyone) to argue that Marx stood for a free, autonomous press open to all citizens. On this view, the centralised press systems of the Soviet Union and China depart radically from Marx. Yuan, in an article first published in 2017, contends that this reading misunderstands Marx and Engels and cuts their words out of context. The article sets out to establish which kind of press freedom they actually endorsed.

The analysis rests mainly on three texts from Marx's Rheinische Zeitung period: the 1843 essay on the latest Prussian censorship instruction, the first article on the debates of the Sixth Rhenish Provincial Assembly on press freedom, and the trial of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung. The article has five parts: Marx's opposition to Prussian feudal censorship; his critical assessment of bourgeois press freedom; his shift from idealism to materialism; his recognition that no press freedom serves all estates alike; and his views on press freedom and law.

Yuan argues that Marx attacked censorship and welcomed the bourgeoisie's progressive struggle for press freedom, while also seeing that under capitalism this freedom stays a privilege of capital. Printing and buying publications cost money, so material conditions limit it. Marx's early reasoning, Yuan says, still rested on Hegelian appeals to reason and the human spirit. Experience of material-interest conflicts then pushed him towards materialism, and he came to see that no press freedom exists above class. Yuan reads the Assembly debate as showing this: princes, knights, townspeople and peasants wanted different things, so no single demand could speak for 'everyone'. Marx's answer, in Yuan's account, was that the press should express the people's reason and the general interest of the majority, and this was his first statement of the people-oriented character of a free press.

On law, Yuan notes that the early Marx called for a press law as the guarantee of freedom, a position that still reflected Hegelian faith in the rational state. Later, with Engels, Marx came to see law as an expression of the ruling class's will and interests. Yuan concludes that class analysis of press freedom is faithful to Marx, and that selecting 'absolute' phrases without regard to the development of his thought is unscientific. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist rebuttal of liberal readings of Marx on press freedom, with close attention to the Rheinische Zeitung texts.
quoteEn: Marx recognised that within the state, a press freedom that is independent and stands above the state and class does not exist.
quoteZh: 马克思认识到，在国家中，独立的、超越国家、阶级的新闻出版自由并不存在。

t: Freedom enslaved by new imperialism: a critique of neoliberalism
zh: 新帝国主义奴役的自由：评新自由主义
source: Journal of Hebei University of Economics and Business, 2017 no. 4
paras: Yu Bin, writing in 2017, argues that neoliberalism is the freedom of capital to exploit and enslave workers, and that it serves as the policy doctrine and hegemonic tool of what he calls new imperialism. The article opens with a domestic dispute: a prominent professor's "steamed bun" parable, which blames high taxes and fees for weak demand, is read by Yu as an attempt to steer supply-side structural reform towards the neoliberal supply-side school.

The text has two parts. The first dismantles the bun parable, examining pricing, taxation, logistics, rent and the effects of tax cuts on workers and the state. The second turns to Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom and to neoliberal doctrine more broadly, covering unemployment, minimum wages, wages and productivity, free trade, privatisation, international institutions and Latin America's experience of the Washington Consensus.

In the first part, Yu contends that a product too expensive to sell is not "overcapacity", that tax cuts would not much lower bun prices, and that cutting taxes would only shift overcapacity from buns to steamed bread. Taxes, the author adds, would be better used to subsidise the cheaper product, and a property-tax pilot should not be halted. In the second part, Yu reads Hayek's "socialism" as Nazi state socialism and Second International revisionism, which Yu equates with forms of state capitalism rather than Marx's scientific socialism. Yu argues that Hayek's passages on unemployment, minimum wages and postwar British austerity burden workers alone, and uses a numerical example to claim that the neoliberal "iron law" that wages must grow more slowly than productivity does not hold where surplus value is extracted.

Yu holds that neoliberalism rose together with new imperialism in the 1970s, as Keynesian state intervention obstructed the plunder of other countries' resources. In the author's account, equal opportunity and free trade favour transnational monopoly capital, while the IMF, World Bank and WTO impose liberalisation on developing countries. Yu says China's reform did not fully uphold the principle of unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector, so state enterprises were privatised and some utilities came under foreign capital. Read the original if you want a Marxist polemic against neoliberalism and Hayek that ties debates on China's supply-side reform to the theory of imperialism.
quoteEn: What we are carrying out at present is supply-side structural reform, not the supply-side reform of the neoliberal supply-side school; our reform is meant to adjust the structure and to meet the shock of the international economic tide with innovative products.
quoteZh: 当前我们进行的是供给侧结构性改革，而不是新自由主义供给学派的供给侧改革，我们的改革是要调结构的，用创新的产品去应对国际经济大潮的冲击

glossary.explanation: An economic policy line announced by Xi Jinping in 2015. It aims to improve the quality and structure of supply, for example by cutting overcapacity, rather than only stimulating demand.

glossary.zh: 毫不动摇巩固和发展公有制经济
glossary.pinyin: háobù dòngyáo gǒnggù hé fāzhǎn gōngyǒuzhì jīngjì
glossary.en: unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector
glossary.explanation: The official principle, one half of the Two Unwaverings, that the public sector must be consolidated and developed. It is paired with support for the non-public sector.
The author's term for the final phase of imperialism, which he dates from the 1970s. He defines it by weakened state sovereignty and free plunder of other countries' resources.

t: Rethinking the relationship between Marx's thought and the Western cultural tradition
zh: 重新理解马克思思想与西方文化传统的关系
source: Zhonghua dushu bao (China Reading Weekly), 17 January 2018
paras: Many commentators, in the East and the West alike, detach Marx's thought from the Western cultural tradition and read it as a uniquely self-standing theoretical construction. Nie Jinfang argues the opposite. Based on his recent book Origins and Flourishing: An Inquiry into the Origins of Marx's Thought, the article holds that Marx's thought was nourished and shaped by that tradition. First published in the Chinese-language Zhonghua dushu bao in January 2018, it is a short account of the book's findings.

Nie reports a close reading of Marx's surviving youthful writings and traces three Western sources in the period when his thought took form. The first is the "Trier tradition", the religious and humanistic atmosphere of his birthplace, family and school. The second is his own literary writing: 111 poems, one play and a fragment of a novel. The third is ancient atomism, which he studied after turning to the Young Hegelians.

On the first source, Nie contends that the Trier milieu gave Marx religious feeling and humanistic concern. He argues that his father's "Enlightenment" outlook meant conversion to liberal Protestantism rather than rejection of theology. In Nie's view, Marx's image as an atheist and fighter against religion was greatly exaggerated in later Marxism, because he attacked particular doctrines and the worldly basis of religion, not ultimate concern as such. On the second, Nie reads the poems as teaching Marx the meaning, the complexity and finally the limits of emotion, and as leading to reflection on German national character and on Kant, Fichte and Hegel. On the third, Nie presents atomism as showing Marx that the world contains manifold contradictions (atom and void, space and time, necessity and chance). In Nie's account, the atom's swerve from the straight line stands for freedom and the emergence of self-consciousness, and this made up a fairly well-formed philosophical system, which Nie calls the most important result of Marx's formative period.

Nie concludes that the twentieth-century practice of international communism, and the confrontation between capitalism and socialism, raised Marx's influence but also produced extreme and irrational evaluations. Admirers and opponents alike, he says, removed Marx from the history of thought, either as a figure towering over all predecessors or as an eccentric to be expelled. Nie maintains that Marx's critique was "German-philosophical": sublation and carrying forward, not wholesale rejection. Read the original if you want a concise statement of this argument about Marx's youth, religion and atomism, and a pointer to the book behind it.
quoteEn: My research shows that Marx's thought was nurtured and shaped by the long-standing Western cultural tradition.
quoteZh: 我的研究表明，马克思思想是西方源远流长的文化传统哺育和塑造的。

t: Mao Zedong's lifelong bond with the Communist Manifesto
zh: 毛泽东与《共产党宣言》的不解之缘
paras: Marking 170 years since the first German edition of the Communist Manifesto (London, 24 February 1848), this newspaper commentary by Qi Ji traces Mao Zedong's relationship with the text. The author argues that the Manifesto was the first Marxist classic Mao read and the one he cherished all his life, and that he treated it as a guide to practice and theoretical innovation.

The piece follows Mao chronologically through three stages: the formation of his Marxist faith after the May Fourth Movement; his repeated reading and his promotion of the text among cadres from Yan'an to the 1970s; and his reading after 1949, including the Chinese preface he offered to write and his study of the English edition. It draws on Mao's 1936 conversation with Edgar Snow and on recollections by his librarian Xu Zhongyuan and his English tutor Lin Ke.

Qi presents Mao's own testimony that the Chinese translation by Chen Wangdao, with works by Kautsky and Kirkup, fixed his belief in Marxism by summer 1920. According to the article, Mao said in 1939 that he had read the Manifesto more than a hundred times, consulted it when writing On New Democracy, and held that Marxist theory must be read in order to be applied. Qi then lists his repeated placing of the Manifesto first on required-reading lists (1942, 1945, 1949, 1963, 1970), and his plan in 1965 to annotate it in light of China's revolutionary experience.

The author concludes that Mao's reading was unusually deep, citing dense annotations in his English copy and the six copies, two of them English, found by his bed after his death. Read the original if you want a short, anecdotal account of Mao's reading habits and of how his study of the Manifesto is presented in Party-oriented commemorative writing.
quoteEn: He not only liked to read it, but read it attentively, repeatedly and selectively, more than a hundred times.
quoteZh: 不仅自己喜欢读、用心读、反复读、重点读，阅读次数超过一百遍

t: The Communist Manifesto and the ideals and convictions of Communists
zh: 《共产党宣言》与共产党人的理想信念
source: Study Times (Xuexi Shibao), 2018; posted on marxism.cass.cn 28 March 2018
paras: Published in Study Times to mark the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto (1848–2018), this commentary asks why Communists still need to reread the text today. Wang Haibin answers that the Manifesto, as the first programme of the Communist Party, supplies firm support for the ideals and convictions that Xi Jinping describes as the foundation of a Communist's life, the spiritual "calcium" and the "political soul" of the Party.

The piece is organised under three headings: the Manifesto as the theoretical foundation of Communist ideals, as a source of intellectual nourishment, and as a stimulus to spiritual strength. It moves from Marx and Engels's analysis of bourgeois and proletarian development, through three guiding ideas the author draws from the text, to the Manifesto's remarks on the nature of Communists and on the Marxist spirit of self-reflection.

Wang argues first that the Manifesto's conclusion that the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable rests on historical materialism, not on class sentiment or values. It points to recurrent commercial crises of relative overproduction and to the proletariat as the product of large-scale industry. Second, Wang reads the Manifesto through "two inevitables", "two most radical ruptures" and the "free development of all". On the first, the author notes that capitalism is growing socialist elements, such as taxation adjustment, joint-stock companies and social security, and that the inevitable outcome comes only once capitalism has exhausted its capacity for productive forces. On the second, Wang says Marx and Engels targeted the private-ownership form and ideas such as money worship, egoism, despotism and bureaucracy, not markets or capital as such. Third, the author notes that the Manifesto credits capitalist civilisation with material achievements but not with spiritual ones, so Communists must keep raising their own spiritual level.

Wang concludes that grasping these historical laws, and pursuing the free development of all, gives Communists a continuing source of wisdom and moral drive for the basic conviction of serving the people. The author also holds that the 1872 German preface, which says the practical application of the principles depends on historical conditions, requires reading the Manifesto in light of the contemporary world and China's realities. Such a reading is said to strengthen belief in Marxism, socialism and communism, and in the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Manifesto was presented to Party members in 2018 as a basis for ideological conviction.
quoteEn: Ideals stand above reality, but they cannot be divorced from it.
quoteZh: 理想高于现实，但不能脱离现实。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era, combining Marxism with China's conditions and market mechanisms.
A staple Party term for members' commitment to communism and socialism. Xi Jinping has stressed it as the spiritual foundation of Communists.
The Marxist theory that material production and class relations drive historical change.

t: On the integrity of Capital as a whole
zh: 论《资本论》的整体性
source: Economic Vertical and Horizontal (Jingji zongheng), 2017 no. 11
paras: Marking 150 years since the first German edition of Capital Volume I, Yu Bin takes up a familiar reading habit: many readers return repeatedly to Volume I and never reach Volumes II and III. Yu argues that the three volumes form one whole and that Capital cannot be understood without recognising this. Those who claim a contradiction between Volume I and Volume III, in Yu's view, have simply not understood the work.

The article proceeds almost entirely through close reading of Marx's and Engels's own statements: Marx's 1868 letter to Danielson, his letters to Engels and Kugelmann, and Engels's essays, letters and prefaces from 1869 to the 1890s. These are used to establish the relative independence of Volume I, its one-sidedness, the reasons the later volumes were unpublished in Marx's lifetime, and what unifies the three volumes. Yu also answers critics, including Achille Loria and a contemporary view that Marx withheld the later volumes because his theory no longer fitted reality.

Yu's central claim is that Capital narrates the whole career of surplus value: Volume I covers its production, Volume II its circulation and Volume III its distribution. Volume I is relatively self-contained, but Engels called it one-sided and abstract, and Yu holds that concepts such as money, capital, the transformation of surplus value into profit and average profit, and the refutation of bourgeois economics only come into full view with the later volumes. On the delay, Yu rejects the idea that Marx doubted his theory. Yu points instead to poverty, illness, political work for the International, repression, Marx's perfectionism and the priority given to new editions and translations of Volume I. Yu adds that Volume I's treatment of value is developed in Volume III, where value is determined by the labour-time needed for reproduction.

Yu concludes that the missing final chapter on classes, and even the last part on revenues and their sources, do not damage the unity of the work, since production, circulation and distribution of surplus value are already complete. Capital should therefore not be regarded as an unfinished work, and Yu asks rhetorically whether any work could then count as finished. New developments in capitalism, Yu says, would enrich the later volumes rather than negate earlier content. Read the original if you want a text-based argument, built from Marx's and Engels's correspondence, for reading Capital as a unified three-volume theory of surplus value.
quoteEn: Capital in essence narrates the whole career of surplus value, and this is precisely where the integrity of all three volumes lies.
quoteZh: 《资本论》本质上叙述的是剩余价值的整个生涯，这也是《资本论》全部三卷的整体性之所在

t: The programmatic document of scientific socialism
st: Commemorating the 170th anniversary of the publication of the Communist Manifesto
zh: 科学社会主义的纲领性文献
zhSub: 纪念《共产党宣言》发表170周年
paras: Marking 170 years since the Communist Manifesto first appeared in 1848, Yang Haifeng argues that it remains the programmatic document of scientific socialism and the most influential text of the world socialist movement. Writing as China enters what the article calls a new journey of building a modern socialist country, Yang holds that rereading it has real contemporary significance.

The article has three parts. The first traces the Manifesto's role in the socialist movement: its worldwide circulation, its guidance for the Bolsheviks and the October Revolution, and its arrival in China through Chen Wangdao's 1920 translation. The second sets out the ideas Yang sees as laying the theoretical and ideological foundation of scientific socialism. The third explains why the text is still alive today.

In the second part Yang identifies four contributions. The first is the 'two inevitables' (the downfall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat), derived from the contradiction between socialised production and private ownership of the means of production. The others are the free and all-round development of the individual, the theory of proletarian revolution and proletarian dictatorship, and the doctrine of the proletarian party. In the third part Yang argues that the nature of capital has not changed, even though its forms have. Capital's harm and control are said to be greater in the age of globalisation. The Manifesto's method is presented as a tool for analysing today's Western societies, where movements over inequality, environment, race and gender intertwine with capitalism's basic contradictions.

Yang concludes that the Manifesto supplies spiritual strength for communist ideals and that socialism with Chinese characteristics proves its vitality after the post-1989 setback of world socialism. Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, established at the 19th Party Congress (2017), is described as a contemporary expression of the Manifesto's spirit, with the Communist Party of China as its present-day practitioner. Read the original if you want an example of how the Manifesto was presented in the official Party press in 2018, linked to ideological education and to the new-era theory.
quoteEn: Critically analysing contemporary capitalist society under changed historical conditions is the historic mission of today's Marxists.
quoteZh: 在历史条件变化了的情况下去批判分析当代资本主义社会，是当代马克思主义者的历史使命。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution at the 19th Party Congress in 2017.
The official name for China's path of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership with a market economy.
The thesis, attributed to the Manifesto, that capitalism's collapse and socialism's victory are both historically inevitable.
The term for Marx and Engels' socialism, which they distinguished from earlier utopian socialism by its basis in laws of historical development.

t: Raising high the ideological banner of twenty-first-century Marxism
zh: 高举21世纪马克思主义的思想旗帜
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Shuang Chuanxue takes up Xi Jinping's call, made at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences and in his letter marking the 40th anniversary of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, to develop "twenty-first-century Marxism" and "contemporary Chinese Marxism". Shuang argues that this is the historic mission of the age and that Xi Jinping's thought on governance is its most concentrated expression. Shuang adds that the banner can be held high only by clearing away several mistaken ideas.

The commentary has three parts. The first presents the development of twenty-first-century Marxism as a task the times have set for Chinese communists. The second sets out why Xi's ideas on governing the country count as the latest result of adapting Marxism to China. The third lists the intellectual obstacles to be removed and ends with a call to philosophers and social scientists.

In the first part, Shuang holds that Marxism's essence is to ground itself in developing practice, and that Marx and Engels offered no formulas valid for every era. The author traces this through Lenin and the Chinese Party's adaptation of Marxism, and credits the Party with a tradition of learning and theoretical innovation.
