The practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics, Shuang says, poses new problems that neither the classics nor foreign experience can answer. In the second part, Shuang describes Xi's thought as an "Four Comprehensives"-centred system that answers the Chinese Dream question, enriches the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and has been tested in practice, citing the May 2017 Belt and Road forum as evidence. In the third part, Shuang opposes three forms of the claim that Marxism is outdated, along with the "Westernisation" and "Confucianisation" of guiding ideology. Shuang also opposes currents such as historical nihilism, neoliberalism, "universal values", Western constitutional democracy and democratic socialism.

Shuang concludes that scholars should study and implement Xi's speeches and his new ideas on governance, and should take on the task of upholding and developing twenty-first-century Marxism. The author says that opposing Westernisation and Confucianisation does not mean rejecting Western civilisation or traditional Chinese culture. Instead, Marxism should absorb the best of human civilisation and creatively transform traditional culture. Read the original if you want an example of how the Party's theoretical press in 2017 presented Xi Jinping's governance thought as Marxism for the twenty-first century, and which ideological currents it named as opponents.
quoteEn: Practice has proved that keeping pace with the times is the most important theoretical character of Marxism.
quoteZh: 实践证明，与时俱进是马克思主义最重要的理论品格。

glossary.explanation: A formula used in Party theoretical discourse for the latest stage of Marxism's development, which the article ties to Chinese practice and Xi Jinping's thought. Xi urged scholars to develop it alongside "contemporary Chinese Marxism".

A strategic layout put forward under Xi Jinping: building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform, governing the country according to law, and strictly governing the Party. The article treats it as the framework of Xi's governance thought.
Xi Jinping's formula, from 2012, for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It is presented as the nation's greatest modern aspiration.
In Party discourse, a label for views that question or negate the official account of Chinese revolutionary and socialist history.

t: A textual study of Marx's category of totality
zh: 马克思总体性范畴的文本学研究
source: Journal of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee, 2017 no. 1
paras: Marx never explicitly put forward "totality" as a concept, yet Georg Lukács claimed to derive the category from Marx's texts, and it has shaped Marxist scholarship in China as well as abroad. Peng Hongwei argues that Chinese scholars have accepted Lukács's version uncritically and applied it to other fields. The article returns to Marx's own texts to test whether Lukács's totality matches Marx's meaning, and concludes that it differs significantly.

The article is a close reading, mainly of the Grundrisse chapter on capital and of Capital and its manuscripts. It has three parts: what Marx meant by "totality" (the object), how Marx moves beyond the opposition of whole and part, and totality as a fundamental attribute ("totality-ness") and a method of thought. Peng also cites Lukács's own 1967 self-criticism, in which Lukács said that placing totality at the centre of Marxism had produced a Hegelian distortion.

Peng's first move is to argue that, for Marx, the totality is a living social organism, and in capitalist society it is above all capital. Capital subordinates other social elements and creates the organs it lacks. Marx distinguishes this real totality from the "totality of thought", the product of the thinking brain, which he separates from Hegel's idealism. Peng treats "collective worker" and "collective capitalist" as the two categories under the capital totality. The second move is to argue that what corresponds to totality in Marx is the particular, not the part. The totality is therefore not a mechanical sum but a set of organically connected particular relations, and it is a process that unites production and circulation. Peng's third move defines totality-ness as the process by which capital becomes a totality, which he dates to the age of large-scale industry. He lists four attributes: maintaining balance through alienation, unity of continuity and discontinuity, self-generation, and the building of organic relations.

Peng concludes that totality-ness is a method that Marx originated and that enriched materialist dialectics. It brings will and spirit into the analysis, which rules out mechanical and supposedly neutral thinking, and it surpasses old materialism and idealism. Peng lists five tasks for studying a totality: its internal connections, its stages, its links with external elements, its relation to its derivatives, and its will. Read the original if you want a text-based challenge to the Lukácsian reading of totality, or want to see how Chinese scholars return to Marx's manuscripts on this question.
quoteEn: The totality is not the sum of its parts but one built from particular relations, and totality and the particular are inseparably linked.
quoteZh: 总体不等于部分的加和，而是特殊关系构建而成的总体，总体与特殊不可分割地联系在一起。

t: Multiple dimensions of research on Marx's political economy since the twentieth century
st: New readings of Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and Capital
zh: 20世纪以来马克思政治经济学研究的多维度开展
zhSub: 马克思《1844年经济学哲学手稿》、《资本论》新解
paras: He Ping asks how three major strands of twentieth-century Marxist theory grew out of Marx's two central economic works. The article argues that the immaturity of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 in economics, and the unfinished state of Capital, are strengths rather than defects. In the author's view they make Marx's political economy an open system that later theorists could develop. Published in Tianjin Social Sciences in 2017, it traces the link between Marx's texts and later theory.

The article has three main sections. The first follows the concept of practice and the theory of alienated labour from the 1844 Manuscripts into Marxist cultural critique. It covers Labriola, Gramsci, Althusser and Williams, and then the Frankfurt School and Lefebvre. The second section follows the question of capital accumulation, from Rosa Luxemburg's dispute with Hilferding, Bukharin and Lenin through underconsumptionism and world-systems theory to post-2007 readings of Capital. The third examines ecological Marxism's use of the labour theory of value, from James O'Connor to John Bellamy Foster and others, and compares it with Engels.

In the cultural strand, He presents Gramsci's cultural hegemony as a relatively independent social power exercised by consent, which develops the cultural content of Marx's practice concept. He presents the Frankfurt School's critique of modernity and the culture industry as a later form of the theory of alienated labour. In the economic strand, Luxemburg's problem of realising surplus value is said to recur through Baran and Sweezy's 'utilisation of surplus' and Wallerstein's core–periphery scheme. He judges that Wallerstein neglected Capital and so could not explain the 2007 financial crisis. The author says that readings of Capital by Paul Zarembka and others restore accumulation, money demand and crisis to the centre, and so avoid a 'productivist' reading confined to Volume 1. In the ecological strand, He argues that O'Connor's rejection of historical materialism left ecological Marxism a blend of Marxism and ecologism. Foster, Burkett and Clark are credited with a way out through Marx's concept of social metabolism.

He concludes that accumulation has become the central theme of contemporary Marxist political economy. Citing Ben Agger's three-part summary of Marx's dialectic, the author holds that the 1844 Manuscripts and Capital remain the most valuable works of our era. He also argues that Foster's ecological Marxism explains Western capitalist crises but fits socialist China poorly. Engels's more abstract treatment of labour and nature is presented as a better resource for a Chinese ecological Marxism suited to national conditions. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's survey of how Gramsci, the Frankfurt School, world-systems theory and ecological Marxism relate to Marx's economic texts.
quoteEn: The immaturity of the 1844 Manuscripts in political economy and the unfinished state of Capital are not a defect but a strength, because they make Marx's political economy an infinitely open system of thought.
quoteZh: 《１８４４年经济学哲学手稿》在政治经济学上的不成熟性和《资本论》的未完成性并不是一个缺点，而是一个优点，因为它使马克思的政治经济学成为一个无限开放的思想体系

t: Is the Chinese path the "right way in the human world"? We should have this confidence
zh: 中国道路是“人间正道”吗？我们应该有这份自信
paras: This is the text of a speech Ma Ya gave on 24 April 2017 at the launch of a public reading event in Hengnan County, Hunan, later revised and published by Guancha.cn on 3 July 2017. Starting from a book on the "Republic generation", Ma asks why China must hold to its own path. The answer is that only the Chinese path can protect national interests and the people's well-being, and Ma urges confidence in it.

The speech has three main parts. The first argues that national sovereignty and the people's welfare come first. The second sets out why China must keep to its path and why the Chinese Dream requires it. The third turns to cultural confidence and "telling China's story well", covering the troubles of Western democracy, the lessons of the Soviet collapse, the ideological imbalance between China and the West, and the Belt and Road Initiative.

Ma names three pillars of the Chinese path: Communist Party leadership, a socialist orientation aimed at common prosperity, and economic development. Ma presents the Soviet and Eastern European collapse and the Iraq intervention as proof that following Western models or "universal values" brings disaster. Ma points to China's growth, the Wenchuan earthquake reconstruction and its "institutional strengths" as evidence of success. Ma also warns that privatisation in health care, citing the shrinking number of public hospitals, runs against public ownership as the mainstay and could cost the Party its legitimacy. Citing US polling, Trust Barometer results and figures on the Chinese and Japanese economies, Ma argues that Western democracy is in decline and that Western discourse dominates ideologically.

Ma concludes that China cannot copy the American model and that its pursuit of common prosperity could offer other developing countries a model. Ma calls for a discourse that is both Chinese and universal, which would "give a Chinese account of the world's stories and a universal account of China's". Ma sees the Belt and Road as a vehicle for this, along with a culture of coexistence and win-win cooperation that contrasts with Western zero-sum rises. Read the original if you want a vivid example of the confident, polemical case for the Chinese path that circulated in nationalist and left-leaning Chinese commentary in 2017.
quoteEn: This discourse system must give a Chinese account of the world's stories and a universal account of China's story.
quoteZh: 这个话语体系要对世界的故事给出中国的说法，对中国的故事给出普世的说法。

glossary.explanation: A goal of socialism that Deng Xiaoping and later leaders endorsed. It means that the fruits of development are shared widely rather than concentrated among a few.
A slogan Xi Jinping popularised from 2012 for national rejuvenation. It is tied to the "two centenary goals" for 2021 and 2049.
A Chinese infrastructure and connectivity initiative launched in 2013 that links China with Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

t: The origins of the Communist Party of China in Leninism
zh: 列宁主义与中国共产党的渊源
paras: Lü Xinyu argues that the organic link between Mao Zedong Thought and Leninism is an urgent but deliberately or unintentionally obscured question. In the author's view, Marxism reached China through Leninism, and the Communist Party of China has its source there: without the October Revolution there would have been no Party. Lü contends that what is being hidden is the dictatorship of the proletariat and the nature of the state, a major historical issue of the Comintern movement, and that the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics depends on how this succession is understood.

The article, first published on the website Utopia (Wuyouzhixiang) in 2017, reads as a historical argument in five sections. It covers Lenin's attention to the 1911 Revolution, his treatment of Chinese revolution and Russian populism, his defence of the revolutionary character of the peasantry, the difference between proletarian Social Democrats and populists, and the passage from the 'New Democracy' to socialism via Lenin's April Theses, State and Revolution and Mao's writings. Lü draws on Lenin's Collected Works, memoirs and Mao's On New Democracy.

Lü's central move is that the Chinese and Russian revolutions shared the peasant question, which set them apart from the Western bourgeois revolutions. Lenin, who had once fought the populists, revised his view after 1905–07 and concluded that Russia's revolution had to be a peasant land revolution led by a proletarian party. Lü treats this as a key content of Leninism. Lü reads the Comintern's line of supporting peasants and allying with, but not merging into, bourgeois democrats as the theoretical source of Communist–Nationalist cooperation in the 1920s. Mao's New Democracy is then presented as the Chinese answer to the April Theses, with its two-step revolution and its peasant-centred politics.

Lü attacks what the author calls the liberal right, which denies the October Revolution and Lenin, sets Engels against Marx and Stalin against Lenin, and recasts China's path as European social democracy or a truncated New Democracy. The article also faults this camp for never explaining the Second International's betrayal in 1914. Lü calls for a renewed understanding of the historical succession from Marxism through Leninism to Mao Zedong Thought, which the author identifies with the Party's own history. Read the original if you want a Chinese leftist account of Lenin's writings on China and the peasantry, and of how Leninism is said to underpin the Party's path.
quoteEn: Marxism reached China through Leninism.
quoteZh: 马克思主义是通过列宁主义抵达中国的。

glossary.explanation: The Communist Party of China's official designation for the adaptation of Marxism-Leninism to Chinese conditions, associated with Mao Zedong and enshrined in the Party constitution.
Mao Zedong's 1940–41 theory of a transitional stage of revolution. In it a proletariat-led, anti-imperialist and anti-feudal bourgeois-democratic revolution is a first step toward socialism.
A Marxist-Leninist term for working-class state power in the transition to communism. Lü treats it as the core issue of the state's nature.
The Communist (Third) International, founded in Moscow in 1919 under Lenin to coordinate communist parties worldwide, including the early Chinese Communist Party.

In the Russian context discussed here (narodnichestvo), a peasant-based socialist current that expected to bypass capitalism through the village commune. Lenin first opposed it, then reassessed its peasant-democratic content.

t: What is meant by the resilience of the Communist Party of China
zh: 什么叫中国共产党的韧性
paras: This is an interview with Jin Yinan, a military scholar and author of the book Kuonan huihuang (Glorious Suffering), conducted by the Theory Weekly of the Beijing Daily and published on 3 July 2017, shortly after the Party's 96th anniversary. Asked what resilience means for the Communist Party of China, Jin answers that it comes from the resilience of its members, who endured sacrifice for their ideals. He presents the Party's history as 'the greatest study of success', won through tenacity and sacrifice rather than good fortune.

The interview moves through several episodes. It opens with Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je's visit to the site of the First Party Congress and with Jin's own account of German and French officers on a military exchange course who asked to see Sun Yat-sen's residence and the Congress site. It then turns to the fates of the 13 delegates at the First Congress, to Mao Zedong's search for a revolutionary path, to Zhu De's role after the Nanchang Uprising, and finally to national dignity, security and the 'hundred years of national salvation, hundred years of rejuvenation'.

Jin argues that the revolution was never favoured to win. Seven of the 13 First Congress delegates left or were expelled, and two became collaborators with Japan. In his reading, only Mao's path, which relied on the weak points of enemy rule and on warlord wars between 'white' regimes, answered why a red regime could survive. He holds that earlier leaders had dogmatised Comintern instructions and Soviet experience, and that Mao's strategy emerged from close knowledge of China's conditions. He credits Zhu De with holding together some 800 men at Tianxinxu when the Nanchang forces collapsed. He also argues that the Party is a combative body, and that collective self-esteem, restored by the revolution and the Korean War, is a basic national interest.

Jin concludes that national salvation was not begun by the Party but was completed by it, and that 1949 opened a second century of rejuvenation that will also be hard. He links China's larger economy to wider security duties, citing the navy's 2008 Gulf of Aden deployment, and holds that responsibility requires strength. He closes by saying the Party's leadership explains China's transformation and will secure future victories. Read the original if you want an example of how a prominent military commentator told Party history in 2017 as a story of struggle, sacrifice and the leadership of Mao Zedong and Zhu De.
quoteEn: The resilience of the Communist Party of China, at bottom, comes from the resilience of its Communists.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的韧性，从根本上说源于中国共产党人的韧性。

glossary.explanation: Jin Yinan's popular 2009 history of the Communist Party's early decades, which stresses hardship, sacrifice and eventual victory. The title is a literal rendering and not an official English title.

t: China's "internal logic" of democracy under Western discursive hegemony
st: Interview with Ding Yifan, Deputy Director of the Institute of World Development, Development Research Center of the State Council
zh: 西方话语霸权下的中国民主的“内在理路”
paras: This is an interview with Ding Yifan, conducted by the website Guancha.cn and published on 2 July 2017. The interviewers start from the point that Western countries hold the power to "certify" what counts as democracy. They ask whether China can build its own interpretive framework and how other developing countries fare. Ding answers that Chinese and Western definitions differ because each reflects a different historical experience: the West stresses form, China stresses content.

The interview moves through five topics. These are the definition of democracy and its Confucian roots, the inertia of historical tradition in the political system, populism and popular participation, Hong Kong's political system, and the 1950s–60s Asian-African context of China's foreign policy. Ding draws on a passage from Mencius, the civil service tradition, and episodes from decolonisation and China's return to the United Nations.

Ding defines democracy as popular recognition of a regime. He reads Mencius's dialogue with Wan Zhang as showing that "Heaven" in the Mandate of Heaven in fact means the people. Contemporary Chinese practice, in his account, combines recommendation, consultation and election, and rests on a professional civil service and meritocracy (xiánnéng zhèngzhì). The National People's Congress and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference let people outside the system voice demands. Ding says participation is not the same as democracy and that talking with Westerners about it is a "dialogue between chickens and ducks". He adds that decision-makers cannot accommodate every minority interest. On Hong Kong, Ding attributes the unrest to British colonial design, "divide and rule" and economic hollowing-out. He says the central government's bottom line is that Hong Kong must not become a base for subverting China. Ding then recalls China's support for Asian-African nationalism, the Bandung Conference of 1955 and the 1971 UN vote.

Ding concludes that China's political system should draw on historical experience while continuing to innovate. He argues that Western criticism will never be satisfied by Chinese evidence of progress, because the two sides use different standards. He says China's Belt and Road Initiative and Xi Jinping's renewed emphasis on the relation between righteousness and interests (yì and lì) are helping China regain moral discourse power in international affairs. Read the original if you want a candid example of how a Chinese policy adviser grounds the Chinese concept of democracy in Confucian tradition and in the history of Third World solidarity.
quoteEn: Westerners define democracy in terms of what they have experienced, so they regard form as most important. The Chinese definition of democracy is likewise what China has experienced, so content is regarded as most important.
quoteZh: 西方人对民主的定义是他们经历过的东西，所以认为形式最重要。中国人对民主的定义也是中国经历过的事情，因此认为内容最重要。

glossary.literal: politics of the virtuous and capable
glossary.explanation: A term for a system in which officials rise by ability and experience through a professional civil service. It is often traced to Confucian tradition.
A Chinese international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative announced by Xi Jinping in 2013.

t: Capital and the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
zh: 《资本论》与中国特色社会主义政治经济学
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 27 April 2017
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2017, Zhang Chen asks what role Marx's Capital should play in the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author argues that this political economy is a 'Chinese version' of socialist political economy, combining basic Marxist theory with the practice of reform and opening up, and that Capital is its 'soul'. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's 2015 and 2016 statements, including that calling Marxist political economy and Capital outdated is arbitrary.

The commentary sets out three ways Capital guides the Chinese project: its standpoint and basic ideas, its methodology, and its stock of theoretical resources. It then adds a caveat about Capital's historical specificity and closes with a list of theoretical results the Communist Party has produced since the founding of the People's Republic.

Zhang contends that Capital unites scientific rigour with a working-class standpoint, which the author links to the people-centred development philosophy and to common prosperity. Its method, in Zhang's reading, includes historical materialism, the unity of the historical and the logical, and the ascent from the abstract to the concrete, all organised around surplus value. Zhang also holds that its analyses of the law of value, supply and demand, competition and social reproduction apply under certain conditions to a socialist market economy. The author concedes that Capital's concrete content is modelled on nineteenth-century Britain, but says its standpoint, viewpoint and method keep it 'unfinished' and open to development.

Zhang concludes that Party theories such as the primary stage of socialism, the socialist market economy and supply-side structural reform are major innovations that extend Capital-based political economy. Read the original if you want a short, official-line statement of how Chinese commentators in 2017 tied Capital to the new category of 'political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics'.
quoteEn: Capital's method of presentation, ascending from the abstract to the concrete, means that Capital, or Marxist political economy, is forever 'to be continued'.
quoteZh: 《资本论》从抽象上升到具体的叙述方法，决定了《资本论》或者马克思主义政治经济学永远是“未完待续”的

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义政治经济学
glossary.pinyin: Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì zhèngzhì jīngjìxué
glossary.en: political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: A category Xi Jinping put forward in 2015–2016 for a systematic body of economic theory drawn from China's reform-era practice and grounded in Marxist political economy.
The official view that China is in a long initial phase of socialism, with underdeveloped productive forces. It justifies a mixed economy and market mechanisms.
A long-standing official goal of prosperity shared across society, presented as a defining feature of socialism.

glossary.zh: 以人民为中心的发展思想
glossary.pinyin: yǐ rénmín wéi zhōngxīn de fāzhǎn sīxiǎng
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping that makes people's welfare the starting point and goal of economic development.
An economic policy line announced around 2015 that aims to improve the structure of supply, for example by cutting overcapacity.
The official description of China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining market allocation with public ownership as the main body.

t: Capital: the inner unity of philosophy and the critique of political economy
zh: 《资本论》：哲学与政治经济学批判的内在贯通
paras: Writing in a newspaper piece of 2017, Bu Xiangji asks how Marx's revolution in philosophy relates to his critique of political economy. The author argues that Marx's new philosophical path grew out of a practical concern: criticising a capitalist society that exploits the people and achieving human freedom and all-round emancipation. In Bu's reading, Capital resolves this concern by taking the critique of political economy as its entry point, so that philosophy and economics are internally united there.

The article traces Marx's intellectual route. It begins with his move from Kant to Hegel and his association with the Young Hegelians. It then follows the political critique in the Rheinische Zeitung, the doubts about Hegel's philosophy of right, and the reflection on the state and civil society. It ends with the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and the Theses on Feuerbach as steps towards Capital.

Bu's central claim is that the 1844 Manuscripts bring together the philosophical revolution and the critique of political economy. There Marx sets out the principles of practical materialism, with "sensuous activity" or labour as the core concept. From labour, Marx asks how alienated labour relates to private property, which differs from humanist materialism's idealised premise and from political economy's habit of starting with private property. Bu holds that this undermines the premises of classical political economy and makes rebuilding it on new foundations a necessary task, completed in Capital. The Theses on Feuerbach then prepare the early materialist conception of history, which accounts for capitalism's origins.

Bu draws two lessons. First, genuine philosophy must reach into social reality, and Marx's philosophy and political economy have no fixed boundary: Capital is itself Marx's "living philosophy". Second, adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions means inheriting this spirit, focusing on the "Chinese path", social justice and ecological civilization, and building a Chinese Marxist philosophical discourse. Read the original if you want a compact account of how Marx's early works lead into Capital and how a Chinese scholar draws contemporary lessons from that path.
quoteEn: Marx's critique of political economy, represented by Capital, is itself Marx's living philosophy.
quoteZh: 以《资本论》为代表的马克思政治经济学批判，本身就是马克思的活的哲学。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy and theoretical concept, prominent since the 2000s and written into Party documents, that stresses environmental protection and sustainable development as part of national development.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义哲学中国化
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxism to China's circumstances and drawing on Chinese culture, here applied to philosophy.

t: Logical differences between Capital and the Grundrisse
zh: 《资本论》与《政治经济学批判大纲》的逻辑差异
source: Social Science Digest (Shehui kexue wenzhai), 2017 no. 1
paras: Scholars widely accept that the 1857–58 manuscripts, the Outline of the Critique of Political Economy (the Grundrisse, here abbreviated the Outline), and Capital are continuous, both in economic content and in philosophical framework. Yang Haifeng challenges this consensus. The article argues that two different epistemes, or philosophical frameworks, underlie the two texts, and that these produce a major difference in their logic.

Yang first sets out the concept of the episteme, drawing on Althusser's problematic and 'epistemological break', Foucault's The Order of Things and Kuhn's paradigm theory. The article then analyses the philosophical basis of the Outline. It then turns to Capital, comparing the way each text treats labour, the subject and the object.

Yang reads the Outline as resting on an anthropological logic of production, which takes the form of an ontology of labour. Labour is the ontological ground of society. Objectification confirms human subjectivity, and labour creates free time as the space of free development. Yet the Outline also contains a second line, a logic of capital in which capital is the subject and labour only its means. In Capital this second line prevails. Labour is split into concrete and abstract labour, and the key distinction is between labour and labour-power. Yang treats that distinction as a break with the modern Western philosophy of labour as well as an economic one. The capitalist becomes only the personification of capital, and the human subject becomes a carrier of structure. Capital is an 'absolute subject' in a Hegelian sense, which makes it an absolute object relative to human beings.

Yang concludes that studies stressing continuity have joined the two texts through surface discourse. The author calls for attention to what Marx does not say and to the deeper structure that constrains his thought. Doing so, Yang suggests, would prompt a rethinking of earlier research and open new space for Marxist philosophy. Read the original if you study the philosophical reading of Capital, the debate over labour ontology versus the logic of capital, or the use of Althusser and Foucault in Marx scholarship.
quoteEn: In capitalist society, what matters is not labour but labour-power.
quoteZh: 在资本主义社会，重要的不是劳动，而是劳动力。

t: Capital's comprehensive analysis of the relations of production
zh: 《资本论》关于生产关系的整体分析
paras: Zhang Leisheng asks how Marx came to fix the relations of production as the object of political economy and what content he gave them, and how this shaped the framework of Capital. The article argues that Marx's understanding developed over a long period, from private property relations, to relations of intercourse, to relations of appropriation grounded in the development of the productive forces. Zhang holds that, whatever scholars debate about the object of study stated in the preface to the first German edition of Volume I, this development shows that Capital treats the relations of production as a whole.

The article is organised in four parts, each tracing one angle of Marx's research and its use in Capital. These are: relations of intercourse (drawing on The German Ideology), ownership of the means of production, the relations of production as a totality (drawing on the 1857–58 Introduction), and the development of the productive forces (drawing on the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy). In each part Zhang moves from Marx's earlier works to concrete analyses in the three volumes of Capital.

Zhang argues that Marx's focus on 'material intercourse' lets Capital show how the equal exchange of labour-power on the market hides unequal relations in production. On ownership, Zhang distinguishes the unity of ownership and appropriation, the separability of ownership from management, and the economic as against the legal form of ownership. These distinctions are applied to the essence of capitalist ownership, to the dispossession of direct producers, to joint-stock companies and to the 'negation of the negation'. On totality, Zhang reads production, distribution, exchange and consumption as an organic whole, and sees the same logic in the three volumes: production, circulation and the overall process of capitalist production. On the productive forces, Zhang uses relative surplus value, the general law of capitalist accumulation and the transformation of values into prices of production as examples. In each, changes in the organic composition of capital are the starting point for analysing class relations.

Zhang concludes that Volumes I to III together form a complete theoretical system for analysing capitalist relations of production. Zhang presents this system as showing the antagonism between capital and wage labour, the contradiction between productive forces and relations of production, and the historical task of the proletariat. Read the original if you want a detailed, text-based account of how Marx's concept of the relations of production developed and how it structures Capital, as understood in Chinese Marxist political economy.
quoteEn: Capital's analysis of capitalist relations of production, with the relation between capital and wage labour as its axis, runs through all three volumes, through the production process of capital, its circulation process and the overall process of capitalist production.
quoteZh: 《资本论》以资本与雇佣劳动关系为轴心对资本主义生产关系的分析，贯穿整个三卷，贯穿资本的生产过程、资本的流通过程，以及资本主义生产的总过程
keywords: ownership of the means of production

t: Marx's thought on "philistines and their state" and its significance
zh: 马克思关于“庸人及其国家”的思想及其意义
paras: Nie Jinfang takes up Marx's idea of the "philistines and their state", developed in his 1842–1843 correspondence around the founding of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher. The article opens by contesting Hannah Arendt, who sought "totalitarian elements" in Marxism and later coined "the banality of evil" in her study of Adolf Eichmann. Nie argues that Arendt never read Marx's key texts closely, and that Marx had already analysed how people survive without independent thought under despotic rule.

The article is built in four parts. It first describes Marx's picture of Prussian absolutism as a "world of philistines". It then sets the principle of monarchy against what Marx calls the principle of man, and examines how despotism corrupts new ideas, taking Schelling as the example. The last part turns to Marx's strategy for struggling against this order. Nie draws mainly on Marx's letters to Ruge and Feuerbach.

Nie's central claim is that rulers and ruled shape one another. In Nie's reading of the letters, Marx held that philistines want slaves and are slaves themselves, so that the "world of philistines" is a world of "political animals" in which dehumanisation is the system's principle. Marx rejected Montesquieu's defence of monarchy and held that the monarchical principle is incompatible with human dignity. Frederick William IV's attempt at renewal ended in restoration of the old order, which for Nie shows that a philistine state cannot be abolished on its own foundations. Schelling's career as an "official philosopher" shows, in Nie's account, how power turns a once sincere youthful philosophy into Prussian politics under a philosophical cover.

On strategy, Nie reports Marx's combination of uncompromising stance and prudence: signing his name, avoiding rash polemic, and letting the newspaper guide its contributors. Marx pinned his hopes on "thinking men" and "suffering men", and called for restoring the human self-confidence that is freedom. Nie concludes that these ideas remained a value premise of Marx's later social critique and still matter for political philosophy. Nie also finds a kinship with Arendt's resistance to banal evil, and reads her remark that Marx was "misused" by totalitarianism as a kind of self-reflection. Read the original if you want a close reading of the early Marx's letters on Prussian despotism and a rebuttal of Arendt's linking of Marx with totalitarianism.
quoteEn: The characteristic and principle of the despotic system is to look down on people, to despise them and to dehumanise them.
quoteZh: 专制体制的特征和原则就是轻视人、蔑视人、使人非人化。

t: Marx's core philosophical idea is the "greater historical materialism"
zh: 马克思的核心哲学思想是大唯物史观
paras: In this piece, published in Beijing Daily on 23 January 2017, An Qinian introduces his own book on Marx's philosophy, titled The Road to Freedom (《通往自由之路》). An argues that Marx's core philosophical idea is a "greater historical materialism" (da weiwu shiguan), of which many views already accepted by scholars are only component parts.

The text first explains why Chinese philosophers since reform and opening up have studied Marx's own philosophy rather than "Marxist philosophy". An cites disputes over what Marxist philosophy means, the publication of the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 (translated into Chinese in 1979), and the fit between Marx's thought and the changes of the reform era. It then summarises the book's seven chapters and ends with remarks on its title and purpose.

In An's account, the greater historical materialism sees history as the interactive, co-developing process of nature, human society and human beings themselves, grounded in labour practice. Its theoretical basis is the dialectics of labour practice and its value goal is human emancipation. Chapter 2, the key chapter, argues that labour practice matters because environments changed by people in turn change people, and this feedback explains human development. An says the textbook historical materialism (the "lesser" one) is part of the greater version, not opposed to it. The remaining chapters treat Marx and dialectical materialism, the systematic character of his thought, his place in the history of philosophy, and methodological value.

An calls for integrating the existing, often conflicting findings to reconstruct Marx's philosophy as an organic whole, and for a Marxist philosophy as Chinese people understand it, so that "Marx speaks Chinese". An adds that whether following Marx's laws of history will lead to the realm of freedom cannot be proved by theory alone but only in practice. Read the original if you want a short statement of An's reading of Marx and of the aims of Chinese Marxist philosophy after 1978.
quoteEn: The greater historical materialism holds that history is the interactive, co-developing process of nature, human society and human beings themselves on the basis of labour practice; its theoretical basis is the dialectics of labour practice, and its value goal is human emancipation.
quoteZh: 大唯物史观认为历史是自然界、人类社会和人本身基于劳动实践活动的相互作用协同发展，这种历史观的理论基础是劳动实践辩证法，它的价值目标是人类解放。

glossary.explanation: An Qinian's term for what he sees as Marx's full conception of history, covering nature, society and the human being, based on labour practice. It contains the textbook historical materialism as one part.
An's name for the theoretical basis of the greater historical materialism: the mutual shaping of humans and their environment through labour.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978.

t: The wholeness of Marxism revisited
zh: 再论马克思主义的整体性
source: Observation and Thinking (Guancha yu Sikao), 2017 no. 1
paras: Following Lenin's division of Marxism into philosophy, political economy and scientific socialism, Zhao Jiaxiang takes up a problem in Chinese universities. The three parts are taught in separate departments, so specialists in one know little of the others, and the unified Marxist system is cut into pieces. Writing in 2017, Zhao argues that Marxism is an internally unified whole and that scholars and teachers must study it as one.

The article builds the case through six perspectives: the social and historical conditions in which Marxism arose; its theoretical sources; the content of its theoretical system; its historical development; the actual character of the classic works; and, finally, the ways to grasp and apply this wholeness. The historical survey runs from Marx and Engels through Lenin to the Sinicization of Marxism under Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and later leaders.

Zhao argues that the three parts emerged from the same conditions: industrial capitalism, its sharpening contradictions and the rise of the working class as an independent political force. The three sources (German classical philosophy, British classical political economy, utopian socialism) did not act separately but interpenetrated, and the three parts share concepts such as productive forces, relations of production and social formation. Zhao reads the 1844 Manuscripts, The German Ideology, Capital and Anti-Dühring as works that fuse all three parts, and proposes correcting the usual view that The German Ideology marks only the formation of historical materialism. The article also holds that mastering this wholeness requires combining history, theory and classic works, and that real problems call for several principles from all three parts, not one.

Zhao concludes that the Marxist basic-principles textbooks written since the Marxism first-level discipline was set up in 2004 remain a 'platter' of three separate parts. Training teachers who grasp Marxism as a whole will be long and difficult, but Zhao says the work should start now. Zhao offers the article as a spur to others and has no finished model for a truly integrated textbook. Read the original if you are interested in how a Chinese Marxist philosopher argues for integrating the study and teaching of Marxism, and in his close readings of the classic texts.
quoteEn: Removing any one of its components would dismember Marxism, leaving it fragmented and incomplete.
quoteZh: 去掉其中的任何一个组成部分，都会肢解马克思主义，使马克思主义变得支离破碎、残缺不全。

glossary.explanation: The official idea that Marxism's basic principles are combined with China's concrete conditions, producing Chinese forms of Marxism such as Mao Zedong Thought and socialism with Chinese characteristics.
A top-level academic discipline category for Marxist theory in China's university system, established in 2004. It groups the study of Marxist theory under Marxism schools.
The socialist theory founded by Marx and Engels, set against utopian socialism. In the Chinese tradition it is the third component of Marxism, alongside philosophy and political economy.

t: The eight major principles of Xi Jinping's political economy
zh: 习近平政治经济学的八项重大原则
source: Originally published on Red Culture Network (红色文化网), 28 March 2016
paras: Writing in 2016, Cheng Enfu takes up what he calls "Xi Jinping's political economy", which he identifies with contemporary Sinicised Marxist political economy, or the political economy of socialism with Chinese characteristics. His thesis is that it contains eight major principles, each derived from a general principle of Marxist political economy and applied to a specific problem of China's economy.

The article is organised in eight sections, each named for a principle: sustained technology-led development, a livelihood-oriented purpose of production, a public-sector-centred property regime, a labour-centred distribution regime, a state-led market, performance-first growth, structural balance, and self-reliant openness. Every section follows the same three-step pattern. It states the relevant general principle of political economy, then sets out what Xi Jinping's thinking stresses on that issue, then draws out what Cheng says must be done now.

Cheng's central move is to present each principle as the application of classical Marxist theory, such as the primacy of productive forces, the purpose of production under public ownership, the law of value and the law of proportionate development, to China's primary stage of socialism. He argues that the basic economic system must keep public ownership as the main body and the state sector in the leading role, while unwaveringly encouraging the non-public sector. He treats the plan and the market as one organic whole, aiming at a "double-strong" pairing of an efficient market and an efficient government. He also makes sharp policy claims. He holds that China's wealth and income gaps are large, that household net assets, not income, are the primary measure of polarisation, and that neoliberal ideas lie behind the "middle-income trap" concept and behind the view that market-generated overcapacity corrects itself.

Cheng concludes that these principles should guide implementation of the Fifth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2015) and the Central Economic Work Conference of late 2015. His specific proposals include innovation-driven growth, supply-side structural reform, a stronger public sector with mixed ownership under public control, employee shareholding in private firms, and more regulation of foreign acquisitions. They also include Belt and Road cooperation and delaying capital-account opening. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how a prominent Marxist economist in China systematised Xi Jinping's economic thinking in 2016, and of his positions on ownership, distribution and the state's role in the market.
quoteEn: It should be noted that the primary indicator of the gap between rich and poor is not income.
quoteZh: 要注意的是，贫富分化的第一指标不是收入。

glossary.explanation: The official thesis that China is at an early stage of socialism, with relatively underdeveloped productive forces. It justifies a mixed economy and market mechanisms.
An economic policy line stressed at the Central Economic Work Conference of late 2015. It focuses on cutting overcapacity and inventories, deleveraging, lowering costs and addressing weak points.

t: Fidel Castro, permanent hero of the poor of the Third World
zh: 菲德尔·卡斯特罗是第三世界穷人的永久英雄
orig: Spanish newspaper Insurgente (Rebelión-type outlet referred to in Chinese as 《起义报》), 28 November 2016
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation, published in 2016 shortly after Fidel Castro's death, of a commentary by Salim Lamrani, a French specialist on Cuba–US relations. Lamrani argues that although Castro is a controversial figure in the West, he is admired across Latin America and the Third World as a symbol of resistance to oppression and of the South's aspiration to independence, sovereignty and self-determination. In Lamrani's view, Western media cannot grasp his historical significance.

The piece sketches Castro's biography and standing in three steps: his armed struggle against the Batista dictatorship (the 1953 Moncada attack and the 1956–58 campaign), his constitutional record as elected head of state from 1976 to 2006, and his popular support as acknowledged by US officials. A linked second article by the philosopher José Sarrión Andaluz, also translated from the Spanish press, adds material on Castro's international role, Cuban culture and the island's shortcomings.

Lamrani's central claim is that Castro held both historical and constitutional legitimacy. He cites a 1960 US State Department memorandum by Lester Mallory, which in Lamrani's reading concedes that most Cubans supported Castro and recommends economic hardship as the means of undermining that support, and later remarks by the head of the US interests section in Havana on Cubans' admiration for him. Lamrani concludes that US sanctions failed to erode this backing. He characterises Castro in three roles: architect of national sovereignty fulfilling José Martí's dream, social reformer who built one of the least unjust societies in the Third World, and internationalist who placed solidarity at the centre of Cuban foreign policy.

The appended article by Sarrión Andaluz presents Castro as a revolutionary who adapted strategy to a colonial, underdeveloped periphery and made Cuba a vanguard of national liberation. It points to medical aid, the literacy method "Yes, I can", and cultural institutions, and says that Cuba's past persecution of homosexuals was met with self-criticism. It also reports that Forbes failed to substantiate its claim about Castro's wealth. It concludes that history has absolved him. Read the original if you want to see how a favourable Latin American and Spanish left-wing assessment of Castro was selected and presented to Chinese readers in 2016.
quoteEn: Fidel Castro possessed a historical legitimacy.
quoteZh: 菲德尔·卡斯特罗拥有一种历史的合法性。

t: The birthplace of Marx's thought: the 1844 Manuscripts
st: Part one of fragments on the logical development of Marx's thought
zh: 马克思思想的诞生地：《1844 年手稿》--马克思思想的逻辑发展片论之一
source: Exploration and Free Views (Tansuo yu zhengming), 2016 no. 8
paras: Where does Marx's thought have its centre, and how should one find it? Zhang Lingyun, writing in 2016, takes issue with the Japanese scholar Kojin Karatani, who reads Marx through Capital and treats the 'early Marx' as a construct of that later work. Zhang argues that the proper method for locating a thinker's centre is to examine the place where the thought was born, and that for Marx this place is the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844. The article holds that the Manuscripts are the founding work of Marx's new philosophy, not an immature Feuerbachian text.

The article has two parts. The first examines the methodology: it reconstructs the original context of Marx's 'anatomy of man is a key to the anatomy of the ape' in the 1857 Introduction, contrasts it with the 'universal light' method, and notes how Marx himself approached Hegel. The second part sets out five ways in which the Manuscripts founded the new philosophy, then rebuts three standard reasons for placing them in a 'Feuerbachian humanist stage': Althusser's 'problematic', alleged over-praise of Feuerbach, and borrowed Feuerbachian terms.

Zhang's central move is to limit the 'key' method to the economic social formations, since primitive society is, in this account, governed by the production of human beings themselves and requires anthropology rather than political economy. Marx's own study of Hegel began with the Phenomenology, 'the true birthplace and secret' of Hegel's philosophy, not with his final system. Applying the same approach to Marx, Zhang finds in the Manuscripts a new conception of science as a single 'science of history', sensuous activity (practice) as the pivot, and a dialectic of free, conscious activity, alienated labour and the sublation of alienation. On the Feuerbach question, Zhang argues that Marx's 'problematic' had already moved beyond Feuerbach's. The article also contends that the Manuscripts give 'species being' a social meaning and treat alienation as labour alienation, a category of historical materialism, so that Marx's view is a 'labour conception of history' rather than an 'alienation conception'.

Zhang concludes that the claim that the Manuscripts belong to a Feuerbachian humanist stage cannot stand. In the author's view, they are the historical and logical starting point of Marx's later theory. The three-stage movement of the Manuscripts is said to correspond to Marx's late anthropological 'three forms' of society, the former giving the philosophical basis and the latter the scientific proof. Read the original if you study the early–late Marx debate, Althusser's reading of the Manuscripts, or Chinese scholarly arguments for the continuity of Marx's thought.
quoteEn: Therefore, the rational method for studying and grasping the centre of a thinker's thought is to penetrate its birthplace.
quoteZh: 所以，研究和把握思想家思想之中心的合理方法是透析其诞生地的方法。

glossary.explanation: A term drawn from Marx's 1859 Preface. Zhang uses it for the antagonistic stages (Asiatic, ancient, feudal, capitalist) in which the production of things dominates human beings.
Marx's image in the 1857 Introduction for the kind of production that determines the position and influence of all others in a given social form.
Chinese rendering of Althusser's concept of the 'problematic', the underlying framework that governs a text's questions. Zhang uses it to dispute Althusser's dating of Marx's break with Feuerbach.
Marx's concept in the 1844 Manuscripts of labour under capitalism that is estranged from the product, the activity, species-being and other people.

t: The threefold meaning of twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism
zh: 21 世纪中国马克思主义的三重蕴意
paras: Writing in 2016, Zhang Jinsong asks what defines "twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism", the stage of adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions that Xi Jinping has urged the Party to develop. Zhang argues that it is at once a summing-up of the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics and a guide for that practice. Its content, in the author's reading, has three layers: insistence on "Chinese characteristics" to solve China's problems, continuation of the Chinese path alongside a stronger Chinese discourse, and the promotion of Chinese culture as a source of "Chinese wisdom".

The article first sets twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism against its twentieth-century predecessor. The earlier stage, Zhang says, sought a way of combining Marxism with Chinese reality and moved China towards independence and strength. The new stage must lead the building of a moderately prosperous society, modernization and the Chinese Dream. Three sections follow, drawing on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, on policy initiatives since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and on China's economic record.

In the first section, Zhang treats "Chinese characteristics" as the methodological starting point. Policies since 2012 are presented as responses to China's primary-stage conditions: the "two centenary goals", the "Four Comprehensives", the "new normal", supply-side reform and the new development philosophy. Zhang then argues that the Chinese path (a mixed ownership economy with public ownership dominant, distribution mainly by labour, Party leadership, and core socialist values) gives rise to a distinct discourse that challenges neoliberalism, Western democracy and universalist values. Third, Zhang holds that traditional ideas such as "people as the root of the state", "unity of heaven and humanity", integrity in office and "harmony in diversity" feed Chinese governance, ecological thinking, anti-corruption work and diplomacy.

Zhang concludes that twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism should do more than solve China's own development problems. It should show other countries that they can seek paths suited to their own conditions, end the equations of "globalization = Westernization" and "modernization = capitalism", and offer Chinese ideas for global governance and a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a representative 2016 statement of how Chinese theorists tied Marxism's Sinicization to national particularity, the Chinese path and traditional culture.
quoteEn: Adhering to \"Chinese characteristics\" is the most important theoretical starting point and core content of twenty-first-century Chinese Marxism.
quoteZh: 坚持“中国特色”是21 世纪中国马克思主义最重要的理论起点和核心内容

glossary.explanation: Slogan associated with Xi Jinping since 2012, meaning national rejuvenation and prosperity for the Chinese people.
A Party development goal, popularised by Deng Xiaoping, of a society with comfortable but not yet affluent living standards.
Xi Jinping's strategic framework from 2014–15: building a moderately prosperous society, deepening reform, governing the country by law and governing the Party rigorously.
Official description of China's economy from about 2014, characterised by slower but higher-quality growth and structural adjustment.
Five principles announced in 2015: innovation, coordination, green development, openness and sharing.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's formula for international relations based on cooperation and shared interests.

t: Lenin's Imperialism: methodology, core meaning and contemporary value
zh: 列宁《帝国主义论》：方法论、核心意蕴与当代价值
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2016 no. 6
paras: Marking the centenary in 2016 of Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, Zhu Bingyuan asks whether the work has become outdated. Zhu notes that it has been attacked for a century and, in the author's account, is again being questioned and marginalised in theoretical circles as capitalism changes. The article argues that Lenin's theory has not lapsed and remains a theoretical weapon for understanding contemporary capitalism, provided it is grasped as a whole and not judged by individual conclusions.

The article has three parts. The first examines the book's methodology under three heads: its view of history, its materialism and its practical character. The second sets out the book's core meaning as four pillars: monopoly, the rule of the financial oligarchy, external aggression and expansion, and parasitism and decay. The third turns to the present and takes four issues: state monopoly capitalism, the virtualisation of financial capital, new forms of imperialist expansion and the continuing historical trend of imperialism.

On method, Zhu argues that Lenin treated imperialism as a stage of capitalist development, in line with historical materialism, and contrasts this with Kautsky, who reduced it to a preferred policy of finance capital. Zhu says Lenin organised the book around monopoly as its core category, much as Marx's Capital is organised around capital. Zhu holds that, because the essence of monopoly profit-seeking has not changed, Lenin's conclusions are not obsolete. State monopoly capitalism is presented as a logical development of private monopoly that adjusts relations within the system without altering its monopoly character. Zhu also contends that finance capital has widened in scope and become more virtual, which strengthens oligarchic rule, and that expansion now operates through ideological and cultural means such as neoliberalism, the Washington Consensus and 'peaceful evolution'.

Zhu concludes that monopoly, oligarchic rule and expansion still define imperialism, so its parasitic, decaying and moribund tendencies persist. The article cites financialisation, hollowing out of the real economy, rising debt and deepening polarisation as evidence that capitalism's basic contradictions are sharpening and that it is heading for eventual demise. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defended the contemporary relevance of Lenin's theory of imperialism in 2016, and the arguments used to reject claims that it is outdated.
quoteEn: Although the concrete forms of contemporary capitalism change endlessly, the economic essence of monopoly, namely the pursuit of monopoly profit, has likewise not changed.
quoteZh: 当代资本主义尽管具体形式千变万化，但是垄断的经济实质即追求垄断利润的本质也同样没有改变。

glossary.en: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
glossary.explanation: Lenin's 1916 work, often abbreviated in Chinese as Dìguózhǔyì lùn, which defines imperialism as the monopoly stage of capitalism.
Lenin's term for the small group that controls both banks and industrial firms through shareholding and interlocking directorships.
A concept in the Marxist-Leninist tradition describing the merging of state power with monopoly capital, in which the state intervenes in the economy on behalf of monopolies.

t: From The German Ideology to Capital: the deepening of Marx's theory of ideology
st: Reflections on a shift in research approach
zh: 从《德意志意识形态》到《资本论》：马克思意识形态理论的深化与思考
paras: Marx's term "ideology" gradually fades from his writings after The German Ideology (1845) and does not appear directly in Capital. Kuai Zhengming asks whether this marks a break in Marx's theory of ideology or its deepening. The article, published in Theory and Reform in 2016, argues for deepening: ideology was not abandoned but moved from external critique to a detailed internal analysis of how capitalism operates.

The article has three parts. The first treats The German Ideology as the work in which Marx's theory of ideology took basic shape, after earlier steps in the critique of Hegel and the 1844 manuscripts. The second follows the theory through the 1857–58 manuscripts, the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and Capital. The third offers four concluding reflections on the continuity and the change between the early and later works.

Kuai reads The German Ideology as establishing three things: ideology as "false consciousness", as the ideas of the ruling class, and as the class consciousness of a rising revolutionary class. The same work also traces the origins of ideology in the division of mental and manual labour and links its disappearance to the abolition of class rule. Later, Marx placed ideology within the "ideological superstructure" determined by the economic base. He criticised classical political economy for treating capitalism as natural and eternal, and analysed commodity, money and capital fetishism as the everyday ideology of capitalist society.

Kuai concludes that, in Capital, ideology is no longer mainly the invention of bourgeois thinkers but is rooted in capitalist relations of production and in workers' everyday consciousness. Marx also looks for the points where capitalism's claims to freedom and equality contradict its reality. In Kuai's account, the disappearance of the word is an "infiltration" of ideology into the whole economic process, so that it becomes an ever-present "spectre". Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language account of how fetishism critique is read as the continuation of Marx's theory of ideology.
quoteEn: "Essentially, this disappearance is in fact an 'intrusion' or 'infiltration' from the outside inward."
quoteZh: “从本质上看，这种隐遁实际上是一种由外向内的‘侵入’或‘浸润’。”

glossary.explanation: In Chinese Marxist usage, the part of the superstructure made up of ideas, such as law, morality, art, philosophy and religion, as distinct from the political superstructure of institutions. It is held to be determined by the economic base.
Marx's term for the way social relations between people appear as relations between things. The article treats commodity, money and capital fetishism as ideology operating in everyday life.

t: From the state to civil society
st: A study of "On the Jewish Question" and the "Introduction to a Contribution to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right"
zh: 从国家到市民社会
zhSub: 《论犹太人问题》和《〈黑格尔法哲学批判〉导言》研究
paras: Han Lixin asks why the young Marx, a firm supporter of Hegel's philosophy of the state up to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right (1843), abandoned Hegel's dual framework of "state and civil society" and moved to a monist framework centred on civil society, never returning to a philosophy of the state. The article completes an argument Han began in a 2009 paper, which left open how the shift was actually accomplished. Han's answer is that Marx did it in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher essays, through his theory of "human emancipation".

The article first recalls the 2009 claim that Marx's change in 1843 was a move from state to civil society, rather than Lenin's move from idealism to materialism. It then reads "On the Jewish Question", a critique of Bruno Bauer, and the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right. It ends by tracing how Marx's view of the state changed through the Paris Manuscripts, the Comments on James Mill, The German Ideology and the abandoned plan for a volume on the state.

Han argues that Marx found political emancipation insufficient: it splits people into an abstract citizen (citoyen) in the state and an egoistic private person (bourgeois) in civil society, and the state ends up serving private property. Human emancipation requires reuniting these two identities in the individual's own empirical life, labour and relations, which Hegel's scheme would place in civil society. This reversed the Hegelian view that only the state is universal, so Marx needed a universality inside civil society. Han holds that the proletariat, which Marx found in the Introduction, offers only an absolute universality that excludes particularity, so it could not do the job. In the Paris Manuscripts Marx instead turned to Hegel's "formal universality" in money, labour, value and the division of labour.

Han concludes that Marx never completed the human emancipation theory, since later ideas such as "freely associated individuals" and the "re-establishment of individual property" still fall short of the required universality. Its significance lies elsewhere. It made civil society a sphere of universality, replaced the dual framework with a monist one, and caused the state to "retire" from Marx's horizon, which Han presents as a break from Hegel. Han adds that the state, once treated as a fictitious community, became an object of criticism, and that this logic helps explain why the planned volume on the state was never written. Read the original if you study the development of Marx's early thought, his relation to Hegel, or the shift from state to civil society in 1843–44.)
quoteEn: Yet here Marx proposes to hand this task to civil society, which is regarded as a sphere of particularity.
quoteZh: 但在这里，马克思竟然要将这一任务交给被视为特殊性领域的市民社会。

t: Interpreting the idea of spatial justice in The German Ideology
zh: 《德意志意识形态》中的空间正义思想解读
paras: Western neo-Marxists and Chinese scholars have written extensively on the spatial theory of Marx and Engels, yet Wang argues that the idea of spatial justice in The German Ideology (1845) has not received due attention. The article contends that, although Marx and Engels do not treat social space explicitly there, their critique of town and country, globalisation, capital expansion, colonies and the family–civil society–state relation implicitly expresses a view of spatial justice. In Wang's account this is not a species of distributive justice but a comprehensive justice covering the production, distribution, exchange and consumption of spatial resources, and a justice of difference.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the methodological premise: Marx and Engels start from the practice of producing space, against the idealists and Feuerbach's anthropological materialism. The second reads the text for the unjust spatial conditions it reveals: the town–country opposition, the opposition between local closure and global scope, and the opposition between family, civil society and state as forms of community. The third examines the routes to spatial justice that the text proposes. Wang closes by placing the book within the development of Marx's spatial thinking, from early writings to the Manifesto, Capital and the later work.

Wang's central move is to argue that Marx and Engels reverse the idealist order. Ideas of justice do not explain spatial practice; spatial practice explains ideas of justice. Wang reads the town–country split as an opposition of advanced and backward, civilised and barbarous, with the countryside subordinated to the town. Globalisation is read as progress that also produces unequal living conditions, a centre–periphery order and colonial exploitation. The community that Marx and Engels call illusory is read as an alien coercive force over individuals. Against this, Wang finds three paths in the text: a vast growth of productive forces, communist revolution, and the building of a true community in which individuals gain freedom through association.

Wang concludes that The German Ideology marks the formation of Marx's scientific idea of spatial justice. In this reading it is an original response to the unfairness produced by capital globalisation, town–country separation and conflicts of communal interest. Wang places it between earlier writings that implied justice for people of different spatial status and later works that developed a spatial dimension of the critique of capitalism, completing what Wang calls Marx's historical-geographical materialism. Returning to this text, Wang suggests, helps defend and develop Marx's spatial justice thought and clarifies the lineage running through later neo-Marxism and postmodernism. Read the original if you study Marxist spatial theory, Lefebvre and Harvey, or the textual basis of Marx's early critique of town–country division and globalisation.
quoteEn: It is not that values of justice determine the practice of producing space, but that the practice of producing space determines values of spatial justice.
quoteZh: 不是正义价值观念决定空间生产实践，而是空间生产实践决定空间正义价值观念。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Marxist and critical geography concerning the fair production, distribution and use of space and spatial resources. Wang argues it is implicit in The German Ideology.

A term Wang uses for Marx's mature worldview, combining historical materialism with attention to the geography of capital. It echoes the 'historical-geographical materialism' associated with David Harvey.

t: Rediscovering civil society
st: The place of Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right in the history of ideas
zh: 重新发现市民社会
zhSub: 马克思《黑格尔法哲学批判》的思想史地位
source: Journal of the Nanjing Municipal Party School of the CPC, 2016 no. 4
paras: Why does Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right deserve a major place in the history of political thought? Tian argues that the work re-opened Hegel's own analysis of modern civil society, which Hegel's successors and Feuerbach had neglected. By breaking what Tian calls the 'spiritualist order' of Hegel's state theory, Marx began a self-critique of modern society and prepared the ground for Capital.

The article is organised in three parts. The first reconstructs Hegel's idea of the state and its structural resemblance to a Christian order governed by 'spirit'. The second assesses Feuerbach's critique of Hegel and its limits. The third follows Marx's critique of Hegel's logical mysticism and of his 'crude empiricism' on monarchy, bureaucracy and legislative power.

Tian contends that Hegel grounded the state on speculative logic, so that rational knowledge of the state stands where the Holy Spirit stands in Christianity. Real states can therefore stay in non-true forms, which Tian maps onto the logical categories of mechanism and chemism, and the logic can be captured by despotic power. Feuerbach correctly exposed this detachment from life through the inversion of subject and predicate. Tian argues, however, that he skipped the intermediate chapters of the Phenomenology and the Logic and so missed Hegel's analysis of modern economic society, leaving only an abstract 'natural man'. Marx, by contrast, treated the family and civil society as the real presuppositions of the state. He read monarchy as resting on the alienation of people in civil society, bureaucracy as the corporations' interests in another form, and Hegel's legislative power as an expression of private property. Tian sees in this the beginnings of Marx's idea of civil society's self-determination and sublation, here still through democracy, and of the proletariat's political significance.

Tian concludes that the Critique opened a new possibility for post-Hegelian political philosophy: the self-criticism of modern society. Marx recognised civil society as the true subject of the state, even though he had not yet studied political economy. He would later find the path to be abolishing private property and the free workers' common possession of the productive forces. Tian therefore calls the Critique a 'great prelude' to Capital. Read the original if you are interested in the Hegel–Feuerbach–Marx relationship and in how Marx's early concept of civil society links to his later economic critique.
quoteEn: Marx's Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right was precisely the first attempt to break this 'spiritualist order'.
quoteZh: 马克思的《黑格尔法哲学批判》正是破除这种“唯灵论秩序”的最初尝试。
keywords: Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right

t: The logical differences between Capital and the Grundrisse
zh: 《资本论》与《政治经济学批判大纲》的逻辑差异
paras: Scholars widely accept that the Outlines of the Critique of Political Economy (the Grundrisse) is a draft of Capital and that the two texts share a philosophical framework. Yang challenges this consensus. The article argues that two different epistemes, or philosophical frameworks, underlie the two texts and produce major differences in their logic. In the Grundrisse the framework is a labour ontology centred on human subjectivity and freedom. In Capital it is a logic of capital in which capital itself is the subject.

Yang begins with method, asking how one can speak of a fundamental difference between two works by one thinker. The article draws on Althusser's "problematic" and "epistemological break", Foucault's episteme and Kuhn's paradigm shift. It then reconstructs the philosophical basis of the Grundrisse and notes that Vygodsky, Rosdolsky, Lukács and Gould stress continuity. Finally it reads Capital's treatment of labour, the subject and capital as an "absolute object" against that basis.

On the Grundrisse, Yang identifies three components of its labour ontology. Labour is the ontological ground of social existence. Objectification of labour confirms human subjectivity, although Marx now sees objectification and alienation as one process under capital. Labour also creates free time as the realm of free human development. Yang finds a second line in the same text: capital as a self-relating, self-augmenting subject, comparable to Hegel's absolute idea. In Capital this second line takes over. Labour is no longer an ontological foundation but a socially specific function. Yang points to the dual character of labour, labour-power as a commodity, the valorisation process, and the critique of the trinity formula, which calls labour a "phantom". Yang also reads the commodity status of labour-power as marking Marx's break with early modern Western thought, which grounded ownership and rationality in labour. Capitalists appear as personified capital, and workers as its living instruments. Capital becomes the absolute subject, and by the same token an absolute object to human beings.

Yang concludes that research focused on what Marx said finds only continuity, and that attention must also go to what Marx did not say, the deep structure that constrains his thinking. The article suggests that this reading opens a new theoretical space and calls for further theoretical resources. Read the original if you work on Marx's economic manuscripts, Althusserian or Foucauldian approaches to Marx, or debates over labour ontology and capital as subject.
quoteEn: But if we examine the philosophical logic of these two texts in depth, we find that they rest on two different epistemes, or two different philosophical frameworks.
quoteZh: 但如果深入考察这两个文本的哲学逻辑，我们就可以发现，支撑这两个文本的是两种不同的认知型，或者说是两种不同的哲学构架。

glossary.explanation: Foucault's term (l'épistémè) for the underlying configuration of knowledge that governs how thought is possible in a given period. Yang uses it for the deep structure behind Marx's two texts.
Althusser's term for the hidden theoretical framework that determines which questions a thinker can pose. It is reached through "symptomatic reading".
The reading that treats labour as the foundation of social being and of human subjectivity and freedom. Yang associates it with Lukács and Gould and with the Grundrisse.
The self-expanding, self-organising movement of capital in which capital acts as the subject and people as its bearers or instruments. Yang treats it as the overall logic of Capital.

t: Capital as a powerful intellectual weapon for understanding contemporary economic problems
zh: 《资本论》是洞察当代经济问题的强大思想武器
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Li Jiang takes up Xi Jinping's rejection of the claim that Marxist political economy and Capital are outdated. Li argues that, among current schools of thought, only Capital can help readers see through today's tangled economic problems and find ways to answer them. The article's thesis is twofold: capitalism still dominates the world but cannot solve the world's problems, and China should meet its own economic challenges with an approach grounded in Marxism.

The article has two parts. The first reviews 149 years since Capital appeared and asks why capitalism has survived despite Marx's prediction of its expropriation, then examines why its basic contradiction persists, drawing on Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century. The second turns to the problems that have emerged in China's development, such as the wealth gap, environmental damage, corruption and overproduction, and sets out four relationships to be handled correctly.

Li gives four reasons for capitalism's endurance: its relations of production could still accommodate some growth in productive forces; reforms forced by Marxism, the labour movement and socialist states; credit-based consumption that turned citizens into lifelong debtors; and the export of crises abroad, above all by the United States through the dollar's international role. None of this removes the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation. Citing Piketty's figures on concentrated wealth and stagnant middle and lower incomes, Li holds that widening inequality makes the "realisation" of products ever harder and that the 2008 crisis shows the problem lies in the system itself. For China, Li calls for both a decisive role for the market and better government macro-control; for keeping public ownership dominant, defending state-owned enterprises against "privatisation" and against the claim that they cannot coexist with markets; for fairer primary and secondary distribution, including property and inheritance taxes; and for a fairer international economic order.

Li concludes that China must follow neither a return to the pre-reform past nor neoliberal marketisation, but a socialist market economy that combines Marxist truth with present realities. A lasting solution to the imbalance between supply and demand, in Li's view, depends on socialism prevailing over capitalism and on effective global macro-regulation. Meanwhile China should set a socialist example and work with developing countries to change the international rules. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party-journal article uses Capital and Piketty to defend public ownership, state-owned enterprises and macro-control.
quoteEn: It can be said that, looking across the various schools of thought today, only Capital can help us see through today's tangled and complex economic problems and find weapons with which to respond.
quoteZh: 可以说，环顾当前各种思想流派，只有《资本论》能够帮助我们洞察当今错综复杂的经济问题，找到应对的武器。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining market allocation of resources with public ownership as the main body and state macro-control.
State management of the overall economy through fiscal, monetary and administrative means, which official doctrine pairs with the market's role in allocating resources.

t: A new reflection on what materialism is
zh: 关于什么是唯物主义的新思考
paras: Marxist philosophy is a materialist philosophy, so, Jie argues, how materialism is understood is a basic precondition for understanding Marxist philosophy as a whole. The article, published in Philosophical Research in 2016, offers a new interpretation of what materialism is, working from Engels's texts. Its thesis is that materialism has an ontological sense and an epistemological sense, and that both rest on the idea that the world finds its ground and source in itself.
